noticias.titulo: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
noticias.resumen: Megaspeed has been accused of funneling AI chips to China after a former executive's affair with Jensen Huang became public.
noticias.texto:
US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
- Published
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.
The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.
When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.
Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.
On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".
The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.
The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.
China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.
Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.
Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.
Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.
Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.
That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.
Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%.
Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too.
Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take.
The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal.
In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations.
Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

noticias.titulo: What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
noticias.resumen: Ukraine's sinking of a Russian battleship at a port in Libya raises the stakes of the war a notch, writes Frank Gardner.
noticias.texto:
What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
- Published
Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.
The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?
The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.
Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes, has called it "a dangerous escalation".
It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.
Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.
Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks â what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" â have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.
The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.
And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.
It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".
Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.
Throughout this year the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has condemned all attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and today the global shipping community will be wondering whether this attack does indeed set a dangerous precedent.
If Ukraine can plan and execute such a bold attack on Russian ships in a nominally neutral harbour so far from home, where does this stop?
Impact elsewhere in Europe
As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe.
On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders, just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine.
This, said Poland's PM Donald Tusk, was "a deliberate provocation" by Moscow.
It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders is becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response.
But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much â but not all â of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants.
Both Romania and Moldova have found themselves frequently struck by overflying Russian drones targeting Ukraine's Black Sea ports, while Bulgaria and Romania have suffered maritime drone attacks on commercial shipping just offshore in the Black Sea.
In the case of Romania, a Nato member, fast jets have had to be scrambled to intercept incoming Russian drones and there is a profound suspicion that these incursions are not all accidental.
The three Baltic states â Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania â all have borders with Russia and all consider themselves right on the front lines in this war.
There have been a number of anonymous attacks on military industrial facilities in these countries, blamed on agents acting on Moscow's behalf.
Russia, for its part, suspects Estonia of being complicit in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Baltic involving overflights through Estonian airspace.
Hybrid attacks
Hybrid warfare isn't new but it is on the rise.
It refers to the practice, by either side, of carrying out largely anonymous and unattributable operations using methods like cyber attacks, the burning down of warehouses supplying military equipment and the dispatching of drones, both for surveillance and loaded with explosives.
This autumn, Germany's Leipzig-Halle airport, which is used as a resupply hub by Ukraine's cargo aircraft, was targeted by three explosive drones that were discovered before anyone was hurt.
There have been other incidents involving explosive packages sent across Europe targeting Germany, Poland and the UK. Moscow denies any involvement.

noticias.titulo: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
noticias.resumen: Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were reportedly given 74 lashes in Qom.
noticias.texto:
Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
- Published
A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.
Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.
Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.
This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.
In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.
At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.
There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.
On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.
"We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.
"The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."
Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.
"Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).
Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.
In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".
Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.
Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.
In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.
Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.
According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.
Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

noticias.titulo: What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world
noticias.resumen: Interests of oil-producing countries, a US boycott and a dispute over finance may have torpedoed climate talks.
noticias.texto:
What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world
- Published
Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.
Yet that is what happened in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.
The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.
Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".
Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".
And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.
Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?
The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.
Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed.
This time, some of the opposition was public - mostly from oil-producing nations.
Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking on behalf of the 22 Arab League countries, argued that Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions. It was wealthy industrialised nations, he said, that bore the overwhelming responsibility for the problem.
He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances.
Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko went further. Cutting oil and gas supplies before demand fell, he warned, would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty.
"For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said.
The wider political backdrop was still more revealing.
The US, which in previous rounds of talks had helped broker compromises - sometimes working alongside China - had no official delegation in Antalya. President Donald Trump has rejected the entire international climate process.
And while delegates argued over fossil fuels in Turkey, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.
The priorities of some of the world's most powerful governments appeared very different from those being discussed in the negotiating rooms.
A majority that may yet offer hope
Yet, perhaps, the picture is more optimistic than it first appears. About 130 governments backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels - roughly two-thirds of the countries represented in Antalya.
Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker political commitment that might undermine the progress already made.
Looked at this way, the collapse is not evidence that the world has lost its appetite for climate action. Quite the opposite - a substantial majority of governments were demanding more ambitious action.
So why not simply find a way for them to move ahead without waiting for the countries determined to block them?
The difficulty becomes clearer when you look beyond the dispute over fossil fuels.
Kononuchenko had another target in his sights: climate finance. Much of the money wealthy countries provide to poorer nations, he complained, comes as loans rather than grants. He said that developing countries ended up repaying more than they received.
"This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner," he declared.
Then, in a striking moment, he leaned towards the microphone and switched from Russian into English to address his criticism directly to the Europeans: "First of all distinguished representatives of the EU."
Russia has its own reasons for attacking Europe, but the complaint about finance is one that many developing countries share. They argue that they are being asked to pay for damage they did little to cause while receiving too little help to adapt to climate change or build cleaner economies.
The EU had ruled out significant new funding before the negotiations began. Mohamed Adow, the Kenyan campaigner who heads Power Shift Africa, accused Europe of rejecting a flawed deal while refusing to acknowledge its own responsibility for the failure on finance.
So is it possible for a majority of countries to outvote those blocking progress?
The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, has acknowledged the need to "improve, modernise and reform" the process. Some governments have proposed introducing voting when consensus proves impossible. Others want countries prepared to move faster to make their own agreements outside the formal talks.
But there is a reason the UN climate process depends on consensus. International climate co-operation is largely voluntary.
Voting might produce more ambitious agreements on paper, but would it persuade the governments that had been outvoted to act? Consensus also offers some protection to smaller and poorer nations that might otherwise find themselves overruled by the most powerful countries.
Meanwhile, the failure to agree a summit declaration does not mean climate action stops. Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles are becoming increasingly competitive, while the upheaval in global oil and gas supplies is giving countries another reason to generate their own electricity rather than depend on imported fossil fuels.
The energy transition is moving forward, whatever happens in the UN negotiating rooms. The problem is that it is not moving nearly fast enough for the climate.
- Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed 
  - Published20 hours ago
- Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31 
  - Published19 hours ago
A rare moment of agreement
Perhaps the most poignant aspect of the failed Antalya Pact is what the countries had apparently been prepared to accept.
The final draft expressed "deep concern" that global warming was expected to exceed 1.5Â°C in the next few years. It warned that further warming would cause increasingly serious damage, some of it irreversible, and called for urgent action to limit how far temperatures rose above that threshold.
This remarkably strong language had survived into the final version, apparently without provoking the opposition that sank the agreement. Even countries bitterly divided over fossil fuels and finance seemed prepared to acknowledge the scale of the danger.
Yet they couldn't agree on how to respond.
And that, perhaps, is what Antalya tells us about the state of international climate co-operation. The problem isn't simply finding the right words or changing the voting rules. It is persuading countries with very different interests to take action that no international authority can compel them to take.
That was always going to be difficult. In today's divided world, it looks harder than ever.

noticias.titulo: India pledges $1.6bn to Nepal in reset of ties
noticias.resumen: As Nepal rebuilds after deadly floods, its prime minister sets contentious issues aside to secure Indian funding, port access and a new train service.
noticias.texto:
India pledges $1.6bn to Nepal in reset of ties
- Published
Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah has repeatedly called for his country to be treated as an equal by its powerful neighbours. His first visit to the Indian capital, Delhi, put that approach to the test, as both sides sought to reset a relationship strained by years of friction.
The contrast between the two leaders was striking.
Shah, 36, wearing his trademark black suit and sunglasses, stood beside Prime Minister Narendra Modi, 76, dressed in white. Shah rose to power after a wave of Gen Z-led protests toppled his predecessor.
Modi, meanwhile, is serving a third term and has recently faced student-led protests in India.
Yet, the two leaders seemed determined to project warmer relations. They exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service.
For Nepal, the stakes were about far more than repairing diplomatic ties.
The two countries announced a series of agreements covering trade, hydropower, transport and education for Nepali youths.
India, more crucially, unveiled a $1.6bn (Â£1.22bn) support package as Nepal recovers from devastating floods earlier this year.
The floods killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing. Shah's government has faced criticism over support for families which lost homes and loved ones.
The country faces a huge reconstruction challenge. The government estimates rebuilding could cost as much as $4.8bn. Addressing the UN General Assembly in September, Shah warned that when climate disasters devastate poorer countries, "the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan".
Modi pledged nearly $1.6bn in Indian support. Most of it will come as a line of credit for energy projects, alongside about $400m in grants for reconstruction and infrastructure.
While Nepal would have preferred a larger package, former senior Nepali diplomat Vijay Kant Karna says it is still "a significant amount" and could help stabilise a relationship that has often been uneasy.
A Hindu-majority nation wedged between India and China, Nepal has long had to navigate competing interests from its two giant neighbours. Allegations of political interference and an unresolved border dispute have frequently complicated ties with India.
Nepal's former Prime Minister, KP Sharma Oli, who leads a communist party, was widely viewed as being closer to China. Shah, by contrast, emerged as a political outsider when he was elected earlier this year. The former rapper, then 35, led a party that was only four years old.
His new approach of dealing with India may explain why the border dispute was largely absent from the leaders' public remarks, although the joint statement acknowledged that outstanding issues remained.
According to Govind Pokharel, a former vice-chairman of Nepal's National Planning Commission, Shah's government may have chosen to set contentious issues aside in order to secure progress on more immediate development needs.
"Right now you can go home and convince the young Nepalis that it will be handled later," Pokhrel says, "but if they don't deal with these issues in the future, there will be criticism."
Veteran Indian diplomat Anil Trigunayat says both sides appear to have opted to leave the dispute to established mechanisms rather than engage in what he calls "cartographic aggressions".
There were other gains for Nepal as a result of the Delhi visit.
As a landlocked country heavily dependent on India for trade, Nepal secured access to two additional Indian ports, Kandla and Paradip. The two sides also agreed to improve road and rail connectivity.
The leaders jointly inaugurated a train service linking Ayodhya in India, revered by Hindus as the birthplace of Lord Ram, with Janakpur in Nepal, traditionally regarded as the birthplace of his wife Sita.
There was, however, disappointment on aviation.
Nepal has long sought greater access to Indian airspace in order to attract international traffic to its airports at Bhairahawa and Pokhara.
Some analysts believe the lack of an agreement reflects Indian concerns over Chinese involvement in the two airport projects.
"The airport in Pokhara can pose certain security challenges for India, so it is a more complicated issue to resolve," says Trigunayat.
India did, however, agree to make an existing air route linking Kathmandu, Bhairahawa and Lucknow bidirectional.
"Nepal invested a huge amount of money in those airports," says Pokharel. "It fell short of expectations, but the bidirectional route is a breakthrough."
Shah must now manage relations with China as he seeks to balance the interests of Nepal's two much larger neighbours.
For now he returns home with substantial financial commitments from India as Nepal continues the long task of rebuilding.

noticias.titulo: Search and rescue teams race against time to find survivors after Nigeria boat tragedy
noticias.resumen: The government blames overcrowding, poor maintenance, and missing life jackets for boat accidents.
noticias.texto:
Search and rescue teams race against time to find survivors after Nigeria boat tragedy
- Published
Nigerian search and rescue teams are racing against time to find survivors after a boat carrying mourners travelling to a funeral capsized on Friday.
Twenty-nine bodies have been recovered and 50 people rescued so far, a spokesperson for the National Emergency Management Agency (Nema) told the BBC.
The government has responded by ordering stricter enforcement of safety standards on the country's inland waterways.
Overcrowding, poor maintenance and failure to observe safety regulations have contributed to previous deadly accidents on Nigeria's rivers.
The boat was travelling from Ayama community when it developed mechanical problems, according to police spokesperson Musa Mohammed.
Passengers asked the boat operator to steer towards land, but he allegedly declined, leading to the accident.
Survivors have described the panic that followed as passengers struggled to swim and stay afloat while waiting for emergency rescue services.
"As I swam, people were dragging me to the bottom, and I bit one woman and saved myself," Charity Ebikaboaere told local media outlet Arise News.
"Our things, our money, phones, everything lost, but me and my siblings are alive," said another survivor, Tari Samuel.
- Why do Nigeria's boat disaster keep happening? 
  - Published20 July
Nema spokesman Manzo Ezekiel raised concerns about the use of untrained boat operators and passengers travelling without life jackets.
"Some of them believe they're from river areas and they know how to swim," he said, warning that familiarity with waterways should not replace basic safety precautions.
There have been reports that the boat was carrying more than 300 people but the Nema spokesperson said this wasn't correct. He did not say how many people were on board but said it was overcrowded.
The accident happened in a region where waterways are a key means of transport, especially for communities with limited road access.
"Overloading, speeding, recklessness and traveling without life jackets must stop. No journey is worth a life," Bayelsa Commissioner for Information Ebiuwou Koku-Obiyai said in a statement on Saturday.
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has relayed his condolences to the victims' families.
In a statement posted on X, Tinubu said he had directed relevant federal disaster response agencies to work together to ensure a successful rescue and recovery operation.
He also ordered that his election rally on Saturday, in Ibadan, Oyo State, be held without much fanfare in honour of those who lost their lives.
Boat accidents are a recurring problem in Nigeria, particularly in riverine communities where boats are a major means of transport.
In August, at least 50 people, mostly children, died after an overloaded boat capsized in the north-western Sokoto state. In January, at least 25 people died when a leaking boat capsized in Yobe state, in the north-east.

noticias.titulo: Prominent Zimbabwean preacher arrested on sexual assault allegations
noticias.resumen: Uebert Angel, a British-Zimbabwean national, leads a charismatic church with branches in several countries.
noticias.texto:
Prominent Zimbabwean preacher arrested on sexual assault allegations
- Published
A well-known Zimbabwean preacher has been arrested on indecent assault and sodomy allegations, local police said.
Uebert Angel, who leads an international charismatic church with branches around the world, was arrested during a church service in Harare on Sunday. Pictures and footage of the dramatic arrest have since been circulated online.
In one video, a convoy of vehicles is seen escorting the self-styled prophet as he sits in the back of a police van surrounded by armed police officers.
The controversial founder of Spirit Embassy was also appointed Zimbabwe's special presidential envoy and ambassador-at-large to Europe and the Americas back in 2021 by President Emmerson Mnangagwa.
In 2023, he made headlines when an undercover report by Al Jazeera claimed that he had offered to use his diplomatic status to launder large amounts of money through a gold-smuggling scheme in the country.
According to the Qatar-based network, Angel, 48, told reporters working undercover that the scheme was approved by President Emmerson Mnangagwa.
Zimbabwean police only released a brief statement confirming his arrest but a member of his team told reporters the British Zimbabwean national was still in police custody and it was unclear when he'd make an appearance in court.
"It can be in the afternoon or tomorrow [Tuesday]. We are still within the legal framework [for him to appear in court]," Professor Lovemore Madhuku told state-owned broadcaster ZBC in a clip posted online.
This is not the first time the prominent preacher has been accused of improper behaviour.
A report by local online publication ZimLIVE in 2021 said that Angel had previously faced allegations of sexual impropriety from several women, at least five of whom are in England. The charismatic preacher has denied the allegations, the outlet added at the time.
Angel's church has branches in Zimbabwe, South Africa and the UK and he known for his ties to other African preachers like Malawian televangelist Shepherd Bushiri.

noticias.titulo: Comedian impersonates Trump's dance moves, mocks trade talks at Canada press dinner
noticias.resumen: The impersonator, Canadian comedian Mark Critch, poked fun at the US president's search for a new press secretary and US-Canada trade talks.
noticias.texto:
Comedian impersonates Trump's dance moves, mocks trade talks at Canada press dinner
- Published
Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Canada relations and on-again, off-again trade talks.
The impersonator, played by comedian Mark Critch of the sketch comedy show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, came out after Carney jokingly pressed an "emergency comedy button" during his speech.
Critch appeared alongside another actor impersonating Carney, played by Canadian sketch comedian Mark McKinney.
"We've got two Carneys here, it's a disaster," the Trump impersonator said after he walked on stage.
Using some of Trump's signature mannerisms, like his dance moves and his slightly hunched posture, he joked about the latest US midterm elections, which led to Trump's Republican Party losing control in Congress.
"I'm so popular we just had a big BLUE WAVE in the states," the impersonator said at the Saturday press gala.
He also took aim at ongoing US-Canada trade negotiations, saying,"We're going to have a great deal. There's only one thing standing in the way: me, because I'm crazy."
There were also jabs at Trump's search for a new White House press secretary following Katie Zacharia's exit, and at US ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, who is unpopular among Canadians.
"I said 'find somebody who is less likeable than me,' and we got one," the Trump impersonator joked about Hoekstra.
Carney stood behind him occasionally laughing. The prime minister also delivered his own zingers, saying at one point: "This is a tough room. And I've been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator."
Both Critch and McKinney - the two impersonators - are fixtures of This Hour Has 22 Minutes, a long-standing Canadian sketch comedy show that has recently enjoyed viral internet fame for its timely skits mocking the Trump administration.
The skits, published directly on Tik Tok and YouTube, have depicted Zacharia's quick ouster, external and poked fun at rapper Nicki Minaj's, external support for Trump.
They have garnered millions of views, and even captured the attention of major US media., external
Critch and McKinney's appearance at Saturday's dinner is part of an evening of traditionally light-hearted humour, where Canadian politicians poke fun at one another at a gala hosted by the Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery.
In a separate speech, Canada's governor general, Louise Arbour, joked about Carney's popularity and frequent global travel.
"Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he's supposed to be," Arbour said.

noticias.titulo: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
noticias.resumen: Finnish defence forces say that Ukraine was likely behind the drone strike on Saturday. Kyiv has yet to comment.
noticias.texto:
Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
- Published
A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.
The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.
It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.
The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
While Besprozvannykh initially said the crew of the Sparta II intended to repair the ship and carry on their journey, the Finnish Border Guard later said they had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was en route to Russia.
Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, said during a news conference on Sunday that one Sparta II crew member had suffered minor injuries.
The Russian rescue vessel Murman is leading towing operations with the support of a Finnish guard ship and a Estonian naval patrol vessel.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Finnish Defence Minister Antti HÃ¤kkÃ¤nen said that the Border Guard was responsible for the investigation into the attack and was co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

noticias.titulo: 'I want to destroy capitalism, not France': On the streets with the French ultra left
noticias.resumen: The BBC meets the far-left protesters French President Emmanuel Macron says are trying to bring down the Republic.
noticias.texto:
'I want to destroy capitalism, not France': On the streets with the French ultra left
- Published
France is in turmoil. Crippling public debt, a "lame-duck" president with six months left in office, and massive social unrest - sparked by student protests which have erupted into looting and violence.
This Saturday marked the sixth weekend in a row of demos against soaring prices, worsening public services and alleged police brutality. Violence by protesters is down on last month but still present.
President Emmanuel Macron has publicly blamed riots on "delinquents" and "ultra-left groups" whose aim, he says, is to bring down the French Republic.
That's quite a claim â and one that needs examining.
The unrest in France has become a political football ahead of key presidential and parliamentary elections next year. The left in France blames the centre and right for the cost-of-living crisis that's making French people so upset and angry. They blame the hard left for fomenting violence (which they deny). While the nationalist right pledges, if elected, it will return order and security to France's streets.
So, who exactly are these "ultra-left" groups Macron speaks of? And how organised and dangerous are they?
It's infamously hard to speak to members of the radical left. They don't much like what they call mainstream media. We're viewed as part of an establishment many of them despise.
My best bet was to head out into the protests and try to approach people dressed in all black and ski masks or balaclavas (worn, they say, to hide their identity from police). It's a quasi-uniform associated with left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block.
You see them at demos all over Europe. In France, they tend to appear from city side streets, as daytime protests are dying down, dusk is falling and riot police begin to emerge in full force.
French intelligence drastically underestimated the outpouring of anger, looting and destruction following protests last month. More than 1,000 police officers were reportedly injured, young protesters had bones broken and two reportedly lost a hand in altercations with police armed with stun grenades. Le Monde newspaper has an article, external it is constantly updating to investigate a rising number of reports of protester injuries. The French Insurers Federation estimates damages to shops and private property on 17 October alone - the day of the biggest riots - came to around â¬207m (Â£175.5m).
Since then, the French authorities are trying to tightly manage demos. Police presence is heavy. Protesters say heavy handed.
Towards the end of one of the protests this month, we saw would-be rioters vastly outnumbered, glass bottles and homemade paint bombs at the ready to throw at police. They were no match for the batons, stun grenades and tear gas the officers had to hand.
As we were being forcefully kettled in by police, I tried to talk to would-be rioters. Few wanted to engage but I then met 18-year-old Nas (not his real name) and friends. They would only speak to me if they could hide their identity. This was to avoid police detection, they said.
Milling, you could say provocatively, by baton-at-the-ready police â they seemed to fit a radical-left rioter stereotype.
"How can you justify the violence?" I ask them.
"Without violence, you don't achieve anything," one of them tells me. "It's the only way to get our voices heard."
"We come from an area with a bad reputation. Our schools are a mess. Our teachers quit. You need qualifications to get a decent job. There is supposed to be equality in France. We won't give up our fight."
These young men, we discover, come from the sprawling housing estates common on French city outskirts - the banlieues - associated with deprivation, unrest and second or third generation immigrant families.
They weren't politicised or organised by the radical left, they insisted. Just angry.
Earlier, I had spotted two hard-left student activists, standing masked on top of a bus shelter, above the thronging crowd of protesters waving banners sporting the red anarchist sign and the symbol for the Antifa (anti-fascist) movement.
I put it to them that France has a proud tradition and respect for the right to protest but that the country has been horrified by the violence it's seen over the last weeks.
They were keen to downplay the rioting but - again â would only speak if they could remain anonymous.
"Violence ends up reflecting badly on our movements. We don't like it. But what's a smashed shop window compared to police using stun guns on protesting school kids? Also, people [in France] are regularly going cold and hungry. They're losing faith in this society."
How could they believe violence would bring about a juster society, I wondered?
They shrug off my question. In France, these days, the real violence is state violence, they say.
French intelligence estimates there are 5,000 "ultra-left" activists in the country.
Anticapitalist Starflix (that's his codename) counts himself as one of them. The 17-year-old is also a member of the violent Black Block movement. We'd arranged to meet on the edge of the protest, by a narrow canal.
Fearful about being apprehended by police, he asked to remain anonymous.
He showed me a couple of homemade paint-bombs - eggshells filled with paint and sealed with medical tape that he throws at police officers. He carries them in his rucksack, wrapped in a royal blue Italia football shirt.
"We throw the paint bombs at the visors on riot police helmets, so they have to lift them up in order to see and that makes them suffer their own tear gas that they've sprayed at us," he tells me.
"We pick up stones and rocks too. Anything we find on the streets of Paris, to throw."
I put it to him that he and others in the Black Block are causing a lot of problems on French streets: damaging businesses, hurting police officers, destroying the demos for peaceful protesters. What is he trying to achieve?
As he's under 18, his parents give us permission to speak to him. They share his politics, Starflix tells me, but not all rioters - masked and dressed in black as he is - do.
"The Black Block isn't a single organisation. It's a technique. Some of us use violence to get government reform. I want to bring about a revolution.
"Other people are opportunists who use anonymity to steal things. When we all wear the same clothes, it makes it harder for police to identify us."
When I ask if he is scared he might get hurt or arrested, he admits he is but says what frightens him more is the thought that society might not change.
Social media plays a huge role in the riots. Starflix tells me he and his friends use Signal and Telegram to arrange to meet at protests.
There are numerous websites and Instagram profiles, mainly hosted by left-wing organisations, offering tips for protesters and rioters, such as: keep your phone at home so police can't track you, cover your face to avoid being identified and emulate martial arts expert Bruce Lee and "be like water" - appearing and disappearing into crowds. That's advice passed on by the Hong Kong protesters eight years ago.
While not formally organising the protests or violence with these posts, could the fact groups host this information online be viewed as a kind of incitement or manipulation of youngsters whose feelings are running so high in France?
All the young rioters I spoke to insist they are not being herded or directed, but is there something bigger behind what's happening?
It takes our team a long time, but they manage to find a seasoned activist with the Black Block who would speak to us. I put to him Macron's assertion that the ultra left has organised groups that aim to bring down the French Republic. Is that true?
"It's totally false of the authorities to say we are all organised. And the intelligence services know it," the activist scoffs. "It's a manipulation of the French public to make them think there is an enemy within."
"Basically, people turn up to a protest, get dressed in black and do their own thing. The uniting factor is rage and not just in France. You see the same rage [in protests] in Italy, Germany, Spain. It's exploding by itself."
I ask if the anti-capitalist presidential candidate Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon and his France Unbowed party (LFI) are somehow linked to the violence. They are present at most protests, supporters handing out campaign pamphlets to the chanting crowds.
But the activist denies this, telling me MÃ©lenchon is "a capitalist because he's part of the system". He says the LFI and the trade unions try to "calm" unrest, while he believes things need to be "stepped up a notch".
Why had he decided to talk to us, I ask - does he want to collapse the French government?
"I just want to say we don't love violence. I don't want to destroy France. We want to destroy a system that is a capitalist system, of course, but to change the society in a way that we think will be better for the most people, for more people.
"More and more find it hard to make ends meet. In the countryside, people can't even afford to fill their tank with petrol."
You have to leave the city, heading out into the gloriously autumnal French countryside, to meet some of the more organised, hardcore elements of the ultra left.
This is a world of eco activism and known saboteurs. One man remains in police custody linked to the fire during protests at Limoges Town Hall last month. The devastated, yet somehow still elegant, 19th century building has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be in. An acrid smell still hangs in the air one month on.
The 34-year-old arson suspect, who insists he's innocent, comes from a hamlet near Limoges, known for its anarchist, environmentalist community. His father, a fellow activist, is also known to French intelligence. We approached the father and the suspect's lawyer for comment. They didn't want to speak.
Instead, we met a 39-year-old father of one, a local full-time ultra-left activist for more than two decades. Like the other individuals we spoke to for this investigation, he would only talk to us on condition he could remain anonymous.
"We were all shocked by the [town hall] fire â even as we watched it happen in front of us - but it's our duty to take action," he tells me.
"I can't leave this world to my son in the state that it's in. Look how military vehicles and brute force are used by the state against our young students.
"It's amazing the people haven't taken up arms against them. Do we need a policeman killed in order for the state to listen?"
How can you say that, I want to know?
"As a child, I was educated with French values â liberty, equality, fraternity - but when I look at the social injustice in the world now, I'm disgusted. As a father, I can't let this go on. If I have to, I would take a bullet to protect the youth of this country."
These are dangerous-sounding words - but the radical left doesn't appear to be big, armed or united enough to seriously threaten France.
We repeatedly approached French intelligence. They didn't want to comment. A sign perhaps of the huge sensitivity of the current situation, especially with France hurtling towards an extremely charged presidential election.
But Michel Klein, a recently retired former police commissioner, told me he didn't think the radical left posed a serious threat to the French state.
"I believe there is a will from the radical left and the anarchists to try and destroy the Republic but they obviously don't have the means to do it," he told me.
He sees no risk of civil war in France (a possibility you hear some in the country discuss these days) but he identified a rising risk of clashes between far-left and far-right groups ahead of the presidential election.
Polls currently predict a run-off in the vote between nationalist candidate Marine Le Pen and anticapitalist MÃ©lenchon.
Far-right vigilante groups have begun appearing on the edge of protests in a number of cities across France to "protect French streets", they say.
The popular hard-left presidential candidate MÃ©lenchon attends most demos, his supporters handing political pamphlets to the chanting crowds, but he denies any links with violence.
France is so polarised, there's little sign next year's presidential vote will calm things. This turbulent mix of left and right, social and political unrest, feels like a perfect storm.

noticias.titulo: Appeals court renews Trump bid for federal jurisdiction in hush-money case
noticias.resumen: The ruling could clear the way for Trump to argue prosecutors relied on evidence protected by presidential immunity.
noticias.texto:
Appeals court renews Trump bid for federal jurisdiction in hush-money case
Monday’s ruling could clear the way for Trump to argue prosecutors relied on evidence protected by presidential immunity.
A federal appeals court has revived United States President Donald Trump’s bid to transfer his New York criminal hush-money case to federal court, months after a district judge rejected the effort for a third time.
On Monday, a three-judge panel of the 2nd Circuit Court of Appeals reversed a lower court ruling that had kept the case in New York state court.
In a two-page order, the 2nd Circuit panel said it disagreed with the late US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein’s denial of Trump’s request for the “removal” of his case to federal court.
The appeals court said Hellerstein had “erred in holding that removal is categorically unavailable in a state criminal case” after conviction.
It directed a federal judge in Manhattan to consider whether the proceedings could be brought under federal jurisdiction.
In a written statement provided to The Associated Press news agency, a spokesperson for Trump’s legal team said the president “appreciates the 2nd Circuit’s prompt and correct ruling, as he continues to win against Democrat weaponization of our Justice System”.
Trump has sought to use presidential immunity in federal court to have his conviction overturned. He was convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records in 2024, though he has denied any wrongdoing.
Trump’s New York criminal conviction
The case stems from a $130,000 “hush money” payment made shortly before the 2016 presidential election to adult film performer Stormy Daniels.
Daniels had claimed she had an affair with the Republican leader while he was married — an allegation he denies — and prosecutors alleged that the money was intended to buy her silence during a tense campaign season.
Trump ultimately won the 2016 presidential election, ushering him into his first term in public office.
The payment was made through Trump’s former lawyer and fixer Michael Cohen. Prosecutors argued that Trump fudged his business records to pass off his reimbursements to Cohen as legal expenses, thereby concealing them from voters.
While falsifying business records is normally a misdemeanour offence, it can be charged as a felony if done in service of another crime. In Trump’s case, prosecutors said he violated state election laws.
In May 2024, a New York jury found him guilty, making Trump the first US president to be convicted of a crime.
At a sentencing hearing in January 2025 — shortly before his second term as president began — Trump received an unconditional discharge, meaning he faced neither imprisonment nor a financial penalty. But his conviction remains on the record.
Why does Trump want the case heard in federal court?
For years, Trump has sought to overturn that conviction.
Monday’s ruling leaves the jury’s guilty verdict intact, but it also clears the way for the president to seek a hearing in federal court.
He is expected to argue that state prosecutors secured his conviction by relying on evidence that would have been shielded by presidential immunity in federal court.
His legal team is likely to point to a landmark 2024 ruling as justification for that argument.
At the time, the Supreme Court’s conservative majority ruled that presidents could enjoy “presumptive immunity” for any “official acts” conducted while in office.
What constitutes an “official act”, however, is an open question. Previously, the Supreme Court had only conferred immunity to actions taken within a president’s constitutional authority.
Monday’s ruling reverses a series of setbacks for Trump’s legal team.
In August, federal judge Hellerstein rejected Trump’s third attempt to transfer the case, finding that the president’s arguments were insufficient to justify moving it out of state court.
Hellerstein, a senior federal judge in Manhattan’s Southern District of New York, died last month at the age of 92.
The move also stalls Trump’s state-level appeal in New York’s Appellate Division, which heard arguments earlier this month but has yet to rule on his challenge.
A federal judge has been directed to rule promptly on whether the case should indeed be transferred from New York state court to federal jurisdiction, although no deadline has been set.

noticias.titulo: Israeli minister approves return of Flydubai flights
noticias.resumen: Final resumption of carrier's route between Dubai and Tel Aviv depends on Israeli security authorities' approval.
noticias.texto:
Israeli minister approves return of Flydubai flights
Final resumption of carrier’s route between Dubai and Tel Aviv depends on Israeli security authorities’ approval.
Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev has approved the resumption of Flydubai flights to Tel Aviv, according to Israeli media, almost two months after an onboard incident where a co-pilot was accused of attacking his captain.
Regev made the announcement on Monday, though Israel’s security authorities’ approval is still required for flights to resume. The ministry expects operations to resume within a week or two, Israeli media said.
The minister’s approval comes after talks between Israeli officials, led by ministry Director-General Moshe Ben-Zaken, and Emirati aviation officials took place in Dubai on November 16.
Authorities discussed potential security measures that would allow for airlines to fully resume flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv.
“The delegation today presented Regev with the steps the company has taken in the wake of the incident,” Israeli media reported, citing a transportation ministry statement. “As a result, Regev approved the return of Flydubai, subject to clearance from security authorities.”
“The move is a significant step toward restoring air connectivity between Israel and the UAE and expanding flight options for passengers,” the statement added.
Flydubai halted flights to Tel Aviv on September 30 as it began an investigation into the events that transpired on board a Boeing 737 Max 8. Israeli carriers also stopped running routes to Dubai, making Etihad, which flies to Abu Dhabi, the only carrier flying between the UAE and Israel, according to Israeli media.
The co-pilot, who was identified as an Omani national, was arrested when the plane diverted and made an emergency landing in Tabuk, northwestern Saudi Arabia.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused the co-pilot of trying to crash the plane and of attacking the captain, Smit Machchhar, an Indian national.
The emergency came a day after Netanyahu warned of possible attacks in the lead-up to Israel’s October 27 parliamentary elections.

noticias.titulo: Bukele shares details on deaths of Salvadoran troops in Haiti intervention
noticias.resumen: Bukele's military intervention in Haiti comes after four Salvadoran technicians were kidnapped by gangs in October.
noticias.texto:
Bukele shares details on deaths of Salvadoran troops in Haiti intervention
Bukele’s military intervention in Haiti comes after four Salvadoran technicians were kidnapped by gangs in October.
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele has identified the three soldiers from his Central American country who were killed while on an anti-gang mission in Haiti.
Late on Sunday, Bukele posted on social media that their names were Lieutenant Cristian Daniel Palacios Santos and Corporals Emerson Alexander Zepeda Zelada and Wilber Manuel Serrano Medina.
He explained that the two corporals were trying to dislodge a grenade from a drone as its battery was about to run out. They died when the grenade exploded.
“It was not possible to steer the drone toward a completely safe area for it to crash,” Bukele said, adding that Serrano Medina held the drone off the ground as Zepeda Zelada manually disarmed the grenade. “They were fully aware of the immense risk they were taking, yet they chose to act to protect others. And they succeeded.”
Palacios Santos was killed in the same incident, but Bukele provided no details about how he died. The president said Palacios Santos was admired for recently taking control during a “critical moment” in an operation in which some contractors allegedly retreated.
“He acted with speed and determination, managing to save several lives, including those of his own colleagues,” Bukele wrote. “We all applaud his bravery.”
He didn’t identify the contractors.
Bukele also used his post to pledge that Salvadoran troops who want to leave Haiti could do so immediately without facing reprisals.
Bukele makes a promise to Salvadorans
The Salvadoran soldiers killed last week were among 2,500 deployed to Haiti last month after four of their own went missing during an October 18 attack in gang-held territory. They have not yet been found.
Bukele said that his government would award the families of the three soldiers killed on Friday $200,000 in addition to a monthly income.
He also stressed that any soldier who wants to leave Haiti immediately may do so “without fear of reprisal and without concern that their return might jeopardise the mission, as many of their comrades have volunteered to relieve anyone who wishes to be relieved”.
Salvadoran troops have come under increased scrutiny as experts and the United Nations note they are operating in a largely unilateral way. Thousands of Haitians recently demonstrated to support Bukele.
The agreement between Haiti and El Salvador hasn’t been made public.
“There is no information on the scope and limits of its mission, nor on its accountability mechanisms,” according to a report published Monday by NAL Human Rights, a Netherlands-based consulting company focused on Central American issues.
It noted that, regardless of what that deal stipulates, Salvadoran and international laws require that El Salvador’s armed forces comply with human rights and humanitarian laws.
The report also underscored that the Central American country and the International Criminal Court have jurisdiction to prosecute Salvadoran military personnel if they are accused of war crimes, genocide or crimes against humanity.
More than 20,000 people have been killed in gang-related violence across Haiti in the past five years.
US lawmakers demand answers about the situation in Haiti
The deaths of the Salvadoran soldiers come as local and international forces fight powerful gangs entrenched in Martissant, a community located in a key corridor that links Haiti’s capital to the country’s western and southern regions.
Dozens of suspected gang members have been killed since last week as the battle in Martissant continues, police have said.
It is the first major operation in Martissant in the more than five years that gangs have controlled it.
As Haitian police and others continue to battle gangs in Martissant, a UN-backed gang suppression force said it killed several suspected gang members on Sunday as part of ongoing operations in Tabarre and Cite Soleil, located in Port-au-Prince, and in the northern town of Gros Morne.
As fighting intensifies, two Democratic lawmakers on Monday accused the administration of US President Donald Trump of failing to “name and sanction the political and economic elite fueling Haiti’s insecurity”.
The concern was outlined in a letter penned by New Hampshire Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking member in the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and New York Representative Gregory Meeks, the ranking member in the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
“At a time when the Haitian people are preparing to vote for the first time in over a decade, Congress, the American public and the Haitian people deserve transparency about the nature and scale of collusion between gangs and their political and economic support networks,” they said.
The letter was addressed to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
Haiti is scheduled to hold the first round of elections in July 2027. Among the candidates running are some previously sanctioned by the United States and Canada.

noticias.titulo: US adds Megaspeed, firm at centre of Nvidia scandal, to export control list
noticias.resumen: Bureau of Security and Industry adds Singapore-based firm and six other entities to export control list.
noticias.texto:
US adds Megaspeed, firm at centre of Nvidia scandal, to export control list
Bureau of Security and Industry adds Singapore-based firm and six other entities to export control list.
The United States has added the Singapore-based company at the centre of the alleged spying scandal involving Nvidia to its trade blacklist.
The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) placed Megaspeed International and six other firms based in Southeast Asia on its Entity List on Monday, hours after Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia as CEO in a stunning comeback that sent tech stocks soaring.
Megaspeed and the six other entities were determined to be “acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States”, BIS, which sits under the US Department of Commerce, said in a filing to the Federal Register.
The designations mean that anyone seeking to ship advanced US technology, including Nvidia’s top-end graphics processing units (GPUs) used to train and run AI, to the firms must first obtain an export licence.
Megaspeed’s blacklisting comes as divisions in the Trump administration over China’s access to Nvidia chips have been laid bare in recent weeks amid claims Huang was romantically involved with an alleged Chinese spy.
While US officials have been scrutinsing Megaspeed’s compliance with export controls for years, US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s department had until now declined to place the company on its trade blacklist, prompting recriminations from administration officials known to hold more hawkish views on China, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
US officials have accused Megaspeed International’s former top executive Alice Huang of working with China’s Ministry of State Security to target Huang in an intelligence-gathering operation.
Beijing has rejected the claims as “groundless speculation” and “an attempt to smear and malign China.”
The other six entities added to Washington’s entity list are MSFusion, PT Megaspeed International and Speedmatrix, based in Malaysia; Apex Enterprise Solutions and Swiftdata, based in Singapore; and Megaspeed, based in Thailand.
Malaysia’s Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation, Singapore’s Ministry of Digital Development and Information, and Thailand’s Ministry of Industry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Megaspeed International, which is under investigation by the US Department of Justice on suspicion of diverting high-end chips to China in violation of export controls, did not respond to a request for comment.
The Singapore-based data centre company has previously insisted that it is a “legitimate and lawful business” and that media reports about its operations contained claims that were “not supported by verifiable evidence.”
More to follow…

noticias.titulo: What could Democrats do with their expanding congressional majority?
noticias.resumen: The Democratic Party is debating how best to use its large margin of victory in the US midterm elections.
noticias.texto:
What could Democrats do with their expanding congressional majority?
The Democratic Party is debating how best to use its large margin of victory in the US midterm elections.
The Democratic Party has continued to expand its already sizeable majorities in the United States Congress as counting concludes in the final races of the 2026 midterm elections.
As of Monday, the Democrats hold a 258-seat majority in the 435-member House of Representatives. Four races remain uncalled.
All the races have been decided, meanwhile, for the Senate, where Democrats gained a 56-seat majority out of 100 total seats.
Flipping both chambers gives the party a strong hand to shape legislation during the last two years of Trump’s term in office.
How might the Democrats approach their role in government once the new Congress is sworn in on January 3? Find out in this quick explainer.
What do the results say?
The midterm results give Democrats their largest House majority since 1992 and their largest Senate majority in more than a decade. Republicans, meanwhile, saw their tally in the House drop to 173 seats, their lowest figure in years.
The vote also served as a firm rebuke of Trump’s second term as president, with voters venting their frustration over cost-of-living issues, the US-Israel war on Iran, aggressive immigration raids and corruption.
Democratic victories also extended well beyond traditional left-wing strongholds, with candidates racking up wins in Republican-led states such as Texas, Mississippi and South Carolina.
Which races remain?
Four House seats have yet to be called: one in Minnesota, one in Tennessee, and two in Louisiana that will be settled by a run-off on December 12.
Those races could see the Democrats further expand their majority in the House. The final count is now a question of just how large the party’s majority will be.
What will Democrats do with their majority?
Democrats have long pledged to use any congressional majorities they win as a check on Trump’s agenda.
But the scale of their success in the 2026 midterms has prompted discussion about embracing a more ambitious legislative agenda.
In the House of Representatives, Democrats have outlined a 100-day agenda that includes potentially reversing tax cuts that largely benefit wealthy earners and restoring healthcare subsidies that expired under Trump.
Lawmakers have also said that they will act to end the war on Iran, although divisions remain within the party over how to rein in Trump’s military actions. Under the US Constitution, Congress alone can authorise military operations.
Progressives have accused the party’s moderate wing of playing down expectations of firm steps to end the war, including cutting off funding.
Democrats have also pledged to use their newfound position to exercise oversight over the executive branch by launching probes and issuing subpoenas.
On Monday, for example, House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said that a Democrat-led Congress would conduct a “swift, thorough, and wide-ranging” investigation into the actions of the chip manufacturer Nvidia.
He also said it would delve into the “corrupt abuse of power” by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
In the Senate, Democrats have also threatened to block Trump’s nominees for high-level government positions, which require the chamber’s confirmation.
What role will Trump play?
While Democrats will hold substantial majorities in both chambers of Congress, Trump will retain the power to veto legislation.
Some lawmakers, however, have tried to persuade the president that he could benefit from working with Democrats after his party’s stark defeat in the midterms.
Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, for example, has shared a series of tongue-in-cheek social media posts suggesting that a universal healthcare programme — a long-term progressive goal — could be named after the president in a bid to win his support.
“Donald, this is on the table,” El-Sayed said in a social media post showing a card for a hypothetical health insurance programme titled “Trumpcare”. “Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”
Could Trump work with the Democrats?
There is little evidence, however, to suggest that Trump is planning a political pivot after the midterms.
Within a week of the vote, for instance, Trump named Stephen Miller — one of the architects of his hardline policies on immigration — as White House chief of staff.
The staffing shake-up was seen as a doubling-down on right-wing policy priorities.
While Trump has, at times, suggested that he could cooperate with Democratic lawmakers, he has also promised to use his veto power aggressively.
He has also taken to social media to disparage Chuck Schumer, who is currently seeking to become the next Senate majority leader, a position he previously held from 2021 to 2025.
“It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader,” Trump said in a Truth Social post on Sunday.
“He failed badly as ‘Leader’ once before, one of the worst in history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again.”
Trump’s White House has also threatened to take action if Democrats aggressively use their oversight powers in Congress.
“Members of the new Congress have evinced a clear intent to transgress” the constitutional limits of their power, White House counsel Will Scharf wrote in a letter on November 9, gesturing to the prospect of congressional investigations.
