noticias.titulo: Europe Tonight: NATO security warnings, COP31 fallout, and Spain’s elections
noticias.resumen: NATO chief Mark Rutte warns of escalating hybrid threats as Ukraine pushes for membership, COP31 collapses without a climate deal, Spain faces a pivotal right-wing electoral shift, IG Metall workers strike across Germany, and Paris illuminates the Champs-Élysées for the holidays.
noticias.texto:
NATO chief Mark Rutte warns of escalating hybrid threats as Ukraine pushes for membership, COP31 collapses without a climate deal, Spain faces a pivotal right-wing electoral shift, IG Metall workers strike across Germany, and Paris illuminates the Champs-Élysées for the holidays.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte warned in Berlin that malign activities targeting Alliance members (including sabotage, cyberattacks, and airspace violations) are expected to intensify. "We are all targeted, we are all affected," Rutte stressed, calling on allies to bolster defense spending and industrial production. Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has renewed his call for Ukraine to join NATO, following a proposal by US negotiator Jared Kushner for security guarantees modeled on NATO’s Article 5.
COP31 Ends in Disappointment Over Fossil Fuels and Finance
The UN climate conference in Antalya, Turkey (now remembered as both the longest and one of the most disappointing in history) concluded without a major new agreement after deep divisions emerged over fossil fuel phase-outs and climate financing. Tonight, Green MEP Michael Bloss joins us to break down the key takeaways from the summit and discuss what Europe’s role should be moving forward.
Spotlight on Spain elections
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, a prominent standard-bearer for European left-wing politics, faces the growing threat of being unseated in Spain’s parliamentary election. With the center-right conservatives leading most opinion polls, a potential alliance with the far-right Vox party could secure a governing majority, raising broader questions about whether Europe’s political firewall against the far right is eroding. Chief Correspondent Maria Tadeo joins us with the latest analysis from the ground.
Industrial Tensions Escalate as German Workers Walk Out
Labor disputes in Germany’s vital metal and electrical sectors are intensifying. The country’s largest trade union, IG Metall, called on more than 23,000 workers across 19 northern sites—including Mercedes-Benz, BMW, Siemens Gamesa, and shipbuilder Meyer Werft—to stage a 24-hour warning strike. The walkouts follow Friday’s nationwide strikes that mobilized 151,000 workers, affecting major hubs such as Audi’s main plant in Ingolstadt and three BMW plants in Bavaria.
Paris Kicks Off the Festive Season on the Champs-Élysées
Finally, we turn to Paris, where the holiday season officially began on Sunday evening with the illumination of the Champs-Élysées. Joined by Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire, Oscar-winning actress and 2026 event patron Cate Blanchett flipped the switch on 52 kilometers of lights and two million LEDs spanning 400 trees. Through January 4, 2027, visitors can enjoy a five-minute light show every 15 minutes from 5:00 PM to 1:00 AM, cycling through three distinct visual themes: Nature's Awakening, Winter's Arrival, and Starry Night.
When and where to watch Europe Tonight?
You can join Euronews’ Mared Gwyn live on TV and Euronews' website as well as digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, TikTok, and Instagram), every weekday at 6 pm, 7 pm and 8 pm Brussels time.
In just 28 minutes, our new format brings the day's top stories through a European lens, with live analysis and debate with MEPs and leaders.

noticias.titulo: How artists from Qatar, Canada and Mexico are connecting cultures through creativity
noticias.resumen: Artists from Qatar, Mexico and Canada explore shared traditions, personal histories and new creative connections through the 2026 Year of Culture.
noticias.texto:
Artists from Qatar, Mexico and Canada explore shared traditions, personal histories and new creative connections through the 2026 Year of Culture.
What happens when artists from different corners of the world come together to share ideas, traditions and creative techniques?
As part of the Qatar–Canada–Mexico 2026 Year of Culture, artists and designers are crossing borders to explore unexpected connections between their cultures.
Mexican designer Fernando Laposse is bringing traditional materials and agricultural knowledge to Doha. His exhibition, The Sower, combines Mexican natural dyes with Qatar's pearls, while exploring how ancient farming practices could help communities adapt to a changing climate.
Qatar-based designer Yasamin Shaikhi travelled to Mexico, where she collaborated with Mexican artisans to blend traditional craftsmanship with experimental design. What began as an exchange between two seemingly different cultures revealed surprising similarities in their creative approaches.
Meanwhile, Canadian photographer Joanna Johnston is exhibiting deeply personal images of Alberta's prairies at MIHAD, a new contemporary art and design gallery in Doha. Captured during a journey with her late father, the photographs offer a window into family, memory and belonging.
Through their work, these artists are discovering that creativity can bridge cultural and geographical divides. And while the exhibitions may be temporary, the relationships, knowledge and inspiration gained through these exchanges could endure long after the Year of Culture ends.

noticias.titulo: Dutch court bans BYD model from EU over likeness to Land Rover's Defender
noticias.resumen: The Chinese carmaker plans to appeal, and the ruling doesn't stop the car going on sale in Britain in January.
noticias.texto:
The Chinese carmaker plans to appeal, and the ruling doesn't stop the car going on sale in Britain in January.
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) on Monday welcomed a ruling by a court in The Hague, the Netherlands, that bars Chinese carmaker BYD from selling its Ti7 SUV in the European Union because it copies the Land Rover Defender too closely.
On Friday, the district court found that the Ti7 shares distinctive and protected elements of the Defender L663's design. These include the curved "shoulders" of the bodywork, the rounded corners and wheel arches, and the overall silhouette.
The ruling bans BYD from importing, manufacturing, stocking or selling the Ti7 anywhere in the EU. When products are sold across the bloc, a national court in Europe can issue intellectual property rulings that apply throughout the EU.
However, the ban does not cover the United Kingdom. The court said it had no jurisdiction over BYD's British arm, and it rejected JLR's claims based on its UK design rights.
The Ti7 went on sale in China last year. It is not yet available in the EU, but deliveries to Britain are expected to begin in January, according to the court.
"JLR continues to invest in creativity and innovation. We protect our intellectual property and take legal action when necessary," a JLR spokesperson told Euronews. "Legal proceedings are ongoing and we won't be commenting further at this time."
BYD said it would appeal.
"BYD strongly disagrees with today's judgment and will appeal it. The BYD Ti7 is the result of BYD's own independent design work and infringes none of JLR's rights," the company said in a statement.
BYD's shares fell 4 percent in Hong Kong earlier on Monday and closed the session 1.9 percent lower.

noticias.titulo: Macron announces €350 million research aid for France's aeronautics industry
noticias.resumen: During a visit to the Airbus site in Blagnac near Toulouse, the French president announced 350 million euros in state support for aeronautics research and innovation, plus special industrial zones to ease new factory projects.
noticias.texto:
During a visit to the Airbus site in Blagnac near Toulouse, the French president announced 350 million euros in state support for aeronautics research and innovation, plus special industrial zones to ease new factory projects.
New boost for the French aeronautics industry. During a visit on Monday to the Airbus site in Blagnac, near Toulouse, Emmanuel Macron announced 350 million euros in support for research and innovation in the sector, in particular to accompany the development of new technologies and strengthen the competitiveness of the industry.
"350 million euros for CORAC (Council for civil aeronautics research), that is what we will do. And it was very important to be able to confirm it to you. We are providing visibility", said Emmanuel Macron.
The president also announced the creation of industrial zones "with high potential", in which administrative procedures will be simplified in order to make it easier and quicker to set up new factories.
The aim is to strengthen France's attractiveness for industrial companies and to encourage new investment.
For its part, Airbus plans to adapt a second assembly line to the manufacture of A321 and A32XLR aircraft. This change is expected to allow the European aircraft manufacturer to increase its production rate and create jobs, something Emmanuel Macron welcomed.
This visit took place as part of the Choose France summit, organised this Monday in Paris, which highlights nearly 300 industrial projects led by French companies.

noticias.titulo: AI just cracked the biggest maths problem of all time: what does it mean?
noticias.resumen: Some wonder if the solving of the famous Riemann Hypothesis by Anthropic’s Claude model is the beginning of advanced super intelligence.
noticias.texto:
Some wonder if the solving of the famous Riemann Hypothesis by Anthropic’s Claude model is the beginning of advanced super intelligence.
Anthropic’s announcement on Friday that its Claude artificial intelligence model had helped solve what many had called the ‘biggest maths problem of all time’ has been met by both awe and terror for what the future of AI has in store for humanity.
Anthropic researcher and mathematician Levent Alpöge used Claude to find a solution to the 167-year-old math problem known as the Riemann Hypothesis, one of six remaining unsolved Millennium Prize problems carrying a $1 million (€913,000) reward from the Clay Mathematics Institute.
First proposed in 1859, the hypothesis suggests that the seemingly random appearance of prime numbers — numbers divisible only by one and themselves — actually follows a hidden, strict pattern.
Solving the problem could eventually have enormous real-world consequences, by giving certainty to the way prime numbers are distributed, computer systems, for example, can run more quickly and leaner.
Alpöge worked with Claude for months, submitting a partial result in August. This is not the first time he has explored using AI to solve maths’ biggest problems.
In September, he submitted a partial result proof to the Navier-Stokes and Euler equations, which govern fluid dynamics.
The Anthropic researcher submitted both this and his latest proof to Lean, the open-source, interactive maths proof platform which automatically checks proofs.
The platform is designed to test mathematical proofs and allow independent checkers to verify them. Within 48 hours, MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland and the Lean FRO/ Mathlib Initiative checked the proof and found zero errors.
His released proof spans 17,374,215 lines of Lean code spread across 175,187 separate files, backed by an unpublished, AI-generated text draft exceeding 250,000 pages.
The sheer scale of it means that humans have not yet had time to fully comprehend it, and even Alpöge was in awe of the ability of AI to solve the problem.
"Claude began to leave me in awe" and "far outpaced me near the finish line," adding that "Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."
Reaction
Many mathematicians have welcomed the proof.
Hector Pasten of the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile called it “something like a Rosetta Stone” that completes a dictionary between previously disconnected branches of math.
Oxford University’s James Maynard called it “something to be celebrated” because mathematicians finally know why it is true.
Independent Italian mathematician Alessandro Masullo, who released an incomplete, traditional human-written proof on the exact same day after 12 years of solo work, said he refused to use AI because he didn't trust it.
Some had expected that AI would take much longer to solve the problem, such as Australian American mathematician Terence Tao who predicted in October that AI would solve the Riemann Hypothesis by 2050. One month later, he was wrong.
Meta’s AI Chief Alexandr Wang took to X on Sunday warning that the achievement marked “the beginning of a significant change” that could usher in a “handover of society to AI”, arguing machines will soon supersede human capacity in every field.
Elon Musk meanwhile also saw it as a defining moment in the developing AI. He responded on social media platform X, “Unequivocal super intelligence has arrived. Welcome to the Singularity.”
Others have argued that the sheer length and scale of the proof, coming in at 250,000 pages long, makes it almost unreadable to humans, raising philosophical questions about whether mathematical truth matters if humans cannot comprehend it.
AI critics including Gary Marcus and godfather of AI Yann LeCun have pointed out that AI did not solve the problem by itself, rather it required months of human guidance and open-source infrastructure developed by mathematicians to find the solution, dismissing the finding as more hype than proof of a super intelligence.
What does it mean for society?
The solving of Riemann’s Hypothesis sets a major precedent for how science will be done in the future. By pairing human intuition with AI to solve complicated problems to create genuinely new insights that would normally be beyond human capacity.
In mathematics, hundreds of theorems that previously began with the caveat “assuming the Riemann Hypothesis is true…” are now officially proven facts. In computer science, it also confirms that certain algorithms used to process large prime numbers will always run reliably at high speeds.
It could also remove the need for code that previously treated the hypothesis as a theory, meaning computer systems can be learner and more efficient.
What it does not do is break internet encryption. If anything, the proof helps cybersecurity confirm that certain fast algorithms used to test whether a massive number is prime are 100% reliable.

noticias.titulo: EU goes after Russia's banks, soldiers and athletes in new sanctions package
noticias.resumen: Russian banks, crypto, "shadow fleet", oil refineries, soldiers and athletes are all targeted in the latest sanctions package proposed by Brussels.
noticias.texto:
Russian banks, crypto, "shadow fleet", oil refineries, soldiers and athletes are all targeted in the latest sanctions package proposed by Brussels.
The European Commission has proposed a new round of economic sanctions against Russia as the country disregards calls for an energy ceasefire and continues its relentless attacks aimed at making Ukraine's winter unbearable.
The proposal, unveiled on Monday afternoon, comes amid intensifying efforts to advance the peace negotiations into a multilateral format involving Ukrainian, Russian, European and US officials, although Moscow has yet to commit to taking part.
If approved by member states, it will mark the 22nd sanctions package since February 2022. Brussels aims for a deal in December before the holiday break.
"We will continue to propose new sanctions until Russia shows genuine intent for lasting peace in Ukraine," Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a video statement.
"Our position is clear: we are giving Ukraine the strength to secure peace – and Russia every reason to choose it."
The new sanctions seek to remove an additional 60 Russian banks from the SWIFT system, crack down on the crypto platforms that Moscow uses to bypass restrictions, and prohibit European companies from repairing Russian energy facilities, particularly oil refineries, which Ukraine's long-range strikes have significantly impaired.
The proposal also targets over 70 vessels from the "shadow fleet" that Moscow employs to bypass the oil price cap, currently set at $44 per barrel.
More than 670 of these vessels have already been denied access to EU ports and services. The decrepit ships, which lack standard insurance and often sail under false flags, are considered a security and environmental threat.
Von der Leyen has revived a measure from the previous package that was left pending: an entry ban on Russian soldiers who have fought in Ukraine.
The first attempt in July fell short after France and Italy raised concernsabout the administrative burden and legal responsibility for consular services.
But a recent spike in hybrid attacks, many of them attributed to Russian services, has injected fresh energy into the issue. Denmark has asked for tighter visa rules after foiling a Russian plot to assassinate a US-Ukrainian rapper on Danish soil.
"Russian ex-combatants pose a security risk to Europe. They cannot be allowed to wander freely across our countries," von der Leyen said.
"Therefore, entry into the European Union will be off limits."
The package introduces a novel dimension: sports and culture.
The Commission wants to exclude Russian teams and athletes competing under the Russian flag and the display of official Russian symbols from all sports events inside the bloc. It also wants to prohibit Russians from providing financial donations to and holding posts in governing bodies of European-based sports federations.
In July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) lifted its suspension on Russian athletes ahead of the 2028 LA Olympics, triggering an outcry across Europe.
"Sports events can not be a forum for propaganda activities," von der Leyen said.
Notably absent from the Commission’s proposal is alumina, a key raw material used in aluminium production.
The issue came to prominence earlier this year after a media consortium exposed the links between Aughinish Alumina, a sprawling refinery in western Ireland, and Russia's military-industrial complex. Dublin came under intense pressure from Kyiv to cease the exports and was forced to launch a government probe.
The investigation reached no definitive conclusion because it did not find evidence to either confirm or refute a direct link between Irish-made alumina and Russian weapons.
Though publicly Dublin has said it would not "cherry-pick" EU sanctions, Brussels did not sense enough Irish support to move ahead with restrictions.
Monday's proposal is the first since the Commission established a sanctions office within its Secretary General, bringing together officials from different departments
Lars Danielsson, a veteran Swedish diplomat, has been appointed to replace David O'Sullivan as EU sanctions envoy. O'Sullivan spent the last few years travelling around the world, with a focus on Central Asia, to convince other countries to put pressure on companies that help Moscow bypass sanctions and buy blacklisted items.
China, in particular, remains a headache for Commission officials, dismissing their pleas. The country has become the central passage for circumventing sanctions, providing Moscow an essential lifeline to sustain its resource-intensive war.
"Every time we have a summit with China, we raise this issue," a senior official said.
Ahead of the presentation, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on allies to tighten sanctions on the components that Russia uses to build the jet-powered drones that terrorise the civilian population.
"International sanctions, enforcement of sanctions regimes, and genuinely tougher export controls are what can curb Russia's weapons production. Every country and every leader who helps pressure the aggressor also helps protect lives," he said.
Zelenskyy is set to attend a special EU summit later this week in Brussels.

noticias.titulo: Finland summons Russian ambassador as it condemns Russia's 'dangerous and reckless actions' in Europe
noticias.resumen: It comes after a Russian helicopter was suspected of having violated Finnish airspace on Saturday afternoon, off the coast of Loviisa.
noticias.texto:
It comes after a Russian helicopter was suspected of having violated Finnish airspace on Saturday afternoon, off the coast of Loviisa.
Finland announced on Monday that it had summoned the Russian ambassador as it condemned Moscow's strikes on Ukraine and hit out at what it called Russia's "dangerous and reckless actions" in Europe.
"We strongly condemn Russia's illegal war of aggression and its escalating strikes against civilian targets in Ukraine. We stand in solidarity with Denmark, Poland and our other European partners," the foreign ministry said in a post on social media.
It comes after a Russian helicopter was suspected of having violated Finnish airspace on Saturday afternoon, off the coast of Loviisa.
Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said the incident may have been related to "rescue or monitoring operations" involving the Russian cargo ship Sparta II, which caught fire after being struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday morning as it was sailing to Kaliningrad.
"Ukraine has the right to defend itself against Russia's illegal aggression. Russia must end its war of aggression against Ukraine," the foreign ministry added on Monday.
The Finnish Border Guard confirmed on Sunday that the Sparta II was being towed away by a Russian rescue ship.
"The vessel is slightly listing, but the situation is stable," it said in an update on the situation, adding that a Border Guard helicopter was monitoring the Sparta II and any potential risks to the local marine environment.
The United States announced sanctions against the Sparta II in 2022, shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Ukraine has also sanctioned the vessel.
The Gulf of Finland is a crucial maritime passage for Russia, connecting Saint Petersburg with the wider Baltic Sea.

noticias.titulo: Ukraine releases footage of strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya
noticias.resumen: Ukraine has released footage showing what it says are strikes against two Russian vessels off the Libyan port of Benghazi.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine has released footage showing what it says are strikes targeting two Russian vessels off the Libyan port of Benghazi.
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
The images, shared by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on 22 November 2026, appear to show explosions near the vessels off Libya's eastern coast. "It all took place off the coast of Libya. Our warriors deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones. Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk," Zelensky wrote in a post on X.
The alleged strikes come as Russia's war against Ukraine continues into its fifth year, with the conflict increasingly extending beyond Ukrainian territory.

noticias.titulo: How Iceland's Blue Lagoon is faring after its long-awaited stock market debut
noticias.resumen: Shares in Iceland's Blue Lagoon fell below their offer price when they started trading on Friday. The geothermal spa operator raised 14.3 billion Icelandic krónur (€104mn) in the country's first IPO in nearly three years.
noticias.texto:
Shares in Iceland's Blue Lagoon fell below their offer price when they started trading on Friday. The geothermal spa operator raised 14.3 billion Icelandic krónur (€104mn) in the country's first IPO in nearly three years.
Blue Lagoon, which runs Iceland's famous geothermal spa, saw its shares drop below their initial public offering price on Friday.
The company raised 14.3 billion Icelandic krónur (€104mn) in Iceland's first IPO in nearly three years. The previous one was by fishing company Ísfélag in December 2023.
Its shares opened at 85 krónur, 10.5% below the offer price of 95 krónur a share, and closed at 87.4 krónur, down 8%.
On Monday, the shares were trading slightly lower at around 86.3 krónur.
Listed under the ticker BLUE, Blue Lagoon is the 28th company on the main market of Nasdaq Iceland, the country's stock exchange.
Magnús Harðarson, president of Nasdaq Iceland, said in a statement that the listing gives investors access to a part of the Icelandic economy that has not been represented on the market before.
Blue Lagoon sold 150 million new shares, equivalent to 14.6% of the company after the offering.
The offering drew nearly 4,000 subscriptions, worth about 15.3bn krónur (€112mn), according to the company. That was roughly 7% more than the value of the shares on offer. About 40% of the shares went to individuals and 60% to professional investors and companies.
At the offer price, Blue Lagoon was valued at about 97.4bn krónur (€710mn), based on the 1.02bn shares it now has in issue.
Blue Lagoon began preparing for a listing in 2022 and had hoped to go public in 2023.
More than a lagoon
The company was set up in 1992 to research the lagoon's geothermal seawater. The lagoon lies in a lava field on the Reykjanes Peninsula in south-west Iceland.
The company now runs The Retreat and Silica hotels by the lagoon, the Michelin-starred Moss restaurant and two hotels in Iceland's highlands. It also sells skincare products abroad.
Its revenue reached a record €156mn last year, according to its offering documents.
Blue Lagoon is also buying Arctic Adventures, an Icelandic tour operator.
Including the tour operator, the company has budgeted revenue of €291mn for 2027. On its own, Blue Lagoon expects revenue of about €173mn this year.
It wants to use the IPO proceeds to develop new destinations, strengthen its balance sheet and fund growth.
One risk for the business is that the lagoon sits near Grindavík, a town that has been hit by a series of volcanic eruptions since late 2023.
The company said volcanic activity forced the lagoon to close for 49 days in 2023 and 76 days in 2024, but for only two days in 2025.
Tourism accounted for 8.8% of Iceland's economic output in 2025, up from 8.2% the year before, according to preliminary figures from Statistics Iceland, the national statistics office.
Blue Lagoon has said it expects to complete the Arctic Adventures deal at the end of November, when it will issue about 246 million new shares to the tour operator's owners.
They will then hold about 19% of the enlarged company.

noticias.titulo: 'Return the Marbles': Greece renews demand for Parthenon relics at Acropolis Museum reopening
noticias.resumen: "The place of these priceless masterpieces is here, under the Attic light and in direct contact with the temple they belong to," said Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis.
noticias.texto:
"The place of these priceless masterpieces is here, under the Attic light and in direct contact with the temple they belong to," said Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis.
The goal of having the Parthenon Marbles returned to their original position was at the heart of the Greek prime minister's speech on the Sacred Rock of the Acropolis.
Speaking at the inauguration of the Old Acropolis Museum, Kyriakos Mitsotakis once again referred to Greece's longstanding demand for the sculptures held in the British Museum.
"The return and reunification of the Parthenon Marbles remains our great and non-negotiable national objective. The place of these priceless masterpieces is here, under the Attic light and in direct contact with the temple to which they belong. Since a history of 2,500 years cannot be erased, no solution, no agreement can be accepted if it involves recognising foreign ownership over our national treasures," said the Greek prime minister.
"Today we are returning to the starting point, to the place where one of the first chapters of our modern archaeology was written. This modest building became the first home for the finds from the Acropolis," Mitsotakis added.
The Greek prime minister also noted that when the exhibits were moved to the new museum, the old museum's doors closed for 20 years: "The question remained open, what would its purpose be? The easy option would have been for it to remain downgraded, serving as a storeroom and offices.
"The difficult option was the one our government chose, to reintegrate it into the living fabric of the archaeological site and of the entire city. It is a mission that is now being completed, bringing a landmark from the past into our everyday present," he said, adding: "It is worth focusing on the core of this effort, which is nothing other than the new pulse the old museum is acquiring."

noticias.titulo: South Korea’s education minister resigns after backlash over AI exam cheating rules
noticias.resumen: South Korea’s university entrance exam can shape a student’s future. Hidden cameras and smart glasses have fuelled fears of AI-assisted cheating, prompting last-minute security measures that drew criticism and led to the education minister’s resignation.
noticias.texto:
South Korea’s university entrance exam can shape a student’s future. Hidden cameras and smart glasses have fuelled fears of AI-assisted cheating, prompting last-minute security measures that drew criticism and led to the education minister’s resignation.
South Korea’s education minister has resigned after criticism of last-minute changes meant to stop students from cheating by using AI on the country’s university entrance exam.
President Lee Jae-myung accepted Choi Kyo-jin’s resignation on Sunday, three days after the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), known locally as Suneung. Choi acknowledged that the government had failed to prepare adequately and that sudden changes had caused confusion.
On Monday, the Education Ministry said it was filing criminal complaints against five candidates caught using smart devices during the exam. Some complaints had already been filed, with the remaining cases due to follow by the end of the day, an official told Yonhap news agency.
Concern grew after the top scorer in this year’s certified tax accountant examination admitted on 15 November to cheating with a miniature camera, a smartphone and generative AI.
The confession came days before the university entrance exam, which plays a major role in students’ university choices and career prospects.
The Education Ministry had also reported four cases involving AI-enabled smart glasses in middle and high school exams this year.
Authorities deployed about 8,400 additional staff for the university entrance exam, including specialists checking for smart devices and monitors patrolling corridors. Supervisors were told to inspect students’ glasses and cover clothing buttons with stickers to block hidden cameras.
During the exam, the government sent three nationwide emergency alerts to mobile phones to detect devices that candidates had not handed over.
The ministry reported 111 suspected breaches involving electronic devices. Of those, 54 were detected through the alerts and 52 through other methods, while five involved candidates actually using smart devices. The figures do not establish that all 111 cases involved AI-assisted cheating.
Last-minute changes draw criticism
The government announced the additional staff two days before the exam. Teachers’ organisations questioned whether supervisors could learn to identify sophisticated devices at such short notice.
The Korean Federation of Teachers’ Associations criticised a timetable that left staff being selected on Tuesday, trained on Wednesday and deployed on Thursday.
The day before the exam, the ministry also restricted students to black pencils. Exam centres were to provide other supplies, including erasers and correction tape, to prevent candidates from hiding cameras inside them.
Choi had already drawn criticism for telling a parliamentary hearing on 16 November that his age made him doubt his ability to detect all AI-assisted cheating.
“Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation,” he said in his resignation statement.
Lee has put Prime Minister Han Seong-sook in charge of follow-up measures and ordered a review of how examinations are managed.
One proposal under consideration would add identification marks to question papers, allowing authorities to trace where photographed or leaked questions came from.

noticias.titulo: ‘Batman Returns’: Tim Burton’s iconic Batmobile car heads to auction
noticias.resumen: The iconic Batmobile from Tim Burton’s 1992 film Batman Returns is heading to auction with an estimated price of $5 million to $7 million.
noticias.texto:
The iconic Batmobile from Tim Burton’s 1992 film Batman Returns is heading to auction with an estimated price of $5 million to $7 million.
Fancy taking over Bruce Wayne's night-time business? If the price is right you can pretend to be the "World's Greatest Detective" by buying the unmistakable Batmobile which starred in Tim Burton’s 1992 film Batman Returns.
Soon to be auctioned, the sleek, glossy vehicle known as the “Number One Hero car”, measures just under six metres long and features two distinctive sweeping tail fins. It appeared in most of the film’s driving sequences, including a memorable scene in which Danny DeVito’s Penguin takes control of the car and speeds through the streets of Gotham City.
The Batmobile has spent years on display at the Marconi Automotive Museum in Tustin, California. It retains its original paintwork, Chevrolet V-8 engine and a radio-controlled flaming exhaust system, used in the film when Batman, played by Michael Keaton, torches one of the Penguin’s circus henchmen.
Beyond its impressive design, the vehicle reflects the darker gothic aesthetic that Burton brought to the DC universe, helping influence the visual direction of subsequent superhero films.
It is is expected to fetch between $5 million and $7 million at auction on Monday. It could surpass the record set in 2013, when the Batmobile driven by Adam West in the original 1960s television series sold for $4.6 million.
The future owner will, however, face restrictions on its use. The car is not road legal and must remain stationary when displayed to the public, under an agreement with Warner Bros.
The car is the centrepiece of a Julien's Auctions sale that features dozens of pieces of Batman and other superhero memorabilia.

noticias.titulo: Robotaxis and stock exchanges: Why Bolt's CEO says Europe is way behind
noticias.resumen: Bolt’s CEO spoke to Euronews about the company’s future IPO plans, why he believes Europe is falling behind, and whether the US could offer a more attractive market. He also shared his vision for the future of autonomous vehicles.
noticias.texto:
Bolt’s CEO spoke to Euronews about the company’s future IPO plans, why he believes Europe is falling behind, and whether the US could offer a more attractive market. He also shared his vision for the future of autonomous vehicles.
At just 27 years old, Markus Villig became Europe’s youngest self-made billionaire, thanks to Bolt, the mobility company he founded at the age of 19 in Estonia.
Now generating an annual turnover of more than €2 billion, Bolt’s founder and CEO, Markus Villig, said he knew the company was going to be a big success almost immediately.
“Honestly, after the first 30 days, it was very clear that this product resonates. Customers love it. They get access to more affordable and great transportation, drivers see that they're able to make more income than what they used to do, and it just took off immediately.”
Markus joined Angela Barnes in the studio for the latest episode of The Big Question to discuss the company’s future, the latest technological developments coming to Europe and Bolt’s IPO plans.
How soon will we see robotaxis in Europe?
While Bolt started its life as a ride-hailing taxi app, under the names mTakso and Taxify, it has since diversified into e-scooters, e-bikes, food delivery and courier services.
And the company’s next big move is robotaxis – self-driving vehicles that are expected to help bridge the gap between supply and demand, while reducing road traffic accidents.
“The technology is ready today,” Markus told The Big Question.
“When we look at what's going on in the US or China, robotaxis today are serving hundreds of thousands of passengers every single week. So this is no longer a fictional technology, this is something that works in the real world. And yet, at the same time, there's zero robotaxis operating in Europe at the moment.”
According to Markus, a combination of factors is holding back the bloc: a lack of domestic technology, regulation blocking adoption and fragmented regulation making widespread roll-out even more complex.
“Today in the European Union there's not a single advanced self-driving car company who could produce this technology domestically,” he criticised.
As a result, Bolt has had to look elsewhere.
Bolt has signed a deal with US electric vehicle maker Lucid to provide a 25,000-strong fleet, equipped with technology from Chinese company Pony.ai, for roll-out across Europe. Pilot programmes are expected to start within the next year.
Will Bolt IPO in Europe?
In short, no – not in the current climate. But that’s not because Markus doesn’t want to.
“As a European, I'd like to list in Europe. However, when I am looking at this neutrally as a CEO, I look at the facts.
“It's very clear that Europe is just very far behind in terms of access to capital. Today, it just clearly is not as attractive,” he told Euronews.
However, he is in no rush to take the company public, choosing to focus first on delivering its robotaxis and winning in that category. Markus also seemed optimistic that the situation in Europe could be fixed, hopefully by the time he’s ready to hit the stock exchange.
“If we really wanted to, we could reform the European capital markets. We absolutely have the funding we need, but we just need to structure it better so it would actually be competitive versus just going and listing in New York.
“There's absolutely potential to fix that, but we must do that urgently,” Markus added.
The Big Questionis a series from Euronews Business where we sit down with industry leaders and experts to discuss some of the most important topics on today’s agenda.
Watch the video above to see the full discussion with Bolt’s founder and CEO, Markus Villig.

noticias.titulo: At least 24 people killed in Indonesia factory fire, police say
noticias.resumen: Dozens of employees are still reported to be missing after a blaze broke out at a candy factory in Banten province at around 4:30 pm local time on Saturday.
noticias.texto:
Dozens of employees are still reported to be missing after a blaze broke out at a candy factory in Banten province at around 4:30 pm local time on Saturday.
At least 24 people were killed in a deadly fire that ripped through a factory in western Java over the weekend, police have said.
The blaze broke out at a candy factory in the Serang Regency of Banten province at around 4:30 pm local time on Saturday, trapping workers inside. It had been extinguished by 6:30 am the following day.
Dozens of employees are still reported to be missing.
Hendra Kurniawan, the chief inspector general of the Banten regional police force, said on Sunday that the bodies "were no longer physically identifiable" and that DNA testing would need to be used for identification purposes.
The presidential advisor for workers' welfare, Said Iqbal, said in a statement on Monday that the fire could have been caused by a short circuit in the building's AC system, but he stressed that further investigations were needed to determine how it began.
Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency (Basarnas) shared footage on social media on Sunday showing emergency crews looking through the charred remains of the building.
Other images from the scene show extensive damage to the factory's roof as well as burned-out vehicles.
The candy company, Fonusa Agung Mulia, describes itself online as a subsidiary of Indonesia's UNIFAM food company.

noticias.titulo: Nvidia closes up more than 30% after Jensen Huang returns as CEO
noticias.resumen: Nvidia shares soared from their Friday close after the company's board unanimously voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. US President Donald Trump welcomed his return.
noticias.texto:
Nvidia shares soared from their Friday close after the company's board unanimously voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. US President Donald Trump welcomed his return.
Nvidia's stock soared by around 31.5% on Monday after the company moved to reinstate Jensen Huang as president, CEO and board member, just 11 days after his resignation.
The board voted unanimously to bring Huang back after a series of meetings with him left directors satisfied with his "candor and ability to lead," the firm said in a statement.
Monday's rally spread across Wall Street, with both the Nasdaq Composite and the S&P 500 securing their best days since April 2025. The Nasdaq jumped 6.5%, while the S&P 500 was up roughly 4.7% at the close of play.
US President Donald Trump hailed the move in a social media post, writing that Nvidia's board had made the "correct and proper decision" and adding that "the country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the success and prosperity of not only the company, but the American economy".
Trump, who had publicly called for Huang's return and on Friday described him as "one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world," later told CNBC that he had been "speaking to the board directly and indirectly" about the decision.
"The board was placed in a very bad position. I think the board acted really responsibly," he said.
Huang has been one of AI's most visible champions as he fuelled the boom in the sector through deals that helped finance Nvidia's suppliers and customers as they built the infrastructure that runs on its chips.
Huang has built a close relationship with Trump since the president returned to the White House, making frequent trips to Washington and negotiating directly with the administration over chip exports to China.
Nvidia also gave $25 million (€23m) to Trump's White House ballroom project, according to a donor list published by The Washington Post.
His departure left investors asking whether Nvidia could keep up the pace of dealmaking and whether its customers would stick to the spending plans that had helped drive the AI boom originally.
The decision came less than two weeks after the Nvidia co-founder resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who was alleged to be a spy.
US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on 12 November that the FBI was investigating reports that she had worked for the Chinese government and that the Justice Department had yet to reach a conclusion.
Meanwhile, Beijing has rejected the espionage allegations.
Reacting to the Nvidia board's decision, Trump rebuffed the claims by stating that "the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security."
He also told CNBC that Huang "didn't know about" advanced Nvidia chips going to China.
The board said it had received input from senior US government officials and was also confident that Huang's return posed no national security risk.
The decision stands in stark contrast to the board's position last week.
Nvidia had said it would consider internal and external candidates to replace Huang, who had signalled he was willing to return if asked. While Nvidia reported better-than-expected quarterly results last week, board chair Harvey Jones told investors that the board did not intend to reinstate Huang.
On Monday, Jones said the board believed Huang was "the right person to lead NVIDIA" and that bringing him back was in the interests of shareholders, employees, partners and customers.
He also thanked Colette Kress for serving as interim CEO. Kress will remain CFO, and Jones will stay on as chair.
Huang said he was honoured to return and would take on the role with "the greatest humility and renewed commitment."
Nvidia also clarified that a committee of independent directors would continue investigating reports that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The committee has hired independent lawyers, and Huang supports the investigation and has pledged to cooperate, the company said.
A separate committee of independent directors will oversee trade compliance and national security risks, with help from specialist lawyers and advisers.
The company said it would continue to cooperate with any government investigations and inquiries.
Huang is still due to face questions from three US House committees on 1 December in a session that will be a transcribed interview, but will not be open to the public.

noticias.titulo: Portishead join ‘No Music For Genocide’ campaign alongside Massive Attack, Fontaines D.C. and Björk
noticias.resumen: Iconic trip-hop band Portishead has joined the ‘No Music For Genocide’ campaign, a cultural boycott initiative encouraging artists and rights-holders to pull their music from streaming platforms in Israel.
noticias.texto:
Iconic trip-hop band Portishead has joined the ‘No Music For Genocide’ campaign, a cultural boycott initiative encouraging artists and rights-holders to pull their music from streaming platforms in Israel.
Hundreds of artists have joined the No Music For Genocide movement, a cultural boycott initiative which encourages artists and rights-holders to pull their music from streaming platforms in Israel, in response to the ongoing humanitarian crisis in Gaza.
Among the 400+ artists are Massive Attack, Fontaines D.C., Kneecap, Björk, and the estate of legendary Japanese composer Ryuichi Sakamoto.
The most recent addition is iconic British trip-hop band Portishead, who has also geo-blocked their music from streaming platforms in Israel.
The band’s three albums are no longer available on Spotify, Apple Music and their YouTube page in Israel, according to a recent report by Israeli outlet Haaretz.
This was confirmed by the band, with Portishead member Geoff Barrow sharing an Instagram post that shows Gaza in 2023 and 2026, with the caption: “And people wonder why we boycott Israel."
Other major artists who have joined the movement include Lorde, IDLES, Wednesday, Amyl & The Sniffers, Wolf Alice, Paramore, Rina Sawayama, Primal Scream, Soccer Mommy, Shygirl, Lucy Dacus, MJ Lenderman, MØ and AURORA.
A statement released last year from ‘No Music For Genocide’ stated: “Culture can’t stop bombs on its own, but it can help reject political repression, shift public opinion toward justice, and refuse the art-washing and normalization of any company or nation that commits crimes against humanity.”
“This initiative is one part of a worldwide movement to erode the support Israel needs to continue its genocide," the statement added. “Many of our peers have felt, like ourselves, unsure how to use music in this moment. Our first goal with No Music For Genocide is to inspire others to reclaim their agency and direct their influence toward a tangible act. We are so grateful for all of the artists, managers and labels who have already committed to this first step, and we’re excited to expand this together. The more of us there are, the stronger we will be. This is just the beginning.”
Hamas launched an attack on Israel on 7 October 2023. The Gaza health ministry has reported more than 73,000 deaths in the last three years of Israeli bombardment.
Organisations including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the United Nations have described Israel's actions as "genocide" - as well as a report published in June by a UN independent commission which found that "Israeli authorities and security forces have deliberately targeted Palestinian children, resulting in genocide and atrocity crimes in the Gaza Strip and war crimes in the West Bank."
Israel has rejected accusations it is waging genocide and maintains that it is not committing any war crimes. It rejected the UN Commission’s findings as “distorted and false” and a “libellous sham”.

noticias.titulo: How a winemaker found his home and his market in Macao
noticias.resumen: From Portuguese heritage and independent restaurants to luxury resorts and quiet hilltop runs, winemaker Eddie McDougall explains how Macao shaped both his career and his life since he moved there for his wife’s work.
noticias.texto:
From Portuguese heritage and independent restaurants to luxury resorts and quiet hilltop runs, winemaker Eddie McDougall explains how Macao shaped both his career and his life since he moved there for his wife’s work.
“Macao has been an amazing place for me professionally because I work in wine,” says McDougall, Oenologist & Founder, E.J. McDougall & The Flying Winemaker.
He says the city’s push to become a gastronomic hub “plays perfectly” for his work, and its luxury venues help him seal deals. “Meeting clients in a luxury environment of course helps get the deal done,” he says. He also created the Wynn Signature Chinese Wine Awards, which he describes as the biggest of their kind in the world.
Macao’s Portuguese and Chinese heritage runs through his view of the city. “Take the Portuguese heritage, plant it in China, grow it there, bottle it in Macao,” he says.
