noticias.titulo: China: 5,000 drones illuminate sky over Three Gorges at autumn festival
noticias.resumen: Five thousand drones lit up the night sky over Wushan, southwest China, creating giant images of autumn leaves, mountains and river landscapes. The spectacular display celebrated the region's annual Red Leaf Festival.
noticias.texto:
Flying in carefully synchronised formations over the Wu Gorge, the drones created enormous illuminated images inspired by the region's autumn scenery, from mountains covered in red leaves to the winding waters of the Three Gorges. The performance, titled Light and Shadow Three Gorges, unfolded across 12 choreographed scenes, depicting cruise ships, local delicacies and the legendary Goddess of Wushan. Crowds gathered to watch the formations shift across the darkness, culminating in glowing Chinese characters welcoming visitors to theregion's red-leaf season.
The display was organised as part of the 20th Chongqing Yangtze Three Gorges International Red Leaf Festival and the seventh Wushan Goddess Cup Art Film Week, held from 20 to 23 November. Wushan is renowned for its dramatic gorge landscapes, which turn vivid shades of red and orange as autumn foliage spreads across the mountainsides. By recreating these natural landmarks in the sky, organisers sought to showcase the area's scenery, cultural traditions and tourism attractions.

noticias.titulo: LEGO to build €1bn factory in Portugal, creating more than 1,000 jobs
noticias.resumen: The Danish toymaker plans to invest around €1 billion over several years in its fourth European factory. LEGO says the plant will be its most technologically advanced and is expected to start production in 2030.
noticias.texto:
The Danish toymaker plans to invest around €1 billion over several years in its fourth European factory. LEGO says the plant will be its most technologically advanced and is expected to start production in 2030.
LEGO announced plans on Monday to invest around €1 billion in a new factory in Estarreja, Portugal, to meet growing demand across Europe, the Middle East and Africa.
The factory will employ more than 1,000 people once fully operational, the company said. It will offer skilled manufacturing jobs and is expected to start production in 2030.
LEGO chief executive Niels B. Christiansen said: “We are excited to announce our new factory in Estarreja. Expanding our global manufacturing network means that we will continue to be well-positioned to grow and bring LEGO play to many more children, families and fans for generations to come.”
The plant will be LEGO’s fourth in Europe, alongside its factories in Denmark, Hungary and Czechia.
“Portugal stood out to us given its proximity to markets, access to transport links, commitment to sustainability and skilled local workforce,” LEGO’s chief operations officer, Carsten Rasmussen, said.
The 115,000-square-metre factory will sit on a 60-hectare site, roughly the size of 120 football pitches. It will be less than half the size of LEGO’s Nyíregyháza factory in Hungary by building area. The new plant will mould and process bricks and pack finished sets.
Rasmussen said it would be LEGO’s most automated factory. “This new factory will be our most automated and advanced site, using innovative technologies to enhance productivity, sustainability and operational resilience.”
Portugal’s prime minister, Luís Montenegro, attended the launch in Estarreja on Monday. He said the government would work to make the land available and speed up construction so the jobs could be created as soon as possible.
Construction is expected to begin in the first half of 2027. The Portuguese plant will be LEGO’s eighth worldwide, following the opening of its Virginia factory, which is due in 2027. LEGO says making products closer to customers will shorten supply chains and reduce the environmental impact of transport.
LEGO aims to meet all of the Estarreja factory’s annual energy needs from renewable sources. It expects on-site infrastructure, including solar panels and battery storage, to account for around 80%.
LEGO expands as sales rise
LEGO’s consumer sales rose 22% in the first half of 2026. Revenue climbed 21% to 41.9 billion Danish kroner (€5.6bn), while operating profit rose 22% to DKK 10.9bn (€1.5bn). The company singled out Western Europe as one of several regions that helped drive revenue growth.
LEGO increased production capacity at its Hungarian factory by 30% in 2025 and opened a manufacturing innovation centre in Billund, Denmark, in June 2026. It also expanded its factory in China and announced plans in September to increase capacity at its Monterrey plant in Mexico.
The company opened a factory in Vietnam in April 2025 and expects to open both a factory and a regional distribution centre in Virginia in 2027.

noticias.titulo: Croatia steps up pressure on Montenegro over border dispute as EU accession deadline looms
noticias.resumen: Zagreb is demanding a settlement over a strategically important peninsula as Montenegro races to conclude its EU accession talks by the end of the year, raising fears that the dispute could derail its membership ambitions.
noticias.texto:
Zagreb is demanding a settlement over a strategically important peninsula as Montenegro races to conclude its EU accession talks by the end of the year, raising fears that the dispute could derail its membership ambitions.
Croatia is stepping up diplomatic pressure on Montenegro to settle a territorial dispute as the candidate country races to conclude its EU accession talks, two diplomatic sources told Euronews on condition of anonymity.
Zagreb has a list of grievances dating back to the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s that it wants Podgorica to resolve before joining the EU. But in recent days, the Croatian government has intensified its demands over a long-running border dispute.
The diplomats say Croatia's real objective is to settle ownership of the Prevlaka peninsula and the surrounding territorial waters, with one dismissing its other demands as "smokescreens".
The other grievances, which Podgorica has already partly addressed, include locating the remains of prisoners of war, compensating Croatian families whose property was expropriated and returning a naval training ship that was in Montenegro when Yugoslavia dissolved in 1991.
"When it comes to the border issues, if we don't find any kind of solution that is for Montenegro and Croatia acceptable, then we can go to an international court or international arbitration. We are not against this kind of mechanism," European Affairs Minister Maida Gorčević told reporters last week.
Zagreb has so far resisted international arbitration. Instead, it wants Podgorica to recognise the findings of the Badinter Commission, established by the European Community in 1991 to provide legal opinions on the dissolution of Yugoslavia.
The commission established the principle that the boundaries between the former Yugoslav republics should become international borders upon independence. Croatia is now demanding that Montenegro formally recognise the existing land border.
On land, Prevlaka is little more than a virtually uninhabited strip of rock. But its strategic location makes it crucial to determining the maritime boundary between the two countries, with implications for navigation, access to the Bay of Kotor and potentially valuable offshore oil and gas reserves.
Since 2002, the two countries have coexisted peacefully under a temporary arrangement, with Croatia controlling the peninsula and Montenegro most of the surrounding waters.
Zagreb is now pressing Podgorica to reach an agreement by December, just as Montenegro is trying to conclude its EU accession negotiations before the end of the year.
Croatia leveraging its membership
Montenegro still has eight of its 33 negotiating chapters left to provisionally close. At an intergovernmental conference on Thursday, Podgorica had hoped to close at least four, but managed only two because of Croatian opposition.
Time is running out for the Western Balkan country to complete negotiations by the end of the year. That would probably require another intergovernmental conference before the end of November, followed by a final meeting in December.
Montenegro is the frontrunner to join the bloc and hopes to become its 28th member by 2028. But the bilateral negotiations are deeply unequal, with Zagreb effectively holding the keys to Podgorica's European future.
"If Montenegrin citizens feel pressured to make territorial concessions, it is the whole EU integration process that would be damaged in terms of public perception. The risk is that Montenegro enters the EU with a growing anti-European sentiment," the second diplomat said.
Germany has also urged Croatia, through the so-called Berlin Process, not to allow bilateral disputes to derail Montenegro's accession, particularly as the EU seeks to use enlargement to strengthen its influence in its immediate neighbourhood.
But the border dispute has become politically sensitive in Zagreb, where the government is eager to demonstrate that it is defending Croatian interests amid reports that it is considering calling early parliamentary elections in 2027.
"Before Montenegro concludes its EU accession negotiations, we want to reach an agreement on the land border. It is crucial that we establish whether the current Montenegrin government understands and recognises this fundamental principle, which is key to the post-1991 settlement," Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković told MPs earlier this month.
Croatia itself has an unresolved border dispute with Slovenia, which did not prevent it from becoming the EU's most recent member in 2013. Zagreb subsequently rejected an international arbitration ruling on the dispute in 2017.
The European Commission has said Montenegro has met the targets to provisionally close all 33 negotiating chapters, and it is now up to all 27 member states to unanimously green light their closure.
As so often in EU enlargement, political considerations have overtaken technical progress.

noticias.titulo: South Korea and China agree wider trade deal covering entertainment
noticias.resumen: South Korean entertainment companies have faced barriers in China since a dispute over a US missile defence system in 2016. New trade commitments could improve access, but content checks on films remain and a return of K-pop concerts is not guaranteed.
noticias.texto:
South Korean entertainment companies have faced barriers in China since a dispute over a US missile defence system in 2016. New trade commitments could improve access, but content checks on films remain and a return of K-pop concerts is not guaranteed.
South Korea and China have largely completed talks to expand their free trade agreement, with new commitments covering entertainment, tourism, and financial services.
The announcement came last week during talks between South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.
Technical details, translations, and legal reviews still need to be completed before the expanded agreement can be formally signed, China's commerce ministry said.
China has agreed to treat film and video game businesses from South Korea the same as companies from other countries. It has also promised not to discriminate against Korean films and online games when reviewing them for approval, said the trade ministry in Seoul.
The agreement would expand joint production arrangements beyond films to include television dramas, animation, entertainment programmes, and documentaries. Productions officially recognised under these deals would qualify as Chinese content and so would not count towards quotas on foreign productions.
Films would still have to pass China's content review process before being released in cinemas, a South Korean official told The Korea Herald.
K-pop concerts remain uncertain
South Korean entertainment has faced restrictions in China since Seoul's decision to deploy a US missile defence system in 2016. Beijing has never formally acknowledged the restrictions, which have affected films, television programmes, and live performances.
A senior South Korean presidential official said the agreement did not require either country to approve concerts, but had opened more channels for discussion with Beijing, The Korea Herald reported.
Industry representatives remained cautious about whether the commitments would lead to practical changes.
"We will have to see whether practical measures that affect the content industry follow," an official at a South Korean drama production company told Yonhap News Agency.
Wider access for tourism and other businesses
South Korean tour operators established in 23 designated areas of China, including Beijing and Shanghai, would be allowed to arrange overseas trips for Chinese citizens and foreigners living there.
Retailers would also be able to operate chains of 30 stores or more without forming joint ventures with Chinese companies and financial services firms would automatically benefit from any further access China grants to businesses from other countries through future trade deals.
In return, South Korea has agreed to expand access for Chinese companies in legal, retail, and audiovisual services. Both countries have also agreed not to require technology transfers as a condition of investment.
China's commerce ministry described the agreement as a joint effort to oppose protectionism and support international trade.
The original free trade agreement took effect in December 2015. Negotiations on expanding services and investment provisions began in March 2018 and continued over 17 formal rounds, gaining momentum after meetings between Lee and Xi.

noticias.titulo: Japan launches Asian oil task force amid Gulf supply disruptions
noticias.resumen: Disruptions to oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran war have pushed Asian countries to look at larger emergency reserves, shared storage, and closer cooperation with fuel suppliers as shortages squeeze their economies.
noticias.texto:
Disruptions to oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran war have pushed Asian countries to look at larger emergency reserves, shared storage, and closer cooperation with fuel suppliers as shortages squeeze their economies.
Japan has launched a regional task force to help Asian countries build up emergency oil reserves and plan joint responses to shortages, as the Iran war interrupts supplies from the Gulf.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi announced the initiative on Tuesday at the Asia Zero Emission Community leaders' meeting in Manila, held alongside the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit. A joint statement by Japan and the International Energy Agency (IEA) confirmed that the task force had been established.
Tokyo also proposed using unused oil storage tanks, including those at closed refineries, to hold reserves for other Asian countries. This would create shared oil storage across the region.
Around a quarter of the world's seaborne oil trade passed through the Strait of Hormuz in 2025, with about 80% of those shipments heading to Asia, according to the IEA.
The task force will work with the IEA and the Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia to assess oil reserves and explore how countries could coordinate their response to shortages.
Japan and the IEA also outlined plans for an oil security centre in Tokyo, supported by the agency's teams in Paris and Singapore. It would help countries develop storage systems, share information on oil markets, and prepare for emergencies.
"We would like to position this as an Asian version of the IEA," Takaichi said.
The energy body coordinates emergency oil releases among its members. Oil-importing countries such as Japan must hold stocks equivalent to at least 90 days of net oil imports.
Countries in the IEAagreed on 11 March to make 400 million barrels from their emergency reserves available to the market in response to the Iran war, the largest coordinated release in the agency's history.
Plans for shared oil storage
Singapore, Indonesia, and Malaysia have expressed support for the storage proposal, Cristina Roque, the trade secretary from the Philippines, said on Monday.
The United Arab Emirates has also shown interest in storing oil in countries with available facilities, she added.
However, arrangements allowing countries to draw on one another's reserves have yet to be agreed.
Japan and the Philippines also signed a three-year agreement on Monday to help Manila develop its own emergency oil reserves, which covers cooperation on storage facilities, financing and rules for managing and releasing supplies.
Takaichi also outlined a separate proposal for closer cooperation between Middle Eastern oil producers and Asian consumers. Japan wants to help connect the two regions and strengthen their energy supplies, its foreign ministry said.

noticias.titulo: Hungary's PM to visit Transcarpathia, pledges support to Ukrainian people and local Hungarians
noticias.resumen: Ties soured sharply under Hungary's previous PM Viktor Orbán, whose government repeatedly clashed with Kyiv over Ukraine and blocked its progress towards EU membership.
noticias.texto:
Ties soured sharply under Hungary's previous PM Viktor Orbán, whose government repeatedly clashed with Kyiv over Ukraine and blocked its progress towards EU membership.
Hungary's Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Monday that he planned to visit the southwestern Ukrainian region of Transcarpathia and pledged his support for Ukrainians there under attack from Russia and ethnic Hungarians living in the border region.
"The vast majority of Hungarians, including ourselves, stand by our Hungarian compatriots in Transcarpathia, and we also stand by the Ukrainian people who have been attacked, even if someone in Moscow takes a dim view of this," Magyar said in parliament.
He said the government in Budapest is also raising the issue of Hungarian schools, the use of the Hungarian language and Hungarian education, and is calling Ukraine to account over the fulfilment of the commitments made to the Hungarian community.
Magyar said that no elected Hungarian prime minister had visited Transcarpathia and the Hungarians living there since 2015.
"This will change shortly...I will return to Transcarpathia as an elected Hungarian prime minister and personally take the message of support from the mother country to our Hungarian brothers and sisters" he said.
Last month, Hungary and Ukraine came close to ending a long-running dispute over the rights of ethnic Hungarians in Ukraine, potentially clearing a major obstacle in relations between Budapest and Kyiv.
Ties soured sharply under Hungary's previous PM Viktor Orbán, whose government repeatedly clashed with Kyiv over Ukraine and blocked its progress towards EU membership.
But Magyar has sought to repair relations since taking office in May, but the rights of ethnic Hungarians in Ukraine's Transcarpathia region remain a source of tension.
In June, the two countries agreed an 11-point plan to strengthen minority rights. Hungary responded by allowing two negotiating clusters to open in Ukraine's EU accession talks.
But Budapest has blocked further progress, insisting that Ukraine's parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, first pass the legislation required under the deal. The laws are due to be adopted by the end of the year.
Deal could ease tensions
The breakthrough follows another flare-up between the two governments earlier in October.
Magyar and Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha clashed over Volodymyr Zelenskyy's C8 regional development initiative, with Sybiha accusing the Hungarian leader of following in Orbán's footsteps after Magyar said Hungary had been included against its will.
A bill covering language and cultural rights is due to go before the Rada later in October. Kyiv has not officially commented on the latest developments.
Ukrainian outlet LIGA.net reported that experts from both countries held intensive talks this week and agreed which parts of the 11-point plan Kyiv can deliver.
Dániel Hegedűs, deputy director of the Institut für Europäische Politik, told Euronews that the move could help reverse recent negative trends in bilateral relations, but that the legislation could still run into obstacles in the Rada.
"Given the absence of stable majorities in the Verkhovna Rada, passing the legislation in October is an ambitious goal and a real test of whether the Ukrainian administration can regain political control over issues of strategic importance to the country's EU integration," Hegedűs said.

noticias.titulo: CrowdStrike buys Zscaler in €40 billion cybersecurity deal
noticias.resumen: The merging of the two companies is one of the biggest cybersecurity deals in history.
noticias.texto:
The merging of the two companies is one of the biggest cybersecurity deals in history.
US cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike bought rival Zscaler for $43.9 billion (€40.4 billion) on Monday in the largest cybersecurity deal of all time, bringing together cloud cybersecurity services to offer customers a single service provider.
The companies share a long history of working together as they both operate in the cloud cybersecurity sector, with CrowdStrike offering device protection and Zscaler securing network traffic and application access from cyber threats and attacks.
The merger comes at a time when cyber incidents and threats to infrastructure have become commonplace in recent months.
Since September, Europe has been hit with cyberattacks on supermarket fridges, crypto wallet firm Binance has been hit by North Korean hackers, a Google Cloud outage has knocked out financial services companies including Revolut, and Microsoft's servers have gone down, taking Outlook, Teams and other platforms with them, to name but a few.
CrowdStrike itself was at the centre of a cybersecurity issue in 2024, when a software defect crashed approximately 8.5 million Microsoft Windows devices worldwide. As a result, flights were grounded, hospitals closed, and banks and other services were disrupted globally.
On top of this, AI has uncovered new cybersecurity vulnerabilities in software and programming languages underpinning the internet, including PHP and Java.
It was Zscaler's speciality in AI systems, including its Zero Trust Exchange system, which secures enterprise AI usage, protects sensitive data in AI workflows and governs AI applications and agents in real time, that was a key factor behind CrowdStrike's decision to buy the company.
"The network used to connect people to places. Now it connects agents to data. With Zscaler, we're building cybersecurity's operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely," said George Kurtz, CEO and founder of CrowdStrike.
In a press release published on Monday, the companies cited several reasons for the deal, including the potential to combine device and network data security, unlock cross-selling opportunities across customer bases, expand markets and ecosystems and, most importantly, offer customers a common, single solution.
"We see a path to become the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen," added Kurtz.
The companies expect the deal to expand their total addressable market by more than $185 billion (€168.7 billion), bringing CrowdStrike's platform to roughly 8,000 Zscaler customers and raking in an estimated $10 billion (€9.1 billion) more in combined annual recurring revenue.
Under the deal, CrowdStrike will buy Zscaler in an all-stock transaction, based on the company's share price on Friday 20 November 2026.
CrowdStrike expects to complete the transaction in 2028, subject to approval by Zscaler shareholders, with Zscaler CEO Jay Chaudhry remaining in charge of the business and joining CrowdStrike's board.

noticias.titulo: EU opens antitrust probe into Coca-Cola's European distributor
noticias.resumen: Discounts that depended on drinks staying inside national borders, and a refusal to sign supermarket deals covering more than one country, are among the practices under scrutiny.
noticias.texto:
Discounts that depended on drinks staying inside national borders, and a refusal to sign supermarket deals covering more than one country, are among the practices under scrutiny.
The European Commission on Monday opened a formal antitrust investigation into Coca-Cola Europacific Partners (CCEP), the largest supplier of fizzy drinks in eight EU countries. It suspects the company abused its dominant position to stop retailers buying across borders.
"People across Europe enjoy soft drinks every day. But they should not have to pay more simply because they live in one EU country rather than another," said Teresa Ribera, the Commission's executive vice-president for clean, just and competitive transition, who oversees competition policy.
"We are investigating whether Coca-Cola has been putting barriers between national markets, making it harder for retailers to buy products across borders and secure better deals," she said.
CCEP is headquartered in the UK and is one of the two largest European bottlers of Coca-Cola brands. It sells those drinks, along with other brands, in Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden.
The Commission is concerned that CCEP may have abused its dominant position in the wholesale supply of carbonated soft drinks and sports drinks to supermarkets and other retailers. Restaurants, hotels and cafés are not part of the case.
The investigation will look at whether CCEP:
- made wholesale price cuts conditional on drinks not being exported to other EU countries
- sold different packaging volumes in different countries to restrict cross-border trade
- gave retailers incentives to limit imports of fizzy drinks into Spain
- refused to let retailers negotiate deals covering several countries at once, insisting instead on separate national negotiations
"This could undermine the Single Market, limit competition and ultimately mean higher prices and less choice for consumers," Ribera said.
If proven, the practices could breach Article 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU, which bans companies from abusing a dominant position. Here the alleged abuse is dividing the Single Market along national borders.
The investigation comes three days after an EU-UK summit in Brussels, Belgium, where UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham sought to show he is delivering the closer post-Brexit ties promised by his predecessor, Keir Starmer.
The case follows unannounced inspections at CCEP's premises in several EU countries in March 2025. The Commission said it would treat the investigation as a priority. It added that opening a probe does not prejudge the outcome, and that there is no legal deadline for completing it.
Because the Commission has opened proceedings, national competition authorities can no longer apply EU competition rules to the same practices.
CCEP said it would continue to "engage fully" with the Commission's inquiries. It said it took competition law very seriously and was "firmly committed to complying with all applicable laws and regulations".

noticias.titulo: Mercedes, BMW hit by 24-hour strikes as German pay dispute widens
noticias.resumen: IG Metall, Germany’s largest trade union, called on more than 23,000 workers at 19 northern sites to join a 24-hour strike. The walkouts hit Mercedes-Benz, BMW, and Siemens Gamesa, with Meyer Werft workers also called out.
noticias.texto:
IG Metall, Germany’s largest trade union, called on more than 23,000 workers at 19 northern sites to join a 24-hour strike. The walkouts hit Mercedes-Benz, BMW, and Siemens Gamesa, with Meyer Werft workers also called out.
Workers in Germany’s metal and electrical industries walked out this week after three rounds of pay talks ended without a deal. IG Metall called on more than 23,000 workers at 19 sites in northern Germany to take part in a 24-hour strike.
Further walkouts are expected in Berlin and the union's central district, which covers Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saarland, and Thuringia.
The latest "warning strikes" follow nationwide walkouts on Friday that drew 151,000 workers, according to IG Metall. Audi’s main plant in Ingolstadt and three BMW plants in Bavaria were among the sites hit.
Three rounds of negotiations for around 130,000 employees in northern Germany have so far been unsuccessful.
IG Metall is seeking a 5% pay rise over one year for 3.7 million workers, including those in the automotive sector. Employers have offered a one-off payment in July 2027 worth 1% of gross annual pay, and a 1.3% pay rise from July 2028. The union said the offer would leave workers worse off after inflation.
Strikes began at several factories on Sunday evening as night shifts started, including at Mercedes-Benz plants in Bremen and Hamburg.
Tagesschau, the news service of German public broadcaster ARD, reported that production lines at Mercedes-Benz’s Hamburg plant have been idle since 10pm on Sunday.
"So far, the plant is completely sealed off and no one has been allowed in to work," an IG Metall representative told the news service on Monday morning. "Only plant security is present, and otherwise nothing is happening here."
Mercedes-Benz confirmed to Euronews that its plants were affected and said they were adjusting operations. The carmaker did not specify which plants were affected or give details about the impact on production.
Mercedes-Benz said employers' associations were negotiating with IG Metall and that it fully supported a statement by Südwestmetall. The employers' association called the 24-hour strikes an "unnecessary escalation" and urged the union to resume talks.
Wind turbine maker Siemens Gamesa in Cuxhaven is also impacted.
The union also called on workers at the Meyer Werft shipyard in Papenburg to walk out on Monday, NDR reported.
Volkswagen, which owns Audi, is seeking a two-year pay freeze and more flexible working hours in separate talks with IG Metall covering about 120,000 employees, according to Reuters.
BMW previously sought to cut nearly 8,000 jobs through voluntary severance, according to Münchner Merkur.
Mercedes-Benz is seeking €800 million in annual savings in Germany, Handelsblatt reported. Longer working hours without extra pay and cuts to benefits were among the options under discussion, German public broadcaster SWR reported. Mercedes-Benz has also said it would suspend investment in Germany.
Euronews contacted BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Volkswagen for comment.

noticias.titulo: Exclusive: China-backed hackers suspected behind ongoing EU Commission cyberattack
noticias.resumen: The European Commission suspects a China-backed hacking group is behind a cyberattack that has hit its systems for a month and is still ongoing. The first confirmed leak of personal data involves EU Academy users.
noticias.texto:
The European Commission suspects a China-backed hacking group is behind a cyberattack that has hit its systems for a month and is still ongoing. The first confirmed leak of personal data involves EU Academy users.
The European Commission suspects that a large-scale cyberattack, still spreading through its IT systems, is the work of a China-backed network of threat actors, according to two sources with knowledge of the matter.
"Panda" is the codename circulating inside the Commission for the suspected perpetrators. In the cybersecurity community, the animal name is used to loosely tie threat actors to their state sponsors, in this case China.
Publicly, the Commission has so far declined to formally attribute responsibility for the attack as the internal investigation is still ongoing.
"When it comes to the attribution, we would need the investigation to be concluded to be able to find out who is behind this. So, for now, no attribution from our side," Commission spokesperson for technology Thomas Regnier told reporters on Monday.
On 22 October, the Commission's IT department detected a malicious actor in its internal networks. A month after the attack began, the EU executive has yet to fully contain the breach and was forced to take the EU Academy website offline on Saturday.
The EU Academy is an online platform offering professional development and specialised learning to young people.
"The incident is still under investigation. Public access to the platform has been disabled and measures to contain, mitigate and limit the impact of the incident have been taken, including the implementation of preventive, detective and corrective controls," reads the EU Academy's website.
The Commission has confirmed a leak of names and email addresses and is warning users of possible follow-ups from the attacker, such as phishing campaigns based on their personal data.
That is the first major consequence of the incident. For other IT systems, EU cyber experts have not confirmed data theft affecting Commission staff, though several internal apps were taken offline as a precaution and some remain unavailable.
According to the current threat assessment, the China-linked actor was not targeting specific systems or individuals, which would have called for a less visible attack. Instead, it wanted to test more broadly how far it could compromise the Commission's IT networks.
Suspicion of a link to Chinese security services rests on the sophistication of the attack and on the use of ARTEX, a Chinese-developed cybersecurity tool that uses AI to detect vulnerabilities that hackers can then exploit.
Leading cybersecurity firms like Microsoft and CrowdStrike have attributed to the China-linked groups Storm-0940 and Panda Vapor attacks using ARTEX for AI-driven global espionage campaigns targeting hundreds of organisations globally.
The Commission has been hit by two other cyberattacks this year: one on the cloud infrastructure hosting its Europa.eu website and one on its mobile infrastructure in January.
Both are also deemed to stem from China's cyber threat landscape, but from different groups, and neither was ever formally attributed.
The Chinese government has consistently denied sponsoring, directing or supporting hacking groups accused of conducting cyberattacks on foreign governments and institutions.
Since the hack became public last week, the main trade union of Commission staff has vehemently criticised management of the incident, notably for leaving civil servants to learn about it from the press.
A Commission official rejected that criticism, stressing that public communication is not foreseen in such cases because it would tip off the malicious actor that mitigation measures are under way.
Secrecy also prevents the spread of panic, which makes life harder for the security experts trying to contain the incident, Euronews understands.
This article was updated with a statement from Thomas Regnier.

noticias.titulo: EU military chief warns of escalating hybrid threats as Europe races to strengthen defences
noticias.resumen: General Seán Clancy says Europe is better prepared to defend itself but must speed up efforts to close critical military gaps, amid growing threats from Russia and uncertainty over US military commitments.
noticias.texto:
General Seán Clancy says Europe is better prepared to defend itself but must speed up efforts to close critical military gaps, amid growing threats from Russia and uncertainty over US military commitments.
Europe faces an escalating wave of hybrid threats, stretching from the Baltic to the Black Sea, and must urgently accelerate its military preparedness to confront them, the EU's most senior military official has warned.
General Seán Clancy, chairman of the EU Military Committee, told Euronews on Monday that the proliferation of asymmetric attacks was his greatest security concern, pointing to incidents in Poland, Denmark and Germany.
"The main concern is the spread and escalation of hybrid threats," he said in an interview with Europe Today. "We've seen this particularly over the past six to twelve months, from the Baltics to the Black Sea."
His warning follows another weekend of Russian attacks on Ukraine and comes as European governments grapple with growing concerns about sabotage, drone incursions and other forms of hybrid warfare.
Clancy said the threats were designed to destabilise not just Ukraine but European democracies more broadly.
"That's why readiness and preparedness are at the centre of the EU's strategy," he said. "The sooner member states can act collectively in a crisis, the better our chances of containing it."
Military chiefs meet
Europe's military chiefs will meet in Brussels on Wednesday to assess the continent's defence readiness, with Ukraine and the Coalition of the Willing high on the agenda.
Clancy acknowledged that enormous challenges remained, particularly in building up weapons stockpiles, industrial production capacity and the ability to sustain military operations over time.
"We're in a better position than we were. But we need to move faster and accelerate our preparedness," he said.
"Europe is stepping up. It's leaning in. We're closing the gaps."
However, Europe remains heavily dependent on the United States for critical military capabilities, including air defence, air-to-air refuelling and other strategic support.
Clancy dismissed fears that Washington's ongoing review of its military presence in Europe would undermine the continent's security, insisting that any transition would be managed jointly.
The transatlantic partnership, he said, was "without equivocation, our most important relationship, and it will remain so, now and into the future."
Asked whether Europe could defend itself against Russia without American support, Clancy expressed confidence in its armed forces.
"We are ready to defend and secure Europe," he said, while stressing that NATO remained ultimately responsible for the continent's collective defence.

noticias.titulo: Donald Trump urges Nvidia to rehire former CEO Jensen Huang
noticias.resumen: US President Donald Trump has urged Nvidia's board to rehire Jensen Huang, joining calls for his return that include a petition with more than 200,000 signatures. The former CEO is due to face questions in Congress on 1 December.
noticias.texto:
US President Donald Trump has urged Nvidia's board to rehire Jensen Huang, joining calls for his return that include a petition with more than 200,000 signatures. The former CEO is due to face questions in Congress on 1 December.
US President Donald Trump has called on Nvidia's board to reinstate Jensen Huang as its CEO.
Trump's appeal adds to growing calls for Huang's return, including a petition with more than 200,000 signatures that Elon Musk has signed.
Huang, who co-founded the AI chip giant in 1993, is due to answer lawmakers' questions in Congress on 1 December.
"I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the company, and also, for the U.S.A.," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Sunday.
Trump has stepped up his support over the past week for Huang's return.
Last Monday, he said he "would not mind" seeing Huang reinstated. On Friday, he told reporters at the White House that he "would love to see Jensen be given a second chance".
Huang resigned on 12 November after it emerged that he had two extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.
Beijing has rejected the espionage allegations and US authorities said they have not reached a conclusion.
Musk and other tech leaders back a return
The "Stand with Jensen" petition, an open letter to Nvidia's board, had more than 206,000 signatures as of Monday morning, according to its website. More than 10,000 signatories claim to be current Nvidia employees.
The letter asked the board to "bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts". It also highlighted that Nvidia and Huang have not endorsed it.
"A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I'm signing it too," Musk wrote on X on 13 November.
Tobi Lütke, CEO of e-commerce platform Shopify, and Tim Sweeney, CEO of Fortnite developer Epic Games, have also signed it.
Huang said on 17 November that he would be "honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO" if the board judged that best for the company, its staff, its shareholders, and America.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on 15 November that Nvidia needed "a dramatic shake-up" and a CEO from outside the company.
However, in an interview with CBS on Sunday, he stated: "I said they should go to the outside, but he's on the outside now".
Thus far, Nvidia's board does not plan to bring him back. Chair Harvey Jones told analysts during the company's earnings call last Tuesday that the board had "unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO".
Colette Kress, Nvidia's finance chief, has taken over as interim CEO during the search for a permanent replacement. An outside law firm is currently undertaking an investigation.
Nvidia's shares closed around $125.5 on Friday, representing a 48% collapse since their intraday all-time high price of roughly $243.3 on 6 October.
They lost over 20% just last week, their seventh weekly decline in a row and the longest losing streak since 2008.
The slide continued despite Nvidia beating earnings forecasts last Tuesday.
Friday's 14% drop followed a Reuters report, citing two people briefed on the matter, that the Securities and Exchange Commission, the US markets regulator, was examining possible accounting issues at Nvidia.
Questions in Congress
Huang will answer questions from three House committees behind closed doors on 1 December: Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.
The committees are looking into the possible diversion of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese businesses.
The session will be a transcribed interview and will not be open to the public.
Huang's public testimony will come before the Senate Banking Committee, according to the office of its chair, Republican Senator Tim Scott. No date has been set, though Scott had originally asked for 3 December.
Two Nvidia shareholders, the investment firms Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management, have asked the board to keep Huang's return open and to hold off on a permanent CEO until all the facts are known.

noticias.titulo: Iran vows 'every means' to counter US blockade of Hormuz after Trump threat
noticias.resumen: Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei called the blockade an "act of crime" a day after Trump said Iranian ships trying to break it would go "to the bottom of the sea".
noticias.texto:
Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei called the blockade an "act of crime" a day after Trump said Iranian ships trying to break it would go "to the bottom of the sea".
Iran's foreign ministry condemned the US naval blockade as "military aggression" on Monday and said Tehran would use "every means" to counter it, a day after US President Donald Trump threatened to sink Iranian tankers attempting to breach it.
Spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei, speaking at his weekly press briefing, described the blockade as a violation of the UN Charter and an "act of crime," adding that Tehran considered itself entitled to use any means to defend itself.
"We will certainly not tolerate this situation and will use every means to counter US aggression," Baghaei said.
On Sunday, Trump warned that Iranian ships attempting to break the blockade would be sent to the "bottom of the sea."
Asked about the possibility by a Fox News reporter, he said: "I hope they do it; they'll all go down to the bottom of the sea, just like the rest of their navy."
Convoy uncertainty
Media outlets and figures close to the IRGC have called in recent days for a convoy of Iranian oil tankers to be dispatched to break the blockade, with some threatening that Gulf oil facilities would be targeted if the vessels came under attack. Iranian officials have said they have no concrete plan to do so.
IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency published an article on Sunday acknowledging the wave of reports, and said no competent or official authority in the armed forces, the Supreme National Security Council or the government had announced such a plan.
Tasnim said the reports stemmed entirely from proposals put forward by individuals in the media and on social media.
The news agency added that "Iran's plans to break the blockade are certainly being drawn up," but that no one outside the circle of security and military decision-makers had knowledge of them.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) confirmed on Sunday at least one incident involving an oil tanker in the Gulf of Oman, saying military forces had been involved in the encounter.
No further details were released about the identity of the forces involved or whether the tanker had been attempting to circumvent the blockade. The US Central Command (CENTCOM) had not commented on the incident as of Monday.
Also at Monday's briefing, Baghaei was asked how Tehran might respond to reported US planning for a possible attack on Iran.
"The best scenario is for them to get the hell out of the region," he said, adding that IRGC Air Force commander Majid Mousavi would deliver Iran's response to any potential attack "in a neat and elegant package."
Mousavi said on Sunday that IRGC aerospace capabilities had grown since the previous round of conflict and that "the field is ours and we determine the battlefield."
IRGC deputy commander-in-chief Major General Mostafa Izadi said Iran's missile range had been significantly upgraded and that any threat would draw an immediate response "without geographical limitations."
Azizi, chairman of parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, reiterated the same position, saying Iran had determined it would face no geographical limitations in any future confrontation.
Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf cited remarks by Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei about the need to end the current situation, saying "sustainable deterrence" was the way out of the crisis.
"We must remove the shadow of war from ourselves," Ghalibaf said. Iran needed to fulfil "the directive of the Supreme Leader" Khamenei, he added.
What will it take to reopen Hormuz?
Baghaei elaborated on remarks by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who said the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened within two hours of the other side fulfilling its commitments.
Baghaei said the comment was meant to signal Iran's readiness to act quickly, not to minimise the complexity of a potential agreement.
Tehran's conditions, he said, include lifting US sanctions, ending the naval blockade and implementing commitments Washington accepted under the Islamabad memorandum of understanding.
Trump has described the Islamabad memorandum as a waste of time and declared it null and void, and has characterised ongoing negotiations with Iran as "a load of nonsense".
Diplomatic efforts are continuing despite the standoff. Qatar's prime minister is expected to meet US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Monday, with Doha serving as a key mediator between Tehran and Washington.

noticias.titulo: Bomb threats emailed to German schools present no 'concrete danger,' police say
noticias.resumen: It comes after more than 300 schools across Italy were evacuated earlier this month after receiving emailed bomb threats, which also claimed that an explosive device had been planted in Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s car.
noticias.texto:
It comes after more than 300 schools across Italy were evacuated earlier this month after receiving emailed bomb threats, which also claimed that an explosive device had been planted in Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s car.
Bomb threats were emailed to schools in Germany but there appeared to be no "concrete danger" at present, police said on Monday, after a wave of hoax bomb warnings at schools across Europe in recent weeks.
More than 450 schools in the southwestern state of Baden-Wuerttemberg were sent the threats, police said.
Police in the eastern state of Thuringia also said "numerous" schools there received bomb threats, which were not considered to be genuine.
Meanwhile, police in Denmark also said they were investigating bomb threats that had been sent to several schools across the country but maintained there was no cause for concern.
It comes after more than 300 schools across Italy were evacuated earlier this month after receiving emailed bomb threats, which also claimed that an explosive device had been planted in Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s car.
"At present, based on the checks carried out, no element has emerged that would suggest there is a concrete danger," Meloni wrote in a Facebook post.
Italian media reported that 312 schools had received threats.
Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said around 300 alerts had been recorded across the country, adding that "it is clear that there is a strategy".
The emails began: "We have come to annihilate you. We will carry out genocide against the Italians." They claimed a "powerful explosive device" with a "remote trigger" had been placed in each building.
"We have placed a bomb in the engine of your prime minister’s car," the emails continued. They were signed "Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan".
Bomb threats sent to media outlets in Ireland and Bulgaria in the past week were signed with the same name.
Similar hoax threats were also reported at schools in the UK and Ireland on 11 November, prompting some evacuations.
Almost a week after that scare, at least 100 other schools in Italy received email and poison threats, triggering a new security protocol introduced by the government.
Speaking in Brussels, Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said there was a "shared vision and desire to be increasingly united in responding to attacks and preventing different types of threats by email, cyber or hacking."

noticias.titulo: Can AI help detect breast cancer faster? Major new trial will find out
noticias.resumen: Researchers will test whether an AI tool helps radiologists detect breast cancer.
noticias.texto:
Researchers will test whether an AI tool helps radiologists detect breast cancer.
Researchers in the United Kingdom will test whether artificial intelligence tools can help improve breast cancer detection, in the world’s largest study of its kind.
Early breast cancer detection can save lives, but diagnosis can be a time-consuming process. Currently in the UK, at least two radiologists review every mammogram, or breast x-ray, but very few — less than 1% — of these scans actually show signs of cancer.
In the trial, known as EDITH, radiologists will use an AI-assisted tool to help detect cancers that are too small to see or feel. The goal is to give specialists more time to diagnose and care for women with cancer, while reducing the time they spend reviewing mammograms with no signs of disease.
“If successful, this technology could help women get a breast cancer diagnosis and start treatment much more quickly, giving them the best possible chance of recovery,” said Yvette Cooper, the UK’s health and social care secretary. The UK government is backing the trial with £10 million (about €12 million).
The study will enroll about 660,000 women aged 50 to 71 who are due for a routine breast cancer screening, which is offered every three years in the UK. Women can opt out if they do not want to take part in the trial.
Women will be split into three groups: the first group will undergo a standard breast cancer screening, with two radiologists reviewing the x-rays. In the second group, a radiologist and the AI tool will both review the mammograms to see if the AI tool catches any signs of cancer the radiologist may have missed.
In the third group, the AI tool will take the first look at an x-ray and determine whether the likelihood of cancer is high or low. If it is low, one radiologist will review the images, but if it is high, two radiologists will check the images and decide whether to refer the patient for additional testing.
The AI tool could “help experts review images more efficiently,” said Fiona Gilbert, a radiology professor at the University of Cambridge and one of the study’s lead researchers. She is also studying whether AI can help identify women at higher risk of developing breast cancer.
Every mammogram will still be reviewed by at least one radiologist, according to the trial announcement, and the AI-assisted tool will only be integrated into routine breast cancer screening if the study shows it is as safe and effective as the existing screening programme.
Currently, around 2.1 million women in the UK undergo breast screening each year, preventing around 1,300 deaths.
Breast cancer is the most common form of cancer in the European Union, with an estimated 360,000 women diagnosed in 2024, EU data shows. That accounts for 29% of all cancer diagnoses in women.

noticias.titulo: 'We should not be okay with a handover of society to AI', warns Meta's AI boss
noticias.resumen: Alexandr Wang has raised concerns over the latest achievements of AI and the risk posed by super intelligent AI models to humanity.
noticias.texto:
Alexandr Wang has raised concerns over the latest achievements of AI and the risk posed by super intelligent AI models to humanity.
The world is entering the era of superintelligence, and the AI industry must prioritise safety and human control rather than allowing an unconstrained handover to machines, Meta’s AI chief has warned.
Alexandr Wang, Meta’s Chief AI Officer, made the warning in a post on social media platform X on Sunday in light of rival Anthropic’s announcement on Friday that one of their mathematicians had used their Claude AI model to solve the famous Riemann Hypothesis mathematical problem.
The hypothesis suggests that the seemingly random appearance of prime numbers actually follows a hidden, strict pattern. Solving the problem could eventually have enormous real-world consequences, by giving certainty to the way prime numbers are distributed, computer systems, for example, can run more quickly and leaner.
It comes at a time when global debate over AI has reached fever pitch, with concerns among the public over the risks AI poses not only to jobs and the economy but also to security and human rights.
Young people in 20 countries took to the streets on Friday to protest the cost of living, with the lack of AI regulation and fears over autonomous weapons following talks over killer robots also among concerns.
The AI chief said he sees the discovery as “marking the beginning of a significant change” and argued that “nothing humanity has ever accomplished compares to proving the Riemann Hypothesis in terms of sheer intellectual might and strength”.
It’s for this reason Meta’s AI chief is concerned that the intelligence of AI models may outpace humans, raising questions of what the future holds.
“It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” said Wang.
“It is equally hard to imagine a world where humanity maintains control with superintelligence that is 1,000-times smarter and more capable than humans in every field.”
Wang criticised the “lazy thinking within the AI industry” that advanced AI capable of surpassing human intelligence across all domains is “inevitable” and cannot be stopped.
“We should not be okay with a 'handover' of society to AI,” warned Wang.
“We should endeavour ourselves to build a technology which delivers a positive future for humanity, where all humans have greater agency and empowerment.”
Wang concluded saying while he believes it is possible, it means “the whole industry taking meaningfully different actions from the ‘default path’ in front of us”.
The latest in a series of warnings
His warning echoes similar statements made by other leading AI research labs.
On Friday, Google DeepMind researchers including Tim Genewein warned that artificial general superintelligence could soon be within reach, opening the door for recursive self-improving AI models.
On Sunday OpenAI publicly urged rival AI labs to agree on shared safety limits until better monitoring and control tools exist, amid Anthropic’s claim of solving the Riemann Hypothesis.
In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for “pacing the frontier”, to slow down the development of advanced AI models to give time for sufficient safety guardrails to be put in place.
His call was welcomed by some leaders such as European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen who reiterated his call to slow down development and establish global rules.
However, US President Donald Trump has taken a different approach. At the end of September, he convened a summit with America’s biggest AI firms and made an agreement that the companies can police themselves.
Last week in China, America’s approach to AI safety was at loggerheads with the Chinese premier Xi Jinping, who called for global action to keep “AI under human control”.
Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney also warned last week that global governance on AI is an “enormous risk”.

noticias.titulo: From COP31 Antalya to Copenhagen: UN climate summits where no agreement was reached
noticias.resumen: Since 1995, UN climate and environment summits have often seen deadlock, delays and frustration.
noticias.texto:
Since 1995, UN climate and environment summits have often seen deadlock, delays and frustration.
The COP31 climate negotiations in Antalya have ended without a final deal. The EU and other countries rejected a cover decision because it did not cover how to quite fossil fuels or fund climate action in developing countries.
As the COP process depends almost 200 countries reaching a consensus, it is far from easy, especially with geopolitical tensions as they are.
Since the first United Nations' Conference of the Parties (COP) in 1995, many summits have seen fierce arguments when countries failed to find common ground.
Here we take a look back at previous COP summits where tensions ran high.
2000: COP6, The Hague
At COP6 in 2000, held in The Hague, the negotiations were suspended. Talks resumed months later in Bonn, where the secretariat of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change is based.
The summit took place at a time when the United States was locked in an extremely tight presidential election. Negotiators did not know whether the next leader of the world's largest economy would be George W. Bush, who was sceptical of climate policies, or Al Gore, who would later share the Nobel Peace Prize for his climate advocacy.
Ironically, Bush's election victory, and his subsequent rejection of the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, encouraged other countries at the resumed Bonn talks to push ahead with plans to implement the protocol.
However, France's former chief negotiator Paul Watkinson criticised the summit, saying it ended in "chaos".
2009: COP15, Copenhagen
Expectations rose after the election of US President Barack Obama. But COP15 failed to deliver the binding global climate agreement many countries had hoped for.
Deep divisions between developed and developing countries, especially disputes between Washington and Beijing, blocked a deal on mandatory cuts in emissions.
In the end, the conference only agreed to "take note" of the non-binding Copenhagen Accord. The accord included a goal of keeping the rise in global temperatures below 2 degrees and a pledge by rich countries to provide 100 billion dollars a year in climate finance by 2020.
2012: COP18, Doha
Countries agreed a second commitment period under the Kyoto Protocol. But major emitters such as the United States, Russia and Canada did not take part.
Critics of the deal argued that the targets were not ambitious enough and that the arrangement covered an ever-shrinking share of global emissions.
2019: COP25, Madrid
Talks in Madrid overran their scheduled finish time by more than 40 hours, as they did this year at the summit in Antalya.
At COP25, countries failed to agree rules to govern international carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.
The summit's final text disappointed the countries most vulnerable to climate change and environmental groups, because it did not include a significant increase in emissions reduction pledges.
2022: COP27, Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt
Countries agreed to establish a historic "loss and damage" fund to support those most affected by climate change.
But negotiators were unable to strengthen commitments to phase down the use of fossil fuels. Many governments and climate activists criticised the outcome, arguing that there had been insufficient progress on cutting emissions.
2024: COP29, Baku, Azerbaijan
At COP29 rows over climate finance for developing countries pushed the negotiations beyond their planned end date.
Negotiators struggled to bridge differences over the scale of financial commitments between rich and poor nations.
The summit eventually produced an agreement, avoiding a complete breakdown. But many developing countries judged the outcome to be inadequate.

noticias.titulo: Eight EU countries join forces to defend carbon market against calls for delay
noticias.resumen: The eight countries warn that further delays to the EU's expanded carbon market would undermine energy security, prolong dependence on fossil fuel imports and jeopardise investment in clean technologies.
noticias.texto:
The eight countries warn that further delays to the EU's expanded carbon market would undermine energy security, prolong dependence on fossil fuel imports and jeopardise investment in clean technologies.
Eight European Union countries have joined forces to defend the bloc's expanded carbon market, warning against any further delays or changes to its implementation.
In a letter to Climate Action Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra, seen by Euronews, the climate ministers of Denmark, Finland, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden argue that the EU's dependence on imported fossil fuels is a major economic and security vulnerability.
They see the new Emissions Trading System (ETS2) as part of the solution, pushing governments and businesses to accelerate the shift to electrification.
"By providing a cost-effective means to accelerate the decarbonisation of the road transport and building sectors, ETS2 strengthens Europe’s energy security by reducing dependence on fossil fuel imports and promoting electrification," reads the letter dated 23 November.
The intervention comes amid mounting political pressure from the four-nation Visegrad Group, Italy and Greece to soften or delay the system following the 15-16 October EU summit in Brussels.
Resisting calls to scrap ETS2, EU leaders instead agreed to assess its impact ahead of its introduction in January 2028, after it was already delayed by a year.
ETS2 will put a carbon price on fuels used for road transport and heating, with energy suppliers expected to pass the additional costs on to consumers through higher bills.
The scheme has become increasingly politically sensitive as EU governments grapple with high energy costs and growing concerns about the impact of climate policies on households and businesses.
Energy security before climate goals
In their letter, the eight ministers invoke the disruption of energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz to argue that reducing fossil fuel consumption is no longer simply a climate objective, but a matter of strategic autonomy.
The EU imported €340 billion worth of fossil fuels in 2025, the ministers noted. Since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year, the additional cost of imports resulting from higher prices has reached €127 billion.
The ministers warn that Europe's continued dependence on imported oil and gas leaves its economies exposed to geopolitical tensions, volatile prices and political pressure from suppliers.
They argue that the ETS2 can help reduce that vulnerability by accelerating electrification in buildings and road transport, reducing fossil fuel imports and creating demand for clean technologies manufactured in the EU.
Danish Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa said ETS2 was essential to the EU's electrification ambitions.
“We need to accelerate the clean transition so the EU can reduce its dependence on expensive and unreliable fossil energy imports. That is crucial for lowering energy prices, strengthening our long-term competitiveness and stepping up our efforts to combat climate change," Nawa reacted.
A warning against reopening the ETS2
The eight governments also warn against allowing the Commission's review of ETS2 to become an opportunity to reopen the legislation and water down its provisions.
They argue that the system is part of a carefully balanced climate framework, combining emissions reductions with financial support for those most affected by the transition.
Central to that balance is the Social Climate Fund, designed to cushion vulnerable households and businesses against higher heating and transport costs.
Changing ETS2 in isolation, the ministers warn, risks undermining that broader agreement.
They also insist that sticking to the agreed timetable would provide businesses with the regulatory certainty needed to invest in cleaner technologies, while generating revenues for national governments.
"A strong implementation of ETS2 without further delays provides regulatory certainty and investment signals that are crucial to ensure the necessary investments towards decarbonisation and electrification," reads the letter.
Czech Deputy Prime Minister Karel Havlíček said the energy crisis, Russia's war in Ukraine and continued geopolitical tensions have let to "exceptionally high energy costs" for households and businesses across the EU.
"Implementing ETS2 under these circumstances, when the system was designed and agreed upon under completely different geopolitical and economic conditions, simply does not seem reasonable to us," Havlíček told Euronews.
"It will also be increasingly difficult to explain to our citizens across the EU why additional costs should be imposed at a time when many households are already struggling with high energy prices and the cost of living."
