noticias.texto:
Watch: Moment troops raid home and capture Mexican drug lord
Newly-released bodycam footage shows the moment troops entered a house and detained a Mexican drug lord who had managed to evade capture for years.
The video shows armed personnel entering via a garage and finding Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, also known as 'El Chapo Isidro', who was on the FBI's most wanted list.
Seven suspects were killed in last Friday's operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
The arrest of Meza Flores in the northern Sinaloa state sparked a wave of unrest, which led to eight alleged drug cartel members being detained for their involvement in the retaliatory violence.

noticias.titulo: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police
noticias.resumen: South African communities tell the BBC of measures they're taking to keep women safe after a wave of horrific killings.
noticias.texto:
Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police
- Published
Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.
It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.
Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured.
"When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle," says Tuku, 50.
After seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country.
But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn't until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle's body.
When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten.
"It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it."
Okuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student.
She is among 581 women who were killed in the country between July and September, according to the South African Police Service.
Overall, there were 5,590 murders - 204 fewer than in the same period last year.
It is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years as police had stopped releasing this breakdown until now.
There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer.
South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide - the intentional killing of a woman or girl - in the world.
Am I Next? Fear and Survival in South Africa
The BBC World Service visits communities struggling to confrontÂ widespreadÂ violence against women
In response to this summer's killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas.
But in places like Kokstad, as well as Kempton Park, in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands.
For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter's killing himself.
Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested.
"It was just silent after we buried Okuhle - there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate."
He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says.
The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received.
The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has said there needs to be "greater efforts" to prevent violence against women and children.
According to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing.
This year, Amnesty International said South Africa's police service was "under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence".
Tuku says he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads.
Despite Ramaphosa's promises, he has little faith anything will change.
"I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us."
Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa said the government would be allocating extra money in February's budget to deal with gender-based violence.
Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years "and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing".
Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad.
Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases.
In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children.
Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.
Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them.
The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, says Kamvalethu.
Most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He says the group will call police when they need back-up.
Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu says the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers.
"With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there's nothing we can do."
Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets.
Kgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempton Park.
She was in a taxi when the driver locked the doors and started driving in the wrong direction.
When Kgothatso told him he had missed the turn, she says he started punching and slapping her.
"Immediately, I just knew my life was in danger," says Kgothatso, who is now 35.
Kgothatso says she forced the passenger door open and threw herself out of the moving taxi, badly injuring her knee and causing nerve damage to her eyes. Two security guards, who were nearby, came to her aid.
She says her attacker was later jailed for a number of crimes, including what he did to her, but was released last year. Kgothatso says she now fears for her life.
Yet while Kgothatso was attacked by a stranger, according to the South African Medical Research Council, 60% of women murdered in the country between 2020-21 were killed by an intimate partner.
In the wake of her attack, Kgothatso has made changes to how she lives, including buying an imitation gun to scare off would-be attackers.
She has also stopped running alone, and insists on someone accompanying her if she goes to meet a client she hasn't met before at work.
Such precautions are all too familiar to many women in South Africa.
In September police urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone, "particularly in isolated areas" - after the killing of 38-year-old mother Elizabeth Moselakgomo.
She vanished on 9 September while out running. Her badly bruised, partially clothed body was found dumped near a busy motorway in Kempton Park three days later.
It was a killing that resonated deeply within South Africa's running community, including sisters Zonke and Zama Mthethwa. They started The Pack, a women's running group in Johannesburg nine years ago. Elizabeth would sometimes attend The Pack events.
- Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa 
  - Published19 September
Runners across the city joined the search efforts following Elizabeth's disappearance, and took part in protests calling for violence against women to end.
Zonke and Zama's group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles. They also get cars to follow them and have started offering self-defence coaching to the women in their running group.
"We need to try and rally and create safe spaces for women to show up authentically and to do what they love doing," says Zama, 37.
Following her ordeal, Kgothatso moved from Kempton Park and now lives closer to her parents in another part of the country.
Her mother, a community activist, recently organised a prayer march to remember women who have been killed.
Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at the march.
Wiping away tears, she said: "To a survivor listening right now, I want to say you are not dirty, you are not broken beyond repair. You are not to blame and you are not alone."
- This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

noticias.titulo: The ‘eighth front’: Why Israel’s influence war in the US is failing
noticias.resumen: Despite quadrupling its hasbara budget, Israel is losing American hearts and minds, and its PR may be making it worse.
noticias.texto:
The ‘eighth front’: Why Israel’s influence war in the US is failing
Despite quadrupling its hasbara budget, Israel is losing American hearts and minds, and its PR may be making it worse.
Israeli efforts to maintain the public goodwill of its principal ally, the United States, appear to be continuing despite a series of setbacks.
According to filings with the US Department of Justice’s Foreign Agent Registration Act on October 28, US influencing company Starboard was contracted by Israeli firm LDRS Group LLC, which declares itself as acting on behalf of the State of Israel to conduct “strategic communications and public relations services in the United States to promote the interests of the State of Israel”.
This builds on previous efforts to influence the US public. The Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft estimates that more than $1bn has been spent in direct funding for programmes to influence US public opinion in favour of Israel since the genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023. That figure stands independent to the fundraising and political efforts of domestic organisations supporting Israel, such as the highly influential American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).
US support for the multiple wars Israel has embarked on since the Hamas-led attack of 2023 has been close to unconditional. In addition to the annual grant, agreed under former President Barack Obama in 2016, the US has provided at least $25.5bn in appropriations and at least $21.7bn in military support, according to Brown University’s Costs of War project. Almost as critical has been the diplomatic support, which has seen the US use its veto to block United Nations Security Council ceasefire resolutions as well as allowing Palestinian full UN membership.
Collapsing support
However, evidence that US public support for Israel is collapsing is growing and has, for lawmakers in both countries, become unavoidable. Numerous polls point to growing hostility to Israel, especially among the young, stretching to include those on the right who hold Israel responsible for gulling President Donald Trump into an unwinnable war with Iran that is forcing their own cost of living, and gas prices, still higher.
President Donald Trump’s announcement that the US would end an Obama-era grant to Israel early, made on the day of the US midterms, was widely seen as an attempt to stave off the worst consequences of waning support for Israel across the political divide. But it did little to halt the rout that followed. The heavy spending by AIPAC and its affiliated organisations, estimated at $84m, in support of explicitly pro-Israel candidates, such as Senator Susan Collins of Maine, was largely considered a waste.
“The shift that has occurred in American public attitudes toward Israel is paradigmatic, generational, and lasting,” pollster Shibley Telhami, the director of the University of Maryland’s Critical Issues Poll, said.
“You cannot unsee what you saw in Gaza, over three years. Israeli public relations campaigns are thus swimming against the tide. When they are visibly connected to Israel, they are even toxic, achieving the opposite results, as we have seen in the midterm elections.”
The pro-Israel campaigns are seeing the biggest impact among Republicans, especially among the Evangelical right. “But even there, there is evidence younger people are less impacted by these active and expensive campaigns,” Telhami said.
Losing battle
Concerns that Israel may be losing the battle for American hearts and minds reach beyond the state’s traditional allies on the right. Speaking with US media in May, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attributed the loss of US public support to unspecified foreign states’ manipulation of social media, ignoring the genocidal war on Gaza that has killed more than 70,000 people, including about 20,000 children, in the past three years. He characterised this as an “eighth front” in Israel’s ongoing wars with regional powers.
In March, Israel quadrupled the budget for its public diplomacy or “hasbara”, to $730m, much of it earmarked for US social media and American eyeballs. In November, it appeared to go further, bringing more than 250 of what Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs determined to be the next generation of US officials, journalists, influencers and community leaders to tour sites associated with the October 7 attack and cement relations with leading Israeli officials.
“Quadrupling the hasbara spend just means they’re more stupid than I thought they were and I already thought they were pretty stupid,” former Israeli ambassador and consul general in New York Alon Pinkas said. “You change the conversation by changing the policy … So far, they haven’t let any foreign media into Gaza. Can you imagine what happens when they do? No amount of spending on their social media is going to mitigate what international journalists find there.”
Israel and its place in the Middle East had already been losing their relevance to the US before the war on Gaza, he said.
Washington had achieved energy security, the bogeyman of the USSR had been consigned to history, China had emerged as an area of critical interest, and both the public and politicians had grown weary of the kind of forever wars, he said, such as the current US-Israel war on Iran that shows no signs of ending.
“Add to that a resentful and angry president in the White House, and you have some idea of the job [potential incoming prime minister, [Gadi] Eisenkot or whoever, has ahead of them: One that no amount of Hasbara is really going to help.”
Long-term damage?
How far Israeli efforts to entrench US support among future leaders, or to game the country’s social media platforms, might go in reversing negative perceptions of Israel among the American public remains unclear. The midterm elections saw several of the country’s most vocal critics of Israel elected to Congress.
The prospect of renewed war with Iran, initiated through a partnership of two deeply unpopular leaders in the US and Israel, is unlikely to win hearts and minds.
“There’s no doubt that the three pillars of US support for Israel – the public, congressional, and the executive – are at an all-time low, certainly the lowest in my experience,” former State Department Middle East negotiator Aaron David Miller, now a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment, said.
“It’s not just that we’ve seen the US engage in talks over Israel’s advice with Hamas, Yemen’s Houthi rebels and zeroing out aid [in] US weapons, but we’ve also seen a US president talk of his Israeli counterpart in extraordinary terms, and allowing highly critical phone calls of him discussing him to be leaked. However, this doesn’t mean we’re looking at a permanent rupture. A new Israeli government following different policies will take a good part of the tension out of public perceptions and Congressional angst.”

noticias.titulo: Why are Russian warships off Libya, and will Ukraine’s attack change that?
noticias.resumen: Ukraine is stepping up 'long-range sanctions' attacks on Russian vessels far beyond the battlefield.
noticias.texto:
Why are Russian warships off Libya, and will Ukraine’s attack change that?
Ukraine is stepping up ‘long-range sanctions’ attacks on Russian vessels far beyond the battlefield.
Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli has condemned Ukraine’s deadly attack on a Russian warship in Libya, in what Kyiv claimed was an “exemplary” operation.
Libya’s Foreign Ministry said the country would not accept being drawn into the Russia-Ukraine war and that its sovereignty and territorial integrity were non-negotiable, according to a statement posted on Facebook on Monday.
“The continuation of the war between Russia and Ukraine gives neither side the right to conduct military operations on Libyan territory or in its territorial waters,” it said.
Sunday’s drone strike on the Merkury, one of Moscow’s newest warships, resulted in the deaths of at least 10 Libyan and Russian crew members, local authorities said.
The attack sent shockwaves through Europe and the Middle East and raised new fears that the months-long war had already spilled over far from the front line.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Ukraine’s attacks represented a “very dangerous trend”.
Here’s what we know:
What happened?
On Sunday, Ukrainian drones targeted the Merkury in Libya’s coastal city of Benghazi after the Russian corvette docked to refuel and resupply under a cooperation agreement between Russia and Libya’s eastern rival government based in Benghazi. It is led by Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army (LNA), which is based in Tobruk.
Sources told Al Jazeera that the warship was moored in the civilian area of Benghazi seaport, close to a naval base, when it was hit.
In a Monday post on X, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed that the attack had been carried out by Ukraine’s intelligence security service, the SBU, and involved seven Ukrainian drones. The strike also destroyed a Russian Ka-27 combat helicopter. A second Russian ship was also hit. Zelenskyy said the cargo vessel Angara was transporting weapons.
“Despite all the enemy’s efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk,” he wrote.
Ukraine’s security service justified the attacks in a Monday statement, saying that both vessels were “legitimate military targets for Ukraine because they directly supported Russia’s military capabilities”.
Satellite images on Sunday showed that most of the vessel ‌‌‌‌had capsized, with only its bow still visible above water. Smoke from the initial explosion rose from the ship’s superstructure. Along the pier, debris from the strike lay scattered around.
However, officials in Libya told the Associated Press that the Merkury was only heavily damaged.
Unnamed sources also told AP that Ukraine had launched the drones from a military base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya.
Tripoli, in its condemnation of the attack on Monday, did not confirm Ukraine’s alleged presence.
Earlier on Sunday, Prime Minister Osama Hammad of the eastern Libyan government said it had submitted an investigation request to the United Nations General Assembly and Security Council.
What’s happening in Libya and why does Russia have a base there?
Oil-rich Libya is a focal point of the long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.
The North African country has been divided since 2011, when a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi. Moscow’s close ally was killed later that year.
The UN recognises the western Libyan government in Tripoli, while the Benghazi-based administration in the east is a close ally of Moscow. Russia has long maintained deep ties with Haftar in a bid to keep eastern Libya as a logistical hub for its widening military operations across Africa, including in Sudan and the Sahel region.
In 2024, following the fall of the Russia-aligned regime of Bashar al-Assad, Moscow shifted attention to Libya as a potential new site for the vast military infrastructure it had built up in Syria over the previous decade during the civil war there.
Moscow managed to maintain relations with the new government in Damascus, although its footprint is much smaller, according to analysis by the Atlantic Council think tank. Some estimates put the number of Russian troops there at 1,000, significantly fewer than around 10,000 in previous years.
How significant is Russia’s presence in Libya?
Russia is believed to have planned and funded projects at multiple Haftar-controlled Libyan military bases in its search for a “plan B” following the fall of the Assad regime in Syria: Al-Jufra, Al-Khadim, Al-Qardabiyah, Brak al-Shati, Maaten al-Sarra and Tamanhint.
An estimated 1,800 Russian troops, including those from Africa Corps, which succeeded the paramilitary Wagner Group, are presently based in Libya.
The United States is meanwhile leading efforts to reunite the two Libyan militaries, partly to counter Russia, analysts say, with Washington focusing on relations with the 35-year-old LNA deputy commander and Haftar’s son, Saddam Haftar.
That is likely why Moscow has not yet secured a port in the southern Mediterranean: Libya’s eastern authorities do not want to damage improving ties with the US, Turkiye and European partners by giving Moscow port access, which would be more visible and invite scrutiny, unlike the inland military bases, the Atlantic Council noted.
What does Ukraine’s attack mean for Russia?
It means that Ukraine is achieving results in its push to target Russia thousands of kilometres from the battlefield with what Zelenskyy calls “long-range sanctions”, even as Moscow has focused on overwhelming Kyiv with swarms of killer drones daily.
A particular focus is Russia’s so-called ‘shadow fleet’, the network of tankers Moscow uses to evade Western oil sanctions.
Around the same time the Merkury was hit, a suspected Ukrainian drone struck the Russia-bound dry cargo ship Sparta II in the eastern Baltic Sea, near Finland. Finnish authorities blamed Kyiv, while Moscow called it “terrorism”.
In July, Kyiv said it hit a Russian missile boat and the Iran-linked cargo ship, Anna, in the Caspian Sea, resulting in a diplomatic fallout between Tehran and Kyiv.
Ukraine’s long-range drones have also hit deep inside Russia, targeting oil terminals and other energy infrastructure.
In June 2025, Ukraine’s secret service smuggled components of 117 attack drones into Russia, then arranged and deployed them to hit multiple military bases in five regions. The covert operation, nicknamed Operation Spider’s Web, caused around $7bn in damage to Russian military equipment.
In the Sahel region of western Africa, Ukraine has been accused of working with armed groups fighting against Malian forces and their allied Africa Corps members, although Kyiv denies that.

noticias.titulo: Iraq orders takeover of oilfields in areas under Kurdish control
noticias.resumen: PM Ali al-Zaidi also orders his government to seize all crossings in the Kurdish region after an oil smuggling inquiry.
noticias.texto:
Iraq orders takeover of oilfields in areas under Kurdish control
PM Ali al-Zaidi also orders his government to seize all crossings in the Kurdish region after an oil smuggling inquiry.
Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has ordered the federal Ministry of Oil to manage oilfields in areas under Kurdish security control, potentially deepening tensions between Baghdad and the semi-autonomous region in the north of the country.
The prime minister’s order covers oilfields in Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahuddin and Nineveh provinces, according to a statement from his office on Tuesday.
It said Baghdad would “secure and monitor all oilfields with cameras, including fields within the administrative boundaries of the federal government that are under the security authority of the regional government”.
Al-Zaidi also ordered the border crossings authority to take over all crossings in the Kurdish region and directed the regional government to approve exports of crude oil and petroleum products only through the federal Oil Ministry.
“The Border Forces Command shall close unofficial crossings along the international borders with neighbouring countries, including crossings in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq,” the statement said, adding that “all seasonal roads” between the four governorates and the Kurdish region would be closed.
Al Jazeera’s Mahmoud Abdelwahed, reporting from Baghdad, said the latest development might exacerbate tensions and disputes over control of oil and the sharing of budgetary resources between the national government and the autonomous regional government.
“The federal government is keen to keep all excavation and marketing of oil under its state organisation, SOMO, but this has been totally rejected by the Kurdish region,” he said.
A dispute over Kurdish authorities selling oil without Baghdad’s approval halted pipeline shipments to Turkiye for more than two years before the sides agreed in September 2025 to restart them.
Al-Zaidi, meanwhile, removed the head of the border crossings authority and suspended North Oil Company’s director general and his deputies pending further investigation, Iraq’s state news agency reported.
In a separate case, Iraqi officials accused Kataib Hezbollah, an armed group backed by Iran, of running an oil smuggling network in its stronghold of Jurf al-Sakhar, south of Baghdad.
The group denied the accusation.

noticias.titulo: Vietnam restaurant blast kills at least six
noticias.resumen: At least 10 wounded after blast at restaurant in the Dong Da district in Hanoi as rescue operations under way.
noticias.texto:
Vietnam restaurant blast kills at least six
At least 10 wounded after blast at restaurant in the Dong Da district in Hanoi as rescue operations under way.
An explosion in a crowded residential part of Vietnam’s capital Hanoi has killed at least six people and injured 10, according to local authorities.
The blast occurred at a restaurant in the Dong Da district at about 8am (01:00 GMT) Tuesday, shattering windows, tearing metal shutters from their frames and heavily damaging surrounding buildings and homes, according to local media reports.
The restaurant was full of people at the time of the explosion, which the Ministry of Public Security believes was related to cooking gas. More people are feared to be trapped under the rubble, which rescuers have spent hours searching through, reported Vietnam’s VnExpress newspaper.
One nearby resident described the blast as “deafening”.
“There was a flash of light, and doors, glass and everything around me were sent flying,” the unnamed resident told the state-affiliated VietNamNet newspaper.
Photos published by VnExpress showed the restaurant, located on the ground floor of an apartment block, almost completely collapsed. Rubble was scattered across the narrow street outside, where several cars and motorbikes were damaged or overturned.
Dozens of firefighters and other rescue officials were dispatched to the scene. They were still digging through rubble more than four hours later, said VnExpress, adding that the city’s mayor was also present.
Authorities have since evacuated people from nearby buildings deemed structurally unsafe, said the report.

noticias.titulo: Was Jensen Huang too big to fire? Why Nvidia, Trump brought him back
noticias.resumen: Nvidia chief's 'mistakes' had consequences far beyond Silicon Valley. He is back nonetheless, in less than two weeks.
noticias.texto:
Was Jensen Huang too big to fire? Why Nvidia, Trump brought him back
Huang’s ‘mistakes’ had consequences far beyond just chip giant Nvidia. He is back nonetheless, in less than two weeks after spy scandal sacking.
Jensen Huang has returned as Nvidia’s chief executive officer, just 11 days after he resigned from the board of the chip giant over an affair with an executive of a client company, alleged to be involved in a Chinese spy plot.
On Monday, Huang returned to a cheering crowd of employees at Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California – a week after the board said it would not reinstate him.
US President Donald Trump took the credit for bringing back Huang – even as multiple inquiries continue, including an FBI-led counterintelligence review of his alleged links to a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.
The White House said: “We need to protect our geniuses.”
So, was Huang simply too big to fire? We look at what factors compelled Nvidia, the world’s most valuable semiconductor company, which controls 90 percent of the data centre graphics processing unit (GPU) market globally, to roll out the red carpet for Huang’s second coming.
What happened at Nvidia?
Huang, the 63-year-old cofounder and chief of Nvidia, resigned on November 12 amid reports of extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who led Singapore-based Megaspeed – and is believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset by some in the Trump administration. The New York Times first reported the alleged Chinese spy plot.
Beijing has denied that Alice Huang is a spy for China. Nvidia’s board began an investigation into the allegations, but Jensen Huang resigned before it concluded.
He was reportedly romantically involved with at least two other executives at Nvidia as well.
Analysts warned that losing Huang could significantly undermine Nvidia’s market value, with some estimating that his departure could wipe as much as 30 percent off the company’s roughly $4 trillion valuation. In the event, the share price fell by 27.7 percent to a November 20 low of $3.04 trillion.
Following news of his reinstatement, shares rebounded, propelling the company back to a valuation of $3.98 trillion at the close of trading on Monday.
Several investigations are under way, including a Justice Department antitrust probe into Nvidia’s business practices and an SEC inquiry into its accounting. Congress is also examining the potential diversion of Nvidia chips to China through Megaspeed.
Amid mounting pressure from the market and the Trump administration, Nvidia brought Huang back to lead the company by Monday.
“I am honoured to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said in his statement.
Who was pushing to bring back Huang?
Huang’s departure prompted a backlash from influential figures in Silicon Valley.
A petition calling for his reinstatement attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
“Bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA’s best interests,” stated the letter published on the petition’s website.
But it was the Trump administration that made the decisive move, after a group of Silicon Valley insiders reportedly put together a so-called war room and lobbied the White House for support.
“The board decided to do what we wanted them to do,” Trump told CNBC in an interview, adding that he had spoken with board members and Huang.
“Basically, I was represented at the board,” Trump said, adding that Nvidia’s board asked for assurance about reported threats to national security.
“And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know and we know a lot,” the president said.
How did Nvidia’s board flip?
Huang does not have the voting power to control Nvidia’s board. In fact, he only has a 3.58 percent ownership stake – unlike, for example, Mark Zuckerberg, who leads Meta and holds a 13.4 percent economic stake, but commands nearly 60 percent of the company’s voting power.
Amid the campaign to reinstate Huang, the ousted CEO added that he would be “honoured” to ‌‌‌‌return if the board deemed it best.
Board Chair Harvey Jones, however, told investors that Huang left voluntarily and would not return.
The board announced a new committee to investigate the matter internally and also formed a so-called National Security and Export Control Committee to oversee trade compliance and national security risks.
Then came the about-face, with Jones saying on Monday that the board “believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers”.
“In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government and based on that input the Board is confident that Mr Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk,” the statement added.
What made Nvidia bring back Huang?
There are several reasons.
Trump’s influence
The US president’s administration, including Vice President JD Vance, pressured the board to chart a path for Huang’s return.
Trump claimed that he played a central role in Huang’s reinstatement to the consequential company, which had lacked a clear succession plan.
In the middle of the heated scandal, Trump repeatedly backed the “genius” Huang, who built Nvidia over three decades and was deeply involved in its technology strategy, relationships with customers and governments.
“I think this move is unprecedented in the sense that a sitting president has exerted very public pressure on a corporate board to make a particular decision,” Aleksandar Tomic, associate dean for strategy, innovation and technology at Boston College, told Al Jazeera.
Stock market
Huang’s departure created concern among investors and employees about whether Nvidia could maintain its momentum without him – as reflected in its tumbling stock price.
Nvidia’s share price fell nearly 28 percent between November 11, when the board accepted Huang’s resignation, and November 20, amid mounting uncertainty over its leadership.
It surged 31 percent in early trading on Monday after the board announced his reinstatement – adding about a trillion dollars to the company’s valuation – lifting stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq climbing 6.5 percent and the S&P 500 by 4.75 percent.
Tech and AI companies make up about 40 percent of S&P 500 valuations.
On Tuesday, major Asian stock indices in Seoul, Tokyo and Taipei all rose as well.
In Taiwan, where Huang was born, the market soared by more than 9 percent, while South Korea’s Kospi index increased more than 6.8 percent and Japan’s Nikkei 225 by 3.8 percent.
Nvidia’s role in AI
Huang’s company makes chips that literally power the modern AI revolution as we see it.
Nvidia holds an extraordinary near-90 percent share of the market for GPUs – graphics processing units, which are specialised AI processors – used in AI data centres, giving it an oversized influence over the infrastructure powering the global AI boom.
That also makes the company central to the AI rivalry between the US and China.
Hours after Huang returned to Nvidia, the US added Megaspeed – the Singapore-based company at the centre of the alleged spying scandal involving Nvidia – to its trade blacklist.
Washington does not allow the sale of advanced chips to Beijing in order to maintain its lead in the rapidly developing industry and says it would punish those who try to circumvent the restrictions.
Nvidia’s customers include tech giants such as Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta, which rely on Nvidia hardware to build and operate their AI data centres.
Huang has spent years lobbying in Washington against such restrictions, arguing that restricting sales would surrender a strategically important market to domestic Chinese competitors. That puts him at odds with US legislators who view access to Nvidia’s advanced chips as a national security risk, particularly given their potential military applications.

noticias.titulo: Israeli air strikes in Gaza kill 7 as doctors warn of meningitis outbreak
noticias.resumen: Gaza health officials say meningitis cases rose to 272 in October, more than eight times the typical monthly rate.
noticias.texto:
Israeli air strikes in Gaza kill 7 as doctors warn of meningitis outbreak
Gaza health officials say meningitis cases rose to 272 in October, more than eight times the typical monthly rate.
At least seven Palestinians, including a child and police officers, have been killed and dozens injured in Israeli air strikes on the Gaza Strip.
Health officials confirmed the deaths on Tuesday morning while a public health warning was issued about an outbreak of meningitis.
Three Palestinians, including a child, were killed in an Israeli air strike on the Wadi Gaza area in the centre of the Strip, medical sources said.
Earlier on Tuesday morning, a further three Palestinians were killed and five wounded when an Israeli drone struck the al-Mawasi area west of Khan Younis in southern Gaza while a fourth Palestinian died from injuries after being targeted in the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.
Al Jazeera’s Hind Khoudary reported from Gaza that the three people killed in the al-Mawasi attack were Palestinian police officers. “Dozens of others have been injured in different areas across the Gaza Strip,” she said on Tuesday. “According to the Ministry of Health, it was very hard to recognise who these people were who were attacked by Israeli forces, and the same thing happened yesterday when Israeli forces targeted a vehicle in Gaza City.”
“There have been attacks on a daily basis by Israeli forces despite the fact that there has been a ‘ceasefire’ that has been agreed on between both parties,” Khoudary said. “Israel continues to violate this ‘ceasefire’ every single day.”
On Monday night, two civilians were also killed and others injured in an air strike by Israeli forces on Gaza City, Wafa reported.
The Ministry of Health in the Gaza Strip has also issued an epidemic alert across all parts of Gaza due to a rapid rise in cases of meningitis. It warned that the spread of the disease poses a direct threat to the lives of thousands of Palestinians, particularly children, given the deteriorating health and environmental conditions in the Strip.
Dr Nidal Ghoneim, deputy director general of primary care for public health affairs, said at a news conference that cases of meningitis rose to 272 in October, more than eight times the normal monthly rate, which ranges from 30 to 50 cases.
Ghoneim explained that 15 deaths resulting from the disease have been recorded since the start of this year, including five deaths in August, September and October. He noted a rise in cases of bacterial meningitis, which is the most serious form of the illness, from 10 to 20 cases per month to 108 cases in October. Since the start of November, another 100 cases have been recorded, he said.
According to health officials, casualties from Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza have risen to 74,746 people killed and 176,234 injured since it began on October 7, 2023. That includes 1,679 people killed and 6,100 injured since the “ceasefire” went into effect on October 10 last year.

noticias.titulo: Why S Korea issued air raid alert after Russian jets flew near its airspace
noticias.resumen: South Korean authorities issue air raid warnings after several Russian jets were on verge of entering its airspace.
noticias.texto:
Why S Korea issued air raid alert after Russian jets flew near its airspace
South Korean authorities issue air raid warnings after several Russian jets were on verge of entering its airspace.
South Korea has scrambled fighter jets and issued brief air raid warnings for residents of an island after Russian military planes approached its airspace over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan.
Russian jets on Tuesday briefly entered South Korea’s air defence identification zone (ADIZ), an aerial buffer area between countries, South Korea’s military said, adding that “multiple” Russian aircraft were “on the verge” of entering the country’s airspace over Ulleung Island.
“Airspace intrusion was anticipated. Therefore, to protect the safety of our people, we issued a warning pre-emptively,” Jang Do-young, a spokesperson for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said.
Authorities had earlier issued an alert that a North Korean plane had made an incursion, which would have been a significant escalation in tensions between the two Koreas, which remain technically at war after the 1950-1953 Korean War ended with an armistice and not a peace treaty. South Korea later issued a correction saying no North Korean jet was involved.
Here’s everything we know about the incident:
Why did South Korea tell residents to take shelter?
According to the Joint Chiefs of Staff, about five Russian military aircraft entered South Korea’s ADIZ on Tuesday morning. There was no intrusion of South Korea’s airspace by the Russian aircraft in the end, the South Korean military said.
Jang said the aircraft came “very close” to the airspace above Ulleung Island, which is home to 9,000 people and lies 120km (75 miles) off the northeastern coast of South Korea. South Korean fighter jets conducted “tactical manoeuvres” to prevent any incident, the Joint Chiefs of Staff said.
But confusion ensued over the alert and who was responsible for the intrusion.
The government of North Gyeongsang province, which includes Ulleung, sent out an alert saying the jets were suspected to be North Korean, which it later corrected.
Still, the Ministry of the Interior and Safety issued the shelter warning at 7:52am (22:52 GMT on Monday) and lifted the alert three minutes later after the aircraft had left the area.
The last time the island in the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, was sent into panic was in 2022 after North Korea fired more than 20 missiles into the sea during a period of heightened inter-Korean tensions. After one missile headed towards Ulleung, it triggered air raid sirens and led to residents evacuating.
What has South Korea said about Russia?
South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it had conveyed its regret over the incident to Russia and called for measures to prevent a recurrence, South Korea’s Yonhap News Agency reported.
The ministry also sent the message to the Russian embassy in Seoul but stopped short of summoning the Russian ambassador, diplomatic sources told the agency.
Still, the Ministry of National Defence called in Russia’s military attache, Nikolai Marchenko, to lodge a formal complaint.
Russian military aircraft have entered South Korea’s ADIZ five times so far this year.
Last week, South Korea announced Russian military aircraft had temporarily entered the ADIZ.
On the same day, Japan protested to Moscow after also saying two suspected Russian aircraft had entered its airspace off its southwestern coast.
In 2019, South Korean fighter jets had fired warning shots after a Russian A-50 early warning aircraft, flying alongside Russian and Chinese bombers in a joint patrol, entered its territorial airspace near the island of Dokdo.
At the time, Moscow denied violating South Korean airspace.
What has Russia said about the incident?
So far, Moscow has not commented.
Russia does not recognise South Korea’s authority over its ADIZ and has argued it has no basis in international law.
What is the status of Russian-South Korean relations?
The two countries have fairly strained relations.
Moscow has a close relationship with North Korea, and Pyongyang deployed troops to help Russia’s soldiers during its war in Ukraine. Meanwhile, Seoul has joined Western sanctions against Russia due to its invasion of Ukraine.
However, recently, the leaders of the two countries have signalled interest in restoring ties.
Last week, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and Russian President Vladimir Putin held a 10-minute meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and agreed to pursue cooperation where possible while also working to ease tensions on the Korean Peninsula, an official in Seoul told reporters on the condition of anonymity, Yonhap reported.

noticias.titulo: Russian strike kills two in Ukraine, days after ship attack off Libya
noticias.resumen: Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia destroyed a house and damaged a five-storey apartment building, Ukrainian officials said.
noticias.texto:
Russian strike kills two in Ukraine, days after ship attack off Libya
Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia destroyed a house and damaged a five-storey apartment building, Ukrainian officials said.
A Russian air attack on Zaporizhzhia in Ukraine has killed two people and wounded more than 40, including an infant, the day after Kyiv said its drones sank a Russian warship in a Libyan port far from the front lines of the war.
Russia’s dawn raid on the city in southeast Ukraine destroyed a house and damaged a five-storey apartment building, regional officials said on Tuesday.
It came as the two warring sides continued long-range attacks, launching hundreds of drones overnight.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said air defences intercepted and destroyed 699 Ukrainian drones over seven regions, occupied Crimea and the Black Sea.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 355 drones flew towards the capital overnight and 63 were shot down as they approached.
Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Amin Dorghami said it had been a “long time” since Moscow had been targeted with as many drones.
Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia launched 96 drones overnight, with hits at 13 locations and 73 shot down or jammed.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces hit an electricity substation in Pryluky, in Ukraine’s Chernihiv region, which it said powered Ukraine’s military. Russian forces also hit a dry cargo ship southwest of Odesa that the ministry said was carrying military supplies.
“This too could be considered routine, since Russia is enforcing a blockade on Ukraine’s Black Sea ports,” Dorghami said.
Late on Monday, the Polish military said a Russian drone briefly entered Poland’s airspace during an attack on western Ukraine but was not shot down because of the risk to civilians. Deputy Defence Minister Pawel Zalewski said he assumed the incursion was deliberate, coming three days after three Russian cruise missiles crashed in eastern Poland.
Reporting from Kyiv, Al Jazeera’s Abdelaziz Mujahid said the incursion “may also signal that the conflict and these confrontations are widening”.
It follows Ukraine’s attack on the Russian corvette Merkury in the Libyan port of Benghazi on Sunday. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said seven Ukrainian-built naval drones were used in the “completely legitimate operation against enemy ships”.
“The strike in Benghazi has left Russia without one of its newest combat ships,” said Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow. “It was commissioned only three years ago.”
Russia’s UN envoy, Vassily Nebenzia, accused Western countries of backing Ukraine’s recent attacks and said Moscow would keep using military means to ensure its security.
On Monday, debris from Russian drones fell in central Kyiv, close to the president’s office and set a five-storey building on fire. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said five people were injured, including a foreign national.
“All of this is a bit too close for comfort for Ukrainians, especially considering that the presidential palace is just a few hundred metres up the road,” reported Al Jazeera’s Audrey McAlpine from the scene.
Zelenskyy said on Monday evening that Ukrainian intelligence warned that Russia was preparing a new series of strikes and urged residents to heed air raid alerts.

noticias.titulo: US army says detonation of lead explosives in Iowa will proceed
noticias.resumen: Public outcry led to a legal battle when details of the plans to conduct two controlled detonations surfaced.
noticias.texto:
US army says detonation of lead explosives in Iowa will proceed
Public outcry led to a legal battle when details surfaced of the plans to conduct two controlled detonations.
The United States military will proceed with its plan to blow up a deteriorating stockpile of toxic lead explosives in rural Iowa, according to the army’s top civilian official, after a federal appeals court gave clearance to the waste disposal operation.
In an announcement late Monday on X, Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle called the choice to move forward a “consensus decision” among all the federal agencies involved, as well as the courts and state officials.
“Every expert agency agrees, and both Iowa’s current and incoming governors say the call belongs to the experts,” Telle said.
“We are proceeding with the controlled removal in full coordination with all state, local and federal authorities.”
The Army prompted a public outcry last week when details surfaced of its plan to conduct two controlled detonations of 68 drums containing almost 4,500kg (10,000lb) of degraded lead azide, a chemical used in munitions, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa.
Legal battle
Environmental groups immediately filed suit to block the plan, raising public safety concerns over the likelihood that the explosions would release a plume of toxic lead dust over homes, crops and livestock far beyond the detonation site, about 240km (150 miles) southeast of Des Moines.
The lawsuit challenged a special permit granted for the operation by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
The EPA countered that a managed detonation would be far less risky than an uncontrolled, spontaneous explosion of the highly volatile material, a scenario the agency said was growing more likely as the weather turns colder in Iowa.
According to the EPA, any attempt to chemically neutralise or relocate the storage drums would also risk an uncontrolled blast.
A three-judge panel of the 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals last Thursday issued a temporary stay blocking the EPA’s permit while the court more thoroughly reviewed the case.
But Trump administration lawyers filed a legal notice two days later asserting that the Army intended to carry out the controlled detonation with or without court approval, citing an emergency exemption to federal environmental laws.
Then, in another twist on Monday, US President Donald Trump weighed in on the controversy, ordering the Army to hold off on its disposal plan until the appeals court had ruled in its favour.
Hours after Trump’s edict on Monday pausing the army’s demolition plan, the 8th Circuit sided with the EPA and lifted the court’s earlier stay, removing the final legal obstacle. But the status of the detonation plan remained unclear until Telle’s announcement on Monday night.

noticias.titulo: Malaysia set to return thousands of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar
noticias.resumen: The announcement comes five days after the ICJ ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority.
noticias.texto:
Malaysia set to return thousands of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar
The announcement comes five days after the ICJ ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority.
Malaysia will send more than 6,500 Rohingya refugees back to Myanmar in a new round of repatriations, said Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.
The announcement on Tuesday comes five days after the International Court of Justice in The Hague ruled that Myanmar’s security forces committed genocide against the Rohingya minority.
Malaysia has historically offered safe haven to exiles from Myanmar but has grown increasingly frustrated by large numbers of refugees, saying that hosting them has become a financial burden and security risk.
In late September, around 1,500 migrants were sent back to war-torn Myanmar in an opaque scheme that concerns rights groups.
Addressing the Malaysian parliament, Anwar said 1,500 Myanmar nationals will be returned on three navy vessels from December 6 to 7. “For the month of December, 5,303 will be brought back by aircraft at the expense of the Myanmar government,” he said.
As of August, there were 225,740 refugees and asylum seekers registered with the UNHCR in Malaysia, around 90 percent of them from Myanmar, according to the agency’s data.
The UN’s highest court ruled last week that Myanmar authorities must “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return” of refugees displaced either within Myanmar or abroad.
Malaysia hosted Myanmar’s former junta chief-turned-President Min Aung Hlaing last month, despite criticisms from rights groups that the move risked legitimising Myanmar’s government and posed dangers for those being returned.
Anwar said his engagements with Myanmar’s former leader were part of efforts to safeguard Malaysia’s interests and in line with the ruling by the International Court of Justice, which was “to guarantee a safe and dignified return” for those fleeing persecution.
The PM acknowledged that many asylum seekers in Malaysia were “victims of atrocities carried out by the Myanmar regime”, but said Malaysia could no longer afford to ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌host refugees and that hoping for them to be resettled in third countries had not worked.
Late last month, Malaysia said it would seek clarification from Myanmar about reports that hundreds of migrants recently returned to the country were being held in military detention.
Anwar did not mention the request for clarification, but said Malaysia reiterated its stance over concerns about the Rohingya and other ethnic groups, which was also underscored by the ICJ’s ruling.
The mainly Muslim Rohingya – described as the ‘world’s most persecuted minority’ – make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the United Nations.
