noticias.titulo: Pakistan’s Zeeshan Ali set for historic flight to China’s space station
noticias.resumen: The Pakistan Air Force pilot will spend about a week on board the Tiangong, conducting experiments with China’s crew.
noticias.texto:
Pakistan’s Zeeshan Ali set for historic flight to China’s space station
The Pakistan Air Force pilot will spend about a week on board the Tiangong, conducting experiments with China’s crew.
Islamabad, Pakistan – Pakistan is poised to send an astronaut into space for the first time on Wednesday, when an air force pilot joins China’s Shenzhou-24 mission to the country’s Tiangong space station.
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, will fly as a payload specialist alongside commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi. The spacecraft is scheduled to launch from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China at 8:18am Beijing time (00:18 GMT), or 5:18am in Pakistan.
Speaking at a news conference in Jiuquan on Tuesday, China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) spokesperson Zhang Jingbo said the mission would mark the first joint flight by Chinese and foreign astronauts in the country’s crewed space programme.
After reaching orbit, the spacecraft will carry out a rapid, autonomous rendezvous lasting about three and a half hours before docking with the forward port of the station’s Tianhe core module, Zhang said.
Ali’s stay will be brief. He will return to Earth on board the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft after a short joint flight, while Zhu Yangzhu, a member of that crew, remains in orbit for a year, Zhang said.
Pakistan’s Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO) has said Ali will spend about a week on the station.
“I want to assure you that I am not flying for myself. I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis,” Ali told reporters during the crew’s conversation with the media.
The two pilots
Ali and Khurram Daud, a second Pakistani selected for astronaut training, are Pakistan Air Force pilots.
They were selected through a three-stage process that began with screening in Pakistan and included medical, psychological and technical assessments.
CMSA named them reserve astronauts on April 22 earlier this year. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif met them in Islamabad the following day, and on April 24, China’s Space Day, they joined the Astronaut Center of China in Beijing for training.
Before leaving, Daud asked Pakistanis to pray for him in a video released by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.
“My message to you all is to pray for me, so that I can complete this training and this mission well, and make my nation and my country proud,” he said in Urdu.
Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, who is in China for the launch, paid tribute to both men on X on Tuesday.
“They trained in centrifuges and simulators, in emergency drills and in a new language. Both performed exceptionally well in training. Though Zeeshan Ali will fly tomorrow both have already made Pakistan proud,” he wrote.
Thanking his instructors, SUPARCO and CMSA, at Tuesday’s news conference, Ali said: “No matter who flies, we have already made the history together.”
Daud was not named in the crew, and it is not yet clear whether he will fly on a later mission.
In written responses to Al Jazeera, SUPARCO said the backup astronauts would serve as experts to help carry the programme forward.
Scientific experiments
Zhang said Ali would take part in the crew’s daily work but would mainly oversee China-Pakistan experiments, install samples and equipment and conduct tests in orbit.
The mission will include four joint science projects in biotechnology and materials, Zhang said. Ali will also conduct an experiment involving cyanobacteria, photosynthetic microorganisms.
Pakistan’s Information Ministry said in April that the experiments would cover materials science, fluid physics, life sciences and biotechnology, with potential applications in climate resilience, food security and industrial innovation.
Qamarul Islam, a space scientist and former senior official in the state-affiliated Institute of Space Technology (IST) in Islamabad, said the experiments had been shortlisted after SUPARCO invited research institutes in Pakistan to submit proposals.
“Primarily these experiments are the experiments of the research institutes, universities and others, from Pakistan,” he told Al Jazeera.
SUPARCO said the station was a fully equipped laboratory. It added in its response that Ali’s week in orbit was meant to start and install the experiments, and to record data confirming that the equipment had survived launch loads and vibrations and was safely installed in microgravity.
“Completing the four experiments takes between six and 12 months,” it said.
Training for orbit
According to Zhang, preparations focused on professional skills, crew coordination and language.
“We focus on Chinese commands and technical terms to ensure accurate execution,” he said, in the English interpretation of his remarks.
In a promotional video by the Chinese space agency, Ali, who described himself as a fighter pilot, said centrifuge, rescue and survival, and emergency procedures training were part of his preparation.
“But the real challenge, honestly speaking, was mastering the Chinese language, because all the switches, all the software, all the programmes, all the voice announcements, everything is in Chinese. So we had to learn that and master that technical Chinese,” he said.
SUPARCO and CMSA signed their astronaut agreement in Islamabad in February 2025. Ali said the two countries had since moved quickly.
“The two great nations of China and Pakistan have turned a pilot into an astronaut in a remarkably short span of time,” he said.
A new milestone
This year marks 75 years of diplomatic ties between the two neighbours. Zhang described the flight as another milestone in their cooperation.
“Pakistan is China’s all-weather strategic cooperative partner,” Zhang said, according to the English interpretation of his remarks.
Pakistan’s Information Ministry said in April that the programme placed the country among a select group of nations involved in human spaceflight.
China built its own space station after being excluded from the International Space Station (ISS), in part because a 2011 US law bars NASA from bilateral cooperation with Beijing.
“Chinese were left out. And obviously China developed their own space station. Pakistan is also out of the International Space Station as far as the astronauts are concerned,” Qamar said.
He said China’s decision to choose Pakistan for its first foreign visitor reflected the two countries’ closeness.
Asked by a reporter on Tuesday whether China would expand cooperation, including joint flights with Russia, Zhang pointed to the station’s transport and astronaut-training systems. He said China hoped to explore space with more countries and regions.
SUPARCO said Pakistan was opening a path for international collaboration on the Chinese station and could now offer its expertise to other countries.
Moon by 2035?
Asked by China’s state-run CGTN about the future of the partnership, Ali looked beyond the current mission.
“I believe what comes after this flight matters more than the flight itself. This mission is not a finish line; it is a launchpad. And I hope the next chapter of China-Pakistan space cooperation to grow from one astronaut, one flight, to multiple joint flights, to Moon, Mars, and beyond.”
Pakistan’s government has also set a lunar target.
Asked about lunar plans, SUPARCO said Pakistan was already working with China on a lunar mission tentatively planned for 2028. It said it could not yet disclose details.
Pakistan’s lunar programme has so far focused on robotic missions. The iCube-Qamar satellite, developed at IST, reached the lunar orbit on board China’s Chang’e-6 mission in 2024. A SUPARCO-developed rover is due to fly on the Chang’e-8 about 2028.
Qamar, who was the project director for iCube-Qamar, said lunar missions ranged from flybys and orbiters, such as the satellite, to landings and eventually permanent bases.
“In the long term you will see stations on the Moon, a utilisation of the Moon,” he said.
China is also advancing its lunar programme. Zhang said preparations were under way for tests of the Long March-10 rocket and Mengzhou crewed spacecraft. The first flight of the Lanyue lunar lander was on track, he said. Beijing aims to put astronauts on the Moon by 2030.
For Pakistan, Qamar said, sending a person into space would introduce scientific challenges beyond the technology of getting there, including coping with isolation and supplying oxygen and food.
“I think it will be really good learning for Pakistan to be involved in such thing because then it has many other applications on ground, applications in the medical field and other aspects,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Wars choke global food routes, threatening aid for 7.3 million, WFP warns
noticias.resumen: WFP Executive Director Luke Lindberg decries ‘political problem’ as grain is 'not reaching the people who need it'.
noticias.texto:
Wars choke global food routes, threatening aid for 7.3 million, WFP warns
WFP Executive Director Luke Lindberg decries ‘political problem’ as grain is ‘not reaching the people who need it’.
The head of the World Food Programme (WFP) has warned that disruption to three critical trade routes is pushing up food and humanitarian costs, threatening assistance to millions of people.
Addressing the United Nations Security Council in New York on Monday, WFP Executive Director Luke Lindberg said a “triple chokepoint” in the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab al-Mandeb and the Black Sea had “dramatically tightened the supply of food exports and farming inputs”.
“Combined with a surge in conflicts and climate shocks like El Nino, the effect on food production and prices has been very real,” he said.
If current conditions persist, the agency expects $727m in additional costs by mid-2027, potentially putting assistance for 7.3 million people at risk.
“This is taking money straight out of WFP’s operations, directly translating into less food for fewer families,” Lindberg said.
The warning comes as 266 million people worldwide face acute hunger, with a risk of famine in parts of Sudan, South Sudan and Somalia.
About 30 percent of global fertiliser supplies pass through the Strait of Hormuz. The Black Sea is a key source of grain for countries including Somalia and Yemen, which imports 90 percent of its food.
By mid-October, 63 percent fewer wheat and maize vessels were moving through the Bosphorus than a year earlier, the WFP said. About 10 million tonnes of Russian and Ukrainian wheat could fail to reach global markets, enough to feed an estimated 44 million people.
“This is not a problem of production. It is a political problem,” Lindberg said. “Grain is available, but it is not reaching the people who need it.”
In Sudan, the cost of a basic diet has risen by 130 percent since February.
Lindberg urged member states to commit to three “red lines”: no more famines, no more weaponisation of food and no more attacks on humanitarians.

noticias.titulo: Why has Yemen’s offensive against the Houthis in al-Bayda stalled?
noticias.resumen: Government forces made early gains in September, but Houthi fighting on multiple fronts has slowed the offensive.
noticias.texto:
Why has Yemen’s offensive against the Houthis in al-Bayda stalled?
Government forces made early gains in September, but Houthi defences and fighting on multiple fronts have slowed the offensive.
When Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched a counteroffensive against the Houthis in the strategically important al-Bayda province in September, it appeared to open a major new front against the group.
Al-Bayda, a province in central Yemen, has become one of the flashpoints since the Yemeni government launched its response to a series of Houthi advances on the coast and around Taiz in September.
Fighting continues in and around the central province, but government forces have failed to achieve a significant breakthrough since the September counteroffensive.
There have been hundreds of air raids on Houthi positions in al-Bayda since then, but initial advances on the ground have failed to develop into a broader push towards the provincial capital.
Houthi fortifications, minefields and difficult terrain reportedly slowed the offensive, while government forces faced pressure from simultaneous fighting elsewhere in Yemen.
On November 21, Houthi media reported eight air strikes on telecommunications towers in al-Bayda’s Mukayras district.
In mid-November, government-aligned forces withdrew from areas near the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb Strait to reinforce their defences around Aden, the government’s main base of operations.
Why is al-Bayda important?
Located southeast of Sanaa, al-Bayda occupies a strategic position connecting northern and southern Yemen and holds several important military fronts.
For the Houthis, the province provides a defensive buffer and access to supply routes linking their positions in neighbouring areas.
For government forces, retaking al-Bayda could disrupt Houthi supply lines, ease pressure on surrounding provinces and potentially open routes towards the capital Sanaa, held by the Iran-backed rebels since September 2014 and triggering an ongoing war with forces linked to the government.
But the province’s mountainous terrain, winding roads and valleys make it difficult for attacking forces to advance, secure territory and maintain supply lines.
Brigadier General Mohammed al-Kumaim, a Yemeni military analyst, previously told Al Jazeera that if the government took control of al-Bayda, it would cut Houthi supply routes and increase pressure on the group’s other strongholds.
Such gains, however, would depend on the government’s ability to hold this territory and sustain military operations.
Al-Bayda has seen repeated clashes since the Houthis expanded their control beyond Sanaa in 2014. Government forces and allied tribal fighters have periodically captured territory, only to lose it during subsequent Houthi counteroffensives.
In July 2021, government forces advanced into parts of the province before the Houthis recaptured the lost territory.
What has prevented a breakthrough?
Beyond the military challenges, divisions among forces opposed to the Houthis have complicated efforts to sustain the government offensive. There remain deep divisions between forces aligned to the Yemeni government and the Southern Transitional Council (STC), a coalition of separatist groups who want independence for south Yemen.
While officially dissolved earlier this year, armed groups once under the STC umbrella remain important actors in Adan and southern Yemen. Continued differences between the Yemeni government and southern separatists reportedly remain a problem in creating a united front against the Houthis.
Ali al-Dhahab, a Yemeni military and strategic analyst, told Al Jazeera that local resistance groups had repeatedly suffered from inconsistent government support, disrupted supply lines and political rivalries among anti-Houthi factions.
He said violence in neighbouring southern areas had also prevented fighters in al-Bayda from establishing reliable supply routes and securing the support needed for prolonged operations.
The latest fighting reflects the broader difficulties facing Yemen’s fragmented anti-Houthi forces, which are attempting to defend multiple fronts while challenging the group’s control of strategically important territory.
The government’s recent withdrawal from areas near Bab al-Mandeb has added to those pressures, as forces concentrate on defending Aden against further Houthi advances.
The central challenge for the government in al-Bayda remains unchanged: Converting the province’s strategic importance into lasting territorial gains.

noticias.titulo: Sheikh Hasina plans to return to Bangladesh from exile on December 16
noticias.resumen: Hasina urges Dhaka to arrange her return on the national airline, as government says she can only be extradited.
noticias.texto:
Sheikh Hasina plans to return to Bangladesh from exile on December 16
Hasina urges Dhaka to arrange her return on the national airline, as government says she can only return through extradition.
Sheikh Hasina, the former prime minister of Bangladesh who was overthrown more than two years ago, plans to return home from exile in India on December 16, her spokesperson said, as the government said she can only return through extradition.
Hasina went into exile in August 2024 after a student-led mass uprising forced her to end her 15-year rule.
She was later sentenced to death by a Bangladesh court in her absence for ordering the deadly crackdown on the uprising in which hundreds of protesters were killed.
Hasina rejected the verdict and has said she is ready to fight the case once she is back.
Announcing her plan to return on the anniversary of the end of her country’s 1971 liberation war with Pakistan, she urged Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to arrange her flight on the national airline.
“Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5, 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka,” spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali said in a statement on Tuesday.
Government position ‘very clear’
Abu Abdullah M Saleh, Prime Minister Rahman’s press secretary, told the Associated Press news agency that the government would stick to its position on Hasina’s extradition as a convict.
“My government’s stand is very clear. She has been convicted in a tribunal. We have sought her extradition,” he said by phone.
Hasina is expected to be arrested upon her return and sent to jail.
Aminul Islam, chief prosecutor of Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal, which sentenced Hasina to death, said it was unreasonable for a convicted fugitive to expect the government to arrange her return.
The judiciary had earlier said that Hasina would not be able to appeal her death sentence as she missed the required deadline and there would be no legal basis to stop her execution.
In Bangladesh, presidential clemency is allowed, but Hasina has never sought that in earlier statements and has rejected the verdict outright.
The United Nations has said as many as 1,400 people were killed during the unrest that forced Hasina from power.
Hasina’s father led the war against Pakistan and after independence was the first leader of the new People’s Republic of Bangladesh.
He was killed in a military coup in 1975, along with most of his family members. Hasina and her younger sister survived as they were out of the country.

noticias.titulo: Member states must not betray the ICC
noticias.resumen: Succumbing to US pressure to change the Rome Statute would be devastating for international justice.
noticias.texto:
Member states must not betray the ICC
Succumbing to US pressure to change the Rome Statute would be devastating for international justice.
The International Criminal Court (ICC) is in danger of being hollowed out. There are growing signs that its member states are preparing to change the Rome Statute, which governs the court, to meet the demands of US President Donald Trump.
Amnesty International Secretary General Agnes Callamard recently warned that ICC member states are undertaking “a dangerous step towards ‘constructive dialogue’ with the Trump administration”. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has acknowledged that the Netherlands, which hosts the ICC, is engaged in negotiations with the US, but has refused to provide details.
The Trump administration has given a six-month “grace period” before implementing crippling sanctions on the ICC, framing it as a chance for member states “to demonstrate meaningful progress on diplomatic and legal resolutions”.
What the US wants is for the Rome Statute to be amended to ensure that no citizen of a state that has not joined the court can ever be subjected to its jurisdiction, regardless of where their crimes are committed. This flies against the principle that the ICC can investigate anyone if they commit war crimes, crimes against humanity, or genocide on a territory the court has jurisdiction over.
Members of the Trump administration have periodically claimed that US attacks on the ICC are intended to protect Americans from falling under the court’s scrutiny. But that hasn’t happened and isn’t the case now. ICC judges recently decided to end an investigation into alleged US crimes committed in Afghanistan, yet another signal that US citizens are not at risk of investigation by the ICC – even if there are grounds to believe they should be.
According to Callamard, the US also demands that heads of state are granted immunity from prosecution by the court and that the investigation into the situation in Palestine is dropped. Currently, the court is investigating not just possible war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza, but also atrocities committed in the occupied West Bank.
It would take more than a few states to change the ICC’s jurisdiction, but it is notable that none of the 125 member states has come out and explicitly stated that the Rome Statute is not up for negotiation – especially when the court and its supporters are being held over a barrel by the Trump administration.
Accepting American terms would be as damaging to the international justice system as any ICC sanctions Washington could muster. If US efforts to destroy the court – via sanctions or neutered jurisdiction – succeed, those who would benefit the most would be perpetrators of some of the worst crimes we have seen in the past few decades.
Those include first and foremost, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. It is for “Bibi”, more than anyone, that the US has gone all-out in its ambitions to crater the ICC. Trump has made that much clear, openly stating that the sanctions against the court weren’t about protecting American citizens, but Netanyahu.
If Trump is successful, the Israeli prime minister – who faces charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity over his prosecution of the war in Gaza – will enjoy impunity. Israel is not a member state, but Palestine is, which is what allowed the Court to take action against the Israeli prime minister.
The ICC’s investigations into Palestine are something of a litmus test for the institution’s independence and impartiality, and its ability to speak truth to power. If it is forced to drop the warrants it has already issued for atrocity crimes committed in Gaza, many will conclude that the court is operated in line with the narrow interests of the powerful and not the law or the needs of victims and survivors.
Another immediate beneficiary of the gutting-out of the ICC would be Russian President Vladimir Putin. The Trump administration has long been interested in currying favour with the Kremlin, despite the fact that its leader faces an ICC arrest warrant for abducting Ukrainian children and giving them to Russian families. Indeed, at the recent ASEAN conference, Trump openly offered to work with Putin to attack the ICC.
That warrant was made possible because Ukraine accepted the jurisdiction of the ICC. But if the US campaign against the court succeeds, Putin’s warrant will evaporate, since Russia is not a member state.
Then there are Myanmar’s junta leaders. It is well established that Myanmar’s military committed a litany of atrocities against the Rohingya minority in what many states – including the United States – officially consider genocide. Last week, the International Court of Justice also found that Myanmar carried out a genocide against the Rohingya, concluding that this was the “only reasonable inference” that could explain Myanmar’s actions towards the Muslim minority.
In 2024, the ICC Prosecutor applied for a warrant for Myanmar’s Senior General and Acting President Min Aung Hlaing, alleging he committed the crimes against humanity of forced deportation and persecution against the Rohingya.
Myanmar is not a member-state of the ICC. But Bangladesh, where many Rohingya were forcibly displaced to, is what gave the court jurisdiction. If Trump achieves his goal of castrating the court, Min Aung Hlaing and other suspected genocidaires in Myanmar won’t ever have to worry about facing justice in The Hague.
This is all bad enough. But it is not just that those who have already committed atrocities that will be let off the hook if the US campaign against the ICC succeeds. New perpetrators will also be emboldened. While the court has not been able ensure that the warrants against Netanyahu, Putin or Min Aung Hlaing are enforced, what would the likes of these atrocity perpetrators do if they knew that no court would ever hold them to account for their crimes?
There’s no straight line between the ICC’s actions and the deterrence of international crimes. But a world without legal consequences for atrocities is one in which violence, death, and destruction become the international system’s normal function rather than its failure.
ICC member states should therefore reject any negotiation with the US that would weaken the court’s jurisdiction and instead double down on protecting it from the impacts of sanctions. Washington alone cannot destroy the ICC. It needs the cooperation of the court’s member states to achieve their aims. Those states must not cave in.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: Australia warns tech giants of multibillion-dollar fines for online ‘harm’
noticias.resumen: New internet safety bill expected to pass this week could impose fines of up to 5 percent of firms' global revenue.
noticias.texto:
Australia warns tech giants of multibillion-dollar fines for online ‘harm’
New internet safety bill expected to pass this week could impose fines of up to 5 percent of firms’ global revenue.
Australia’s government has announced plans to impose hefty fines on tech companies if they fail to pull harmful content off their platforms.
Companies, including Google and Meta, could be hit with fines of up to five percent of their worldwide revenue under a proposed digital duty of care law detailed by the government on Tuesday.
That represents a sizable increase from the previously proposed financial penalty of 109 million Australian dollars ($72.2m), given that some platforms bring in hundreds of billions of dollars in annual revenue.
The new bill, agreed by the centre-left Labor government and the left-leaning Greens in the Senate, would also give individuals the right to sue platforms for enabling wrongdoing. It is expected to be approved in Parliament this week.
“This is seismic reform, this ‌is urgent reform and this is reform we will deliver to Australians in Parliament this week,” Communications Minister Anika Wells told reporters.
The law would replace a patchwork of enforceable codes of conduct drawn up by various online industries, from messaging apps to search engines to AI chatbots, with a single underlying law that forces them to proactively check for and stop harmful user experiences.
Targeted harms include material involving child sexual abuse, nonconsensual fake nude material, gender-based violence, self-harm promotion and terrorism.
‘World-leading reform’
In an effort to curb addictive features, Australians aged 16 or older will also have the option to turn off algorithm-driven feeds.
“It’s about Australia taking action on the side of parents and children, not foreign-owned tech companies,” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told Parliament.
“World-leading reform and we are getting it done. Just like we have led the world when it comes to the under-16s social media ban. This is the next step.”
Though tech firms generally agreed with the government’s aim of improving child protection and minimising harmful content, most opposed the bill on the grounds that it gave some discretion to government officials to decide what counted as harmful content.
Even before the government raised the potential fine, industry groups had said the law might encourage platforms to become heavy-handed when deciding what content ‌to take down as they sought to avoid punishment.
Greens Senator Sarah Hanson-Young said the legislation would help stop Australians from being exploited.
“Big tech for far too long has run our lives, dictated what we see in our social media feeds, and pumped our feeds full of addictive, harmful content and thought that they could just get away with it,” she said at a news conference.

noticias.titulo: Why Eisenkot is negotiating with Netanyahu
noticias.resumen: Talks with different political powers give Yashar leverage. But they also give Likud renewed political relevance.
noticias.texto:
Why Eisenkot is negotiating with Netanyahu
Talks with different political powers give Yashar leverage. But they also give Likud renewed political relevance.
Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot has an unusual problem. He holds the presidential mandate to form Israel’s next government after 67 members of the Knesset recommended him to President Isaac Herzog, yet those 67 votes do not constitute a ready-made coalition.
They come from parties that disagree not only on policy but also on the most basic question of who they are prepared to engage with politically. This is why Eisenkot is now negotiating with the very party he spent the entire election campaign vowing to remove from power.
His Yashar party and incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud have held repeated talks over a possible unity government. Simultaneously, Eisenkot is negotiating with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which were part of Netanyahu’s governing coalition, and is keeping open the possibility of a minority government supported by the Palestinian parties.
The latest round of talks with Likud ended without agreement. The two sides are still divided over who would serve as prime minister and over who would be included in the government.
At a first glance, engaging with Netanyahu does not make sense. Eisenkot is the leader of a camp whose main unifying purpose was to end Netanyahu’s rule. His ally, Avigdor Lieberman, refuses to serve in any government that includes Netanyahu. Other members of Eisenkot’s bloc remain deeply suspicious of returning Likud to government under its current leadership.
Yet the talks still serve Eisenkot politically, even if they lead nowhere. That is because he cannot allow Likud to monopolise the language of national unity. Since the election, Netanyahu has repeatedly presented a broad Jewish-Zionist unity government as the responsible answer to Israel’s political deadlock.
If Eisenkot had refused to enter negotiations, Netanyahu would have had an easy political argument: Likud offered unity, but the other side refused because of petty personal hostility towards its leader.
Negotiating changes the equation. Eisenkot can say that he did not reject unity; he tested it. He sent negotiators, held discussions and gave the option a genuine chance.
Demonstrating that he has done what it could matters even if the talks collapse. If they fail over Netanyahu’s insistence on serving first as prime minister in a rotation, Eisenkot can try to shift responsibility for the failure back onto him: the problem, he can argue, was not his refusal to sit with Likud, but Netanyahu’s refusal to relinquish the premiership after losing the election.
The talks also give Eisenkot leverage elsewhere. He currently has three possible routes to a government: some version of a unity government with Likud, an agreement with the Haredi parties, or a minority government dependent on support from Palestinian parties. He has publicly acknowledged all three. None is easy.
A Likud agreement requires resolving the much larger question of Netanyahu himself. The Haredi route requires compromises over military service, one of the central issues on which Eisenkot’s camp campaigned. The Palestinian-backed route faces opposition from Lieberman and others inside his own bloc.
Keeping all three options alive therefore has value. It tells every negotiating partner that Eisenkot may have somewhere else to go, and it strengthens his claim that he is exhausting every possible route before choosing a narrower and politically more controversial coalition.
The problem is that the negotiation process also works in Netanyahu’s favour. To push the conversation away from his election loss, he and his allies have zeroed in on the Palestinian parties, accusing them of “stealing” the vote.
Netanyahu has insisted that a “unity government” must mean the exclusion of the Palestinian parties. By doing so, he is attempting to remove any possible coalitions that include Palestinian representation from the Israeli political scene altogether. By trying to define which political forces are legitimate and which are not, Netanyahu is seeking to retain and even grow his political relevance.
This strategy seems to be working. Before the election, much of Eisenkot’s camp was organised around a simple idea: Netanyahu must go. Now Netanyahu is once again a viable coalition partner. Some of Eisenkot’s allies, like Naftali Bennett, have also held discussions with Likud.
The line has therefore shifted. Netanyahu has moved, at least partially, from being the political problem around which the opposition organised itself to being one of the possible solutions that the party with the mandate is required to consider.
That leaves Eisenkot in a strange position. He is trying to use negotiations with Likud to show that Netanyahu is the obstacle to unity. But the more he negotiates, the more a coalition with his political nemesis is becoming normalised. Meanwhile, a cabinet supported by Palestinian parties is beginning to look a lot more like an unacceptable option, even though those parties helped Yashar get the mandate in the first place.
For Eisenkot to win this game, he would have to find a way to bring the focus back on Netanyahu’s toxicity. He would have to convince the Israeli public that Netanyahu’s political demise is worth whatever painful political choice he would have to make.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Arsenal and their fans were left frustrated at the weekend despite opening up a six-point lead at the top of the Premier League with a 2-2 draw at Newcastle United.
But a firm grip on their English top-flight title defence and a 10-game unbeaten streak across all competitions give Mikel Arteta’s side plenty of reasons to be optimistic for Tuesday’s UCL fixture in north London.
Dortmund, too, have been impressive in their own ways. Unbeaten in Germany this season, they sit two points clear of defending champions Bayern Munich atop the Bundesliga table. Niko Kovac’s team are also on an eight-match unbeaten run.
Eberechi Eze, who also scored in the last game, has been Arsenal’s leading scorer in this year’s Champions League with two goals so far, while fellow stars Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard have also bagged a goal each.

noticias.titulo: Pennsylvania reports ninth measles death in ongoing state outbreak
noticias.resumen: CDC and state figures on measles deaths differ as Pennsylvania faces an escalating health crisis in 46 counties.
noticias.texto:
Pennsylvania reports ninth measles death in ongoing state outbreak
CDC and state figures on measles deaths differ as Pennsylvania faces escalating health crisis in 46 counties.
Pennsylvania health officials have reported another death linked to the ongoing measles outbreak, bringing the state’s death toll associated with the highly contagious viral disease to nine.
The state Department of Health confirmed on Monday the death of an unvaccinated resident of Centre County in central Pennsylvania who tested positive for measles.
Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit US state, has recorded 1,638 confirmed measles cases across 46 counties so far in 2026, including 330 hospitalisations.
The nine deaths were recorded across five counties, as Lancaster County accounted ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌for three deaths, while Jefferson County reported two.
Virginia recorded its first measles-related death in more than three decades on Friday, just days after the United States lost its hard-fought designation as having eliminated the highly contagious virus.
Meanwhile, Wisconsin has reported two deaths, and New York state has recorded one child death linked to the disease.
However, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reported only six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, without specifying the states where the deaths were recorded.
The discrepancy between state and federal tolls emerged earlier this year after the health agency, under US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures.
The US Department of Health and Human Services said it was “saddened to hear of another death in Pennsylvania”, adding that the CDC has provided the state with nearly $4m in one-time emergency funding for response efforts in 2027.
A total of 5,838 measles cases were confirmed across the country this year as of November 19, according to CDC data. The figure is the highest number reported by the CDC since 1991.
Children below the age of five account for 18 percent of cases, while children between the ages of five and 19 make up 41 percent of cases.
The number of confirmed cases in November 2026 is more than double the 2,289 confirmed measles cases reported for the full year of 2025.

noticias.titulo: WHO chief visits Cuba as healthcare system deteriorates
noticias.resumen: Analysts say fuel shortages blamed on US sanctions are worsening the crisis.
noticias.texto:
WHO chief visits Cuba as healthcare system deteriorates
Analysts say fuel shortages blamed on US sanctions are worsening the crisis.
The World Health Organization’s top official is in Cuba, as the island continues to suffer under an ailing healthcare system amid an economic crisis deepened by United States sanctions.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus visited a paediatric cardiology centre in Havana on Monday alongside the country’s Public Health Minister Dr Jose Angel Portal Miranda.
“Hola, Havana!” Tedros wrote in a post on X during his tour. “Here for a visit to discuss Cuba’s health situation, challenged by sanctions, fuel and electricity shortages.”
The WHO leader arrived Sunday at the invitation of health authorities in the Caribbean nation for a three-day visit, the second time he has visited Cuba as WHO director-general.
Portal Miranda welcomed Tedros, saying it was an opportunity for him to see firsthand the reality of the Cuban healthcare system and the challenges that it faces.
Sharp decline
Cuba’s once-vaunted system of free universal healthcare has deteriorated sharply.
Analysts say the crisis has been compounded by fuel shortages that they blame on stricter US sanctions on the island’s energy sector, worsening an economy that already had been limping for years.
A government report released in June said that the survival rate for children with cancer had fallen to 65 percent from 85 percent, before the energy blockade began in January.
Hospitals across Cuba face shortages of supplies including syringes, gauze, vaccines and anaesthetics. They also lack spare parts to repair equipment such as haemodialysis and CT scan machines.
“The situation is shocking,” said Mario Cruz Penate, the Pan American Health Organization and WHO representative on the island.
He noted that Cuba has long enjoyed health indicators comparable to those of developed nations, including low mortality, high life expectancy, broad vaccination coverage and widespread prenatal care.

noticias.titulo: Five women killed every hour by family members or partners — UN report
noticias.resumen: On average, 129 women or girls were killed every day in 2025 by someone in their close social circle, UN data showed.
noticias.texto:
Five women killed every hour by family members or partners — UN report
November 24, 2026
Around 47,000 women and girls — or five every hour — were killed by intimate partners or family members in 2025, according to a United Nations report released on Tuesday.
This figure equates to around 60% of women and girls who were victims of intentional homicides last year, the report said ahead of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25.
The total fatalities were calculated based on statistics from 122 countries and territories. They translate to an average of 129 women and girls killed by their close social circle each day.
Africa recorded the highest number of femicides, at 22,100. Asia followed, with 15,100 victims, ahead of the Americas with 7,400, Europe with 2,100 and Oceania with 300.
Femicide is a hate crime broadly defined as "the intentional killing of women or girls because they are female."
One in three women experienced physical or sexual violence
The report also found that although global homicide rates have declined, femicide rates have fallen at a slower pace, particularly in the Americas and Europe.
According to the UN, this shows the barriers women often face in accessing the justice system and that "these crimes are deeply rooted in social norms and gender stereotypes."
Nearly one in three women worldwide have experienced physical or sexual violence, yet only 7% reported it to the police, a separate UN Women report found.
According to estimates by UN Women and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC, the number of women and girls killed by a family member or an intimate partner has wavered between 45,000 and 51,000 over the past several years.
"Frightening attitudes, social norms, and the failure of institutional safeguards create an environment in which killing a wife, daughter, mother, or sister becomes 'tolerable,'" UNODC director Monica Juma said. "Changing this reality calls for sustained action across all levels of society."
Sima Bahous, executive director of UN Women, said that the world needed to "act urgently to ensure no warning sign is ignored, no survivor is left without protection, and no perpetrator escapes accountability."

noticias.titulo: Bombed factories, billion-dollar opportunity: Why German companies keep investing in Ukraine
noticias.resumen: German companies remain committed to Ukraine despite million-dollar losses, an unreliable energy supply and a shortage of skilled workers. They are betting on new markets and long-term growth.
noticias.texto:
German business bets on Ukraine despite war damage
November 24, 2026
Power plants, train stations, shopping centers, warehouses, and residential buildings: the massive Russian attacks on civilian targets across Ukraine continue unabated. Industrial facilities have also come under attack, affecting German companies.
"Over the past few months, goods and facilities worth several hundred million euros have gone up in smoke," reported Oliver Gierlichs, who heads Bayer's operations in Ukraine and serves as president of the German-Ukrainian Chamber of Industry and Commerce (AHK Ukraine). The damage is estimated at €500 million ($544 million).
At the 9th German-Ukrainian Business Forum, held in Berlin on November 20, Gierlichs described the situation on the ground. Together with two other German business associations, the AHK had invited around 500 participants from politics and industry, including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi.
According to the AHK, just over 2,000 German companies are active in Ukraine. German direct investment in the country totals around €1 billion ($1.1 billion). The situation remains critical due to the ongoing attacks, Gierlichs said. "We are preparing for a difficult winter."
Ukrainian economy under pressure
After posting comparatively strong growth rates in recent years, Ukraine's economy has slowed sharply since the summer.
"The intensified Russian attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure and production capacity in recent months have significantly worsened the economic outlook," according to the latest analysis by the Kyiv School of Economics (KSE), which warns of "substantial risks."
Energy supplies are under strain, and electricity remains in short supply. Companies are also grappling with a worker shortage, as many people have been mobilized for military service or have fled abroad to escape the attacks. German business leaders also cite burdensome approval processes and unclear regulations in Ukraine.
"Not a single German company has left Ukraine since the start of this war," Merz emphasized at the business forum. He also pointed out that "in 2025, trade between Germany and Ukraine exceeded €12 billion, an increase of 4.4% compared with the previous year."
Benefits extend beyond Ukraine
Military cooperation currently tops the agenda in German-Ukrainian relations. Germany continues to supply large quantities of defense equipment, but new capabilities are increasingly being developed through joint ventures. At the business forum, held at the House of German Business Associations in Berlin, the long-range combat drone "Anubis," produced by the German-Ukrainian joint venture Auterion Airlogix, was displayed in the foyer. The drone was developed in Ukraine, and the software in Germany.
A total of 5,000 drones are to be produced near Munich. This marks the first time Germany has established industrial-scale production of heavy attack drones on its own soil. "Through this cooperation, Germany's technological capacity for innovation is expanding in ways that would have been unimaginable just a few years ago," Merz said.
The chancellor is convinced that cooperation between the two countries will also benefit Germany's civilian industries. "What we invest in Ukraine today will be repaid many times over through stability, export opportunities, joint projects, and economic growth," Merz said.
$524 billion for reconstruction
For foreign companies operating in Ukraine, it is a continuous balancing act: on the one hand, substantial risks persist; on the other, Ukraine represents a land of opportunity, with a market size virtually unmatched anywhere else in Europe. In February 2025, the European Commission and the Ukrainian government estimated that Ukraine would need $524 billion in funding for reconstruction and recovery over the following ten years. This figure has likely grown even larger since then.
In this context, Ukraine is increasingly seen not merely as a recipient of aid but also as a potential future business destination. The country aims to modernize its economy, bring it into alignment with EU standards, and achieve deeper integration into the European single market over the long term.
Mechanical engineering, energy, and infrastructure opportunities
"We see significant opportunities in the defense industry, the energy sector, infrastructure, information technology, and many other industries," Ukrainian Prime Minister Koretskyi said in Berlin. "German expertise and Ukrainian drive, combined with unity and determination, make for a powerful partnership," Oliver Gierlichs noted.
However, achieving this will require greater support, the AHK president emphasized. "Companies need reliable financing and investment guarantees, as well as effective instruments to protect themselves against war-related risks." Reliable logistics, predictable business conditions, and faster administrative procedures will also be essential, he said.
Investment guarantees and reforms as prerequisites for new projects
At the business forum, Chancellor Merz pledged support in these areas while also calling on Ukraine to pursue further reforms, particularly to strengthen the rule of law and combat corruption. "These reforms are a prerequisite for additional financial assistance and investment."
Another challenge stems from the differing interests of the partners. German companies are seeking to expand into new markets, while their Ukrainian counterparts seek technology transfers and local production to keep as much value creation as possible in the country. "Export fees or legal restrictions on the transfer of intellectual property rights stand in the way of joint innovation efforts," the chancellor cautioned.
Who is financing Ukraine's reconstruction?
Representatives of Ukrainian business associations estimate that the private sector could cover up to 40% of Ukraine's reconstruction costs in the long term. For now, however, many projects rely on support from international development banks, government guarantees, or public funding programs. Without such support, many investments would be difficult to undertake.
In principle, business investment follows a straightforward model: companies commit their own capital and bear the losses if a venture fails commercially. When bank loans are involved, the risk is initially shared by the company and the lending institution. Government-backed projects are different: when investment guarantees are in place, companies are compensated for any losses incurred.
This does not apply when companies incur losses as a result of their own business decisions. Compensation may, however, be available in cases involving political actions, such as expropriation, or when war destroys assets and disrupts operations. Under a government guarantee, the taxpayer ultimately bears the risk in such circumstances. By the end of 2025, the German government had provided investment guarantees covering a total investment volume of €558 million ($611 million) in Ukraine.
German companies hoping to benefit from Ukraine's reconstruction need to establish partnerships and build a long-term presence in the country now. After all, the competition is already heating up. At the German-Ukrainian Business Forum, participants noted that German business leaders have often been more risk-averse than their counterparts from Turkey, India, and China. International interest in Ukraine's reconstruction is considerable, and German companies are far from the only ones vying for contracts.
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: How the AI trade could trap even cautious investors
noticias.resumen: From Nvidia to Coreweave, AI and tech stocks have swung sharply in recent months. Some investors still see plenty of room to run, while others are trying to diversify — and finding it harder than expected.
noticias.texto:
How cautious investors are struggling to avoid the AI bubble
November 24, 2026
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index roared back to life this week after a worrying sell-off recently that saw huge falls in technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks.
After suffering its worst week since the pandemic crash of March 2020, the Nasdaq opened Monday nearly 1,700 points, or 7%, higher.
The AI trade received a further boost after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced to resign amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
The chipmaker's stock rose more than 30% on the news, opening at nearly $170 (€155.5) per share and recovering most of the losses since last month, when the affair was first reported.
How passive investing is fueling the AI trade
The recent volatility around AI, memory chips and other technology stocks has unnerved even the most experienced and bullish investors.
Yet, those seeking a safe haven away from the United States stock market, which has enjoyed the majority of the AI hype — along with Taiwan and South Korea — are increasingly finding few places to shelter.
Economists warn that this is partly due to the way index funds, including exchange-traded funds (ETFs), work. These funds hold the pensions and other savings of hundreds of millions of passive investors.
These indices have become increasingly exposed to the AI boom.
Riding the winners works — until it doesn't
Most flagship index funds are keen to ride winners, so they automatically buy stocks according to a company's market value. The bigger a company grows, the more of it they hold.
The values of Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet and other US technology giants have benefited from this effect, with many soaring after ChatGPT was first released in late 2022.
The US also has an outsized position in funds that track the global economy. Nine of the top 10 holdings of the MSCI All Country World Index (ACWI), an index of more than 2,400 firms across 47 developed and emerging markets, are US Big Tech names.
The other is TSMC, a Taiwanese chipmaker that produces 90% of the high-end AI semiconductors.
Together, these 10 holdings make up nearly a quarter of the index.
Although it's a global index, nearly two-thirds of MSCI ACWI's value is in US-listed companies, even though they make up only around a fifth of its firms.
Don't put all your chips in AI stocks
"A well-diversified portfolio should ... reasonably represent the entire global economy," Gerd Kommer, founder of the Munich-based asset manager Gerd Kommer Invest, told DW.
"That's not the case if 70% of the portfolio is concentrated in just one country — the US. The global economy is more resilient than any national economy."
Kommer, who is known as Germany's "ETF pope," said investors need exposure to all economic sectors and that no single sector should make up more than a quarter of a portfolio.
Yet, even if investors want to avoid US-dominated World funds altogether, the AI trade still overshadows several other top index funds.
In MSCI's Emerging Market index, for example, the top 10 make up 37.5% of its value and TSMC alone accounts for almost 16%. Tech, chip and internet firms make up eight of the largest holdings, alongside two banks — one Chinese, one Indian.
How funds fuel investor hubris
That matters, according to Dimitri Vayanos, a finance professor at the London School of Economics who studies how passive investing pushes up the prices of the biggest firms.
"My model suggests that the effects of flows into index funds are larger when the large stocks happen to be in the same industry," Vayanos told DW.
When some investors get over-optimistic about a company and push the stock price up, index funds add to that price pressure.
Professional investors then often bet against overpriced stocks, a practice known as "shorting," which helps pull prices back down. But that's far riskier with, say, a tech giant than with a small firm.
"Being short 1% of SpaceX involves much more risk than being short 1% of a small company," said Vayanos.
The problem gets worse when the biggest firms are all in the same sector, as they are now. As short-sellers hold back, the biggest stocks climb further, creating what he calls an "amplification-overpricing spiral."
Lower AI risk outside of US, Asia
To cut exposure to AI-related stocks, investors may have to turn to developed market funds outside the US and Southeast Asia. These funds have offered lower returns over the past decade.
In the MSCI Europe, Australasia and Far East (EAFE) index fund, the top 10 holdings make up about 14.5% of the index, about 40% lower than the all-country world index.
EAFE's major holdings include healthcare giant Roche, oil major Shell, HSBC bank and Nestle — the world's largest food and beverage company.
However, its biggest holding, ASML, is still very much part of the AI trade. The Dutch tech firm sells the equipment that firms such as TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix and Micron need to make their chips.
AI crash will have ripple effects
If Monday's rebound in the AI trade is sustained, stock prices may move sharply higher over the next few months. Yet if history is a guide, the bubble will eventually burst, leaving both institutional and passive investors nursing heavy losses.
Kommer warned that if the AI bubble bursts, "in all likelihood it will drag down the global stock market," though the damage would be most severe in tech and AI stocks.
Those hit hardest would be retail investors "with heavy portfolio weights in tech and AI stocks," he told DW, including "a lot of people who have bought individual AI-related stocks on top of their equity ETFs."
LSE's Vayanos thinks it is still "certainly safer to hold an ETF than to hold individual stocks."
But as index providers add mega-IPOs such as SpaceX and Claude-maker Anthropic to benchmarks within weeks of their debut, and money continues to pour into passive funds, he warned that "the conditions are present for the effects of our theory to be even stronger."

noticias.titulo: EU imposes import quotas for hybrid vehicles from China
noticias.resumen: The EU is trying to protect its own car manufacturers from what it called "overcapacity" in China. Carmakers in the bloc, especially in Germany, have been lagging behind their Chinese rivals.
noticias.texto:
EU imposes import quotas for hybrid vehicles from China
November 24, 2026
The European Union announced on Tuesday that it was capping the number of hybrid vehicles that can be imported into the bloc from China.
The quota is to stand at around 15% on top of the volume imported in the previous year.
The announcement follows an agreement made between the EU's trade commissioner Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Trade Minister Wang Wentao in October.
China, on Tuesday, called on the EU to stick to the "compliant, and balanced" agreement the two sides had reached.
The cap is set to come into effect on December 1.
What did the EU say about the import quota for Chinese hybrid vehicles?
"These restrictions are needed to protect EU industry against a sharp recent increase in imports of such vehicles … [following] an investigation that showed imports of hybrid vehicles into the EU have increased significantly since 2023," the European Commission said in a statement.
"The surge in imports of hybrid passenger vehicles into the EU has been driven by growing global production overcapacity. It is also prompted by increased use of trade-restrictive measures in other major markets," it added, in reference to the range of tariffs introduced in the US under the Trump administration.
According to the statement, the import quota covers two types of hybrid vehicle: "full hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), including mild hybrid electric vehicles (MHEVs)."
Although specifically designed to deal with the influx of Chinese cars into the European market, the country-specific import quota will be valid for all countries whose imports made up more than 2% of EU imports in 2025. Other importers will face a residual cap.
Why is an EU import quota important for Germany?
The goal behind import quotas is to protect a country's, or in this case the European Union's, own producers.
China has become a major player in the car manufacturing market in recent years, especially when it comes to electric and hybrid vehicles, a sector where European manufacturers have fallen behind.
Germany, as the EU's largest economy and a major exporter of vehicles, is a primary beneficiary of the import quota. Several of Germany's car manufacturers have announced widespread layoffs as they see their market shares shrink.
In October, German car manufacturers saw their sales fall by 5.7% in the EU despite a growing market. This meant their market share in the bloc fell from 41.5% to 38.2%, according to consulting firm EY.
Europe's booming hybrid and electric market
A report by the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) published on Tuesday found that electric vehicles and hybrids have seen a large uptick in new registrations in Europe in October over the same time last year.
It found that new electric car registrations were up 61.4% across the bloc while plug-in hybrids were up in particular in Italy (+73.1%), Spain (+32.3%), and Germany (+11%).
Hybrid electric vehicles were around a third of all new registrations, with plug-in hybrids making up around 10%.
"The main beneficiaries of this trend are in China," EY said in comments to AFP. "Chinese manufacturers, which are heavily focused on electric cars and plug-in hybrids, increased their EU sales by 73.4% and achieved a new record market share of 13.1%."
"The market share losses suffered by German manufacturers are not an outlier and are not a problem limited to individual countries — it is a clear trend that is now evident in all major European markets," said Constantin Gall of EY. "This is alarming, because Europe is the home market of the German auto industry."

noticias.titulo: German directors' doc on stolen film wins International Emmy Award
noticias.resumen: Two German film students confronted the American who won festival prizes with their animated movie. "The Talented Mr. F," their documentary on their fight against plagiarism, is now in the spotlight.
noticias.texto:
German directors' doc on stolen film wins International Emmy Award
November 24, 2026
It sounds like the plot of a screenplay, but it happened to two Berlin film students in real life. The documentary they made out of their unusual story, "The Talented Mr. F," has now won an International Emmy Award.
Moritz Henneberg and Julius Drost had created an animated short film for their final project at university.
"Butty" tells the tale of a household robot that gets kicked out when it can't do its job properly.
When the two filmmakers posted the work on YouTube, this touching tale quickly went viral. After generating a huge amount of hits, the duo decided to submit their work to festivals — but they were in for a shock: Organizers told them the film had already been submitted under a different name.
How could that have happened?
US student Samuel Felinton downloaded the film, made minimal edits, gave it a new title, "T-130," and removed the original credits. As the alleged author, he went on to win numerous prizes and made a name for himself in the United States.
A story turned into a documentary, 'The Talented Mr. F'
Shocked by the blatant theft of their work, Henneberg and Drost sought legal advice. They were told that if they opted to sue, the process would be arduous and costly. So, the filmmakers took matters into their own hands and went to the US to confront Felinton — filming their journey along the way.
"We'd already made documentary films," Henneberg told DW. "And the idea just popped into our heads: This is a brilliant story — let's make a documentary about it."
The two directors had developed a kind of fascination for the man who'd stolen their film.
"We looked at his vlogs and sort of took a deep dive into his world," said Drost. "We almost saw him as a kind of celebrity. We discovered a lot about him and really wanted to meet him in person."
Fascination instead of anger
While family and friends reacted with anger, the two young filmmakers remained surprisingly calm. They were more perplexed than anything: "Our families and friends hated Samuel. But we just wanted to understand what had happened," they said.
The pair put together a film crew and traveled to Morgantown, West Virginia — the university town where Felinton lives. With the help of a New York filmmaker pretending to make a documentary about young animators, they won Felinton's trust — and then Henneberg, Drost and Felinton were finally in a room together.
The two German filmmakers had prepared for all manner of scenarios ahead of the meeting: "We expected an emotional reaction — that he'd run away, cry, be ashamed or get aggressive. But he remained completely calm. That was the only thing we hadn't bargained for. We thought his world would implode. But he showed barely any emotion at all," they recalled.
Felinton explained how he'd shortened and "improved" the film and that this was how it became such a success. He agreed to transfer any prize money. His manner was cool and matter-of-fact, which Drost and Henneberg found both unsettling and fascinating. After their chat, the three barbecued together and played a round of basketball.
Sue or stay creative?
Later, many viewers accused the two German filmmakers of being too soft on the plagiarist. Others praised their approach.
"The reactions were very divided," said Drost. "Some said we should've sued him or punched him in the face. Others said we'd shown new ways to resolve conflicts."
"And in the end, it wasn't personal," added Henneberg. "He wanted to make something of himself — he could've taken another film. But if a big studio like Pixar had stolen our film, that'd be quite a different story."
And so, Henneberg and Drost made the conscious decision to keep things respectful.
They didn't want to "publicly embarrass him or punish him any more than necessary," they said, adding that their documentary was sufficient "revenge."
The title of the documentary, "Der talentierte Mister F." ("The Talented Mister F."), is no coincidence. It's a play on the movie title "The Talented Mr. Ripley," the story of a young man who assumes the identity of a wealthy heir and ends up mired in a web of lies, fraud and, finally, murder. And just like Mr. Ripley, Felinton had also assumed a false identity.
Award-winning works
Felinton did actually end up sending them the trophies he had won, as well as a sum of money.
For their part, however, the festivals preferred to keep their distance from the saga. As one organizer said: The prize has been awarded, and there's nothing we can do about it — it's up to these guys to work things out between themselves.
For the original filmmakers themselves, the scandal has also had a positive impact: Since the documentary was released in Germany in October 2025, their animation film has garnered even more attention on YouTube. Henneberg and Drost uploaded it again, and in the credits, special thanks also go out to Samuel Felinton.
And now, the documentary is winning its own awards: Before being honored with the International Emmy Award, it also won a Grimme Prize, one of Germany's most prestigious television awards.
'Don't be afraid to show yourselves'
Felinton was able to steal the film in the first place in part because when it first appeared online in 2023, it could just be downloaded from YouTube.
Drost and Henneberg say uploading "Butty" back then wasn't a mistake, saying that was the risk of putting something online.
The alternative would have been not to show the film at all, they said; then no one would have seen it.
They have a clear message for young creatives.
"Don't be discouraged. Be aware that something like this can happen — but stay creative in how you deal with it. Suing is expensive and often doesn't do much good. Instead, show the world that you're the authors."
What started out as film plagiarism ended up becoming material for another project. And that's perhaps the most unusual twist in this very quirky story.
This article was originally published in German in February 2026 and was updated on November 24, 2026, following the International Emmy Awards.

noticias.titulo: Istanbul 'lion hunt' ends with no big cat found after all
noticias.resumen: After a major search operation for a lion on the loose in Istanbul woodlands, Turkish authorities said "the animal was neither a lion nor any other big cat."
noticias.texto:
Istanbul 'lion hunt' ends after no big cat found after all
Published November 23, 2026last updated November 24, 2026
A large-scale search operation for a suspected lion sighted in woodland north of Istanbul has ended, with the animal in question found to be neither a lion nor any other type of big cat, according to the Istanbul governor's office.
The governor's office first issued a statement on Sunday evening saying that security cameras had captured footage of a lion on the loose in Sariyer, north of Istanbul's European side. It said "the lion has been located and the efforts to capture it were underway."
The parks authority also said in an online statement that police officers in the area had spotted "an animal resembling a lion" on surveillance cameras.
Turkish media published grainy images purportedly showing a lioness walking through a grassy area. Some media reports suggested it had escaped from a nearby home.
The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office also issued a statement saying it had launched an investigation focused on identifying the lion's owner.
After a day of searching, however, the Istanbul governor's office said "no concrete evidence indicating ‌the presence of a lion was found."
It said based on new footage, "it has been determined that the animal in the footage is neither a lion nor any other species of big cat."
The governor's office did not provide further information about what the animal seen in the footage was.
Outcry among activists
The earlier reports about a lion on the loose had sparked an outrage among activists.
Northern Forests Defense, an independent ecology advocacy movement, called for "the individuals who illegally held this lion captive to be identified and brought to justice."
"Removing wild animals from their natural habitats and keeping them in captivity in villas is a crime," the organization said on X.
Wildlife conservationist Gokce Coskun said on X that "there are thousands of people keeping lions illegally in Turkey" and "licensed 'lion parks' have sprung up everywhere."
Last year, a lion that escaped from a "theme park" near the southern city of Antalya was shot dead after attacking a man.
Doganay Tolunay, an ecology professor at Istanbul University, said questions must be asked about how a globally threatened species was brought into Turkey, how it passed through customs and why those keeping it have not been identified.
Although keeping wild animals as pets is forbidden in Turkey, the country has become a hub for the illegal wild animal trade as traffickers exploit its air links to Africa and Asia.
In December 2024, a young gorilla was rescued after being discovered in a crate at Istanbul Airport.

noticias.titulo: Pakistani astronaut to join Chinese space mission
noticias.resumen: A Pakistani astronaut is set to become to the first foreigner to board China's Tiangong space station. Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a payload specialist, will join the Shenzhou-24 mission when it launches on Wednesday.
noticias.texto:
Pakistani astronaut to join Chinese space mission
November 24, 2026
China on Tuesday unveiled the crew for this week's Shenzhou-24 space mission, with a Pakistani payload specialist set to become the first foreign astronaut to board its Tiangong space station.
The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) said that Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a 40-year-old former Pakistani air force pilot, would join two Chinese colleagues when the mission launches from the Jiuquan launch center in China's northwestern Gobi Desert at 8:18 a.m. local time (0018 GMT) on Wednesday.
"I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis," Ali told a news conference on Tuesday, switching between Urdu, Mandarin and English.
"To every child who is watching while I'm in orbit, just look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams," he said.
Pakistan: 'Source of joy and pride'
Pakistani officials welcomed Ali's selection as a significant milestone in relations between Islamabad and Beijing who are this year marking 75 years of cooperation in space.
Information Minister Attaullah Tarar described the mission as a "source of joy and pride for the entire nation" and Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said the mission underscored the "iron brotherhood" between the two countries.
"This mission is not a finish line; I hope the next chapter of China-Pakistan space cooperation will grow from one astronaut and one flight to multiple joint flights, to the Moon, to Mars, and beyond," said Ali.
"Together with my Chinese crew mates, I will show that this friendship is real, not only on paper, but also in orbit."
What will Pakistani astronaut Ali do in space?
Ali will not be the first Pakistani in space, with Monaco-based polar explorer Namira Salim having flown on Virgin Galactic's Galactic 04 mission in October 2023. But he will be the first foreign astronaut to join a Chinese mission.
During a short orbital flight expected to last around five days, Ali will carry out a series of experiments in the fields of biotechnology and photosynthetic microorganisms before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft, which docked at the Tiangong in May.
China has poured billions of dollars into its space program. Its prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.
Beijing is aiming to land Chinese astronauts on the moon for the first time by 2030 and is seen as the main space rival to the United States, which is hoping to return to the lunar surface in 2028.

noticias.titulo: Chinese official gets death sentence in spy case, report says
noticias.resumen: A Chinese official recruited while working abroad was paid more than a million yuan to leak secrets, state-affiliated media reported.
noticias.texto:
Chinese official gets death sentence in spy case, report says
November 24, 2026
A Chinese court has sentenced a government official to death for spying for a foreign country, according to a report published Monday by a state-linked social media account.
The official was reportedly convicted of passing on secret information in exchange for payment.
What do we know?
The report was published on an online account run by Gold Wall Press, a publisher tied to the National Administration of State Secrets Protection.
The report named the man only as Ma. The AFP news agency called him a ministerial official, while Reuters described him as an administrative official in China's central apparatus.
According to the report, a foreign operative called "Kailin" recruited Ma while he worked overseas. Kailin first met him regularly on the pretext of learning Chinese. The talks then turned to politically sensitive topics.
A colleague of Kailin's later threatened to tell Chinese authorities about Ma's earlier disclosures unless he cooperated. Later, Ma signed an agreement committing him to confidentiality and loyalty. He received monthly payments and a laptop for sending and receiving intelligence, the report said.
What is the official accused of selling?
Upon returning to China, Ma kept passing on information, sending more than 100 intelligence reports, 35 of them later deemed "top secret," the report said. He was allegedly paid over one million yuan ($150,000, €138,000).
The sentence also includes confiscation of all his personal property.
The report did not say when or where Ma was sentenced, or whether he had already been executed.
Chinese courts rarely publish details of state security cases, but the secrecy regulator and the Ministry of State Security have increasingly publicized them as a warning to officials not to become spies.
"This shocking case serves as yet another wake-up call," the report said.
In recent years, the US CIA has published videos in Mandarin seeking informants in China's bureaucracy and military, which Beijing has called a "damning confession."

noticias.titulo: What happens if a nuclear weapon explodes in space?
noticias.resumen: Earth's atmosphere offers protection from a nuclear blast in space, but satellites are more exposed. We explain how radiation could damage them, why the effects can linger and what protection is possible.
noticias.texto:
What happens if a nuclear weapon explodes in space?
November 24, 2026
A nuclear explosion in space would be unlikely to cause widespread injuries on Earth. But it could disable satellites that provide services we depend on every day, including some that save lives.
In the United States, satellite failures could make it harder for emergency crews to communicate in remote areas. If GPS were also disrupted, drivers and pilots could lose navigation guidance, and financial networks could lose a source of precise time.
We have some idea of what would happen because it's already been done.
What does history teach us?
On the evening of July 8, 1962, people in Hawaii held "watch-the-bomb parties" and followed the countdown on shortwave radio. Then the night sky lit up. The United States had detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometers (250 miles) above the Pacific. The test was called Starfish Prime.
An electromagnetic pulse knocked out some streetlights in Hawaii, and some Pacific radio links briefly went down. The glow faded within minutes, but some satellites failed months later.
How does the physics change in space?
The air was too thin for a conventional fireball to form or for a destructive shock wave to reach the ground. Charged particles made denser air below glow, creating an artificial aurora. The atmosphere also absorbed much of the initial radiation.
Satellites are especially vulnerable because they orbit above most of the atmosphere that shields people on the ground from the initial radiation.
In orbit, the initial burst of X-rays can damage spacecraft right away. But Earth's magnetic field can also trap electrons released after the blast, as it did after Starfish Prime. Satellites receive another dose each time they cross the resulting radiation belt. Over time, that exposure can damage electronics and solar panels.
Which systems would be exposed?
That would depend on where the explosion happened and which satellites crossed the radiation belt. GPS satellites send signals that help phones, planes and ships work out where they are. They orbit about 20,200 kilometers above Earth and could keep working even if satellites closer to Earth failed.
But satellites do different jobs. A ship's emergency beacon can use GPS to work out its location, then send it to rescuers through a separate satellite network. If part of that network failed, the alert could take longer to get through.
Is it legal, and could it be detected?
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars its parties from placing nuclear weapons in orbit. The 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty prohibits its parties from carrying out nuclear explosions in space.
The Outer Space Treaty has no dedicated system for checking what spacecraft carry. A detonation is easier to detect because US satellite sensors are designed to pick up the signals it gives off.
Can the US protect itself?
Shielding could help protect satellite electronics, and backups could keep some services running. During a GPS outage, pilots over the contiguous US can use ground-based navigation aids. Operators could launch replacements, but those satellites could still face lingering radiation or debris.
Radiation could leave many satellites intact but unable to steer. If two objects collided, fragments from the crash could hit other satellites, creating more debris and triggering further collisions. If enough debris built up for the chain reaction to keep going on its own, it could continue even if no new satellites were launched. This is known as Kessler syndrome.
Whether an explosion would trigger such a cascade is uncertain. If it did, the debris could endanger replacement satellites for years.
Could radioactive fallout reach the ground?
Some radioactive particles could enter the atmosphere and eventually settle on the ground. But a blast in space is too far away to sweep up the soil and water that carry fallout from a surface explosion.
As the particles disperse, their radioactivity decreases over time. The concentrated local fallout that can expose people near a ground-level blast to high doses would be unlikely.

noticias.titulo: Germany news: Volkswagen begins wage talks with IG Metall union
