The plaintiffs are seeking $1.3 million in compensation for health problems and medical expenses, as well as $5 million to restore the environment. Their lawyers say they worry their clients might come under pressure or intimidation to withdraw their testimony.
The mother, however, said she had no such fears. "We have a right to a clean environment," she said, "and to health."

noticias.titulo: Meet Colombia's fuzzy 'water guardians'
noticias.resumen: High in the Colombian Andes, a growing number of volunteers are racing to save an unusual plant that helps supply water to millions — one tiny seedling at a time.
noticias.texto:
Meet Colombia's fuzzy 'water guardians'
MONGUÍ, Colombia — Moisés Moreno greets visitors at his greenhouse 10,000 feet high in the Andes Mountains. Underneath the plastic roof, he nurtures tiny seedlings that can grow to be 30-feet tall.
"Do you know anything about frailejons?" Moreno asks his visitors, who are mostly clueless.
Related to the sunflower, frailejons are the iconic flora of Colombia's high mountain wetlands, which are known as páramos, and are vital for the country's water supply.
The wooly fuzz on their leaves protect frailejons from the cold and absorb water from the cloud cover. This helps maintain moisture in the páramos, which are the source of major rivers, and much of Colombia's water.
But frailejons and the páramos where they grow face a growing array of threats, including farmers, cattle ranchers and coal miners who are gradually pushing higher into the Andes. In addition, climate change is warming the mountains, allowing invasive species to survive at higher altitudes and disrupt their fragile ecosystems.
Of the nearly 150 species of frailejons, two-thirds are at risk and 17 are endangered, says Mauricio Diazgranados, a Colombian expert on the plant who is chief science officer at the New York Botanical Garden.
"They are a keystone species for maintaining the páramos and play a key role in water production," he says. "But most frailejons are in trouble,"
When explorers first spotted the shrubs mysteriously protruding from the mountain fog centuries ago, they reminded them of hooded monks. Hence the name frailejon, which is Spanish for "big friar."
The long, thin leaves of some species bend toward the sky and resemble palm fronds. Many are stout in the middle because, rather than falling to the ground, their dying leaves slump down to form a brownish outer shell to their trunks.
The Muisca Indians, who once populated the area, considered frailejons to be sacred guardians of the water. When he first came across the plants as a teenager in Colombia, Diazgranados says: "I became completely captivated."
By contrast, Moreno, 53, who runs the frailejon greenhouse, used to be one of the plant's predators. Growing up on a mountainside farm near the central Colombian town of Monguí, Moreno and neighboring farmers knew little about them and chopped them down to make way for potato fields and cow pastures.
"We viewed them as a nuisance," Moreno says.
Later, while employed by a coal mine, he was injured during a cave-in and vowed to work above ground in the fresh mountain air.
On his own he began studying páramo ecosystem that he'd grown up in, started his greenhouse and began leading tourists and volunteers on expeditions to replace the frailejons that had been wiped out.
"I felt inspired to do something to protect the páramos," he says.
Elsewhere, Colombia's National Parks agency and even its armed forces have gotten involved in reforestation campaigns after wildfires scorched thousands of acres of frailejons.
Yet many average Colombians have learned about the plant's importance through an enormously popular cartoon character called Ernesto Pérez. Shaped like a frailejon, he exhorts people to conserve the flora and fauna of the Andes, similar to the way Smokey Bear promotes forest fire prevention in the U.S.
In fact, several of the volunteers Moreno is guiding up the mountain say the cartoon and its earworm theme song introduced them to the frailejon.
"The song is very contagious," says Nicolás Coronado, 25, who works for a Bogotá-based plastics company, and is carrying a 6-inch frailejon that he will plant in the páramo.
The hike takes the group up to an altitude of 11,000 feet, past streams, waterfalls and lagoons. Underfoot, the ground is damp and spongy. The area is a state park and frailejons dot the landscape. But there are also barbed-wire fences erected by farmers and a half dozen cows grazing on the mountainside.
Moreno and his assistants show the volunteers how to dig shallow holes, then add a bit of shredded tobacco as fertilizer, before nestling the tiny frailejons into the soil.
Their survival is no sure thing. Many die in the cold, harsh climate and those that take hold grow just a few inches per year.
To help them along, the volunteers hold an impromptu ceremony, with one member reciting a prayer to connect with the mountain spirits and another blowing on a conch shell.
By now, some volunteers have grown attached to the frailejons that they've carried up the mountain and have bestowed names on them. Among them is biologist Julieta Barba has baptized hers "Gerry," in honor of her mother.
After patting some dirt around the plant's roots, she says: "I'm very excited for her future here in the páramo."

noticias.titulo: Democrats probe whether Trump Jr.-aligned businesses benefit from government access
noticias.resumen: Investigators say companies with ties to Donald Trump Jr's investment firm, 1789 Capital, have profited since his father's reelection.
noticias.texto:
Democrats probe whether Trump Jr.-aligned businesses benefit from government access
Congressional Democrats, led by likely House Judiciary Committee Chair Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, are expanding their investigation into the investment firm 1789 Capital, which brought on Donald Trump Jr. as a partner days after his father's reelection to the White House.
Since then, investigators say the firm has grown from "a middling venture capital firm" with $150 million in managed assets to "the darling of the venture capital world" with $3 billion in managed assets.
Investigators want to determine whether the growth was boosted by the president's son leveraging political influence or government information to secure federal contracts and regulatory changes for companies with connections to the investment firm.
Trump Jr. told Axios last week that the timing of his hiring at 1789 Capital was coincidental, noting that he had already been working with founder Omeed Malik for years. He also said he draws a clear line when marketing and raising money for the firm.
"I make it very clear [to foreign investors] that I have nothing to do with government," Trump Jr. said. "[The president is] my father, but he's also busy and I probably haven't spoken to him in three weeks."
He also suggested he doesn't use or need government connections to make smart investments. "Trying to do the things that we're alleged to be doing every day, I think that would last for about two seconds before it was out there very publicly," Trump Jr. said. He added that the firm relies on teams of analysts to make investments in industries where there are obvious public and national security demands but relatively few companies who are able to meet those needs.
NPR reached out to Donald Trump Jr. for comment and did not hear back.
Regarding Raskin's request for documents from 1789 Capital, Bill Burck, an attorney representing the firm, told NPR, "We responded to Congressman Raskin back in September pointing out in detail the many flaws in his understanding of how 1789 has operated and a number of basic factual errors. He never bothered to reply. Facts are facts and Congressman Raskin has them wrong here but persists in his tall tales against 1789. These are personal attacks untethered to actual evidence."
What investigators are interested in
On Monday, congressional investigators sent letters to four companies — military contractor Hadrian, electronic cigarette company Juul, prediction market Polymarket and online weapons dealer GrabAGun — asking them to preserve their records and turn over a broad array of records to the committee.
The committee is interested in Hadrian's contracts with the armed forces, signed in March of this year, worth close to a billion dollars. Investigators allege that, in 2024, the company had a single manufacturing facility and "no history of fulfilling government contracts." They also noted that CEO Chris Power donated tens of thousands of dollars to Trump-aligned political organizations in advance of the 2024 election.
Political donations are constitutionally-protected speech and not necessarily evidence of wrongdoing. 1789 Capital first invested in Hadrian in July 2025. The company is also backed by a number of bluechip investors, including Morgan Stanley, T. Rowe Price, Andreessen Horowitz and JPMorganChase. Hadrian did not reply to a request for comment from NPR.
Investigators also allege that Trump Jr.'s firm took a stake in e-cigarette company Juul in March 2025, as the company teetered near insolvency following rulings during the first Trump administration limiting the sale of various flavor cartridges. Four months after that investment, though before it was publicly disclosed, investigators say the company's fortunes rebounded after the Trump administration authorized five new Juul e-cigarette products. The company has announced plans for more flavor authorization applications moving forward.
In a statement to NPR, a Juul spokesperson said the company had received Rep. Raskin's letter and are "reviewing it closely. As always, we intend to cooperate with any Congressional effort to understand our company, our commitment to combating underage vaping, and our mission to help adult smokers of combustible cigarettes transition completely away from smoking."
Investigators are also interested in betting site Polymarket. They say that following a meeting between Polymarket leadership and Trump Jr. at the 2024 Republican National Convention, 1789 Capital invested in the company — which at the time was banned in the United States. In July 2025, after President Trump took office, the Justice Department and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission notified the company that they had closed investigations launched during the Biden administration, according to reporting from Bloomberg News. The CFTC later authorized a U.S. version of the platform to launch. Investigators allege 1789's investment resulted in a 70-fold return.
GrabAGun, a company that "believe[s] people should be able to use their computers, phones, and tablets to shop for firearms the same way they purchase everything else," became, according to investigators, a publicly-traded company with the help of 1789 Capital leadership, including Trump Jr., who serves of its board.
In May 2026, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) proposed a draft rule that would make it easier to ship guns directly to people's homes. At the time, GrabAGun claimed that the company is "uniquely positioned to capitalize on this potential opportunity." Investigators are seeking to understand what knowledge and involvement Trump Jr. had of the proposed rule change.
In a statement to NPR, GrabAGun said the investigators' letter is "a political document, and its allegations are baseless." It added that the ATF's review of its regulations was well known across the firearms industry, and the agency published numerous proposed rules for public comment.
"GrabAGun's only input came through public comments on several of those proposals," the company said.

noticias.titulo: Right-wing revolt threatens to bog down EU budget
noticias.resumen: A Patriots for Europe official said several other delegations could back a challenge that would slow down budget talks in the European Parliament.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — The far-right Patriots for Europe group plans to challenge the European Parliament’s negotiating mandates on several files in the EU’s next budget, according to four EU officials with knowledge of the discussions — a move that could drag out discussions on the seven-year plan in the chamber. The challenge would stop the files, which have already been discussed at a committee level, from going straight to talks with national governments. Instead, the mandates would need a plenary vote, opening the door to amendments that could rehash positions committees had already settled. “The merger of several programs [in several budget proposals] is accompanied by an increasing concentration of allocation authority in the hands of the Commission,” a PfE official told POLITICO. Moreover, most of the PfE’s amendments in the budget have been rejected, they said. The official added that “several delegations outside of the PfE” have told them they would support the challenge. Another official said the Patriots are set to target the European Competitiveness Fund, the Connecting Europe Facility and FP10, the research program that would succeed Horizon Europe. A third official said the group was likely to challenge all the mandates, but that it was not yet clear whether other groups or lawmakers would back the move. The Parliament fight comes as EU leaders prepare to discuss the budget at a summit on Thursday, following the negotiating box presented by European Council President António Costa on Nov. 21. A drawn-out plenary fight would slow Parliament’s side of the process just as governments try to move toward a deal. Parliament’s rules allow a political group or lawmakers representing at least 72 members to request a plenary vote on a decision to start negotiations. They have until midnight Tuesday to do so, according to a Parliament notice . The Patriots have about 86 members. POLITICO asked the Patriots for comment but did not immediately receive a response. Marianne Gros contributed reporting.

noticias.titulo: ‘Majority’ against Frederiksen’s return hub plan, says Socialist chief in EU Parliament
noticias.resumen: The European center-left will hold a formal debate on the Danish PM's migration stance.
noticias.texto: STRASBOURG — A “majority” of the Socialists and Democrats group in the European Parliament opposes building migrant deportation centers outside the EU, a plan that center-left Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen is pushing. Return hubs in Africa for people denied asylum in the EU “have no legal basis and are not in line with international law,” S&D group leader Iratxe García said at a press conference Tuesday morning. The S&D group will debate Frederiksen’s stance on migration at an upcoming meeting following increased tensions over an agreement involving Denmark and four other EU countries to establish a return hub in Rwanda. “We are going to have the debate, to define, to see what the sensitivity of the whole group is and so that everyone can express themselves,” García said. Asked by POLITICO about potential disciplinary measures on Danish members of the S&D, García didn’t rule it out but said that if “any type of action were to be proposed,” it would have to be “determined” by the Party of European Socialists, the EU-wide umbrella party for the center-left. The formal debate will come after an internal meeting during which MEPs raised objections to the Rwanda deal and Frederiksen’s recent comments on migration that critics said echoed the “great replacement” theory, which falsely asserts that elites are plotting to dilute the white population, chiefly through nonwhite immigration. Frederiksen’s approach has drawn criticism from fellow party leaders before, including after she joined Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni in condemning uncontrolled migration .

noticias.titulo: Donald Trump still thinks the rules don’t apply to him — or Jensen Huang
noticias.resumen: The president’s handling of the Nvidia scandal shows he hasn’t digested his midterm rebuke.
noticias.texto: President Donald Trump’s grandiose self-conception was effectively an official part of his original campaign platform. “I alone can fix it,” he declared in his 2016 speech accepting his first Republican presidential nomination. Eight years later, the notion that Trump is specially commissioned by history took on an even more messianic dimension when Trump narrowly escaped assassination. “I was saved by God to make America great again,” he said in his 2025 inaugural address. Suddenly, this week, the country is once again reckoning with Trump’s Indispensable Leader theory of power and destiny — in a whole new context, and amid wildly cross-cutting cultural currents. Jensen Huang is back in charge at Nvidia , in a move that Trump celebrated and that a top aide said he was “totally involved” in orchestrating. This was a breathtaking convergence of the world of business and the world of governmental power. One squints to think of even an approximate precedent of a U.S. president intervening to lobby a private-sector board of directors to influence its choice of CEO — much less to return to power someone it had ousted for alleged professional misconduct. But the intervention comes when the whole concept of a leader infused with mystical powers to summon winning results — and immune from conventional standards of ethics and accountability — is at a crossroads. In the political realm, the notion has been decisively rejected . Trump’s appeal to voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” put Republicans on the losing end of a historic rout. Was the cause mainly the Iran war or inflation or corruption or personal disdain for Trump? A unifying theme of all of these factors was a repudiation of Trump-era methods of power. A wide majority of Americans no longer believes Trump’s thesis that a president as special as he believes he is should get to do what he wants — start wars without congressional or popular backing, encourage the enrichment of his family business, erect monuments, impose tariffs by personal fiat, or plaster his name on buildings. One thing uniting virtually all Democrats, whether centrists or on the left, is a demand that Washington return to something like normal standards of procedure, and that Trump be held accountable by Congress and courts for his norm-shattering behavior. In the corporate realm, however, plenty of people still believe in the Indispensable Leader concept and prove it with their investment decisions. Nvidia stock soared 31% Monday after the news of Huang’s return. The days preceding and following Huang’s Nov. 12 ouster, after a board meeting, were replete with revelations of the CEO’s affair with a woman that U.S. intelligence officials believe could be a spy, another inappropriate relationship with a subordinate, and a tantrum-throwing leadership style that some colleagues called abusive . The reports suggested that he ran Nvidia as a cult of personality — very much like how Trump sought to run the government. But Huang devotees, including investors and Trump himself, didn’t want accountability and normal procedure. They wanted Huang back on the job, and for now they have him. Ordinarily, the suspicion that a firm’s results hinge on a singular figure at the top would draw skepticism from investors. Companies built sturdily for the long haul typically have succession plans and aren’t vulnerable to a specific person dropping dead or, as in Huang’s case, being struck by reputational missiles. The technology sector may be an exception — or so some of its evangelists believe. Arguably one reason Trump is drawn to tech leaders, who filled prized seats at his second inauguration, is they have fashioned their own mystique as leaders who are bending history as they become incomprehensibly rich and famous, often accompanied by conspicuous consumption and celebrity hobnobbing. The prototype is Elon Musk. Conventional morality doesn’t suit him, with his 14 children from various mothers and his musings about drug use. But, like Huang, he continues to be hailed as a tech visionary who shouldn’t be judged by normal boardroom standards. In politics, it is much harder to maintain the Indispensable Leader mystique for long. Barack Obama was first christened “The One” in the 2008 election but secular realities, including the 2010 midterm elections, brought him back to life size before long. Around the world, leaders such as Boris Johnson in the United Kingdom and Emmanuel Macron in France for a time electrified people with outsized personalities or the belief that they were surfing waves of history. Wipeouts inevitably followed. Some people would like to see similar reputational deflation in Big Tech. Democrats, including Sen. Elizabeth Warren and would-be Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, called the reinstatement shocking and vowed to investigate multiple avenues of the Huang affair, including whether national security was compromised and Trump’s role in getting him back in the CEO chair. More than a few Republicans will also be on board, including China hawks like Sen. Tom Cotton. “The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back,” he warned . The next chapter of the Huang drama will be to see whether this political power is stronger than his grip on power at a company he helped found. In ordinary times, which may not be these times, a ruler acting like the rules don’t apply to them is a way of ensuring that they eventually do.

noticias.titulo: Meta’s AI agent Muse launches in UK
noticias.resumen: Regulators will be watching the U.K. rollout of Muse carefully.
noticias.texto:
LONDON — Meta rolled out its personal AI agent Muse to the U.K. adults on Tuesday, promising users a tool they can trust to lend a “helping hand” on everything from chasing a refund and renewing car insurance to doing the Christmas shopping.
It is the first AI agent product to be launched by a Big Tech company in the U.K., and regulators will be watching closely.
The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum (DRCF), comprising the Competition and Markets Authority, Financial Conduct Authority, Ofcom, and the Information Commission, published a statement last month warning that AI agent products “may amplify and accelerate risks” to consumers.
Advertisement
Reuters reported last week that Meta staffers had raised concerns internally about “undesired actions” carried out by the agent since its debut in the U.S., from accessing encrypted messages to supplying bogus information about purchases (a Meta spokesperson said these were “isolated incidents.”)
In a blog post published Tuesday morning, Meta sought to reassure would-be users that although the agent is built to carry out tasks on their behalf, Muse is “private, safe and secure by design.” For example, users can choose whether their interactions with the agent are used to develop and improve Meta’s AI — though will need to actively switch this setting off.
“We’ve engaged constructively with the appropriate regulatory authorities and will continue to do so,” Meta said in its blog post.

noticias.titulo: Budget de l’UE : c’est Noël avant l’heure pour Emmanuel Macron
noticias.resumen: Plusieurs Etats membres accusent António Costa, le président du Conseil européen, de favoriser la France dans sa nouvelle proposition budgétaire.
noticias.texto: BRUXELLES — Emmanuel Macron se rendra jeudi à un sommet européen des chefs d’Etat et de gouvernement en position de force, après les concessions cruciales qu’il a obtenues sur le budget de l’UE pour 2028-2034 . En privé, d’autres Etats membres se sont montrés optimistes quant à la conclusion d’un accord en décembre. Le président français, dont le mandat se terminera au printemps 2027, est apparu comme le grand gagnant de la dernière proposition dévoilée samedi par le président du Conseil européen, António Costa. C’est d’ailleurs sur ce texte que vont batailler les dirigeants européens lors de leur réunion à Bruxelles. Même s’il a suscité des critiques de toutes parts — y compris venant de Paris —, un projet budgétaire qui penche du côté des positions françaises est le signe qu’un compromis est possible, sachant que la France est à mi-chemin entre les deux principaux camps qui s’opposent dans ces négociations. Le plus beau cadeau de Costa à Macron est d’avoir inclus, parmi ses propositions de nouvelles recettes fiscales européennes, l’instauration d’une taxe sur les géants du numérique — une ville idée française, écartée en 2018 par crainte de représailles américaines. Parmi les autres concessions faites à Paris, António Costa a préservé les aides aux agriculteurs de toute coupe, proposé de nouvelles taxes pour plafonner les contributions nationales au budget de l’UE, et reporté le remboursement de 10 milliards d’euros de l’emprunt commun post-Covid. Preuve de la complexité du débat : la députée européenne Renaissance Fabienne Keller a, d’un côté, qualifié de “ bonne nouvelle ” la proposition de taxation des géants du numérique et, de l’autre, fustigé des coupes budgétaires qui “sapent les ambitions de l’Europe” et “lui coupent les ailes”. Avec une enveloppe globale de 1 780 milliards d’euros sur sept ans, la dernière proposition budgétaire d’António Costa est inférieure de 44 milliards à la version présentée le mois dernier par l’Irlande , qui assure actuellement la présidence tournante du Conseil de l’UE. Les Etats membres se divisent entre ceux qui veulent un budget plus modeste, axé sur les priorités actuelles, telles que la défense et la compétitivité ; et ceux qui veulent que l’UE dépense davantage et se concentre sur les domaines habituels, comme l’agriculture et le soutien aux régions les plus défavorisées. Malgré des divergences importantes, António Costa et la plupart des gouvernements nationaux sont déterminés à parvenir à un accord d’ici la fin de l’année. “On dirait que le père Noël est passé plus tôt cette année pour les Français”, ironise un diplomate européen qui, comme d’autres personnes citées dans cet article, a souhaité garder l’anonymat afin de pouvoir s’exprimer librement sur ces négociations sensibles. “Profondément décevant” Le pas de Costa vers Macron représente une victoire rare en cette fin de mandat compliquée pour le président français. La perspective d’un second tour en 2027 entre une Marine Le Pen eurosceptique et un Jean-Luc Mélenchon qui veut “désobéir aux traités” — tous deux étant actuellement en tête des intentions de vote — est l’une des principales raisons qui motivent l’UE à parvenir à un accord sur le budget cette année. Selon plusieurs diplomates, Costa et Macron entretiennent une relation de travail étroite et partagent des ambitions similaires en matière de dépenses européennes. Ils “ont la même stratégie qui consiste à considérer les nouvelles ressources propres [les taxes] et le report de NextGenEU [le remboursement de la dette post-Covid] comme des questions à résoudre avant la fin de la partie”, observe un deuxième diplomate. Les Etats membres se préparent néanmoins à des négociations difficiles. Scène typique du théâtre politique : le président français a qualifié la proposition d’António Costa de “très décevante”, ajoutant qu’elle “ne constitue pas une base pour un accord”. Ce pourrait aussi être une tactique, les Français étant réputés pour leur fermeté dans les négociations et, comme le fait remarquer un autre diplomate européen, pour vouloir remporter chaque match 10 à 0 plutôt que de se contenter d’une victoire plus modeste. “Je ne comprends pas vraiment les critiques de l’Elysée”, souffle l’un des diplomates. “En gros, ils ont obtenu ce qu’ils voulaient.” Manifestation d’agriculteurs Aux yeux de Paris, la proposition d’António Costa prévoit des coupes budgétaires excessives, et des garanties insuffisantes pour les agriculteurs — une profession puissante aux enjeux importants dans le budget de l’UE. Une critique reprise par le puissant lobby agricole Copa Cogeca, qui a annoncé une manifestation à Bruxelles le jour du sommet européen. Des policiers sont aperçus à côté de tracteurs lors d’une manifestation d’agriculteurs à Bruxelles, le 18 décembre 2025. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images Cependant, d’autres Etats membres n’ont pas tardé à démasquer le bluff de Paris. Ils ont noté qu’António Costa a maintenu 297 milliards d’euros d’aides directes aux agriculteurs, et qu’il a transformé un objectif vague de dépenses “rurales” en de nouveaux fonds destinés au secteur. “Chaque nouvelle [proposition budgétaire] s’accompagne d’un nouveau cadeau à l’agriculture et d’une nouvelle réduction des fonds alloués à la modernisation”, résume un troisième diplomate européen originaire d’un pays dont les contributions au budget dépassent les montants que le pays perçoit. Malgré les plaintes, les diplomates interrogés par POLITICO se sont montrés plus optimistes quant à la capacité d’António Costa à mener les Vingt-Sept vers un accord définitif d’ici la fin de l’année — avant les élections en France, en Italie et en Pologne, qui menacent de faire dérailler les négociations. Les Etats membres doivent d’abord parvenir à un accord entre eux avant de chercher à s’entendre avec le Parlement européen. Dans une déclaration samedi , le chancelier allemand Friedrich Merz a souligné la nécessité de conclure les négociations “avant la fin de l’année 2026”. Le risque Le Pen “pas pris au sérieux” Malgré ces coupes budgétaires — qui touchent la quasi-totalité des dépenses, à l’exception des subventions accordées aux agriculteurs —, le projet de budget reste, en termes réels, supérieur d’environ 25% au cadre financier pluriannuel 2021-2027, même si une grande partie de cette augmentation est due au remboursement de la dette post-Covid. Tout au long des négociations, Emmanuel Macron a plaidé en faveur de nouvelles taxes européennes, appelées “ressources propres”, afin de générer des recettes supplémentaires et de limiter la contribution de la France au budget de l’UE, qui est la deuxième plus importante après celle de l’Allemagne. António Costa a fait une concession à Paris en maintenant largement le niveau de recettes visé avec ces nouvelles taxes — environ 60 milliards d’euros, comme l’avait proposé la Commission européenne l’année dernière. Le Portugais a également mis au point une solution pour reporter certains paiements — et économiser des milliards d’euros lors du prochain cycle budgétaire —, en prolongeant d’un an le délai dont disposent les Etats membres pour dépenser leur part des fonds régionaux. Selon le président du Conseil européen, cela permettra de limiter la hausse des contributions nationales, qui passeraient de 0,80% à 0,82% du revenu national brut des pays — une priorité majeure aussi pour d’autres contributeurs nets, surnommés les “frugaux”, parmi lesquels figurent l’Allemagne et les Pays-Bas. Il se pourrait toutefois que ces concessions ne suffisent pas pour faire accepter un accord d’ici la fin de l’année aux pays frugaux les plus radicaux. “Il y a toujours le sentiment qu’il vaut mieux ne pas conclure d’accord plutôt que de conclure un mauvais accord”, soulève le premier diplomate européen. “Les discours alarmistes concernant Le Pen ne sont pas pris au sérieux dans le camp des frugaux.” Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Marie Thirion et Jean-Christophe Catalon.

noticias.titulo: Türkei sieht Europas Wohlstand in Gefahr – wegen des IAA
noticias.resumen: Die EU plant ein Gesetz zur Stärkung der europäischen Industrie. Der „Industrial Accelerator Act“ könnte aber auch die Autoindustrie schwächen. Die Bundesregierung ist gespalten.
noticias.texto: Wenn ein türkischer Handelsminister nach Deutschland reist, gibt es meist etwas zu feiern. Der Handel hat sich in 30 Jahren verdreifacht, in diesem Jahr jährt sich das Gastarbeiterabkommen zum 65. Mal, das seit 1996 bestehende Zollabkommen zwischen Ankara und Brüssel gilt für beide Seiten als Erfolg. Doch der Besuch von Ömer Bolat vergangene Woche lief anders: Es war eine Abrechnung mit der EU-Politik. Und eine Warnung an Deutschland, dass ein Wohlstandsverlust drohe. Der Grund liegt in einem ganz bestimmten Brüsseler Gesetzesvorhaben. Bolat kam am Donnerstag nach Berlin, um auf dem Deutsch-Türkischen Automobilgipfel zu sprechen. Im Anschluss traf er Wirtschaftsministerin Katherina Reiche unter vier Augen. Er nutzte seinen Auftritt vor der Autobranche für Kritik an einer EU-Verordnung, die, so sagte er es im Interview mit POLITICO, Deutschland und der Türkei schaden könnte. „Die deutsche Wirtschaft hat sich als drittgrößte Volkswirtschaft der Welt dank internationaler Investitionen, des Außenhandels und einer offenen Außenwirtschaft erfolgreich entwickelt“, sagte Bolat. „Würde man sich dem internationalen Wettbewerb verschließen, würde der Wohlstand sofort sinken und die Preise für die Verbraucher steigen.“ Es geht ihm um den sogenannten Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). Dessen Ziel ist es, die europäische Industrie zu stärken und Arbeitsplätze zu sichern – vor allem gegen den unfairen Wettbewerb aus China. Als Mittel sollen bei allen Förderungen innerhalb der Europäischen Union und in der öffentlichen Vergabe sogenannte „Made in EU“-Quoten eingeführt werden. Sie sollen dafür sorgen, dass ein bestimmter Anteil der Wertschöpfung in der EU erbracht werden muss. Die Verhandlungen darüber laufen noch in Brüssel. Ein Abschluss wird Anfang kommenden Jahres erwartet. Die große Streitfrage ist: Zählt für die Erfüllung der Quote wirklich nur Produktion innerhalb der 27 EU-Staaten? Was ist mit Produktion in Partnerländern wie der Schweiz, Großbritannien und der Türkei? Und was mit den rund 80 Freihandelspartnern Brüssels? Nach aktuellem Verhandlungsstand zwischen EU-Parlament und Rat wäre die Türkei raus. Das hätte massive Auswirkungen auf die europäische Autoindustrie, warnt Bolat. 250.000 Jobs in Europa seien in Gefahr, die Kosten für Autos könnten sich um bis zu neun Prozent verteuern, besagen Zahlen des türkischen Handelsministeriums. Da in Deutschland mehr als ein Drittel der europäischen Auto-Arbeitsplätze liegen, stünden 90.000 der noch 887.000 Jobs in der Autoindustrie infrage. Auch für die Türkei könnte der IAA gefährlich werden. Um 68 Prozent könnten die Autoexporte in die EU bis 2035 einbrechen, so Bolats Zahlen. 330.000 türkische Jobs wären weg. Die Ursache liegt in den engen Verkettungen zwischen der türkischen und europäischen Autoindustrie. Da die Montage am Bosporus wesentlich günstiger ist, verlagerten spätestens nach der Einführung der Zollunion 1996 viele Autobauer den letzten Schritt, darunter Stellantis (unter anderem Opel, Fiat und Citroën), Renault und Ford. Nur wenn sie an dieser Stelle Geld sparen, ließe sich der Rest der Industriearbeitsplätze in Europa erhalten, so lautet das Argument der meisten Unternehmen. „Ford ist seit fast 100 Jahren in der Türkei vertreten, und diese Präsenz hat sich im Laufe der Zeit erheblich weiterentwickelt“, sagte Nicola Walker, Chefin des Politik-Teams bei Ford Europa, zu POLITICO. Dort baut Ford seine Nutzfahrzeuge, vor allem den erfolgreichen Van Transit. „Etwa zwei Drittel der Transporter, die wir in der Türkei produzieren, werden im EU-Binnenmarkt verkauft.“ Die elektrische Version des Fahrzeugs bestehe zu 56 Prozent aus Komponenten, die aus der EU stammen. „Sämtliche Batterien beispielsweise werden in der EU hergestellt“, sagte Walker. Weil die Endmontage aber außerhalb der EU stattfindet, könnte so ein E-Transit nach dem IAA nicht mehr gefördert oder vom Staat gekauft werden. Da E-Fahrzeuge hierzulande von der Kfz-Steuer befreit sind, sind 100 Prozent der E-Autos subventioniert. Das Geschäftsmodell von Ford in Europa wäre gefährdet. In Gefahr sind damit aber nicht türkische Standorte. Denn während das Geschäft mit den Nutzfahrzeugen ordentlich Geld in die Kasse spült, und Ford in der Nische zum Marktführer macht, schwächelt das Pkw-Business. Am Kölner Standort wurden seit 2025 mehr als 4000 Arbeitsplätze abgebaut. Das Werk in Köln machte 2024 das erste Mal wieder Gewinn – nach jahrelangen Verlusten. Die Zahlen für 2025 stehen noch aus. Der Anteil an Neuzulassungen an Ford-Wagen in Deutschland schrumpft aber kontinuierlich. Ob durch den IAA am Ende auch das Werk in Köln in Gefahr ist, wollte Walker nicht beantworten. Nur so viel: „Die politischen Entscheidungsträger, die über den IAA beraten, sollten all die Arbeitsplätze und Investitionen in der EU berücksichtigen, die unmittelbar durch die Montage in der Türkei gesichert werden.“ Deutschland hat sich in der Vergangenheit immer für Freihandel ausgesprochen. Katherina Reiche spricht deshalb lieber von „Made with Europe“. Ihrer Meinung nach sollten sämtliche Freihandelspartner integriert werden. Damit würden bestehende Lieferketten weitestgehend erhalten bleiben. Doch innerhalb der Bundesregierung konnte sie sich mit dem Ansatz nicht durchsetzen. Kanzler Friedrich Merz und Frankreichs Präsident Emmanuel Macron haben über den Sommer einen Deal abgeschlossen. Sie verbanden damit verschiedene europäische Themen, bei denen Berlin und Paris unterschiedliche Ansichten haben. Viel Einfluss auf die Verabredung soll Reiche dem Vernehmen nach nicht gehabt haben. Am Ende stand ein Kompromiss: Macron kommt Merz bei der Auto-Regulierung entgegen. Im Gegenzug gab Paris beim IAA klein bei, sodass auch Berlin seitdem offiziell dafür ist, dass „Made in EU“ für Autos gilt. Nur Großbritannien und die Schweiz sollen für die Quote zusätzlich berücksichtigt werden, nicht aber die Türkei. Für Katherina Reiche ist das heikel. Denn sie verhandelt den IAA in Brüssel, obwohl sie selbst weiter für „Made with Europe“ ist. Auch den Termin mit Bolat hat ihr Haus erst auf Nachfrage von POLITICO bestätigt und machte ihn nicht im Nachgang – wie sonst üblich – öffentlich. Der Deal zwischen Kanzleramt und Élysée betreffe nur die Autoindustrie, heißt es aus dem Wirtschaftsministerium auf Anfrage. Der Auto-Deal „verändert nicht die Position der Bundesregierung zum Industrial Accelerator Act im Weiteren“, heißt es weiter. „Die Bundesregierung setzt sich beim Industrial Accelerator Act für die anderen Sektoren und Technologien weiterhin für einen ‚Made with Europe‘-Ansatz“ ein. Die Regierung fährt also zweigleisig: Während für alle Technologien außer Autos alle Partner integriert werden sollen, würde das für Deutschlands wichtigste Industrie bedeuten: Nur Autos, die auch in der EU zusammengeschraubt werden, gelten als europäisch. Davon profitieren dürften die Autobauer Volkswagen, Mercedes und Audi, die große Werke in der EU haben. Doch die Türkei würde zum Kollateralschaden für eine härtere Abschottungspolitik Europas gegen China.

noticias.titulo: Back to 1936? Civil war ghosts haunt Spanish election campaign
noticias.resumen: With the far right poised to enter government, politicians are reopening the wounds of a war that began 90 years ago.
noticias.texto: Back to 1936? Civil war ghosts haunt Spanish election campaign With the far right poised to enter government, politicians are reopening the wounds of a war that began 90 years ago. By AITOR HERN Á NDEZ-MORALES in Belchite, Spain Picture taken in 1936 of Spanish soldiers loyal to the young republic as they arrive in Madrid from Vicálvaro to fight against nationalist troops of Gen. Francisco Franco. | AFP via Getty Images Ninety years after the outbreak of the civil war, Spain’s campaign for the Nov. 29 election has unmistakable echoes of 1936, with politicians resurrecting the rhetoric of a conflict that still runs deep in the polarized national psyche. At a meeting of Socialist Party supporters in Puerto de la Cruz, Tenerife, on Saturday, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez led the crowd in chants of “¡No pasarán!” (“They shall not pass!”), the slogan immortalized by the left-wing forces that resisted fascist leader General Francisco Franco’s three-year siege of Madrid. Meanwhile, both far-right leader Santiago Abascal of the Vox party and Madrid’s regional President Isabel Díaz Ayuso, of the center-right People’s Party, are referring to their left-wing opponents as the “Popular Front,” the name used by the coalition of communist, socialist and republican forces that governed Spain on the eve of the outbreak of the civil war. “The Popular Front that Pedro Sánchez has assembled will not relinquish power democratically,” Ayuso warned during an interview on the Cuatro television network last month, accusing the prime minister of leading Spain toward “revolution.” Tensions over those historic fault lines of 1936-39 have only been heightened by the prospect of the far right entering national government for the first time since the restoration of democracy in the 1970s. Vox is expected to become the PP’s junior coalition partner , meaning old antifascist songs and slogans have become commonplace at left-wing rallies. The resurgent guerracivilismo — rhetoric evoking the divisions and existential stakes of the civil war — underscores Spain’s increasingly divided society today. A September survey tracking social cohesion and political polarization by More in Common found that 70% of Spaniards view their country as divided — the highest proportion since the polling organization began tracking the sentiment in 2021. Pedro Riera, head of the social sciences department at Madrid’s Carlos III University, said he was not surprised to see politicians invoking the conflict. For Spanish society, he said, the war remains the most emblematic example of the country’s divisions and has become less taboo. “Our transition to democracy was built on a pact of silence , but as time has passed, people — and political parties — have become less afraid of addressing the war, and politicians now invoke it to mobilize their supporters,” he said. Riera stressed the civil war was hardly top of mind for most Spaniards, who are far more concerned with “issues like housing or the overall cost of living.” But the conflict still weighs on the national conscience. “The fact that political parties are resorting to this issue indicates that it is a divide that is still not fully resolved for a relatively important segment of the population,” he continued. The battle over the dead That fracture is particularly visible in Belchite, a municipality in the northeastern region of Aragón where the battle over the legacy of the civil war foreshadows the politics a PP-Vox government could bring to the rest of Spain. Fierce fighting devastated Belchite during the war, changing hands between Republican and Francoist forces within a year. Although the town could have been rebuilt, Franco ordered its residents to be relocated to a newly built settlement and decreed Belchite be left as a ruinous monument to the destruction wrought by left-wing forces loyal to the Republic. Today, the shattered streets and bullet-scarred buildings routinely serve as a film set. But the ruins are also a physical reminder that the civil war remains unfinished business — not least for the families still searching for the bodies of those who went missing during the conflict. The ruins of the old village of Belchite, Aragón seen on Nov. 12, 2015. | Gerard Julien/AFP via Getty Images Around 114,000 people disappeared during the war and Franco’s dictatorship. Some 12,000 of the missing victims’ remains are believed to still be recoverable from mass graves and other burial sites across Spain, with more than 200 possibly lying in and around Belchite. José Vidal, president of the Mariano Castillo Association for the Recovery of Democratic Memory, said his group had excavated 11 mass graves and recovered 105 sets of remains. Yet some of the largest burial sites remain inaccessible, buried beneath cemetery niches built in the late 1940s and 1950s. “And there are many more bodies elsewhere,” he said, including on roadsides. The association’s work has become more difficult since the PP and Vox formed a regional coalition government in Aragón in 2023. Within a year of taking office, the new administration repealed the region’s democratic memory law, which recognized victims of the civil war and Francoist repression and established a framework for exhumations. Aragón’s official inventory of mass graves and its dedicated research center were also scrapped. The PP and Vox defended the repeal — which is currently under review by Spain’s Constitutional Court — as a way to end what they called a “partisan interpretation of history,” arguing that victims on both sides deserved recognition. But regional democratic memory groups say this framing obscures the far greater scale of Francoist repression and overlooks how the dictatorship prioritized the recovery and commemoration of its own dead. While those killed on the Nationalist side were given Christian burials and public memorials, many of Franco’s victims were left in unmarked graves , their whereabouts unknown to their families. Since the law’s repeal, relations with the regional administration have iced up and previously discussed projects to commemorate victims have also been postponed indefinitely, according to Vidal. “We think their intention is to cancel them altogether,” he said. An archaeologist is seen working in a mass grave in Belchite on Nov. 15, 2021. | Marcos del Mazo/Getty Images Carlos Villanova Mutilva, spokesperson for Aragón’s PP-Vox coalition government, said that rather than undercutting the associations’ efforts, the region had increased funding for exhumations by 10% in 2024 and 2025, with annual budgets amounting to €110,000. He argued relations had soured due to “pure sectarianism” because “they do not accept replacing the democratic memory law.” In Belchite, Vidal fears resistance to his group’s work will intensify if the PP and Vox take power nationally in the upcoming election. For him, the issue is deeply personal: He is still searching for his grandfather, a trade-unionist farm laborer last seen in 1936, when Francoist forces escorted him away from his field. “This isn’t just about recovering bones: It’s about recovering the dignity of the person and their families,” he said. “Who doesn’t want to know where their relatives’ remains are?” A timeless war The civil war’s relevance in Spanish politics is not simply a question of laws, funding or graves. It is also a cultural phenomenon — a collective fascination with a conflict that refuses to be confined to history books. Since hitting Spanish cinemas last month, “La Bola Negra,” a historical drama that follows a love story between two gay soldiers on opposite sides of the conflict, has drawn over 5 million viewers. The movie, which has become a cultural sensation and is Spain’s pitch for next year’s Oscars, carries a pointed message about the dangers of exclusionary politics. But that message has not been universally embraced. As theaters screened the movie across Madrid on Nov. 20, more than 200 people gathered outside the capital’s Santa Bárbara church to mark the anniversary of Franco’s death, singing the far-right anthem “Cara al Sol” and raising their arms in fascist salutes. Spain has seen greater tolerance for authoritarian ideas in recent years, particularly among younger generations: Almost 20% of 18- to 24-year-olds consider the Franco dictatorship to have been “good” or “very good,” a 2025 survey from the CIS center for sociological research found. Such attitudes are increasingly visible on the streets. After Spain’s National Day parade on Oct. 12, dozens of teenagers converged on a housing-protest encampment in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol , chanting slogans such as “Rojo muerto, abono para mi huerto” (“Dead reds are compost for my garden”), referring to leftist parties. Members of Spanish neo-Nazi group Núcleo Nacional perform the Nazi salute during a demonstration in Madrid on Oct. 3, 2026. | Oscar del Pozo/AFP via Getty Images Gutmaro Gómez Bravo, who directs the civil war and Francoism research group at Madrid’s Complutense University, said Spain has made significant progress in confronting its past: A unanimous parliamentary resolution was passed in 2002, condemning Franco’s July 1936 coup and recognizing the victims of the civil war and subsequent dictatorship. But progress, he says, now appears to have stalled. “Confrontation over the past yields electoral gains for Vox and other parties,” he said. “But what’s interesting is that they are capitalizing on a view of Franco’s regime that is positive but notably not nostalgic.” Gómez Bravo argued that efforts to roll back democratic memory laws, challenge the historical consensus surrounding Franco’s overthrow of the Republic and play down the repressive nature of his regime create a climate in which such views could gain ground. The dispute over how Spain remembers its past could soon move to the national level. In their election manifestos , both the PP and Vox propose rolling back the national democratic memory law. The PP pledges to repeal it and replace it with legislation that would follow the model of the one in Aragón, while Vox calls for the “overcoming” of what it describes as divisive ideological laws that seek to impose an “official truth.” The PP says it remains committed to recovering the war’s victims, but on “humanitarian grounds.” Yet the record of Spain’s last conservative prime minister offers a cautionary precedent: Within a year of taking office in 2011, Mariano Rajoy’s government scrapped funding for historical-memory projects and the office coordinating exhumations, effectively ending state-funded efforts to recover the remains of Franco’s victims. Gómez Bravo warned that reversing these policies would go beyond politics, compounding the injustice suffered by those who endured repression during and after the war. “What’s at stake is the recognition of the victims themselves, their status,” he said. “They will become invisible again.”

noticias.titulo: Estonian foreign minister: Why we’re closing our border with Russia
noticias.resumen: Only through sustained pressure can Europe make Moscow accept a ceasefire.
noticias.texto: Margus Tsahkna is Estonia’s minister of foreign affairs. TALLINN — In response to Moscow’s long-standing escalation of hostile activities against Europe, Estonia has decided to close its land border with Russia. This is about more than border security. We are making Europe safer, closing opportunities for Russia to exploit our openness and increasing pressure on Moscow to end its aggression against Ukraine. Across Europe, we have witnessed a growing number of acts of sabotage and intimidation. In Poland, Russian intelligence services were behind the arson attack that destroyed Warsaw’s Marywilska shopping center. Polish authorities have also attributed two acts of railway sabotage to individuals cooperating with Russian intelligence. In Germany, an explosives-laden drone was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport in an incident that the German government has attributed to Russia . And just last week, Denmark attributed an attempted assassination targeting an American-Ukrainian citizen to Russian intelligence services. These incidents form part of a broader Russian campaign targeting the whole of Europe , including countries far beyond its borders. The aim is to undermine the European security order, intimidate its neighbors and dictate the choices of sovereign nations. Civilian infrastructure, businesses and facilities connected to support for Ukraine have increasingly become targets. Russian intelligence services exploit cross-border movement to gather intelligence, establish contacts and recruit individuals to carry out hostile activities. These operations are often deliberately designed to create fear, sow distrust, divide our societies and undermine confidence in our institutions from within. Closing our border will not eliminate these threats, but it will limit opportunities for hostile intelligence activities. It will also help close channels for sanctions evasion, a crucial part of depriving Russia of the resources it uses to finance its war economy and sustain its aggression. The same logic should guide Europe’s wider approach to forcing Russia to abandon the imperialist ambitions that continue to drive its actions. Let us recall the months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, when Moscow issued ultimatums to NATO and the United States, demanding a fundamental revision of Europe’s security arrangements. Russia wanted NATO to roll back its military presence to the levels of 1997, effectively challenging the sovereignty and security choices of countries across Europe, including Estonia, Finland and Sweden. Five years of war, death and destruction have done nothing to change the Kremlin’s ambitions. Following the talks in Abu Dhabi, Russian representatives have once again referred to the 2021 ultimatums and even suggested going further, adding new demands based on their experience during the war. This should leave no room for illusions. Russia is not genuinely moving toward ending its war against Ukraine. Instead, it is trying to use negotiations to achieve what it has failed to accomplish on the battlefield, forcing sovereign nations to surrender their security choices and restoring Russian spheres of influence in Europe. Moscow made these demands five years ago and continues to make them today. Its latest invitation for European leaders to visit Moscow to hear Russia’s position changes nothing. All this makes one thing clear: The way forward is to continue increasing pressure on Russia and strengthening Ukraine. We still have considerable instruments at our disposal, including tightening sanctions, closing loopholes, making use of frozen Russian assets and restricting the travel of Russian tourists and former combatants. Only through sustained pressure can we make Russia accept a ceasefire, which must be the very first step toward peace, as recently stressed at the Berlin meeting of the Coalition of the Willing . Only then can meaningful negotiations on a lasting peace in Ukraine take place. Discussions about wider European security must not become a precondition for ending Russia’s aggression — nor must they give Moscow an opportunity to dictate the security arrangements of sovereign states. Allowing Russia such a victory would send a dangerous message to the world. It would suggest that force pays off, borders can be redrawn and the sovereignty of smaller nations can be bargained away. The consequences would reach far beyond Ukraine, threatening Europe’s security and emboldening other authoritarian powers to pursue their ambitions through force. Estonia’s decision to close its road border crossings with Russia, following Finland’s decision to close its entire eastern land border in 2023 , is one part of this broader effort to increase pressure on Moscow and strengthen European security. Whatever inconveniences the closure may cause, responsibility lies squarely with the Kremlin. Russia’s hostile actions and aggression are the reason these measures are necessary. Europe has the means to make Russia change course. What we need now is the political will to use them. Russia must emerge from this war facing a stronger Ukraine, a more united Europe and a clear understanding that any future attempt to threaten our security will come at an even greater cost.

noticias.titulo: Sanchez’s snap election, and what his (likely) defeat means for Spain’s Nato spending
noticias.resumen: Prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s rejection of Nato’s five-percent target was less hostile to rearmament than it looks. Military spending rose by 50 percent in 2025, and not even the election campaign slowed this pace down, as earlier this month the Spanish government authorised a further €12.2bn for air defence, counter-drone systems, submarines and ships.
noticias.texto: Spain votes on Sunday (29 November), though its rejection of Nato’s five-percent target will probably survive a change of government. That reluctance is far from a rejection of rearmament itself: Spaniards are willing to spend more, but never alone. Prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s rejection of Nato’s five-percent target is less hostile to rearmament than it looks. Military spending rose by 50 percent in 2025 , the steepest increase among the 15 biggest spenders, and passed two percent of GDP for the first time since 1994. Equipment purchases doubled, to almost €15bn , although under a rolled-over 2023 budget and with a 2025 plan that put only a fifth of its €10.5bn into new weapons. Not even the campaign has slowed this pace down, as on 10 November the government authorised a further €12.2bn for air defence, counter-drone systems, submarines and ships. Abroad, Spain leads Nato’s brigade in Slovakia , sent a frigate to protect Cyprus in March after drone attacks on the island, takes part in a new allied A400M fleet , co-develops the Eurodrone , co-founded the ballistic-missile-defence coalition and joined four of the five European defence projects of common interest. Spaniards would also rather pay through common European debt than through taxes or cuts, which makes Spain a testing ground for Europe. Where Spaniards agree This European faith partly reflects distrust of Donald Trump’s United States. According to an internal ECFR poll ( see chart, 2026 ), 66% expect other Europeans to defend Spain and only 12% think Washington will. From Sumar (Greens/EFA and The Left), now part of the Frente Amplio (FA) coalition , to Vox (Patriots for Europe), every electorate gives net support to European weapons and a European nuclear deterrent. The US, by contrast, divides them, with 38% of Socialist voters (PSOE, S&D) seeing it as an adversary, compared with 8% of Partido Popular voters (PP, EPP). Common debt wins net support in every electorate except Sumar/FA, where it is tied, but putting a price on the national bill is enough to erode even conservative support. Sources: ECFR/YouGov (30 April–11 May 2026; n = 1,542; ±2.6 points) and survey data accessed by ECFR (13–19 August 2026; n = 1,638; tax question). Sumar: n = 67 and 62, before joining Frente Amplio (±12 points). Like most Germans and Italians , 54 percent reject cutting other spending to pay for defence, but for reasons of their own. Only seven percent see the US as an ally, and it is hard to sell a target that began as a demand from Trump. Spaniards also look south as much as east, and in May, before July’s Ceuta crisis , 67 percent already feared a migration crisis at Europe’s borders. What a new government would entail A change of government would alter the tone and the method, but probably not the figure. Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the Popular Party’s (PP) leader and candidate, signed up to the European People’s Party five-percent pledge the day after the Hague summit , but his party’s programme sets no GDP figure , and neither does the far-right Vox’s . The PP promises to honour its commitments with the endorsement of the Cortes, a multi-year defence law and joint European purchases, while its MEPs voted to explore defence bonds . Vox’s Santiago Abascal, for his part, has called for more money “to protect our borders and our interests” , starting with Ceuta and Melilla, and mocks a European army at von der Leyen’s “personal service” , even though his voters back the spirit of “buy European”. Under SAFE, the European Commission borrows on the markets and lends member states up to €150bn for defence, over the long term and at low cost. Nineteen countries applied; others, such as Germany or the Netherlands , which borrow more cheaply on their own, did not. It is credit, not a transfer, and it counts as national debt , so it holds little appeal for the most indebted. Spain is a case in point: it argued that it would reach two percent without straining its accounts and held off requesting the fiscal escape clause until April 2026 . SAFE’s second call, opened on 29 October for the €21.3bn left unallocated, repeats the design, even though common debt has already funded the recovery fund’s grants and now sustains Ukraine, with €90bn agreed and a further €45bn proposed . Yet 53 percent of voters back common European debt for defence and only 28 percent oppose it. Going South ? None of the five projects the EU approved in September looks south. Madrid should propose a southern-flank equivalent of Eastern Flank Watch , including the territories that Nato’s Article 6 does not expressly cover. With maritime surveillance, counter-drone defence and protection of critical infrastructure, it could be shared with Italy, Greece, Portugal and France and partly funded by the EU. The next government should also aim to join the E5, the group of France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK, which is committed to greater leadership within Nato and which, together with the EU institutions, forms the European team that will negotiate peace in Ukraine . To be sure, a European label should prevent any Spanish government from underinvesting at home. Nobody in Ankara accused Spain of failing to meet its commitments, but burden-sharing within Nato is moving against its budgetary position. Even so, Spain is proof that European rearmament wins over a public that rejects spending cuts and is divided over a purely national bill. Rest assured that Spaniards will rearm, but never alone.

noticias.titulo: Listen: Which EU countries are actually respecting the EU budgetary rules?
noticias.resumen: French President Emmanuel Macron could revive an idea that has been around for quite some time: introducing a so-called golden rule around public deficit into the French constitution.
noticias.texto: Production: By Europod , in co-production with Sphera Network . EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms . Find the full transcript below : French President Emmanuel Macron could revive an idea that has been around for quite some time: introducing a so-called golden rule around public deficit into the French constitution. What is it exactly, and how is it different from the EU budgetary rules? The principle of that golden rule would be to require the state to keep its budget more or less balanced. In other words, the government would have to commit to a specific budgetary trajectory, aiming, for instance, for a deficit of two percent or one percent by 2032. The idea is not new. Germany already has something similar, known as the debt brake. Spain or Italy also have constitutional provisions aimed at controlling public debt and deficits. In France, the proposal was already put forward under former president Nicolas Sarkozy. But it never made it through the final stage of the constitutional amendment process. Read more Listen: What do France’s centre-right candidates want for Europe? This time, however, the proposal could gather enough votes, notably with support from the far-right National Rally, which backs the principle of a golden rule. How does this compare with the EU’s own budgetary rules? Well, in principle, it’s quite similar. EU member states have been required to keep their public deficits below three percent of GDP since the Maastricht treaty. But the reality is that at least ten member states are currently failing to meet that target. When a country breaks the rules, the commission can sound the alarm and ask the country concerned to present a plan to bring its deficit down, with a clear timeline. But governments are given time to get their finances back on track. There are several stages in the procedure before sanctions can eventually be imposed by the commission and the council. And, in practice, no EU country has ever had to pay a fine for persistently running an excessive budget deficit. A constitutional golden rule would be different. If the requirement is written into a country’s constitution, failing to comply could become a constitutional issue. Provided the constitutional court enforces it, that would create a much more direct legal obligation. So, which EU countries are actually keeping their deficits below the three percent threshold? There are 14 of them, so slightly more than half of the 27 member states. Read more Europe’s youth take to the streets as the post‑war promise of a better life breaks down But five countries are doing more than simply staying below the limit: they are actually running a budget surplus. That means their governments are collecting more in revenue than they spend. Those five countries are Greece, Cyprus, Ireland, Portugal, and Denmark. Cyprus is particularly striking, with a budget surplus of more than three percent of GDP. That’s a very different picture from France, whose deficit is close to tive percent, or than Poland where the deficit hits seven percent. So, what’s Cyprus’s secret? Its economy is heavily geared towards tourism, financial services and maritime transport. Combined with controlled public spending, this has helped the country maintain economic growth over several years. Of course, that doesn’t mean Cyprus has always had such healthy public finances, or that the situation will necessarily last. And there’s another side to the story. Whether we’re talking about Cyprus, Greece or Germany, keeping public finances under tight control often means limiting increases in public spending. And that can mean public services struggling to meet people’s needs, particularly in hospitals and schools. Austerity is increasingly becoming a political issue across Europe. And even in countries with relatively healthy public finances, citizens are feeling the pressure as their purchasing power continues to come under strain. Because ultimately, balancing the books doesn’t necessarily mean that people’s living standards are improving.

noticias.titulo: Size of Brussels’ legal rulebook doubles, despite EU push to cut red tape
noticias.resumen: The EU has set a new record - more than doubling its legal rulebook over the last 15 years. EU regulations and directives in force in 2025 run to around 47,600 pages - a 118-percent increase on 2010, despite a 'simplification' drive.
noticias.texto: New research on Tuesday (24 November) revealed that the text of EU law has doubled since 2010 – despite the EU betting on cutting red tape and competitiveness as major factors in its ongoing budget negotiations. The study , by Berlin’s European School of Management and Technology (ESMT) found EU regulations and directives in force in 2025 to be contained in around 47,600 pages – a 118-percent increase on 15 years ago. The so-called ‘EU Bureaucracy Index’ did not count the number of legal acts. It measures their volume, and how much regulatory text applies at EU level – affecting companies and public administration. Announcements, strategies and proposals that are never adopted were not counted. “To be fair, volume is not the same as burden. One EU regulation can replace 27 different national rules, which can make life easier for companies operating across borders,” said University of Vienna professor and author of the study, Stefan Wagner. Read more Energy tax and carbon emissions law on chopping block as EU Commission doubles down on ‘simplification’ drive “But a body of law that doubles in 15 years is hard to call simpler,” Wagner told EUobserver. noticias.titulo: El Gobierno amplía el permiso por nacimiento a 20 semanas para cada progenitor
noticias.texto:
El Gobierno amplía el permiso por nacimiento a 20 semanas para cada progenitor
- Es una semana más que el permiso vigente este año para cuidar de recién nacidos, adoptados o acogidos
- Las familias monoparentales contarán con 34 semanas, dos más que en la actualidad
El Consejo de Ministros ha aprobado este martes una ampliación del permiso por nacimiento o cuidado de un menor a 20 semanas para cada progenitor, una más que en la actualidad. El nuevo real decreto-ley también lo extiende en el caso de las familias monoparentales hasta un total de 34 semanas, dos más que en la norma vigente.
"España se convierte en un referente en el mundo en corresponsabilidad", ha afirmado la portavoz del Gobierno, Elma Saiz, al ceder la palabra a la vicepresidenta segunda y ministra de Trabajo, Yolanda Díaz, en la rueda de prensa. Por su parte, esta ha insistido en que criar y cuidar es "cosa de dos", por lo que tiene que implicar por igual a ambos miembros de la pareja.
"Es la gran diferencia de nuestro país frente a los sistemas de permisos retribuidos que hay en el conjunto de los países de nuestro entorno", ha destacado Díaz, que horas antes había avanzado la medida a través de redes sociales de forma coordinada con el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez. "Hoy damos un paso adelante. Nuestro país necesita adecuar la legislación a la realidad social que nos encontramos", ha defendido en la comparecencia.
Deberá votarse en el Congreso
A solo cinco días de las elecciones generales, el Ejecutivo firma una de las mejoras sociales comprometidas en el acuerdo de coalición entre PSOE y Sumar en 2023. El permiso por nacimiento o cuidado de menor, retribuido e intransferible, pasó de 16 a 19 semanas en julio de 2025 y aquel texto ya prometía un avance hasta las 20 semanas.
Estos cambios se suman a la ampliación a 10 días del permiso por fallecimiento de padres, hijos o cónyuges que el Consejo de Ministros también ha aprobado este martes.
Ambas mejores sociales entrarán en vigor cuando se publiquen en el Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE), pero tienen que ser convalidadas por la Diputación Permanente del Congreso, por lo que su continuidad dependerá de la representación parlamentaria que emane de las urnas de este domingo, 29 de noviembre.
Cómo funcionan los permisos por nacimiento o cuidado de menor
El permiso retribuido de 19 semanas se concede por nacimiento, adopción, acogimiento o guarda para cada progenitor implicado. Se reparten de modo que seis de esas semanas son obligatorias, es decir, deben disfrutarse justo después del parto o de la resolución judicial. Las 11 posteriores pueden disfrutarse a voluntad, semana a semana, hasta que el menor cumpla 12 meses. Así, los progenitores pueden decidir si tomarlas a la vez o turnarse. Las dos semanas restantes pueden emplearse de forma flexible hasta que el menor cumpla ocho años.
En el caso de familias monoparentales, es igualmente obligatorio tomar seis semanas de permiso inmediatamente después del parto o de la resolución judicial que confirme la adopción, guarda o acogimiento. Las 22 semanas posteriores pueden distribuirse hasta que se cumplan 12 meses, y las cuatro restantes quedan a disposición hasta que el menor cumpla ocho años.
La ministra Yolanda Díaz ha recordado que estas semanas son retribuidas y se cotizan al completo, además de ser intransferibles para evitar que los cuidados recaigan solo en la mujer, como ha ocurrido históricamente.

noticias.titulo: El Gobierno aprueba la ampliación a diez días del permiso por fallecimiento de padres, hijos o cónyuges
noticias.texto:
El Gobierno aprueba la ampliación a diez días del permiso por fallecimiento de padres, hijos o cónyuges
- El texto recoge un cambio de denominación: ahora se conocerá como "permiso por duelo en caso de fallecimiento"
- El Decreto-Ley incluye también la reducción o adaptaciones de la jornada de trabajo por cuidados paliativos de un familiar
El Gobierno ha aprobado este martes, en el último Consejo de Ministros antes de las elecciones generales del 29N, un Real Decreto-Ley por el que amplía a diez días laborables el permiso por fallecimiento del cónyuge, hijos e hijas, pareja de hecho o parientes de primer grado de consanguinidad dentro de las cuatro semanas posteriores. Hasta ahora era de dos jornadas o cuatro si requería desplazamiento.
"El fallecimiento de un ser querido es uno de los momentos más difíciles en los que las personas tienen que ir a trabajar, seguramente sin las condiciones debidas", ha justificado la vicepresidenta segunda del Gobierno y ministra de Trabajo, Yolanda Díaz, que ha señalado que hasta ahora se daban situaciones "que no eran comprensibles", como tener un permiso de 15 días por casarse, pero solo dos por la muerte de un padre, una hija o una pareja.
La reforma también eleva hasta tres los días de permiso en caso de fallecimiento de parientes de primer grado de afinidad y segundo grado de afinidad y consanguinidad (hermanos, abuelos, nietos, suegros, yernos, nueras y cuñados), ampliables en dos días más hasta un total de cinco en caso de desplazamiento.
Además, el texto recoge un cambio de denominación: ahora se conocerá como "permiso por duelo en caso de fallecimiento". La medida entrará en vigor cuando se publique en el Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE), pero tendrá que ser ratificada por la Diputación Permanente del Congreso en diciembre.
Díaz ya presentó esta iniciativa en octubre de 2025 y alcanzó un acuerdo con los sindicatos (CCOO y UGT). Sin embargo, la reforma contó con el rechazo frontal de la patronal (CEOE y Cepyme) y quedó sin tramitar ni aprobarse en el Consejo de Ministros.
La situación respecto a Europa
Fue el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, quien avanzó la decisión este lunes en un mitin electoral en Córdoba. Posteriormente, publicó una carta conjunta con Díaz sobre las motivaciones de la ley.
"Ninguna ley resuelve el dolor de una pérdida, pero con esta norma damos más tiempo a quien sufre para que pueda sanar", resaltan.
La misiva también destaca que España ha estado durante años entre los países europeos que menos protegían a las personas en estos duros momentos. "Hoy nos acercamos a lo mejor de Europa", aseguran.
En este sentido, los únicos países europeos que hasta ahora contaban con tantos días de permiso son Bélgica (10), Francia (12 para hijos y 14 para hijos menores de 25 años), Reino Unido (14 para hijos menores) y Portugal (20).
Para países como Alemania, Irlanda o Suecia, el permiso depende del contrato laboral o de los convenios de los distintos sectores profesionales.
Reducciones laborales por cuidados paliativos
El Decreto-Ley incluye también la posibilidad de reducir o adaptar la jornada de trabajo para acompañar en cuidados paliativos al cónyuge, pareja de hecho o familiares por consanguinidad hasta segundo grado. "Nadie tendrá que elegir entre su trabajo y sostener la mano de sus seres queridos", aseguran Sánchez y Díaz.
De ahora en adelante, además, habrá un permiso de un día de duración para acompañamiento en procesos de eutanasia para la persona que ejerce su derecho a una muerte digna.
Según el ministerio, estas medidas garantizan que el derecho a morir dignamente se integre también en el ámbito laboral, permitiendo acompañar a un ser querido en momentos cruciales sin perjuicio económico ni profesional.
"Esta es la España que queremos. Un país que no obliga a esconder el dolor para seguir trabajando, que nombra la pérdida y le da su tiempo, que cuida y se deja cuidar. Hoy pensamos en todas las personas que tuvieron que volver al trabajo con el corazón roto", concluye el texto firmado por Sánchez y Díaz.
No obstante, la nueva ley ha sufrido un recorte respecto al texto pactado en 2025, puesto que el borrador original negociado con los sindicatos contemplaba los diez días también para familiares de segundo grado de consanguinidad.

noticias.titulo: El Gobierno limita el coste de los créditos al consumo y prorroga el impuesto a la banca
noticias.texto:
El Gobierno limita el coste de los créditos al consumo y prorroga el impuesto a la banca
- El objetivo es proteger a las familias, en especial a aquellas en situación de vulnerabilidad económica
- Con el gravamen a la banca, el Gobierno calcula una recaudación de 1.400 millones que irán destinados a vivienda
El Gobierno ha situado a la banca en el centro de su agenda en el último Consejo de Ministros antes de las elecciones generales del 29N. Por un lado, ha aprobado un nuevo real decreto-ley que refuerza la protección de hogares frente al sobreendeudamiento y que, entre otras medidas, pone límites al coste de los créditos al consumo y garantiza que la venta de una deuda a un tercero no reduzca los derechos de quienes tienen que devolverlo.
Además, ha prorrogado el conocido como impuesto a la banca, que grava el margen de intereses y comisiones de determinadas entidades financieras para el ejercicio 2027, con una previsión de recaudación de 1.400 millones de euros que irán destinados a vivienda.
El objetivo, ha dicho la portavoz del Gobierno y ministra de Inclusión, Seguridad Social y Migraciones, Elma Saiz, es proteger a las familias, en especial a aquellas en situación de vulnerabilidad económica.
Límite del 22% TAE al coste de los créditos al consumo
El nuevo real decreto-ley que refuerza la protección de hogares frente al sobreendeudamiento, que nace a propuesta del Ministerio de Economía que lidera Carlos Cuerpo, fija un límite general al coste del crédito al consumo del 22% TAE, vigente hasta su desarrollo reglamentario. Para los créditos de alto coste se establecen además condiciones específicas: la devolución deberá poder realizarse en al menos tres cuotas mensuales, el interés no podrá superar el 6% mensual y la comisión máxima será de 15 euros.
A modo de ejemplo, un microcrédito promedio hoy es de 300 euros con una TAE del 3.417% y plazo de 30 días. Esto supone un coste de 103 euros. Con el nuevo régimen, si el cliente reembolsa anticipadamente a los 30 días, el coste máximo será de 33 euros. Si reembolsa en 3 cuotas mensuales, el coste máximo será de 51,70 euros, explica el Ejecutivo.
La norma limita también los mensajes publicitarios que presenten el crédito como sustituto del ahorro, refuerza las obligaciones de evaluar la solvencia para prevenir el sobreendeudamiento y obliga a los prestamistas de alto coste a facilitar información reforzada con 24 horas de antelación, para que al menos exista este plazo mínimo de reflexión para el cliente.
El texto presta especial atención a las familias vulnerables, ha señalado Saiz, "con más garantías y soluciones para afrontar sus deudas", e incorpora al ordenamiento español varias directivas europeas, entre ellas las de crédito al consumo, de contratación a distancia de servicios financieros y de administradores y compradores de crédito.
1.400 millones de recaudación para vivienda
En el caso del impuesto a la banca, su recaudación se destinará a políticas de vivienda, tal como adelantó el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, el pasado sábado. En concreto, a construir vivienda protegida, ofrecer bonificaciones fiscales a los inquilinos o rehabilitar inmuebles.
El impuesto grava los márgenes y comisiones de las entidades financieras con tipos progresivos de entre el 1% y el 7%, lo que ha permitido recaudar 1.351 millones de euros en este ejercicio.
La medida se puso en marcha inicialmente para tres años -de 2024 a 2026-, tiempo en el que las entidades financieras han abonado un total de 5.723 millones de euros. Asimismo, si el PSOE gana las elecciones, Sánchez se ha comprometido a mantenerla durante toda la próxima legislatura.
Las patronales bancarias AEB y CECA han reiterado su oposición a la renovación del impuesto porque, en su opinión, afecta a la concesión de crédito a familias y empresas y resta competitividad a las entidades españolas frente a las de otros países europeos.

noticias.titulo: Entre bloques y rivalidades: el mapa de los duelos que se vieron en el debate a ocho
noticias.texto:
Entre bloques y rivalidades: el mapa de los duelos que se vieron en el debate a ocho
- La vivienda, el modelo territorial y los impuestos, temas principales del debate de portavoces en RTVE
- PP, Vox y Frente Amplio, los más críticos; ERC y EH Bildu, los que más tiempo dedicaron a proponer
Tras el cara a cara del jueves, este lunes ha sido el turno del debate de los portavoces parlamentarios.
