noticias.titulo: The photos from Gaza resonating with the people of Sarajevo
noticias.resumen: From a photography exhibition to a weekly vigil reading out the names of killed children, solidarity grows in Sarajevo.
noticias.texto:
The photos from Gaza resonating with the people of Sarajevo
From a photography exhibition to a weekly vigil reading out the names of killed children, solidarity grows in Sarajevo.
Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina – A mother holds her daughter, trying to shield and comfort her at the same time. It is the eyes you notice first. And something aches deep inside you, especially if you come from Sarajevo, a city that survived a siege by Serb forces from 1992 to 1995.
Then you remember that you are still in Sarajevo, where there is peace now.
The image is the work of Salah Ostaz, who is still in Gaza, where rockets are falling and food and water are scarce, and where the silence of most world leaders may ring louder than the explosions, even as people in the streets around the world are raising their voices.
I have been a journalist for a long time. I took my first steps as a reporter in wartime Sarajevo: front lines, massacres, morgues, mass graves, hospitals, empty markets, cultural events that people risked their lives to attend for some semblance of normality. I wrote about all of it and thought nothing could get to me any more.
Until Gaza.
Another photograph. A girl’s eyes, wide open, as though she were looking back over the past three years at everything she has seen, which I do not even want to imagine.
In the next photograph, people line up for a spoonful of food.
And then something altogether different – children smiling and swimming at dusk off a crowded beach, as if this were the happiest time of their lives. There is hope in that picture.
That is what the people who organised Ostaz’s exhibition in Sarajevo believe. I went over to ask them how it came about.
Valida Hadzimuratovic, a radio journalist and DJ known in Los Angeles as Valida Carroll, was in Sarajevo when Ostaz video-called her in October last year. Alongside other activists, she had been organising weekly TikTok livestreams in which Palestinian journalists spoke about what they had witnessed. That call was the beginning of a friendship. Over the following months, she shared his photographs and learned more about his life, including why he had not been able to collect his diploma.
“I remember thinking how frustrating it must be to finish your studies, put in all that work, and then not be able to get hold of something as basic as your own diploma,” Valida told me.
She and her friend Nasiha, a Bosnian who also lives in Los Angeles, began raising money to cover his tuition fees. In September, they decided to show Ostaz’s work in Sarajevo. He sent them more than 150 photographs. Milomir Kovacevic, who documented life in his own city during the siege of Sarajevo, helped curate the show to include about 60.
A silent auction was held alongside the exhibition, with about two dozen artisans and small businesses donating work and prizes. Volunteers and activists from the Ka Gazi (Towards Gaza) movement helped organise the event.
Every Tuesday evening, Ka Gazi volunteers gather in central Sarajevo at the Eternal Flame, an antifascist memorial commemorating those who died resisting fascism during the Second World War. They read aloud the names of Palestinian children who have been killed. If you pass by, you hear the name of one child, then another.
Last year, the names were also read at Sarajevo’s MESS International Theatre Festival. The year before, the festival opened with Metro Gaza, a production featuring the Palestinian Freedom Theatre from Jenin, in the occupied West Bank. That year’s motto was “Unstoppable Life”.
“No one who lived through the siege of Sarajevo should be indifferent to the suffering of others,” said MESS director Nihad Kresevljakovic, while visiting the photography exhibition.
At the end of the evening, people walked out of the Bosnian Cultural Centre carrying photographs and items they had won at the auction. All the proceeds went towards covering the costs of getting Ostaz his diploma.
“We can’t help everyone in Gaza. The needs are enormous and the destruction is immeasurable. But we can help one person,” Hadzimuratovic said.

noticias.titulo: Senegal reinstated as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations winners over Morocco
noticias.resumen: Court of Arbitration for Sport rules in Senegal's favour over the controversial final in January.
noticias.texto:
Senegal reinstated as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations winners over Morocco
Court of Arbitration for Sport rules in Senegal’s favour over the controversial final in January.
Senegal have been reinstated as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) winners after the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) upheld ‌‌their appeal against being stripped of the title.
The Moroccans will lose the title that was controversially awarded to them by the Confederation of African Football (CAF) two months after the chaotic final on January 18 in Rabat, where Senegal emerged 1-0 winners.
CAS’s ruling follows an appeal by Senegal after they were stripped of the title in March by African football’s governing body.
CAF had declared that Senegal forfeited the match when players walked off the pitch in protest at a penalty awarded to Morocco. The Senegal team returned after 14 minutes and scored in extra time.
The CAS panel, presided over by French sports law expert Gerald Simon with assistance from Italian international law professor Luigi ‌‌Fumagalli and Ulrich Haas, a Hamburg-based lawyer and professor of law at the University of Zurich, found that “the ‌‌referee ‌‌did not commit any error of law”, said CAS secretary general Matthieu Reeb.
Senegal, who celebrated the trophy win with fanfare on their return home in January, were incensed by the penalty decision and lodged an appeal at CAS, the highest court for sports-related disputes.
Announcing its “crusade” against CAF’s ruling, Senegal’s football governing body then claimed the move could “reshape the world of football” and undermine the principle that refereeing decisions are final.
“This decision cannot even be considered a true sporting justice ruling – it is so crude, so absurd, so irrational,” lawyer Juan de Dios Crespo Perez, representing Senegal’s governing body, had said.
What was the Senegal-Morocco AFCON final controversy?
Senegal were enraged after a late penalty was awarded to Morocco in the second half. The players left the pitch in protest as Congolese referee Jean-Jacques Ndala awarded the spot kick, following a VAR review of a challenge on Morocco forward Brahim Diaz by El Hadji Malick Diouf.
The Senegalese had already protested to the referee in the second minute of stoppage time about an Ibrahim Sarr goal which was ruled out for a foul.
Before Diaz could take the penalty, the Senegalese players and coaching staff left the field, with many believing the game might well end there.
Senegal eventually returned and Diaz missed the spot kick before the match headed to extra time, when Pape Gueye’s stunning strike settled the game 1-0 in favour of the Teranga Lions.
How did Morocco win the final?
Senegal were ruled to have forfeited the final after walking off the pitch, led by coach Pape Thiaw, in protest at the potentially decisive penalty awarded to Morocco.
When play resumed after a delay of about 15 minutes, Morocco forward Brahim Diaz’s penalty was saved. In extra time, Pape Gueye scored the decisive goal that saw Senegal become champions of Africa for the second time.
Less than two months later, CAF ruled Senegal to have forfeited the match by walking off and officially recorded the result as a 3-0 win for Morocco.

noticias.titulo: 11 injured in Houthi ‘terrorist’ attack on tower in Riyadh
noticias.resumen: Two Saudi nationals, nine foreigners injured in Houthi attack on building in Riyadh's financial district.
noticias.texto:
11 injured in Houthi ‘terrorist’ attack on tower in Riyadh
Two Saudi nationals, nine foreigners injured in Houthi attack on building in Riyadh’s financial district.
At least 11 people have been injured after an unspecified projectile struck a tower Riyadh’s financial district, according to Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence agency.
Those injured include two Saudi citizens, two Indian nationals, three Nepali nationals and four Egyptian nationals, a civil defence spokesperson said.
Authorities said emergency services responded immediately and took the necessary measures to protect civilian lives and property.
In a post on the social media platform X, the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition called the Tuesday strike targeting the King Abdullah Financial District a “cowardly terrorist attack”, adding that authorities are conducting an on-site investigation.
The strike marks the second attack on Riyadh’s financial district in less than a week. An earlier attack on Riyadh damaged the Public Investment Fund (PIF) tower, the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund and the country’s tallest skyscraper. The strike caused “material damage”.
The Saudi-led coalition has not named the building that was struck on Tuesday. However, three separate witnesses said a strike targeted the PIF skyscraper.
A fourth witness told the news agency AFP that a vehicle fitted with a speaker had warned pedestrians in the area to take cover.
No warning was sent to phones about any threats to the capital, as has been the case during recent strikes.

noticias.titulo: Could Russia-Ukraine war threaten Libya’s fragile reunification process?
noticias.resumen: Ukraine's involvement in Libya raises concerns as Zelenskyy admits targeting Russian vessels in a key port city.
noticias.texto:
Could Russia-Ukraine war threaten Libya’s fragile reunification process?
While the two European powers have long had a presence in Libya’s rivalry, the overt nature of Sunday’s attack introduces new complications.
The recent attack on a Russian warship in the port of Benghazi, Libya, has drawn condemnation from both sides of the country’s fractured political landscape.
On Monday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy took responsibility for the drone strikes on the Russian ship docked in the Libyan port a day earlier.
This led to outcry from Libyan officials from both sides of the political divide, who fear the attack threatens fragile efforts to unify the country after more than a decade of war and division.
Here’s what we know:
What is behind the Russian presence in Libya?
Since the fall of longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, Libya’s fractious political landscape has settled into two rival administrations currently governing the country: the internationally recognised Government of National Unity (GNU) based in the western city of Tripoli and led by interim Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, and authorities linked to renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar in the eastern city of Benghazi.
Haftar, who had moved to the United States when Gaddafi was still the leader, has long cultivated close ties with Russia. Moscow has allegedly provided his self-described Libyan National Army (LNA) with weapons, mercenaries and diplomatic backing, key to helping him consolidate control over much of the east.
In exchange, Russia has retained a military and logistical foothold in the country, including ports, airfields, storage, maintenance capacity, and overland routes critical to supporting its operations in the rest of Africa.
Russia is believed to have a military presence in Sudan, Mali, the Central African Republic, Niger, Burkina Faso, among others.
There are an estimated 1,000 to 1,800 Russian personnel in Libya, including from its Africa Corps, a unit within Moscow’s Ministry of Defence, which has tried to bring Russian private military companies in Africa under government control.
The importance of eastern Libya as a military hub for Russia only increased after Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, a key regional ally of Moscow, fell from power in December 2024, said Ruslan Trad, nonresident fellow of Global Security at the Atlantic Council.
“Russia’s bases in Libya are less about fighting in Libya itself than about sustaining Moscow’s wider military and political footprint across the Sahel and Central Africa. They function as a logistics bridge between the Mediterranean and Russia’s partners and deployments deeper in the continent,” Trad told Al Jazeera.
“Without this hub, Russia would have to sustain operations thousands of kilometres from Russia with far fewer reliable transit options.”
Why is there a Ukrainian presence in Libya?
The internationally recognised government in Tripoli has sought to counterbalance Russia’s involvement in Libya by forming its own international partnerships, most notably with Turkiye. The GNU has also adopted a firmly pro-Ukraine stance in recent years.
In 2022, the GNU issued an unqualified condemnation of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. It was the only Arab country to vote in favour of suspending Russia’s participation in the United Nations Human Rights Council later that year.
The relationship between the GNU and Ukraine deepened in 2023, with Prime Minister Dbeibah pushing for the establishment of an official embassy in Tripoli and opening talks on military cooperation. Shortly thereafter, Ukrainian forces began providing training and technical support to GNU forces.
Russia has long accused Ukraine of arming GNU forces and maintaining a presence in western Libya to target its interests in Africa, including a string of unclaimed attacks on Russian-linked vessels off Libya’s coast in recent months suspected to have been carried out by Ukrainian forces. Zelenskyy’s claim of responsibility for Sunday’s attack left no room for ambiguity.
“Ukraine’s presence in northwestern Libya is a limited, discreet military cooperation arrangement with the Government of National Unity,” Trad said. “Its main function is to support long-range drone operations against Russian shipping and military logistics in the Mediterranean.”
Suspected Ukrainian attacks in the Mediterranean include drone attacks in September on the Russian cargo ship, Lady Mariia, between Crete and Libya, and an attack that set Russian LNG carrier Arctic Metagaz ablaze in December, leaving it adrift between Malta and Libya.
But it is not clear whether Sunday’s attack was launched from Libyan soil.
Libya’s reconciliation process
Groups loyal to the GNU and Haftar’s LNA have fought a gruelling war since 2014, with thousands killed. Efforts to reconcile the eastern and western authorities have repeatedly failed.
Since 2025, regional and international efforts to bridge Libya’s divide have yielded cautious progress, resulting in a cooperation framework that seeks to unify the country’s political, military and economic institutions.
In April, Libya adopted a unified national budget for the first time in more than a decade. The move was welcomed in a joint statement by 10 countries involved in Libya’s conflict or the process to end it, including the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, France, Germany, Italy, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, the United Kingdom and the US.
Russia also welcomed the move in an April 22 statement but warned against the involvement of “external actors” in shaping Libya’s future.
On August 30, the two sides agreed to presidential and legislative elections within 24 months under a single executive authority, in a UN-mediated deal, but questions still linger over their commitments to the process.
Sansom Milton, a senior research fellow at the Doha-based Center for Conflict and Humanitarian Studies, told Al Jazeera that the framework remained the clearest opening for a political settlement between the two rivals in years.
“The Haftar and Dbeibah camps have moved from bargaining over how to share Libya’s oil wealth to how they might share power,” Milton said. “I doubt Sunday’s strikes alone will derail talks.”
Osama Kubbar, a Libyan political and security analyst, agreed that the attack as an independent action by the Ukrainian government was unlikely to disrupt the political process.
“If the boats did indeed depart from Tripoli, it was an independent action by Ukrainian personnel who are primarily present to train Libyan forces in the west of the country,” he said. “It will therefore not affect the reconciliation process between the two sides.”
What comes next?
The condemnation of the attack by both sides could be counterproductive to any Ukrainian efforts to establish a presence in Libya, analysts told Al Jazeera.
“Both the Russian state and the Haftar family will feel compelled to retaliate – somehow. I’m not saying it’s going to be easy, but the pressure is going to be there, because what happened was humiliating for both,” Harchaoui told Al Jazeera.
“So now that this actor, Ukraine, is not just performing covert action, but overt actions against components of the Russian state, then it opens up all sorts of possibilities.”
It could also have an impact on the fragile peace process in Libya, with the country ever sensitive to a new round of conflict.
“I’m not saying it’s likely, but the possibility now can be imagined,” Harchaoui said.
Both administrations insist that they do not want a foreign war between Russia and Ukraine brought to Libya’s shores.
Mousa al-Koni, one of the three members of the Presidential Council that acts as head of state for the country under a UN deal, characterised the attack as “terrorist” and promised legal and diplomatic measures against culprits, including referring the incident to the UN Security Council.
Ukraine will also face further pressure from both sides to limit its role in Libya.
“Both sides have an interest in framing the strike as a violation of Libyan sovereignty,” Trad said. “What follows will likely be less a clean expulsion than a reduction in visibility and control.”

noticias.titulo: Israeli air strike kills senior Hamas security official in Gaza
noticias.resumen: Naim Abu Nahl, 50, was killed in a crowded area while four others, including a Palestinian woman, were wounded.
noticias.texto:
Israeli air strike kills senior Hamas security official in Gaza
Naim Abu Nahl, 50, was killed in a crowded area while four others, including a Palestinian woman, were wounded.
An Israeli strike on Gaza has killed a senior Hamas security official and wounded several others, according to local authorities.
In a statement, Gaza’s Ministry of Interior and National Security identified the official killed in Tuesday’s attack as Brigadier General Naim Abu Nahl, director of the Internal Security Service.
Abu Nahl was 50 years old and head of Hamas’s internal security across the Gaza Strip. A statement from Gaza’s Interior Ministry said the official was walking in the street when a drone strike killed him.
Four others, including a Palestinian woman, were wounded and taken to al-Shifa Medical Complex. The area where the missile struck is crowded with displaced people and shelters.
Hamas has condemned the assassination as a war crime, saying the killing is part of Israel’s efforts to create a “state of chaos” in the Gaza Strip.
“We affirm that these cowardly assassinations will not succeed in breaking the will of our people, nor will they deter our security and police forces from carrying out their national duty in protecting the internal front and preserving security and stability,” the group’s statement read.
Gaza’s Interior Ministry said the assassination came after the Internal Security Service had made significant gains against what it described as “gangs collaborating with the occupation and operating in areas under Israeli military control”.
Israel’s army and its Shin Bet domestic security service said in a joint statement that they had struck a senior Hamas figure, without identifying him, adding that further details would be provided later. Israel’s public broadcaster Kan later said the target was Abu Nahl. Citing Israeli sources, Kan said Abu Nahl had succeeded Moein al-Arbeid, who was detained by the Israeli army and Shin Bet during a special operation in September and remains in Israeli custody.
Several Palestinians were already reported killed earlier on Tuesday, including a child and police officers, while dozens were injured in Israeli air strikes on various parts of the Gaza Strip, according to local health officials.
There have been daily violations of the so-called “ceasefire” in Gaza, with Israeli air strikes continuing regularly in its genocidal war, with at least 1,680 people killed and 6,100 injured since the ceasefire was signed on October 11 last year.
Hamas also called on the guarantor states of the “ceasefire” agreement to intervene immediately “to rein in the occupation, impose a halt to its crimes, and obligate it to adhere to the agreement’s path”.

noticias.titulo: Records tumble as Indian teen Sooryavanshi smashes 53-ball 204 against UAE
noticias.resumen: The 15-year-old Sooryavanshi struck a staggering 28 sixes, the most ever in a senior men's innings.
noticias.texto:
Records tumble as Indian teen Sooryavanshi smashes 53-ball 204 against UAE
The 15-year-old Sooryavanshi struck a staggering 28 sixes, the most ever in a senior men’s innings.
Teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi hammered 204 off 53 balls for India A to break a host of records, including for both the fastest century and double-century in List A cricket.
The 15-year-old Sooryavanshi struck a staggering 28 sixes, the most ever in a senior men’s innings, as India passed their target of 250 against the United Arab Emirates on Tuesday in just 14.2 overs.
Sooryavanshi reached his hundred off 28 balls to take Australian Jake Fraser-McGurk’s record by one delivery.
He raised his 200 off 52 deliveries, smashing the 103-ball mark previously held by Chad Bowes.
Sooryavanshi also broke his own record for fastest 150, reaching that milestone from 40 balls.
“No words to say for him. I would only say it’s like absolute carnage,” India A captain Tilak Varma said after the Asia Cup Rising Stars match.
“The way he played, I think first five overs, the match was done. Five overs, we are 100, and the way he carried on after that, it was tremendous to watch. Honestly, everyone knows how he can hit the sixes.”
In July, Sooryavanshi became India’s youngest men’s international when he made his T20I debut against England in Manchester, eclipsing Sachin Tendulkar’s longstanding record.
He amassed 776 runs for Rajasthan Royals to finish as the tournament’s leading run-scorer in this year’s IPL, at a remarkable strike rate of 237.30.

noticias.titulo: Jensen Huang’s Nvidia return: Who are the big winners and losers?
noticias.resumen: Jensen Huang returns to lead the most consequential company powering the AI revolution. But who wins, who loses?
noticias.texto:
Jensen Huang’s Nvidia return: Who are the big winners and losers?
Jensen Huang returns to lead the most consequential company powering the AI revolution. We take a look at winners and losers from the scandal.
Less than two weeks after Jensen Huang, the leather-jacket-wearing face of the AI revolution, scandalously fell from the throne of the modern AI industry, he has reclaimed his leadership of the world’s most valuable semiconductor company, Nvidia.
It took a war room of Silicon Valley insiders lobbying the White House for US President Donald Trump to crack the whip on Monday and force chip giant Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang, 63, who fell from grace following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, an executive and controlling shareholder of Megaspeed, an Nvidia client company that has since been blacklisted in the US.
What happens at Nvidia extends well beyond the California-based company.
Share values on the US stock market have become concentrated in a small group of increasingly valuable tech giants, which account for more than 60 percent of the Nasdaq-100. Tech and AI-linked companies together represent around half the S&P 500’s market value.
Huang’s return to Nvidia on Monday triggered a 30 percent rise in Nvidia shares, but has raised several questions about the reach of the Trump administration’s dictates as investigations into the company and its CEO continue. It has also heightened worries about the future of AI development amid Washington’s deepening rivalry with Beijing.
We take a look at major winners and losers from this whole scandal.
Winners
There are many.
Jensen Huang
The sacked CEO, who stunningly returned to applause from Nvidia employees on Monday, had left the board, which last week said it would not reinstate him.
From washing dishes at a Denny’s in the 1980s to building a $4 trillion technology giant, Huang led Nvidia for nearly 33 years and became one of Silicon Valley’s defining entrepreneurial stories.
He now joins a number of “cult-style” leaders in Silicon Valley, including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and SpaceX’s Elon Musk, who appear too “big” to fire.
Allegations that Huang’s affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a businesswoman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence, may have exposed restricted chip technology to Beijing were ultimately not enough to keep him out of the CEO’s office.
During the 11 days he was out of the office, media reports detailed at least two more extramarital affairs with employees at Nvidia, and revealed how he toxically berated his subordinates.
“If Jensen comes back, I’m not doing any HR trainings ever again,” an Nvidia employee wrote on an internal platform, reported Wired.
Lloyd Blankfein, the former CEO of investment bank Goldman Sachs, wrote on X: “Guess you can come back from the graveyard if you’re really, really, really indispensable.”
For his part, President Trump argued that he just returned from a trip to China – where he attended the APEC summit and met with Chinese President Xi Jinping, “So I guess I’m involved also.”
Speaking with CNBC, Trump added, “Every time you have a Chinese woman that’s good-looking or beautiful, they say she’s a spy.” However, he said, “I don’t believe that’s true,” in the case of Huang. He did not comment on US intel reports he received.
Nvidia shareholders
The chip giant holds the key to the modern AI computing industry; its customers include Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta, who rely on Nvidia hardware to build and operate their AI data centres.
Nvidia’s shares fell nearly 28 percent between November 11, when the board accepted Huang’s resignation, and November 20, amid mounting uncertainty over its future leadership.
By the end of Monday, November 23, Nvidia recovered approximately $956bn in market value, rising from its November 20 low of $3.04 trillion to $3.98 trillion, and remaining the world’s most valuable semiconductor company.
Among those shareholders is US President Trump. A review of Trump’s financial disclosures, first reported by The Washington Post, found that he held between $13m and $62m in Nvidia stock at the end of August, up from about $1.3m at the end of 2024.
Companies doing business with Nvidia
The AI industry at large felt the ripples from Huang’s exit from Nvidia, and his return is also boosting companies across the chip giant’s global supply chain, which are hoping for continuity in the product roadmap, manufacturing orders and investment plans.
Shares in Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which manufactures Nvidia’s advanced AI processors, surged 9.9 percent on Tuesday, hitting the company’s daily trading limit and adding $158bn to its market value in a single session.
Shares in Foxconn, which assembles AI servers powered by Nvidia chips, also rose nearly 10 percent.
Shares in South Korean memory-chip makers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics gained 6.7 percent and 6.6 percent, respectively.
Japanese chip-testing equipment maker Advantest shares jumped 12.5 percent.
On Tuesday, major Asian stock indexes in Seoul, Tokyo, and Taipei all rose.
Advocates for open access to tech
Huang has spent years lobbying in Washington against restrictions to tech exports, arguing that halting sales will surrender a strategically important market to domestic Chinese competitors.
That puts him at odds with US lawmakers who view access to Nvidia’s advanced chips as a national security risk, particularly given their potential military applications.
The US first introduced export controls on the chips in 2022 and has subsequently tightened China’s access to them.
In one exception, following a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping last year, Trump said he would allow H200 chip sales to approved Chinese customers. The US ‌eased its licensing policy for the powerful H200 in January, allowing export applications to be reviewed individually subject to security conditions.
Despite all the restrictions, Nvidia tech was reportedly still making its way to China, mostly via third countries and smuggling, according to media reports.
Since the Jensen Huang scandal came to light, Nvidia says it has stopped shipping powerful chips to China, but did not specify the reason for doing so.
Losers
Treasury Secretary Scott Besant
President Trump, who backed Huang solidly, was quick to claim credit for the Nvidia board’s decision to reinstate Huang. But his administration has appeared divided over the issue.
The Department of Justice and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) are continuing to investigate the company, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has emerged as one of its most vocal critics.
Bessent earlier questioned whether Nvidia had facilitated irregular chip sales to China to bolster its financial performance, alleging in an interview with Fox News that the AI chip giant had engaged in “seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings”.
He has also called for Nvidia to appoint a new chief executive from outside the company.
Meanwhile, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faces allegations that he delayed restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China, raising questions about whether his decisions were influenced by the financial interests of his former firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, which is now controlled by his two sons.
Nvidia board
Nvidia’s board has 11 directors, including Huang.
After Huang resigned, board chair Harvey Jones told investors that he had left voluntarily and would not be reinstated, amid a mounting “Stand with Jensen” campaign, backed by Silicon Valley executives including Elon Musk.
Then, on Monday, the board said it “believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers”.
“This is an extraordinary development, and the burden falls on Nvidia’s board, not on Washington. The board reinstated its CEO before the investigations into Megaspeed and his ties to it have concluded,” Shiva Rajgopal, Kester and Byrnes professor and chair of the Accounting Division at Columbia Business School, told Al Jazeera.
“For the chip industry, the lesson is that knowing your customer (KYC) is now a board-level issue. Much of the risk sits with intermediaries, especially in cloud providers and resellers in places like Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.”
Competitor chipmakers
Chaos at Nvidia seemed to offer immediate opportunities for competitor chipmakers such as AMD and Broadcom.
Shares in AMD, which competes directly with Nvidia in AI processors through its Instinct accelerator range, and Broadcom, which designs custom AI chips and networking technology for major cloud companies, gained nearly 6 percent on November 12, the day Huang’s departure was announced.
After Huang’s return, their shares rose modestly higher – by approximately 7 percent and 2 percent, respectively – compared with Nvidia’s 31.5 percent surge.
Alphabet, which develops its own Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), had also stood to benefit as companies such as Google and Amazon may have sought to reduce their dependence on Nvidia.
China hardliners
Another loser in the Trump administration appears to be the president’s national security adviser and secretary of state, Marco Rubio, a known China hardliner.
Earlier, The Washington Post had reported that Rubio set in motion the chain of events that eventually led to Huang’s removal from the board at Nvidia.
Rubio was cornered on Monday, as he appeared alongside Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani at the Department of State, by questions being shouted at him about Huang’s reinstatement. He did not respond to any of them.
Washington, however, added Megaspeed to its trading blacklist on Monday, hours after Huang returned to Nvidia.
The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) placed the Singapore-based company and six other firms in Southeast Asia on its Entity List.
Megaspeed and the other entities were determined to be “acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States”, BIS, which sits under the US Department of Commerce, stated in a filing to the Federal Register.

noticias.titulo: Ten years after its 2016 peace deal, Colombia faces a return to conflict
noticias.resumen: Critics fear that a security crackdown under Abelardo de la Espriella could unravel gains made under the 2016 deal.
noticias.texto:
Bogota, Colombia – Ten years ago, Jorge Suarez and more than 13,000 other fighters agreed to a peace treaty with the Colombian government, paving the way for the disarmament of Latin America’s largest rebel group, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC).
“It was an agreement that I never thought would happen,” Suarez told Al Jazeera.
Born in a rebel camp, he had been fighting since the age of 15. But on November 24, 2016, an agreement signed paved the way for Suarez and other FARC members to lay down their arms.
The deal was historic. It was the culmination of more than four years of negotiations and earned Colombia's president at the time, Juan Manuel Santos, the Nobel Peace Prize for his efforts.
But Colombia's six-decade-long internal armed conflict has continued in the years since. Armed groups, new and old, have continued to clash with government forces. Illegal mining and a booming cocaine trade have fuelled the fighting.
Colombia has also turned away from negotiated solutions to the conflict.
In June, the country elected far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella, who pledged to restore security through military force rather than peace talks.
Now, on the 10th anniversary of the peace deal, those involved reflect on what went wrong, what worked, and whether the country can overcome its deep-seated divisions.
The unravelling of peace
“At the moment of signing, we felt that it was truly a historic event,” recalled Humberto de la Calle, a former vice president who headed the government team that negotiated with the FARC.
The deal was seen at the time as a significant step in winding down a war that would kill more than 450,000 people between 1985 and 2018, according to Colombia's Truth Commission.
Some 80 percent of the deaths were among civilians.
The Truth Commission also found that many of the gravest human rights abuses were committed by state-backed paramilitary groups and government security forces tasked with tackling the FARC.
The accord initially ushered in a period of security in Colombia, as violence plummeted and swaths of former rebel territory were opened up for tourism and trade for the first time in decades.
But the demise of the FARC did not spell the end of Colombia’s conflict. In the years since the deal was signed, an assortment of criminal organisations has expanded control over Colombia's land and its illicit economies.
They include former paramilitaries, FARC dissidents who rejected the peace deal, and the National Liberation Army (ELN), Colombia's largest remaining rebel group.
Government data suggest the ranks of these groups nearly doubled from 15,000 in 2022 to 28,000 today. Child recruitment is also on the rise, and drone warfare increasingly threatens civilian populations.
For many, the optimism of the 2016 deal has been dampened by the present-day reality.
“I think we were guilty of being overly enthusiastic, and we were a little naive,” said Javier Florez, director of conflict and security at the Ideas for Peace Foundation (FIP), a Colombian think tank.
The 2016 peace deal stretched more than 300 pages, and it included hundreds of provisions for policies designed to help the rural poor, including land restitution and the voluntary substitution of illicit coca crops for legal harvests.
It also outlined a path for ex-FARC members to transition into civilian life, with amnesty for low-level political crimes and transitional justice mechanisms for more serious offences.
The terms were designed to tackle the root causes of the armed conflict between the FARC and the government.
An unrealised vision
But a decade later, some 43 percent of the stipulations of the accord have seen little or no implementation, according to the Kroc Institute for International Peace Studies, which monitors the deal.
Some of the least-implemented parts of the accord relate to projects promoting gender equality and political representation for ethnic minorities.
Florez supports the “instruments” designed to build peace under the 2016 deal, but he argues that a lack of resources and political will scuttled their implementation.
“Every new government enters office and, instead of following the established roadmap, comes up with something new,” Florez said.
State support for the accord first collapsed when right-wing politician Ivan Duque succeeded Santos as president in 2018, campaigning on a pledge to dismantle the deal.
Though Duque was constitutionally barred from scrapping the accord, his administration neglected to pursue key tenets of the peace deal, like land restitution and transitional justice.
Duque’s successor, Gustavo Petro, was the first left-wing president in Colombia's history — and a former rebel fighter himself.
But while he promised to implement the 2016 deal in full, he too fell short of meeting its commitments.
His "Total Peace" strategy — which sought to expand peace negotiations to other groups — also fell flat. Critics say Petro’s failed negotiations simply gave criminal organisations more time to recruit, regather and resupply.
De la Espriella, meanwhile, has been one of the deal's most vocal critics.
Ahead of its 10th anniversary, he described the accord as "insufficient". In a social media post on Monday, he also accused it of failing the FARC's victims and costing Colombia trillions in pesos.
"On the 10-year anniversary of the pile of trash that the Havana Agreement with the FARC narcoterrorists turned out to be, it’s worth reminding Colombians how much this false peace has cost us," de la Espriella wrote.
He pointed to costs for projects like the Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP), a transitional justice court established under the peace deal. De la Espriella has suggested he would like to see it shuttered.
The president has also pledged to scrap the Office of the High Commissioner for Peace, which advises the president on peace matters, declaring “the complete dismantling of the perverse system of impunity that currently prevails”.
Having dismissed peace talks as ineffective, de la Espriella has instead ramped up the government's military offensives against armed groups.
De la Calle, however, fears that turning away from the 2016 peace deal will backfire.
“I am very concerned about the message coming from the government," said the former negotiator. “I believe that failing to implement the agreement is a monumental mistake for Colombia."
Achievements of the 2016 accord
Though the 2016 deal has yet to be fully enforced, many involved in its creation still view the treaty as a decisive step forward for the country.
De la Calle, for example, believes Colombia's security situation today would be far worse if not for the deal.
“What would Colombia be like today if, in addition to the violence we are enduring, the 13,000 members of the FARC were still fighting?” he asked.
Suarez also highlighted the political impact of the peace deal, arguing that it allowed for new voices to challenge Colombia's political establishment.
“The 2016 peace agreement paved the way for a democratic opening in Colombia," Suarez said.
The Petro administration was widely seen as a product of the 2016 peace deal.
The accord also allowed thousands of former FARC fighters to begin a new life as civilians. Many of them started businesses in eco-tourism, hospitality and textiles.
“Personally, it has allowed me to start over,” said Suarez, who now coordinates government protection protocols for signatories of the peace deal.
New paths to peace
Though both Suarez and de la Calle believe the state must implement the 2016 peace deal, they diverge on how to end Colombia’s conflict.
De la Calle is sceptical of de la Espriella’s hardline approach, which he says lacks “a methodical, clear, and comprehensive” security policy.
But he does believe the military should play a role in ending the violence.
“Force is necessary,” de la Calle said. “The first thing we need is military control of our territory.”
The next step, he said, is creating a permanent police presence in conflict areas and installing a more effective justice system that can identify and prosecute criminals disguised among civilian populations.
Suarez, who spent 17 years fighting, argues that violence will not end the conflict: “War just brings more war.”
Supporters of that perspective point to a surge in unrest under de la Espriella's nascent military campaign.
The first 100 days of de la Espriella’s presidency saw an 11 percent uptick in violence involving armed groups, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data group (ACLED), a nonprofit that tracks political violence.
Suarez instead believes that land reform and government projects to support local economies are the best way to end the cycle of bloodshed.
“The only way out of the Colombian conflict is to give opportunities to the countryside and rural communities," he said.
With Colombia’s new government set on a more militarised path, Suarez fears that history will repeat itself — and Colombia's armed conflict will enter a new phase of violence.
“I don’t want future generations to go through what I had to go through,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Hormuz oil traffic is down 40 percent: Are Iran’s tanker attacks working?
noticias.resumen: Attacks on tankers have increased, impacting the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
noticias.texto:
Hormuz oil traffic is down 40 percent: Are Iran’s tanker attacks working?
Attacks on tankers have increased, impacting the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz, raising the cost of the blockade.
Iran has reiterated that it will use “all available means” to confront the United States naval blockade, as it has stepped up attacks on tankers attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint, signalling potential escalation.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday that they would “definitely not tolerate” the naval blockade, and would use “all our tools to confront this US aggression”.
“Iran has the right to use any available tool to defend itself in this regard,” he said.
The naval blockade has largely halted Iranian oil exports. It was first imposed in April, but was lifted following the June memorandum of understanding. The blockade was reinstated weeks later after the agreement collapsed.
As Iran’s economy is increasingly squeezed by the US-led economic sanctions, attacks on tankers have also gone up, affecting the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz. The disruption to the flow of oil has triggered a global energy crisis.
What do we know about the attacks on tankers, and how frequent are they?
Attacks on oil tankers and commercial vessels have continued throughout the war, but more recently, a rising number of tankers have erupted in flames after hitting naval mines purportedly placed by Iran. More than 25 tankers have been hit in the past week alone.
According to reports, tankers have continued to make the dangerous journey through the waterway without seeking Iran’s approval, often travelling in the dark and without navigation transponders to avoid alerting Iranian officials.
However, this clandestine approach has come with its own problems.
On Tuesday morning, Iran’s navy said two oil tankers had hit mines and caught fire in the waterway, according to a statement reported by Iran’s Tasnim news agency.
According to the statement, the tankers entered a restricted zone east of the strait after turning off their navigation and identification systems.
The statement reiterated that the strait would not be opened until Iran’s objectives and demands were met, including halting hostilities, lifting the blockade and waiving sanctions, adding that “owners of oil tankers are required to coordinate with the armed forces to ensure safe passage through this strategic strait.”
At the same time, the commander of the Iranian army, Amir Hatami, called for tightening the closure of the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, stressing that Tehran needed to make conditions more difficult.
“We must tighten our control over the Strait of Hormuz, our management of it must be stronger, and conditions must become more difficult for the enemy,” Iranian television quoted Hatami as saying, during a speech to senior army commanders at the Command and Staff University.
The head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) navy, Ali Ozmaei, also warned vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz against using unapproved shipping routes.
“The Strait of Hormuz is not a place to test unauthorised routes and ignore maritime warnings,” Ozmaei said, according to the ISNA news agency.
Is the strategy working?
Despite the attacks, oil prices have fallen, with Brent crude futures at $88.35 per barrel as supplies recover. At one point, oil prices went past $120 per barrel.
So far, according to the AIS ship-tracking platform, in the past 24 hours, 28 ships have crossed the strait: 12 into the Gulf and 16 out of it, carrying an estimated 4.18 million barrels of oil.
However, because it only collects data from vessels with transponders on, loopholes – including the no-signal bypass routes – mean it is not an accurate count of how many ships are crossing the strait.
Still, it is a huge drop from pre-war numbers, during which 125 to 140 ships used to pass through daily.
In the past week, Iran has also carried out attacks on US bases in the Gulf, targeting radars.
On Sunday, US President Donald Trump said in a post on Truth Social that Iran had launched “more drones and missiles in the last week than at any time for over a year”, adding that they had all been downed and had caused no damage.
Meanwhile, last week, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said in an advisory that ships receiving cargo from vessels loaded at Iranian ports or along the country’s coastline could be considered to be “evading the blockade”, which had allowed some Iranian petroleum products to reach international markets.
But Iran has repeatedly warned against US efforts to hamper its trade.
Has this impacted oil traffic?
Yes.
According to data from Marine Traffic, a ship-tracking platform, the number of vessels crossing between November 1 and 23 has dropped as the month goes on.
In the first week of November, between the 1st and 7th, 226 vessels entered or exited the Gulf. In the last week of the month, from the 17th to the 23rd, only 125 vessels crossed the waterway. That’s a drop of more than 40 percent.
Throughout the month, the highest day with 29 vessels exiting took place on November 1, and the highest day entering the Gulf was November 7.
In contrast, the lowest day for exiting the Gulf was on Sunday, when only one vessel left the waterway; on the same day, only two vessels entered the waterway, the lowest figure for the month.

noticias.titulo: Heat deaths reach record high in UK in 2026
noticias.resumen: The UK Health Security Agency estimates that the total number of deaths has reached 5,258 for the summer of 2026.
noticias.texto:
Heat deaths reach record high in UK in 2026
UK Health Security Agency estimates that the total number of deaths has reached 5,258 for the summer of 2026.
The United Kingdom registered more than 5,000 deaths linked to this summer’s heat, the highest number of such cases since records began in 2016, according to the UK Health Security Agency’s (UKHSA) estimates.
“Summer 2026 was an exceptional summer with the highest mortality observed since 2016 when the UKHSA began publishing annual heat mortality reports,” the agency said on Tuesday in a provisional report, after the UK experienced its hottest summer on record this year.
The UKHSA said the highest number of heat-associated deaths was recorded between June 21 and 28, when an estimated 2,401 deaths were associated with the period of extreme heat.
It comes after Europe experienced another summer marked by prolonged periods of extreme heat, which scientists say are becoming more frequent and intense because of climate change.
Other European countries have also reported record excess mortality from the heatwaves over the summer.
Researchers from Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine estimated that more than 50,000 heat-related deaths occurred in urban areas across 30 European countries during the summer, the highest toll recorded since 2000.
The announcement of the latest data from the UK comes days after United Nations climate talks ended in collapse on Sunday, as the European Union and others rejected a final deal put forward by COP31 presidents Turkiye and Australia.
The EU claimed the draft text was too weak to advance the fight against global warming with no reference to fossil fuels.
The failed talks reflect the struggle by governments across the world to muster ambitious action to address the worsening consequences of climate change, including heatwaves, wildfires, floods and powerful storms – as wars and economic pressures compete for their attention.

noticias.titulo: Iran files lawsuits in US, EU courts: Will it get justice for ‘war crimes’?
noticias.resumen: As Iran seeks accountability and compensation for alleged war crimes, experts say legal proceedings face steep hurdles.
noticias.texto:
Iran files lawsuits in US, EU courts: Will it get justice for ‘war crimes’?
As Iran seeks accountability and compensation for war crimes, experts say legal proceedings face steep hurdles.
Iran has filed lawsuits in the United States and European countries for alleged war crimes committed during the US-Israel war, including the missile attack on a school that killed at least 178 people, most of them schoolgirls.
Vice President for Legal Affairs Majid Ansari said on Sunday that Iran has begun legal proceedings in courts in the US and four European countries over “war crimes”, months after the deadly attack on a primary school in Minab in February on the first day of the ongoing war.
The lawsuits will cover the killing of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Iran’s official news agency IRNA reported. They will also address the deaths of scientists, military commanders and civilians, as well as attacks on civilian infrastructure, including hospitals, ambulances and emergency facilities.
Speaking at a ceremony honouring the families of children killed in US and Israeli attacks, Ansari said his office is working with the country’s justice and foreign ministries to pursue claims under international law.
The courts in the US and European countries have not been identified, but Ansari said proceedings had been initiated in courts that accepted jurisdiction over the cases. He gave no further specific details.
Experts say the cases in Europe may offer a more viable legal avenue, while proceedings in the US face significant jurisdictional hurdles. But whether Iran can turn these proceedings into meaningful accountability is questionable.
“Iran is pursuing the legal avenues available to it, seeking accountability and preserving evidence,” Saeed Bagheri, an assistant professor in international law at the University of Reading in the UK, told Al Jazeera.
“Compensation may be an objective, but it is far from assured.”
Iran’s expanding legal campaign
Iran is pursuing its cases in the US and Europe because it has limited access to international courts.
Ansari said Iran was considering filing a case with the International Criminal Court (ICC), which tries individuals charged with the most grave crimes. But Tehran – alongside the US and Israel – is not a signatory to the Rome Statute under which the court was formed in 2002. Iran would, therefore, need an independent basis for jurisdiction, such as a UN Security Council referral.
At the International Court of Justice (ICJ) – the world’s top court that handles legal disputes between states – jurisdiction depends on state consent under Article 36 of the ICJ, said Bagheri.
“Iran cannot simply demand a hearing in either court,” said the expert, who is also a fellow at the Max Planck Institute for Comparative Public Law and International Law based in Germany.
Amid the legal hurdles, Iran has filed a number of cases in both domestic and international courts accusing the US and Israel of committing war crimes in the June 2025 war as well as the ongoing war. Iran says more than 3,500 people have been killed and 26,500 wounded in the war, along with widespread damage to civilian infrastructure, including schools, hospitals, bridges and energy facilities.
In March, Iran filed a complaint at the Iran-US Claims Tribunal in The Hague, accusing Washington of military aggression, illegal economic sanctions and threats of force. The Tribunal was formed following the 1981 Algiers Accords brokered by Algeria.
On Sunday, Ansari said preparations were under way for a second complaint to the Tribunal over the current war.
In September, Iran’s judiciary issued indictments against 159 senior US and Israeli political and military officials over the assassination of Khamenei and military commanders, judiciary spokesman Ali Kazemi said.
The Iranian judiciary has also said that about 400 cases have been filed with Iranian courts as part of domestic and international legal proceedings, including one involving 350,000 plaintiffs, Press TV reported.
A judiciary official on Monday said that local courts have demanded $290bn in damages from the United States.
A separate civil lawsuit was filed in the US in September by the National Iranian American Council Action (NIAC), a US civil society organisation, alongside several Iranian plaintiffs, including the father of a girl killed in the Minab school bombing. The case seeks a ruling that the US military campaign in Iran was unconstitutional. This case was not brought by the Iranian government.
The evidence required
The Minab school bombing is a large component of Iran’s pursuit of justice in the US and European courts.
In September, a report by the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission found that the United States likely committed “war crimes” when it struck the school.
But Iran’s arsenal of evidence to prove that the Minab school bombing was a war crime would have to be wide in scope – civilian deaths do not, on their own, establish a war crime, said Bagheri in Reading.
Iran would need to establish who carried out the attack, what was targeted and what the relevant decision-makers knew at the time, he explained.
Calling a strike accidental also does not settle whether it was lawful or not, said Bagheri.
Investigators must assess whether the military followed the rules of distinction, proportionality and precautions to protect civilians, he added.
“For Minab, the crucial evidence would include targeting files, intelligence assessments, no-strike lists, collateral-damage estimates and records showing when the information was last verified,” Bagheri explained.
According to the UN Mission’s report, the civilian nature of the school was apparent and the US failed in its obligation “to do everything feasible” to verify that it was a military objective.
The report’s authors said that photographs and videos depicting the school before and after the attack showed “readily identifiable features” that it was associated with an educational facility for young children.
“According to public reporting, satellite imagery of the school before the strike also appears to show human figures, readily identifiable as children, gathered in its courtyard,” the report said.
Ultimately, the biggest challenge, said Bagheri, would be linking the evidence of what happened to the decisions, knowledge and intentions of specific military commanders or officials, rather than simply establishing that civilians were killed.
In June, US President Donald Trump said that “nobody” purposefully attacked a girls’ school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident, for which the Pentagon has not yet published any findings.
The Pentagon launched an internal investigation, but it has not yet publicly released its report.
Who could be held to account?
Both the US and Israeli states, as well as individual officials and military commanders, could potentially be held responsible for the alleged violations, but under different legal frameworks.
State responsibility depends on whether an action can be attributed to a state and whether it breached international law, said Bagheri.
Individual criminal responsibility, meanwhile, can extend to those who carried out, ordered or assisted crimes, as well as commanders who failed to prevent or respond to crimes by forces under their effective control, the expert said.
Rank alone does not matter and investigators must establish what individuals knew, what authority they exercised and what they could have done, said Bagheri.
Still, immunity may also shield some officials from prosecution in foreign courts, particularly serving heads of state, government leaders and foreign ministers.
“Functional immunity for other officials accused of international crimes is more contested and depends on the forum,” said the expert from the University of Reading.
“But I would treat Khamenei’s killing separately. Article 110 of Iran’s Constitution gives the supreme leader command authority, but that title alone does not settle whether he was lawfully targetable.”
His actual military role and the circumstances of the attack matter, he added.
From courtrooms to accountability
Iran may have a more viable path to pursuing its cases in Europe than in the US.
In some European countries, prosecutors can pursue serious international crimes under universal jurisdiction, regardless of the nationality of the accused or where the alleged offences happened.
But, Bagheri stressed, this route could lead to the prosecution of individuals – not a criminal trial of the US or Israeli governments.
The majority of European Union member states practice universal jurisdiction, according to the European Union Agency for Criminal Justice Cooperation (Eurojust). The principle of universal jurisdiction allows the prosecution of individuals suspected of international crimes regardless of where they are committed.
In recent years, EU member states have been successful in bringing a number of perpetrators of international crimes to court on the basis of universal or extraterritorial jurisdiction, with convictions obtained in situations as diverse as Syria, Afghanistan, Rwanda and Liberia, including for crimes dating back 40 years, reports Eurojust.
Still, EU countries have varying requirements to proceed with a case, spanning their own presence, residence, nationality or territorial requirements, said Bagheri.
In his view, victims or civil parties are more likely to find success in producing investigations and preserving evidence than bringing senior US or Israeli officials to trial.
In the US, however, Iran faces “serious obstacles” in pursuing its cases, Bagheri said.
“That does not make them pointless, but getting a complaint before a court is a long way from securing a trial or compensation,” he said.
The first obstacle is sovereign immunity – the country’s Federal Tort Claims Act excludes claims arising in a foreign country and claims arising from combatant activities during wartime, said Bagheri.
Suing individual officials may not get around those protections either, he added.
The US War Crimes Act allows prosecution for certain offences, but neither Iran nor victims can initiate federal criminal cases themselves – that decision rests with US prosecutors, said Bagheri.
Experts point out that securing compensation could prove even more difficult than obtaining an investigation or court judgement.
State property may be immune from seizure, while a company’s links to a defendant do not automatically make its assets available to satisfy a judgement. US sanctions on Iran could further complicate payments, Bagheri said.
An arrest warrant, Bagheri said, does not guarantee that a suspect will be detained. Suspects generally must enter a country willing and legally able to act, he said, adding that an Interpol Red Notice is not an international arrest warrant and does not compel an arrest.
Despite these obstacles, Bagheri said Iran’s proceedings could still serve the purpose: preserving evidence and, where courts reach the merits, establishing legal responsibility.

noticias.titulo: UK sanctions Yemen’s Houthi group and four of its top officials
noticias.resumen: Group must be held accountable for 'targeting our partners and innocent civilians', says Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.
noticias.texto:
UK sanctions Yemen’s Houthi group and four of its top officials
Group must be held accountable for ‘targeting our partners and innocent civilians’, says Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.
The United Kingdom has imposed sanctions on Yemen’s Houthis as well as four of the armed group’s senior officials.
Announcing the measures on Wednesday, the British government accused the Iran-backed group of “deliberately attempting to undermine stability in the Middle East”.
It accused the four sanctioned individuals – Houthi Interior Minister Abdulkarim Amir al-Din Hussein al-Houthi, security and intelligence chief Abdul Hakim Hashem Ali al-Khaiwani, judge Mohammed Moufleh and prosecutor Sarim al-Din Muffadal – of involvement in human rights abuses.
Muffadal, according to the UK government, “is reasonably suspected of having directly perpetrated, or knowingly permitted or acquiesced in, sexual violence, including rape, torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment of women detainees”.
Al-Houthi, meanwhile, allegedly oversaw the custody of detainees who were “subjected to torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment”. Such abuses included “electric shocks, beatings and sexual violence”, the UK government said.
The sanctioned individuals are subject to an asset freeze and travel ban, it added.
The UK government said the measures reaffirmed Britain’s view that “Houthi aggression is unacceptable and that the group must be held to account”.
It cited the group’s attacks on vessels in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, strikes targeting civil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and “aggression” in Yemen.
Since seizing Yemen’s capital Sanaa in September 2014, the Houthis – also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God – have controlled much of northern and western Yemen, and Yemen’s internationally recognised government has controlled much of the south. While a United Nations-brokered ceasefire largely halted the fighting in 2022, the conflict flared again in July when the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ports.
The group then carried out a lightning offensive in September, seizing much of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline near Bab al-Mandeb. Government forces launched a counteroffensive last month to recapture territory from the Houthis, but earlier this month forces allied to the government said they would withdraw from areas around the strait and focus on defending Aden.
During the latest flare-up in fighting, Saudi Arabia, which leads a coalition in support of Yemen’s internationally recognised government, has been targeted in near-daily Houthi rocket and drone strikes. One attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh in October killed 13 people.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the sanctions sent a message that Britain “will always act in support of British values and interests.”
“The Houthis’ renewed aggression targeting our partners and innocent civilians is unacceptable and they must be held to account,” said Miliband.

noticias.titulo: ‘We’ll keep sinking Russian ships’: Ukraine challenges Putin’s global reach
noticias.resumen: Ukraine's strike off Libya signals Kyiv's ability to challenge Russian influence beyond the front lines.
noticias.texto:
‘We’ll keep sinking Russian ships’: Ukraine challenges Putin’s global reach
Ukraine’s strike off Libya signals Kyiv’s growing ability to challenge Russian influence far beyond the front lines.
Kyiv, Ukraine – The Merkury warship was one of the newest Russian warships equipped with antiship, surface-to-air and cruise missiles and an advanced three-dimensional radar.
The corvette, commissioned three years ago, escorted the Western-sanctioned Angara freighter that was transporting weapons and military equipment to the eastern Libyan port of Benghazi as part of Russia’s “Libyan Express” route, according to Ukrainian intelligence.
Seven Ukrainian-made naval drones launched from a mothership struck the Merkury and MV Angara on Sunday, Kyiv said. Ukraine claimed the corvette was sunk, while Libyan military officials told The Associated Press news agency that it was severely damaged.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the strike, 2,400km (1,500 miles) from the front lines of Ukraine, “exemplary”.
The operation was not, however, just about destroying another Russian warship. It was also intended to demonstrate Ukraine’s ability to strike at Moscow’s naval assets far beyond the Black Sea, undermining Russia’s efforts to project military power internationally.
The Sunday strike is “so far, a political demonstration from Ukraine of ‘we can do it,'” Kyiv-based analyst Igar Tyshkevich told Al Jazeera.
“But if the attacks continue, Russia will find it more difficult to sell itself as a strong player.”
Tyshkevich said the attack could undermine Russia’s image as a powerful international ally, particularly among African governments and military authorities that have developed ties with Moscow.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Ukrainian forces have destroyed or damaged numerous Russian naval vessels.
Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli has condemned the attack.
The Kremlin uses assets in Benghazi, controlled by the eastern-based rival administration led by military renegade and leader of the self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA) Khalifa Haftar, as a gateway to the Mediterranean, according to observers.
Russia has deployed radar and advanced air-defence systems to military facilities in Libya, strengthening its surveillance and military capabilities in the central Mediterranean, close to NATO’s southern flank.
Eastern Libya is a maritime entry and logistics hub for Russia’s military presence in North Africa and the Sahel. While Moscow uses military transport aircraft to move personnel and lighter cargo, heavy equipment and supplies are also transported by sea.
Ports, particularly Tobruk and Benghazi, provide access for Russian cargo vessels, with facilities for docking, unloading and resupply. Eastern Libya also connects Mediterranean maritime routes with inland military airbases, including al-Khadim and al-Jufra, and southern transport corridors leading towards the Sahara and the Sahel, where Russia maintains military deployments.
‘We’ll keep sinking Russian ships’
The strike offers a perfect formula to further interrupt Russia’s Sahel operations, said a drone maker in Ukraine.
“This is the way. We’ll keep sinking [Russian ships] one by one. Easy does it,” Andrey Pronin, a pioneer of drone warfare, told Al Jazeera.
The amount of damage is not clear yet, but Russia has promised revenge.
“Even in Moscow, they don’t understand the scale of the damage; it will have to be assessed,” Ruslan Suleymanov, an associate fellow at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre, a United States-British think tank, told Al Jazeera.
Eastern Libyan areas controlled by Haftar – and Benghazi in particular – have become “a key hub from the logistical viewpoint” for the Russian military in the Middle East and North Africa since the 2024 fall of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, Suleymanov said.
The Sunday attack is “a heavy blow, in terms of [Moscow’s international] image too; it shows at least that the war is going on not just in Ukraine, but also on other fronts, and that of course, the Russian military is very vulnerable, including in the Libyan areas”, he said.
For years, Russia has been expanding its footprint in the Sahel, offering military support and economic cooperation to Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso.
Ukraine said the Angara was carrying Russian military equipment as part of Moscow’s military supply network in Libya, which supports its wider military presence in Africa, including the Sahel.
At least partially, Ukraine “destroyed the sea component of the African Corps supply”, Nikolay Mitrokhin, a researcher with Germany’s Bremen University, told Al Jazeera, referring to the Kremlin-backed military force operating in Africa.
Guided by the “my-enemy’s-enemy-is-my-friend” principle, Kyiv has been trying to aid anti-Moscow forces despite their affiliations.
Syrian rebels who overthrew al-Assad in 2024 received drones and other military supplies from Ukraine, The Washington Post reported.
Kyiv sent about 20 drone operators and some 150 drones to help the Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) opposition group based in Idlib, the paper claimed, citing sources familiar with Ukrainian military operations abroad.
Ukrainian special forces helped Syrian rebels “destroy” Russian mercenaries in southern Syria, the Kyiv Post reported in June 2024.
“Russia as a global player faces the rising influence of Ukraine as a global player – and it happens in the regions where it doesn’t expect to face it,” Mitrokhin said.
He doubts, however, the practicality of hitting Russia wherever it hurts – and suspects the Pentagon’s involvement in strikes against Moscow.
“What I see in it is Zelenskyy striving to prove to Putin that Ukraine can ‘compete with Russia globally’ or at least in hotspots,” he said.
“I don’t rule out that Ukraine causes trouble to Russia at the request or with maximal support from the US military, that tries to limit Russia’s growing clout in these areas without getting their own hands dirty and without a direct conflict with Russia,” he said.
The Sunday operation may complicate efforts by the Malian military and Russia’s Africa Corps to consolidate their positions in northern Mali, Mitrokhin said.
At least 15 Ukrainian drone pilots help the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) fight Mali’s military government despite their links to the Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin group affiliated with al-Qaeda, CNN reported in September.
CNN cited a Ukrainian defence intelligence source as saying Ukrainian drone experts were also stationed in Sudan and trained troops from Chad, Niger and Burkina Faso in Mali.
Ukraine’s use of minimal resources to help Russia’s enemies contrasts with NATO’s slowness and indecisiveness.
“While the alliance’s nations act indecisively, and Putin sees it as a weakness and ups the escalation, Ukraine finds a way to fight the enemy in a very complicated situation,” Lieutenant General Ihor Romanenko, former deputy head of Ukraine’s General Staff of Armed Forces, told Al Jazeera.

noticias.titulo: HIV infections could rise amid aid cuts, UN warns
noticias.resumen: The impact of United States government funding cuts has been dramatic for many HIV programs, UNAIDS warned. The agency expects that 2027 data to show an increase in new infections after being on the cusp of ending AIDS.
noticias.texto:
HIV infections could rise after historic lows amid aid cuts, UN warns
November 24, 2026
New HIV infections could rise next year for the first time in years, reversing a historic decline amid funding cuts and anti-rights campaigns, the United Nations (UN) warned on Tuesday.
"The world has moved closer towards controlling the HIV pandemic, but changes in funding and resulting service disruptions jeopardize this progress," the UNAIDS agency said in its annual global update.
AIDS-related death numbers has fallen to its lowest in more than two decades. According to the organization, this was made possible by broader access to treatment and improvements in the quality of care programs.
The virus claimed roughly 570,000 lives globally in 2025. This means almost 1,600 people died everyday. In comparison, this figure was 600,000 in 2024 and 1.3 million in 2010.
Based on data from 172 countries, the agency estimated that 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV in 2025, of whom 32.1 million were receiving antiretroviral treatment.
The wider use of antiretroviral medication also reduces the risk of HIV transmission, the organization said. It estimates that 1.2 million people contracted HIV in 2025, down from 1.3 million the year before. The peak in 1994 saw 3.5 million.
"HIV, which was once a death sentence, has become a manageable health condition for millions of people thanks to life-saving HIV medicines," said UNAIDS.
'Dramatic impacts' of US aid cuts
Despite the encouraging data so far, cuts to international funding have hampered efforts to fight HIV, the agency warned.
HIV programs faced an 18-percent decrease in international financing over the past year, said UNAIDS.
"Funding losses have destabilized HIV programs worldwide, coinciding with a wider contraction in official development assistance over the years," it said.
Although the United States remains the largest international donor for HIV programs, its contributions dropped by 26% between 2024 and 2025.
After dismantling USAID, the world's largest foreign aid agency, last year, the Donald Trump administration has sought to replace decades of aid with new bilateral deals.
"The impact of the United States government funding cuts has been especially dramatic given the reliance of many countries on its support for core HIV programs," said UNAIDS.
Meanwhile disbursements from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria dropped by 13% in 2025.
Next year's data may show rising infections
"We are on the cusp of ending AIDS – this has been the greatest story of global health – and just when we should finish it, cuts and the rolling back of human rights is threatening to take away our gains," Winnie Byanyima, executive director of UNAIDS, told Reuters.
"We haven't ‌got the data yet, but we see the signs. We see all the signs of reversals," she added.
Byanyima predicted that data released in 2027 would begin to reflect a rise in new HIV infections.
In 2015, the UN set a goal to end AIDS by 2030.

noticias.titulo: Pope Francis diaries recount spiritual crisis, him seeing the 'Devil'
noticias.resumen: Extracts of the late Pope Francis' diaries have been published, the first release of its kind since the 1960s. They discuss his struggles with his role in the Vatican and visions of the devil and the gates of hell.
noticias.texto:
Pope Francis diaries recount spiritual crisis, him seeing the 'Devil'
November 24, 2026
The late Pope Francis suffered a spiritual crisis during his papacy when he struggled with how to lead the Catholic Church and believed he saw and heard the devil on several occasions, according to an annotated collection of his private diaries published on Tuesday.
Francis was pope for 12 years until his death last April.
Cardinal Victor Fernandez, a compatriot and close collaborator of Francis', collated the diary entries and provides accompanying commentary, in the first set of papal diaries to be published posthumously since those of John XXIII, who died in 1963.
What does the book say about Francis' difficulties as pope?
The diary entries speak of the Argentine-born pontiff not wanting to be someone "who uses others like puppets," according to the accompanying commentary.
"It was all mixed with governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation," a December 2022 entry from Francis said.
Although the book does not make clear exactly who Francis worried he was using like puppets or the nature of the internal pressures, Francis encountered stern resistance from more conservative forces within the Church as he urged the staid institution to modernize.
Cardinal Fernandez wrote that Francis "ultimately recognized it was the worst trial that had toremented him ... and that he felt that he was in a continual battle not to fall into this demonic seduction."
What does the book say about Francis' religious visions and dreams?
The 160-page selection of excerpts — starting in 1992 when he was still known as Jorge Mario Bergoglio and running until a few months before his death — are arranged by theme and pay closer attention to Francis' internal spiritual experiences than Vatican politics.
But one of the three occasions listed where the late pope believed he had seen the Devil was during a meeting with Vatican officials in January 2021 early in what he termed a spiritual crisis. In that instance he even believed to have heard the figure speak.
"I can't forget the powerful raspiness of his voice," Francis wrote in an entry. "The Lord granted me an opportunity to leave that meeting, and thus he freed me."
Other entries detail how Francis believed that God spoke to him in his dreams, and one from 2018 stated: "Last night I saw the entrance to Hell. I peeked in to look a little, and it terrified me."
What else features in the diary excerpts?
The papers show Francis to be self-critical at times, chastizing himself for "feelings of disdain, envy, pride" or for ignoring a drunken man who approached him "because I wanted to have a serene walk."
At one point in a 2022 entry he refers to himself as the "proud, self-sufficient, cynical, self-deceptive Jorge."
They also show how in later years he felt anxious to make the most of his remaining years, and regretful about some of his deicsions earlier in his life.
"I want to do good during the little time I have left, desiring to be good," he wrote in 1996 on turning 60. "How much time I've used badly! How much badly done!"
The accounts also list his regret after a visit to Chile in 2018 when he faced stern criticism for initially dismissing allegations of sexual abuse and cover-up against a bishop there before later apologizing.
"It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn't think it was so serious," a "devastated" pontiff wrote three years later.
Fernandez also recounts comments from Francis on some senior officials in the Vatican including his successor, US Cardinal Robert Prevost, now Pope Leo XIV. According to Fernandez, Francis called him "a great pastor, a generous missionary, and an irreproachable man."

noticias.titulo: EU enlargement: Why do some EU member states use their vetoes to block the accession of certain candidate countries?
noticias.resumen: Individual EU member states use their veto powers to block candidate countries in the accession process — often for reasons of domestic politics. DW takes a look at some cases and examines what's behind them.
noticias.texto:
EU enlargement: Who's blocking whom — and why?
November 24, 2026
