It's been quite a while since the European Union's last enlargement, when Croatia joined the bloc back in 2013.
If everything goes according to plan, another might soon be on the cards: Montenegro, with a population of just 620,000, could complete accession negotiations in the coming months and join the EU in early 2028.
But no sooner had EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos made this announcement in October than news emerged that Croatia might veto Montenegro's accession unless the country meets a series of Croatian demands.
EU politicians and MEPs were dismayed.
This is not the first time that something like this has happened: The veto rights that member states have on many EU matters have increasingly been used by individual countries in recent years as a means of blackmail and a political weapon, paralyzing the EU in the process.
DW takes a look at some of the most significant cases, the background to them and what are — in some instances — the serious political consequences of them.
Montenegro: Croatia's eight demands
Montenegro is the most advanced EU candidate country, with a potential accession date of 2028. It has already provisionally closed several of the EU's 33 negotiating chapters.
As of November 23, however, Croatia is blocking the closure of three chapters that have already been negotiated.
Zagreb is demanding, among other things, compensation for former prisoners held in Montenegrin camps during the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s, clarification of the fate of Croatians who have been missing since that time, and more rigorous prosecution of war crimes.
There are also disputes over the precise maritime boundary between the two countries. In addition, Croatia is demanding payment of about €2.4 billion (about $2.6 billion) for assets that belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army, the army of the former Yugoslavia to which both countries belonged before its breakup in the early 1990s.
Montenegro has already responded to some of Croatia's demands, including those concerning compensation for former prisoners. Others, such as the one relating to the assets of the Yugoslav People's Army, are disputed.
It is clear that Croatia's list of demands is also driven by domestic politics. No government in Zagreb can afford to appear compliant on issues relating to the Croatian War of Independence (1991–95).
Moreover, moderate conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic, who is regularly accused in Croatia of being too pro-EU, can use the dispute to portray himself as a staunch defender of national interests.
Ukraine: Hungarian domestic politics in the name of a minority
After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the EU in June 2022 granted Ukraine and the Republic of Moldova EU candidate status through an accelerated procedure as a gesture of solidarity.
Many EU member states have reservations about Ukraine joining the bloc quickly. Nevertheless, only Hungary, under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, adopted an obstructive stance.
Ostensibly, Hungary's obstruction was about getting Ukraine to improve the rights of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia in western Ukraine. Ultimately, however, Orban used the matter for domestic political purposes and as an election campaign issue, portraying Ukraine as a "mafia state."
In an effort to appeal to widespread anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Hungary, the country's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, has also adopted a tough stance on Ukraine.
Nevertheless, Magyar's government lifted several temporary blocks on the opening of new negotiating chapters, among other things after the Ukrainian parliament passed a law in early October strengthening the educational rights of national minorities.
North Macedonia: The never-ending blockade
No EU candidate country has suffered as much or as long from veto politics as North Macedonia: It was granted EU candidate status in 2005 but only began accession negotiations in July 2022.
Greece blocked the start of negotiations for 13 years because it objected to the name "Republic of Macedonia," as the country was previously known, and accused its neighbor of laying territorial claims to the region of Macedonia in northern Greece.
The dispute was settled in 2018 through a compromise that saw the country change its name to the Republic of North Macedonia the following year.
But just as the path to accession negotiations seemed clear, Bulgaria blocked the opening of talks in November 2020.
Bulgaria regards the Macedonian language as a dialect of Bulgarian and disputes the existence of a distinct Macedonian nation.
Here, too, domestic Bulgarian politics is ultimately a factor.
Former Bulgarian President and current Prime Minister Rumen Radev, for example, fueled the escalation with North Macedonia to enhance his political profile.
Serbia: Croatia is not the only country obstructing progress
Although Serbia has been negotiating EU accession since 2014, little progress has been made.
In July, when the country was still led by President Aleksandar Vucic, no less than eight EU member states — including Croatia — opposed opening further negotiating chapters with Serbia.
While the main reservations relate to democratic shortcomings, deficiencies in the rule of law and corruption in Serbia, Croatia also has its own disputes with its eastern neighbor.
These concern the 1991–95 war, including missing persons, war crimes, minority rights and differing interpretations of history. Relations are also strained by nationalist rhetoric on both sides.
Whether the election victory of the Student List in Belgrade in late October after almost two years of anti-government, anti-corruption protests will change this situation is impossible to say.
Albania: Greece threatens to use minority rights as leverage
The EU opened accession negotiations with Albania, which has been an EU candidate since 2014, in July 2022.
Albania could become the bloc's next new member after Montenegro. However, Greece has repeatedly threatened (most recently in June) to block the accession process unless the rights of the Greek minority, particularly relating to property rights, are adequately protected.
An end to the veto system?
In light of all this, Brussels has long been debating a reform of the accession process and the EU veto system.
In early October, the European Commission proposed that decisions to open negotiations with candidate countries be made by qualified majority rather than unanimously. It also proposed that new EU members would be required to give up the right to veto decisions in certain policy areas altogether for a specified period.
The problem with these proposed reforms is that they would themselves have to be adopted unanimously. In other words, any member state could veto the reform.

noticias.titulo: CAS reinstates Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions
noticias.resumen: The Court of Arbitration for Sport has reinstated Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions, overturning a CAF decision that stripped them of the title. Morocco, previously declared winners, are confirmed runners-up.
noticias.texto:
CAS reinstates Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions
November 24, 2026
Just over eight months after Senegal were stripped of their 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON) title, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has announced that Senegal's appeal has been upheld, reinstating them as 2025 AFCON winners. Morocco, who had been declared champions after a Confederation of African Football (CAF) review, has now been confirmed as runners-up.
"The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French)," the CAS statement read.
"The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed."
The statement continued that it felt "the Referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority" and that his "decision was covered by the ‘field of play’ doctrine."
The decision comes after a closed-doors hearing at CAS' headquarters in Lausanne in early October.
Before the verdict was delivered, Morocco captain Achraf Hakimi posted a message on Instagram saying he would disagree with Senegal being stripped of the title because "its players fought so hard to win."
"I respect the authorities responsible for football, but I firmly believe that what happens on the pitch should be the most important thing of all. Senegal won that Africa Cup of Nations final through their performance, their determination, and the effort of every player, just as every player represents his country. They fought for that title, and no one can erase what those players achieved on the pitch," Hakimi wrote.
"African football needs unity, fairness, and credibility. We cannot keep building our game if decisions like these leave players and fans questioning everything."
An infamous AFCON final
The final was played on January 18, with Senegal winning 1-0 after extra-time. However, the game was thrown into confusion when many Senegal players walked off the pitch following the referee's decision to award Morocco a penalty in the final minutes. Around 15 minutes later, and after furious Senegalese fans had attempted a pitch invasion, the players did return. Morocco's Brahim Diaz inexplicably missed the penalty, sending the game into extra time, which is when Senegal scored the eventual winner.
Just 10 days afterwards, the CAF issued fines worth more than $1 million (€835,000) and banned players from both teams.
Two months later, and after the Senegal team had paraded the trophy to their fans, CAF declared that Senegal had "forfeited" the final by leaving the pitch. CAF then overturned the result, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory and the title. The Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) denounced the CAF decision and took the case to CAS.
The aftermath had rumbled on for months, with many believing it damaging for African football as a whole.
"If you look at it critically, the value of African football will definitely go down with this," Collins Okinyo, a former CAF media consultant, told DW after the result had been overturned in March.
Impact on future World Cup host
The ruling brings an end to a saga that had cast a cloud over a well-organized tournament in Morocco.
The country is emerging as a major football hub in Africa. Already confirmed as a co-host for the World Cup in 2030, Morocco also hosted the 2026 Women's AFCON and has been hosting the U17 Women's World Cup annually since 2025 and is set to do so until 2029. It is further rumored that the Morocco, along with fellow 2030 World Cup hosts Spain and Portugal, is keen to host the next Club World Cup in 2029 as a form of preparation ahead of the big event in 2030.
Although it has made significant advances in sports infrastructure, not everyone is happy about Morocco's push into the football world. In 2025, there were major protests by Gen Z questioning the country's priorities in light of struggling health and education systems.

noticias.titulo: Why Iran's medicine supply chain is failing
noticias.resumen: Pharmacies in Iran are closing, hospital deliveries have stalled and patients are rationing doses or turning to black markets.
noticias.texto:
Why Iran's medicine supply chain is failing
November 24, 2026
Ahmad,* 67, visited nearly 20 Tehran pharmacies for the antipsychotic drug chlorpromazine, but left empty-handed.
"When a patient has to go to this many pharmacies just to find an essential drug, you really have to ask who is responsible for supplying medicine," he told DW.
Mitra,* a 37-year-old Tehran resident with diabetes , spent days hunting for insulin. "These are not drugs I can postpone taking or simply give up," she said. "My life depends on regular access to this insulin."
Their ordeal reflects a wider crisis across Iran's health care system.
Along with Tehran residents, DW spoke with an official at Iran's Food and Drug Administration (IFDA) and pharmacy workers in Tehran, Rasht and Mahabad. The interviews were conducted anonymously or using pseudonyms as speaking with foreign media remains dangerous in Iran.
Iran's broken drug supply chain
The official said that Iran's falling currency, along with price controls, has drained domestic drugmaker profits, while unpaid hospital debts have delayed deliveries.
"Add our own hospitals' heavy unpaid debts to distributors, and you can see why distribution has ground to a halt and companies are no longer supplying hospitals," the official said.
"Unless the Plan and Budget Organization makes our currency allocation realistic, banks step in with loans for drugmakers and insurers settle their debts, the Health Ministry's hands will remain tied and this disaster cannot be stopped," the official warned.
IFDA spokesman Mohammad Hashemi told Iran's semi-official ILNA news agency on November 9 that fewer than 40 of roughly 700 essential drugs faced supply difficulties. However, pharmacists told DW about how difficult it can be to get drugs on shelves.
A pharmacy manager in Tehran said insurance payments are often delayed by months, while drug prices continue to climb. Another pharmacist in the northwestern Mahabad region said distributors demand cash upfront for scarce items.
The insurance delays and shifting rules have pushed some pharmacies to drop contracts or refuse costly insured drugs.
The pharmacist in Mahabad, who prefers to be called Leili,* said that general pharmacies can lack about 40 items, and larger specialty pharmacies stocking chemotherapy and complex treatments can lack over 100, including psychiatric and Parkinson's drugs, and insulin vials.
"Many drugs can no longer be found in the official supply chain at all, such as nimodipine tablets [used to treat certain strokes] or hospital injectable antibiotics that have no substitutes," she said.
Turning to low-quality, black market medicine
As common items like cold medication become scarcer or more expensive, some people are turning to home remedies, she said. She added that for essential medicines like insulin, chronic patients are using smaller doses to preserve supply.
Many of those unable to pay are middle-class customers whom pharmacists cannot easily refer to charities, she said, with elderly and psychiatric patients among the hardest hit.
Leili warned that lower quality seen in some reverse-engineered domestic drugs presents a high risk for cancer, transplant and autoimmune patients.
She added that some families are forced to turn to street markets usually located outside of clinics, which lack cold-chain controls and sell counterfeit medicines or drugs with altered expiration dates.
Another pharmacy manager who asked to be called Khadiv* said scarce medicines can fetch up to 10 times their official price.
Sanctions and blockades
Amid the current conflict with the US, Khadiv said US sanctions, along with border disruptions and the US maritime blockade in the Strait of Hormuz inflate import costs.
In a statement, the US State Department told DW its sanctions follow international law to deny Tehran funds for "destabilizing behavior," stressing the measures allow "broad authorizations and exceptions" for food, medicine and medical devices. It pointed to what it called Iran's "corrupt ruling elite" for not properly allocating resources.
Iranian officials, however, reject that claim. In late summer, Health Minister Mohammad Reza Zafarghandi called US exemption claims "a big lie," saying banking, insurance, flight and shipping sanctions block imports.
Earlier this fall, the IFDA's raw materials chief cited currency, banking, customs and shipping hurdles as the main bottleneck.
DW emailed the Iranian Embassy's media office in Berlin for comment but received no reply.
"Seeing so many people unable to afford their medicine or reach medical centers leaves me with a sense of guilt and helplessness," Khadiv said, adding that lack of access can even lead to patient deaths.
For patients like Ahmad and Mitra, the standoff offers no relief, and every day, the gap between official assurances and what is actually on pharmacy shelves grows harder to ignore.
*Names changed for safety reasons.

noticias.titulo: Colombia: Car bomb attack injures at least 23
noticias.resumen: The explosion in Villavicencio coincides with the tenth anniversary of a peace accord with FARC guerrillas, casting doubt on Colombia's peace process.
noticias.texto:
Colombia: Car bomb attack injures at least 23
November 24, 2026
At least 23 people were injured in Colombia on Monday night when a car bomb tore through the central city of Villavicencio, local authorities confirmed on Tuesday.
The explosion occurred at approximately 9:30 p.m. (3:30 a.m. CET Tuesday) in front of the headquarters of the regional government of Meta province and caused severe structural damage to nearby buildings.
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella confirmed the incident and said no deaths had been reported "so far."
Reporters for the AFP news agency said the blast knocked out power across parts of the city center, leaving damaged cars lining nearby streets and ripping open shopfronts.
"The doors were bent in, the windows shattered, some display cases inside broken," said local resident Johan Perez, who owns a hat shop. "We are alive by a miracle."
The Spanish EFE news agency reported that a well-known local restaurant was completely destroyed and suggested that the structural integrity of the government building itself may have been compromised, raising concerns that it could collapse.
Who is behind Villavicencio blast?
The attack has not been publicly claimed by any group but it came on the eve of the 10th anniversary of Colombia's landmark peace accord with FARC guerrillas.
The agreement persuaded the FARC, once Latin America's largest guerrilla army, to lay down its weapons after more than half a century of conflict.
Shortly before Monday's blast, President De la Espriella had denounced the peace accord as a "false peace."
According to the local Caracol radio station, investigators' initial theories point to a FARC commander known as "Antonio Medina" who leads the dissidents' 28th and 39th fronts, known as the "Amazonas Bloc."
De La Espriella blames 'narco-terrorists'
President De La Espriella, who took office in August and has launched a United States-backed military offensive against armed groups and drug traffickers, blamed "narco-terrorists" for the attack.
"I warn the narco-terrorists responsible: you will answer for every drop of blood you have spilled and every business and property you have destroyed," he wrote on social media.
"We will deploy the full power of the state to hunt you down, dismantle your organizations and take you out." De La Espriella added.
The incident marks the latest violent resurgence of a conflict that has shaken Colombia, the world's largest cocaine-producing nation, over the past two years.
Between January and November, authorities recorded 358 drone strikes, more than one a day, according to a Defense Ministry document obtained by AFP.
Last year, a presidential candidate was assassinated on the campaign trail.

noticias.titulo: Germany's Wadephul 'shocked' by Trump's Nvidia intervention
noticias.resumen: The German foreign minister has criticized Donald Trump's interference in the chip-maker's economic activities. Jensen Huang was brought back after stepping down as Nvidia CEO amid multiple scandals.
noticias.texto:
German FM Wadephul 'shocked' by Trump's Nvidia intervention
November 24, 2026
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on Tuesday expressed shock over US President Donald Trump's admission that he persuaded chip-producing giant Nvidia to reinstall ousted CEO Jensen Huang.
Nvidia brought Huang back on Monday in a surprise decision, less than two weeks after the CEO stepped down amid a series of affairs.
What did Wadephul say about Trump's involvement in Nvidia?
"It shocked me, to be honest, because as far as I know, if I'm personally looking back, I have never seen or recognized such an intervention from the political side into a particular company," Wadephul told reporters at a foreign policy conference in Berlin.
"And I do have some doubts whether this is a very good model for the future," he added.
"But OK, that took place in the United States of America," the foreign minister said.
Wadephul went on to say there are enough reasons to defend the rules-based international order, and that includes political power not getting involved in the economic activities of companies.
Trump boasts about interference in Nvidia decision
Huang's shock reinstatement on Monday came on the back of a unanimous vote by Nvidia's board of directors.
The news was welcomed by Trump, who called it the "correct and proper decision" in a post on Truth Social. The president later said he had played a key role, having spoken "directly and indirectly" to the board of directors, urging them to reinstate the scandal-hit ex-CEO.
"I convinced them," Trump said. "I made the deal."
Huang came under massive fire after it was reported he had had an affair with the CEO of the Singapore-based company Megaspeed. She was also accused of being a spy working on behalf of Chinese intelligence.
Nvidia, Trump see stock surge after Huang's reinstallment
Nvidia's shares took a hit on Huang's stepping down, but rebounded by 30% on Monday after it was announced he was being reinstalled, adding over $900 billion (€820 billion) to the company's market value.
This share price surge also appears to have benefited Trump himself, with the Financial Times calculating that the president saw his Nvidia stock go up $15 million.
Huang's return has also brought some calm to the market that appeared to be teetering, with growing concerns about the viability of the AI sector, which now makes up a substantial part of the US stock market.
It also marks a turn around from the poor showing by Anthropic's IPO launch that saw its early gains quickly melt away amid fears that the AI sector has been overvalued.

noticias.titulo: Land mine deaths reach five-year high, watchdog says
noticias.resumen: Myanmar reported the highest annual land mine casualty toll, followed by Syria and Afghanistan, ICBL report says. Since 1999, nearly 50 thousand people were killed by land mines.
noticias.texto:
Land mine deaths hit a five-year high, report says
November 24, 2026
Land mines killed or injured more people in 2025 than in any year since 2020, according to the International Campaign to Ban Landmines' (ICBL) annual report.
The report stated that the number of recorded deaths was at least 6,929, which is a 10% increase compared with last year. According to the campaign, four out of five victims were civilians, and half of those were minors.
Experts say the true figure is likely higher as not all land mine related death and injuries are recorded as such.
Myanmar reported the highest annual casualty toll for the third year in a row, with 1,891 victims, amid a "massive" new mine use.
In Syria, the number of casualties climbed by 50% to 1,602 in 2025, after the large-scale return of displaced people following the ousting of president Bashar Assad.
Myanmar and Syria were followed by Afghanistan with 497 casualties.
'The Ottawa Treaty faces its greatest test,' report warns
The ICBL criticized Ukraine, over its continued use of land mines. Ukraine, which is currently being invaded by Russia, is one of the 162 state parties to the Mine Ban Treaty.
The treaty, known as the Ottawa Treaty, prohibits the use, production, storage and transfer of anti-personnel mines. The treaty was ratified by 166 countries, but not by China, India, Russia, Israel, North Korea, or the US, along with nearly 30 others.
Five European NATO countries, which share a border with Russia, have withdrawn from the treaty last year: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Finland and Poland. Ukraine has also withdrawn, though this will not take legal effect until the war ends.
"The treaty’s norms face their greatest test since 1999," the report said, citing the withdrawals.
In 2025, Ukraine justified its move to withdraw from the treaty by citing the actions of Russia, which has never ratified the treaty and has been using mines on Ukrainian territory.
The campaign said Ukraine was still "fully bound by the treaty" but had breached its ban on producing anti-personnel mines. It said the country had manufactured both 3D-printed mines and mines designed to be dropped by drones.
Report also noted that Russia has used antipersonnel land mines extensively in Ukraine since its full-scale invasion began in 2022.
Nearly 50 thousand people killed by land mines since 1999
Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Cambodia, Iraq, Morocco, North Korea, South Korea and Ukraine have "massive land mine contamination," meaning they have more than 100 square kilometers of land contaminated by land mines, the report assessed.
Since 1999, 49,859 people were killed and 118,525 injured by land mines, according to Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor, the research and monitoring arm of the ICBL, and the Cluster Munition Coalition NGOs.

noticias.titulo: Is North Korea holding back on sending Russia more troops?
noticias.resumen: A North Korean troop buildup Ukraine warned about months ago has yet to materialize, even as strategic cooperation continues. Analysts say Pyongyang is balancing its ties with Moscow and Beijing.
noticias.texto:
Is North Korea holding back on sending Russia more troops?
November 24, 2026
Over the summer, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that he expected between 30,000 and 50,000 North Korean soldiers would be deployed to Russia as part of Pyongyang's ongoing support of Moscow's war effort.
However, it now appears that troop buildup has yet to materialize, and it is unclear whether North Korea will continue sending large numbers of troops to Russia.
Writing on Telegram on November 9, Andrii Kovalenko, who resigned in September as head of Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation, said an August intelligence assessment indicated that the Kremlin had requested more than 30,000 additional North Korean troops for an autumn offensive.
He said a summit between North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and Russian President Vladimir Putin was expected in September, but did not happen. Kviy has claimed that North Korea previously sent thousands of troops to Russia's Kursk region in 2024, where Moscow was fighting to repel a Ukrainian incursion.
Kovalenko believes Pyongyang turned down Moscow's request because taking part in offensive operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine's Donetsk region may still be a red line for North Korea.
However, Kovalenko added that Russia still relies on North Korean material support, particularly ammunition, while assessing that another major deployment of North Korean combat troops was unlikely this winter.
No need for North Korean reinforcements?
Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, told DW that the lull in fighting and the onset of winter give Pyongyang little immediate reason to send reinforcements.
He added that a visit this week to Moscow by Jo Yong-won, a senior North Korean official and close aide to Kim, could shed light on any future plans.
Han said it remained to be seen whether the visit was intended to deepen political ties between the ruling parties, building on their military cooperation, or to lay the groundwork for a visit by Kim himself.
Ahn Chan-il, a former North Korean soldier who defected to South Korea in 1979 and now heads the World Institute for North Korea Studies in Seoul, said Moscow also had reasons to limit the deployment.
He told DW that he expects Russia to weigh its battlefield needs against the costs of bringing in more North Korean troops. Unless the war expands, he said, Moscow is unlikely to request a larger contingent.
North Korean weapons keep flowing
Ukrainian official Kovalenko said North Korea still had a missile unit in Russia's Voronezh region and around 8,500 support personnel in rear areas, including drone operators, engineers and sappers.
He added that Pyongyang was ramping up ammunition production and showcasing new drones and missiles.
In a post on X on November 17, Zelenskyy said that Russia was receiving dozens of North Korean ballistic missiles each month.
He warned that their use in Ukraine was helping Pyongyang refine its weapons and creating security risks for countries around the Korean Peninsula. Battle-testing weaponry is one of North Korea's primary advantages from military cooperation with Russia
Balancing Russia and China ties
Kovalenko said Pyongyang appeared to have adopted what he called a "containment strategy," limiting its military commitment to Russia's war while maintaining ties with both Moscow and Beijing.
In his assessment, this approach allows Pyongyang to retain the benefits of its alliance with Russia while reducing its exposure to the outcome of the war.
Analyst Ahn said he expects Pyongyang's military cooperation with Moscow to continue because Russian assistance is crucial to North Korea's efforts to develop drone technology and strengthen its navy.
Nevertheless, the extent of this cooperation may be more limited in the future, and Pyongyang is also able to turn to China as a hedge.
Ahn said that if Russia limits the deployment of North Korean troops, Pyongyang's foreign currency earnings from those deployments would have less room to grow, giving it another reason to seek more support from Beijing
Jeong Joon Hee, a former South Korean Unification Ministry spokesperson, told DW that recent moves towards building better ties with Beijing may also reflect Pyongyang's dissatisfaction with what Moscow has offered in return for North Korea's help.
By strengthening its relationship with China while keeping ties with Russia steady, he said, Pyongyang could also be trying to persuade Moscow to give it more.
Kim Hyung Suk, a former South Korean vice minister of unification, told DW that North Korea needs China's economic, political and diplomatic backing alongside the support it receives from Russia. He expects Pyongyang to keep pursuing China's support regardless of how it manages its role in the war.

noticias.titulo: How cautious investors are struggling to avoid the AI bubble
noticias.resumen: From Nvidia to Coreweave, AI and tech stocks have swung sharply in recent months. Some investors still see plenty of room to run, while others are trying to diversify — and finding it harder than expected.
noticias.texto:
How cautious investors are struggling to avoid the AI bubble
November 24, 2026
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index roared back to life this week after a worrying sell-off recently that saw huge falls in technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks.
After suffering its worst week since the pandemic crash of March 2020, the Nasdaq opened Monday (November 23) nearly 1,700 points, or 7%, higher.
The AI trade received a further boost after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced to resign amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
The chipmaker's stock rose more than 30% on the news, opening at nearly $170 (€155.5) per share and recovering most of the losses since last month, when the affair was first reported.
The surge helped propel US stock indices to their best day since last year. But in premarket trading on Tuesday, Nvidia fell about 5%, underscoring the volatility of the market and the risks facing the AI sector and the broader tech industry.
How passive investing is fueling the AI trade
The recent volatility around AI, memory chips and other technology stocks has unnerved even the most experienced and bullish investors.
Yet, those seeking a haven away from the United States stock market, which has enjoyed the majority of the AI hype — along with Taiwan and South Korea — are increasingly finding few places to shelter.
Economists warn that this is partly due to the way index funds, including exchange-traded funds (ETFs), work. These funds hold the pensions and other savings of hundreds of millions of passive investors.
These indices have become increasingly exposed to the AI boom.
Riding the winners works — until it doesn't
Most flagship index funds are keen to ride winners, so they automatically buy stocks according to a company's market value. The bigger a company grows, the more of it they hold.
The values of Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet and other US technology giants have benefited from this effect, with many soaring after ChatGPT was first released in late 2022.
The US also has an outsized position in funds that track the global economy. Nine of the top 10 holdings of the MSCI All Country World Index (ACWI), an index of more than 2,400 firms across 47 developed and emerging markets, are US Big Tech names.
The other is TSMC, a Taiwanese chipmaker that produces 90% of the high-end AI semiconductors.
Together, these 10 holdings make up nearly a quarter of the index.
Although it's a global index, nearly two-thirds of MSCI ACWI's value is in US-listed companies, even though they make up only around a fifth of its firms.
Don't put all your chips in AI stocks
"A well-diversified portfolio should ... reasonably represent the entire global economy," Gerd Kommer, founder of the Munich-based asset manager Gerd Kommer Invest, told DW.
"That's not the case if 70% of the portfolio is concentrated in just one country — the US. The global economy is more resilient than any national economy."
Kommer, who is known as Germany's "ETF pope," said investors need exposure to all economic sectors and that no single sector should make up more than a quarter of a portfolio.
Yet, even if investors want to avoid US-dominated World funds altogether, the AI trade still overshadows several other top index funds.
In MSCI's Emerging Market index, for example, the top 10 make up 37.5% of its value and TSMC alone accounts for almost 16%. Tech, chip and internet firms make up eight of the largest holdings, alongside two banks — one Chinese, one Indian.
How funds fuel investor hubris
That matters, according to Dimitri Vayanos, a finance professor at the London School of Economics who studies how passive investing pushes up the prices of the biggest firms.
"My model suggests that the effects of flows into index funds are larger when the large stocks happen to be in the same industry," Vayanos told DW.
When some investors get over-optimistic about a company and push the stock price up, index funds add to that price pressure.
Professional investors then often bet against overpriced stocks, a practice known as "shorting," which helps pull prices back down. But that's far riskier with, say, a tech giant than with a small firm.
"Being short 1% of SpaceX involves much more risk than being short 1% of a small company," said Vayanos.
The problem gets worse when the biggest firms are all in the same sector, as they are now. As short-sellers hold back, the biggest stocks climb further, creating what he calls an "amplification-overpricing spiral."
Lower AI risk outside of US, Asia
To cut exposure to AI-related stocks, investors may have to turn to developed market funds outside the US and Southeast Asia. These funds have offered lower returns over the past decade.
In the MSCI Europe, Australasia and Far East (EAFE) index fund, the top 10 holdings make up about 14.5% of the index, about 40% lower than the all-country world index.
EAFE's major holdings include healthcare giant Roche, oil major Shell, HSBC bank and Nestle — the world's largest food and beverage company.
However, its biggest holding, ASML, is still very much part of the AI trade. The Dutch tech firm sells the equipment that firms such as TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix and Micron need to make their chips.
AI crash will have ripple effects
If Monday's rebound in the AI trade is sustained, stock prices may move sharply higher over the next few months. Yet if history is a guide, the bubble will eventually burst, leaving both institutional and passive investors nursing heavy losses.
Kommer warned that if the AI bubble bursts, "in all likelihood it will drag down the global stock market," though the damage would be most severe in tech and AI stocks.
Those hit hardest would be retail investors "with heavy portfolio weights in tech and AI stocks," he said, including "a lot of people who have bought individual AI-related stocks on top of their equity ETFs."
LSE's Vayanos thinks it is still "certainly safer to hold an ETF than to hold individual stocks."
But as index providers add mega-IPOs such as SpaceX and Claude-maker Anthropic to benchmarks within weeks of their debut, and money continues to pour into passive funds, he warned that "the conditions are present for the effects of our theory to be even stronger."

noticias.titulo: Who really owns the land in Albania that Jared Kushner wants to develop?
noticias.resumen: Albania's Prime Minister Edi Rama has vowed that Kushner's resort project will go ahead as planned. But an ongoing investigation by Albania's state prosecutor into forged land titles could halt the project.
noticias.texto:
Who really owns the land in Albania that Jared Kushner wants to develop?
ZVERNEC, Albania — In the summer of 2021, Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump boarded a yacht owned by Nat Rothschild, an heir to the European banking family. On the way from Montenegro to Greece, the yacht anchored off the coast of Albania.
And, as Kushner told an investment conference last year, that's when Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama arrived at the boat to tell them about his plan for the country.
"I was very impressed by what he wanted to do with the country," said Kushner. "I really didn't know anything about the country and I didn't understand the history, and the darkness of the history with the communism and terrible leadership led to it being fully undeveloped as a nation."
A year later, Kushner was looking for development opportunities in the Balkans. He returned to the Albanian coast — to the city of Vlore, which was finishing the construction of an airport atop a wetland near an undeveloped coastline. "And obviously, a country's going to build an airport by the coast in a place they think is most beautiful," Kushner told the conference, "so we went there and we were looking for opportunities, and we found some incredible opportunities."
Kushner found those opportunities at Hidrovor Beach, an expanse of caramel-colored sand along the southern Albanian coast, with the gentle waves of the Adriatic lapping its perimeter and a view of an uninhabited island. A company working for Kushner purchased this land and 300 acres surrounding it for more than $130 million in April. But several people here tell NPR this is not Kushner's land.
They say it's theirs.
Land grabs and falsified documents
"This land here belonged to my family for centuries," says Gentian Mocka, who claims his family has owned this strip of beach and wetland since the time of the Ottoman Empire. He provided NPR land titles that appear to prove this.
After World War II, Albania's Communist government seized it — along with all private land.
When communism fell in 1991, families like Mocka's embarked on a years-long process to get their land back. "But then our problems started with the guys that were much more powerful than we were — had a lot of political support, were very rich and very well connected with the politics of that time," says Mocka.
In 2005, Mocka learned that someone else was laying claim to his family's land — a fellow Albanian named Artur Shehu. It was a familiar name for those who lived here in the 1990s, when the regional capital of Vlore was outside the control of the country's government. It was instead run by mafia-style gangs. At the time, Shehu was well-known to police in Vlore for his alleged involvement in a crime syndicate that, according to Albanian prosecutors, smuggled drugs and migrants into Europe. He fled Albania in 1999, after what police say was a shootout with a rival gang.
He ended up in the United States, where he received asylum in 2001 and, later, became a U.S. citizen. The 60-year-old Shehu now lives in a villa in Miami Beach. But he's continued to manage a growing real estate portfolio back in Albania through an associate in Vlore named Pellumb Petritaj.
The pair has claimed plots of land — including Mocka's family plot — up and down the southern Albanian coast, and prosecutors have taken notice. In 2018, Petritaj served three years in prison for forging land titles on behalf of Shehu. And on Nov. 18, Petritaj was sentenced to another seven years in prison for falsifying documents to $17 million worth of oceanfront property in the city of Vlore on behalf of Shehu. The court ordered the land — which does not include Mocka's family plot — confiscated from Shehu last week. The pair has also claimed oceanfront farmland in the village of Zvernec, adjacent to Mocka's land.
Albanian prosecutors say land linked to Kushner may have been "illegally acquired"
The pair has also claimed oceanfront farmland in the village of Zvernec, adjacent to Mocka's land.
The quiet village has only a couple hundred residents. Most of them, like Minella Konomi and Natasha Kota, are past the age of 70. On a recent warm and sunny afternoon, the two are resting on benches in the courtyard of the village church after a day of harvesting olives. They nod their heads when asked about Artur Shehu.
"He is from the village of Kanina, far from here and up in the mountains," says Konomi, motioning inland, "but his family has never lived here. He's involved in shady dealings."
Then Kota speaks up. "There wasn't a single soul of that family living here, going back to the Ottoman times," she says. "But we've heard stories about him, and we're very scared of him."
Twenty years ago, Kota, Konomi and dozens of others in this village learned that Artur Shehu had somehow acquired their farmland. They filed suit in Albanian court to reclaim their land, a fight that escalated this past April when Shehu sold the 300-acre parcel that includes what they say is their farmland to a company developing a luxury resort project for Kushner.
That transaction, however, is under review.
In court documents obtained by NPR, Albanian prosecutors argue that the land involved in Kushner's development is "suspected of having been illegally acquired through forgery."
A spokesman for Kushner did not respond to NPR's request for comment by the time this article was published. Kushner had previously issued a statement on his website saying his partnership purchased the land from a private party in a private transaction. "Title was reviewed by counsel and verified," the statement says.
Shehu did not respond to NPR's request for comment. He has previously denied any wrongdoing. However, in Tirana, a former lawyer for Shehu was willing to talk.
Oceanfront properties are now claimed by several parties
"The people that Artur [Shehu] has authorized by power of attorney to deal with his family's properties committed a forgery in which they removed the property from the brother of Artur's grandfather and passed it to Artur's grandfather," says Kujtim Cakrani. "That is the whole story of the property."
Cakrani says Shehu's associates forged an inheritance certificate that made it appear that Shehu's grandfather had owned the land, which was then passed to Artur Shehu himself. And then last April, Shehu sold that land to Moutaz and Ramez Al-Khayyat, Syrian-born Qatari billionaire brothers who are financial partners of Jared Kushner.
Cakrani says that when he discovered that Artur Shehu was involved in this alleged forgery, he dropped him as his client. "I could no longer continue representing him because of the seriousness of the matter," he says. "It is impossible for me, with these documents that he has, to defend him."
And this is why, Cakrani says, Albanian state prosecutors have put Shehu under investigation and froze his bank accounts. Cakrani says he is now representing a group of 30 relatives of Shehu who he claims to be the rightful owners of this land.
Gentian Mocka, as well as Minella Konomi and Natasha Kota in Zvernec, tell NPR that nobody by the name of Shehu — neither Artur nor his relatives — has any legal claim to what they say is their land, oceanfront property that has now been claimed by several parties, including the son-in-law of the president of the United States.
Wealthy speculators have exploited land in Albania since the fall of communism
Albanian real estate law expert Roden Hoxha says he has seen this kind of land battle many times before. "But now that Kushner is in it," he says, "everybody is freaking out."
He says land ownership in Albania is complicated by decades under a Stalinist regime that stole all the land from private owners and collectivized it. When communism fell in 1991, he says Albania became a land grab free-for-all.
"It was basically chaos," he says. "People started claiming land wherever they threw a stone. It was basically the Albanian version of the U.S.' claiming of the West."
Hoxha describes wealthy speculators keen to exploit the chaos of the moment: locals whose families have farmed the land for generations and well-connected operators like Shehu, who aggressively try to claim that land. "And then on the international level," says Hoxha, most recently, "it exploded because it was Kushner and Trump and Arab money behind it."
And so, Hoxha says, what at first appeared to be yet another Albanian land dispute now has ties all the way to the White House. In the end, an Albanian court will likely decide who the rightful owner of this property is. But for now, it has sparked unprecedented public outrage in Albania. Protesters have taken to the streets of the capital, Tirana, every day since May 31, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. But Rama has only vowed to crack down harder on what have become increasingly violent demonstrations against his entire government.
Rama has also vowed that Kushner's resort project will go ahead as planned, but an ongoing investigation by Albania's state prosecutor into forged land titles could halt the project.
When contacted by NPR, Elona Sinaj, Rama's spokesperson, sent a statement saying, "If the seller does not have legitimate ownership of the property, the money will remain within the Republic of Albania, and certainly it will be used for anyone who proves that his claim over the property is grounded."
Sinaj went on to say that the ambition for Rama's government is "to create a new benchmark for sustainable Mediterranean development."
Some Albanians see advantages to having a Kushner-linked resort
That goal aligns with Kushner's vision for a luxury resort — a five-star ecotourism site, as his wife, Ivanka Trump, laid out in a podcast episode called "Ivanka Trump on Building the Authentic Life."
"For me," said Trump, "this is, it feels more like a challenge than anything else, the culmination of all of my experience in real estate, all of my travel, a lot of reflection on how I want to live."
In the podcast, Trump described both the Zvernec beachfront property as well as Sazan — an uninhabited island across from it — as part of a development project belonging to her and Kushner.
Local tour operator Sherif Durmishaj has made a living taking tourists to Sazan by boat, guiding hikes past foxholes and signs along the trail that warn of active land mines scattered throughout the island's forests. For years, this island was a fortified military outpost.
Durmishaj says he's seen the ongoing protests against the Kushner project, but he takes a different view of it.
"I work in tourism, and I'm from here," he says, "and if you've seen how local developers, along with the mafia, have built this region, it's just a massacre. They've destroyed so much of what is a beautiful coastline, and I support the Kushner project because it's going to be ecologically sustainable and it will set a good benchmark for future projects."
"We are a small country," Durmishaj says, "and Kushner and Trump are very big names."
At least one big name will be in the crosshairs of the incoming Democratic Congress in the U.S.
Regarding Kushner, "This is an individual in the Trump family who has essentially been two-timing on the American people," says Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, who is expected to chair the House Judiciary Committee and will have the power to investigate and subpoena members of President Trump's family.
He says he'll be focusing on Kushner, who he says has been splitting his time between foreign policy and making business deals on the side.
"American foreign policy has never seen anything like that before," says Raskin. "And in this, of course, he is only imitating his father-in-law, who declared that he got $2.2 billion on the side in his first year in office. Uh, that's more than $1 million an hour."
Raskin says the luxury resort project in Albania is one of many Kushner-backed deals that have prompted investigative inquiries from his committee, and there could be more as the new U.S. Congress is sworn in in January.
Fjori Sinoruka contributed to this report.

noticias.titulo: MEPs call on the Commission to assess human rights in Rwanda amid return hub plans
noticias.resumen: Seventy-six lawmakers denounced Kigali’s harassment, espionage, and repression, warning that the return hub could expose migrants to violations of their fundamental rights.
noticias.texto:
Seventy-six lawmakers denounced Kigali’s harassment, espionage, and repression, warning that the return hub could expose migrants to violations of their fundamental rights.
A total of seventy-six MEPs have challenged the legality of plans by five EU countries to deport irregular migrants to Rwanda from 2027, and are asking the European Commission for an assessment of the country's human rights record.
In a letter seen by Euronews and sent on Tuesday to EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner, the MEPs warned that Rwanda may not meet the human rights standards required under EU law for return hubs outside the bloc.
“Besides general human rights concerns, Rwanda has a particular reputation for serious maltreatment of refugees and asylum seekers in the recent past,” the letter says, challenging the initiative launched by Austria, Germany, Greece, the Netherlands and Denmark.
Most of the signatories come from centre-left and left-wing political groups, which have consistently opposed the EU legislation paving the way for the creation of return hubs.
They fear that Rwanda is “unable to fulfil the conditions” required to host a return hub, namely compliance with international human rights standards and international law.
Under the law enabling EU states to set up return hubs outside the bloc, only non-EU countries “where international human rights standards and principles in accordance with international law are respected” are eligible.
The MEPs consider this unlikely to be the case in Rwanda, although the final details of the deal are still under negotiation.
“The Rwandan government under President Paul Kagame is notorious for its harassment, espionage, detention and transnational repression of dissidents and political opposition,” reads the letter.
The lawmakers also condemned Rwanda’s involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which has led to “violations of international law and the displacement of millions of persons”.
The European Parliament has previously adopted a firm stance towards Rwanda.
In February 2025, it called for the suspension of an EU-Rwanda memorandum of understanding on critical raw materials, citing alleged war crimes and the occupation of Congolese territory by Rwanda’s defence forces.
Under EU law, the European Commission can initiate an assessment of Rwanda's human rights record, but it has no formal role in approving the plan.
The deportations, expected to begin in 2027, could nonetheless face legal challenges before European courts.

noticias.titulo: Italy watches worryingly as Ukraine strikes Russian boats in Libya
noticias.resumen: Ukraine's naval drone strikes on two Russian vessels in and off Benghazi have alarmed Italy, amid fears that the attacks could reignite Libya's civil war.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine's naval drone strikes on two Russian vessels in and off Benghazi have alarmed Italy, amid fears that the attacks could reignite Libya's civil war.
Kyiv has stepped up long-range drone attacks on Russian ships in the Mediterranean Sea, but Italy fears the strikes could escalate into renewed fighting in Libya, destabilising its southern neighbour in one of Rome's worst nightmares.
Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani voiced his concern over Ukraine's operations in Libya to his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybiha on Tuesday, according to a readout of the phone call.
On Sunday, Ukrainian naval drones hit two Russian vessels, one docked at the Benghazi naval base and the other just off the Libyan city. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it an "exemplary Ukrainian operation."
The attacks appear to be part of a broader maritime campaign against Russian vessels beyond the Black Sea. On Saturday, a Ukrainian drone hit another Russian ship near Finland's territorial waters.
But the strikes in Libya have rung alarm bells in Rome, where even the prospect of civil war reopening across the Mediterranean is enough to send a shiver down officials' spines.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has so far refrained from commenting on the episode publicly to avoid escalating the situation, but according to the Italian daily la Repubblica, she privately slammed the attacks as "unacceptable".
"We were not informed of absolutely anything; we did not provide any kind of support to the Ukrainians, they did everything without informing us," Tajani told reporters on the sidelines of a visit to Baku.
Tajani pledged to work to stop the conflict with Russia spreading across the Mediterranean basin, while respecting Libya's sovereignty and avoiding its destabilisation.
Libya has been split since the civil war that followed the fall of Muammar Gaddafi in 2011. A UN-recognised government in Tripoli controls much of the west, while the east is dominated by military strongman Khalifa Haftar and his Libyan National Army, which is backed by the rival administration in Benghazi.
Russia backs Haftar, while Italy supports the Tripoli government. Turkey has also been increasing its military presence in the region since it intervened in 2019 to stop Haftar capturing Tripoli.
For Rome, a renewed explosion of fighting in Libya, sparked by possible Russian retaliation in the country, is a nightmare scenario that evokes the chaos following Gaddafi's death.
Italy can do little but hope the strikes do not trigger renewed fighting between Libya's rival factions. Domestically, the Italian government also sees the risk that the attacks might undermine political support for the aid to Ukraine.
"We all know that Libya and the Mediterranean Sea have been a zone of Russian intervention for a long time. Italian politics prefers to ignore international developments rather than taking responsibility to try to prevent an escalation," MEP Lucia Annunziata (Italy/S&D) told Euronews.
Annunziata argued that Kyiv should have notified Rome of the attacks, but stressed that the Italian government cannot simultaneously recognise Ukraine's right to self-defence while imposing geographical limits on how it exercises that right.
Italy is not alone in its concern over the new flurry of Ukrainian attacks on Russian vessels. On Tuesday, a German government spokesperson warned against escalation in the Baltic Sea region.
In May, Greek fishermen found an unexploded Ukrainian naval drone in the Ionian Sea, prompting a strong reaction from Athens, which wants to keep the Mediterranean from becoming a theatre of military operations.
"Ukraine's right to self-defence cannot justify such actions," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lana Zochiou said when Athens lodged a formal protest in June.
According to an EU official who spoke with Euronews on condition of anonymity, Ukraine intended to send a clear signal that Russian vessels in the Mediterranean are within arm's reach, forcing them to reroute and raising the costs for Moscow.
"No member state wants to see the war in its backyard," the official said. "But the spillover didn't start two days ago. Russia is violating EU territory every day of the week. Russian vessels are a legitimate military target."

noticias.titulo: Colombia: At least 25 injured in bombing as armed violence resurges
noticias.resumen: At least 25 people were injured in a bombing in Villavicencio, damaging government buildings, businesses and vehicles. Meanwhile, hundreds of residents marched with candles in Cúcuta following a separate attack, amid a resurgence of armed violence in Colombia.
noticias.texto:
Footage filmed on Tuesday 24 November reveals the scale of the destruction in Villavicencio, southeast of Bogotá, after a car bomb exploded outside the Meta departmental government headquarters on Monday night. Collapsed building façades, burnt-out vehicles and streets strewn with shattered glass bear witness to the force of the blast. Several businesses and homes were damaged, including a shop selling religious images located near the cathedral and parish house.
The explosion comes amid a resurgence of violence in Colombia, fuelled by rival armed groups competing for control of lucrative illegal economies and trafficking networks, particularly along the Venezuelan border.
In Cúcuta, hundreds of residents, police officers and military personnel joined a candlelit march on Monday in solidarity with families affected by a recent attack on the city's police headquarters. Three people, including a child, were injured and more than 80 homes damaged, according to the regional government. Police chaplain José Rodríguez joined the procession, blessing a damaged home with holy water.
Authorities suspect the involvement of the National Liberation Army (ELN), although responsibility has yet to be officially established. Figures from Colombia's Defence Ministry point to a growing use of explosive drones by armed groups, with 358 attacks recorded between January and November 2026, 157 of them attributed to the ELN.

noticias.titulo: Italy develops 'ambitious' business with 'strategic partner' Azerbaijan, Tajani tells Euronews
noticias.resumen: Italy's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani told Euronews that Rome has sought to expand its business relations with Baku now that peace has brought stability and improved connectivity to the region.
noticias.texto:
Italy's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani told Euronews that Rome has sought to expand its business relations with Baku now that peace has brought stability and improved connectivity to the region.
Italy has sought to invest in the emerging Middle Corridor transit route connecting Asia to Europe through the South Caucasus and boost its business volumes with its "strategic partner" Azerbaijan, Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani told Euronews in Baku on Monday.
With Italy as the top EU importer of energy from Azerbaijan and one of its largest commercial partners, Tajani and Azerbaijan's Economy Minister Mikayil Jabbarov led an Azerbaijan-Italy Business Forum that brought together business leaders from both countries, with the two countries sharing a "strong relationship built on trust and common interests."
During a Euronews interview at the forum, the Italian foreign minister, who is also deputy prime minister, told Euronews that "we must be ambitious," describing the forum's objective as "a leap in quality" and calling for a stronger economic partnership between Italy and Azerbaijan.
"Azerbaijan is at the heart of a region that is increasingly important to our foreign policy," Tajani said in a statement, adding that he "reaffirmed Italy’s full support for the peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia, which is essential to the region’s stability and growth."
Tajani announced that Italian exports to Azerbaijan increased by 14% in the first 8 months of this year.
Tajani described Italy's strong interest in Azerbaijan’s role in the Middle Corridor transit project, saying Italian companies can bring their engineering expertise and technology, together with AI, machinery, agri-food and railways.
"We devoted considerable attention to connectivity and the diversification of energy and logistics corridors: from the Middle Corridor to the Green Energy Corridor, which could bring energy to Europe and is already attracting strong interest from our Italian companies," Tajani said.
"We are working together in a spirit of friendship towards a common goal: strengthening links between Europe and Asia and creating new opportunities for growth for our countries," the Italian foreign minister added.
The Middle Corridor is an emerging strategic transit and trade route between Asia and Europe and a strong Eurasian alternative amid global supply chain disruptions in the Middle East.
EU countries are actively exploring new investment opportunities along the Middle Corridor, a rail and maritime transport network that will connect China, Southeast Asia, and Central Asia to European markets via the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus, then to the Black Sea and onward to the Mediterranean.
Tajani also met with Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev and shared on X that he was on a “mission” to Azerbaijan, describing the country as “a strategic partner of Italy with which we share a strong relationship built on trust and common interests.”
Italian and Azerbaijani officials and business delegations discussed investments and cooperation in manufacturing, infrastructure, transport, technology, and critical raw materials.
Tajani said the two countries should work together on critical raw materials, including in Africa and other parts of the world, after signing a Joint Declaration on Strategic Cooperation in Critical Raw Materials in Rome in October.
"If you want to compete at a global level", Tajani told Euronews, "you need to reduce the price of raw materials for example."
"It's also possible to invest in Italy for companies coming from Azerbaijan, but also for Italian companies to export to Azerbaijan", he said.
Tajani also reflected on the role peace might play in the future of business, saying "peace is a good choice for paving the way for new investments."
"I want to thank Azerbaijan for its engagement in favour of peace, not only with Armenia but also in this part of the world, during the difficult situation", he said.
"We need countries working for peace," the Italian foreign minister added.
Economic diversification and development
Azerbaijan’s Jabbarov told Euronews that the two countries signed several agreements during the forum covering AI, industrial production, construction, public transport and investment cooperation.
As both countries aim to increase Azerbaijan's gas supplies to Italy, Jabbarov said economic diversification and business developments in the non-oil sector were also a focus of the talks, including industrial parks and free economic zones, adding that “cooperation with Italian companies opens up very good opportunities for our companies.”
Jabbarov told Euronews that Azerbaijan wanted to improve the competitiveness of locally produced goods and increase their access to foreign markets.
"The initiatives are aimed at modernising industrial enterprises, expanding production capacity, facilitating access to international markets for industrial products, accelerating the adoption of digital technologies and strengthening business and investment ties," Azerbaijan's minister of economy said.
Italy’s Leonardo, a major aerospace, defence and security company, and Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Economy signed a memorandum on cooperation in high-performance computing systems and artificial intelligence.
Italy’s development finance institution, Cassa Depositi e Prestiti (CDP), signed an agreement with Azerbaijan’s Business Development Fund, and its Head of International Markets Development Laurent Franciosi described the platform as being "capable of connecting the different dimensions of the bilateral economic relationship between the two countries.”
Speaking about the agreement with Azerbaijan’s Business Development Fund, Franciosi said: “We don’t want it to be just an institutional framework.”
**Role of small and medium-sized businesses **
Vice President of Confindustria’s Small Industry section Fausto Mazzali led the talks on cooperation among smaller businesses, telling Euronews that “for the Italian industry, Azerbaijan does not just want to be a market for development, but a country with which to build new investment opportunities and collaboration.”
Mazzali highlighted potential cooperation in infrastructure, transport and logistics, critical materials, metallurgy, automation, robotics, electronics, pharmaceuticals, and agricultural machinery, and said Italian companies could contribute through exports, but also by sharing technology, expertise, and industrial solutions.
Head of Foreign Relations at the Italian Union of Chambers of Commerce Pietro Infante said that he would like to propose "a change of paradigm,” calling for businesses to move “beyond the traditional commercial partnerships” and the “logics of pure import and export”, towards joint ventures, industrial partnerships and technology development.
Società Italiana per le Imprese all'Estero (SIMEST), majority-owned by CDP, also discussed support for Italian companies seeking to expand abroad.
Its Chief External Relations Officer Francesca Alicata outlined the institution’s role in helping businesses enter new markets, saying their mission was to support the companies, and in particular, " small and medium-sized companies.”
Alicata explained that SIMEST provided financial instruments to support international expansion, including financing, grants and support for joint ventures.
She also described supplier credit, which allows Italian companies to offer overseas customers extended payment terms for machinery and industrial equipment.
SIMEST signed an agreement with the Italy-Azerbaijan Chamber of Commerce and the Small and Medium Business Development Agency of Azerbaijan; Italy’s Investment and Export Promotion Agency and the Italian Trade Agency signed a memorandum to support trade and investment links.
Attracting investment into Italy was another subject covered at the forum.
Augusto Reggiani, Director of the Foreign Investments Attraction Unit at Italy’s Ministry of Enterprises and Made in Italy, explained the support available to international investors.
Meanwhile, Baku Steel Company signed an agreement with Italian companies Dismas Trading and Edgar H. Greenham to promote exports of locally manufactured industrial products.
The Azerbaijan Construction Products Manufacturers Association and Italy’s FINCO agreed to develop cooperation in construction and building materials.
Iveco and AZ Tex Import signed an agreement in the public transport sector.
Another contract, between North West Construction and Italy’s Falorni Tech, concerned the modernisation of the Garadagh Glass Plant.
The business forum follows Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni's talks with President Aliyev in May, focusing on expanding Azerbaijan's oil and gas supplies to Italy, which Meloni said had been "decisive for the energy security" of Italy since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
At the time, Meloni said she wanted Italy to serve as Azerbaijan's "privileged gateway to the European market" as a hub between Europe and Asia.
Bilateral trade reached €10.2 billion last year, making Italy Azerbaijan's largest commercial partner, while Azerbaijan has invested around €3 billion in Italy.

noticias.titulo: Two arrested on suspicion of burglary at Prince and Princess of Wales' UK country home
noticias.resumen: Two men were arrested on the Sandringham estate on suspicion of burglary and trespass and remain in custody, Norfolk Police said. The force added that the property was unoccupied at the time of the incident.
noticias.texto:
Two men were arrested on the Sandringham estate on suspicion of burglary and trespass and remain in custody, Norfolk Police said. The force added that the property was unoccupied at the time of the incident.
Two men have been arrested on suspicion of burglary after a reported break-in at the Prince and Princess of Wales' country home on the Sandringham estate in the UK.
Police were called out shortly before 6 pm on Monday following a report of "suspicious activity at the address," Norfolk Police said in a statement to Euronews.
British media outlets are reporting that the property was Anmer Hall, which Prince William, his wife Catherine and their three children occasionally use as a retreat in the holidays. Their main residence is Forest Lodge in Windsor.
"Officers attended and specialist resources, including police dogs, drones and the National Police Air Service helicopter, were deployed to assist with searches in the area," police said.
The force added that two men were arrested on the estate on suspicion of burglary and trespass and remain in custody.
The property was said to have been unoccupied at the time of the incident. Inquiries are ongoing.
News of the break-in came as William travelled to Westminster on Tuesday to meet with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street - marking his first ever visit to the PM's residence.
The Sandringham estate, located in Norfolk in the East of England, is the private country retreat of King Charles III and Queen Camilla.
Sandringham House, the Jacobean-style jewel of the estate, has been open to the public since 1977. The house and gardens are open from 28 March to 9 October each year.

noticias.titulo: Why French pharma firm Sanofi is paying $41 billion for US company Insmed
noticias.resumen: French drugmaker Sanofi has agreed a $41 billion (€37.4bn) all-cash takeover of Insmed, a US biopharma company. The deal, one of its biggest ever, is meant to refill its pipeline of new medicines before its best-selling drug loses patent protection.
noticias.texto:
French drugmaker Sanofi has agreed a $41 billion (€37.4bn) all-cash takeover of Insmed, a US biopharma company. The deal, one of its biggest ever, is meant to refill its pipeline of new medicines before its best-selling drug loses patent protection.
French pharmaceutical group Sanofi said on Tuesday it would buy Insmed, a US company specialising in treatments for lung diseases, for $41bn (€37.4bn) in cash.
The acquisition is one of the largest in Sanofi's history as it aims to strengthen the group's line-up of new medicines before the main US patent on Dupixent, its best-selling drug, expires in 2031.
Sanofi will pay $175 for each Insmed share, a premium of around 17% to the New Jersey-based company's share price at Monday's close on the Nasdaq.
Sanofi expects the deal to start lifting its adjusted earnings per share by the end of 2028.
The takeover is the first major deal for CEO Belén Garijo, whose appointment was announced in February and who took over in May. Her mandate is to bring new treatments to market faster after several setbacks in Sanofi's research.
Two lung drugs and more in the works
Insmed sells two main drugs.
Brinsupri treats bronchiectasis, a long-term condition in which the airways widen and clog with mucus. Arikayce is used to treat adults with mycobacterium avium complex (MAC), which is a bacterial lung infection.
Brinsupri brought in $1.1bn (€1bn) between its US launch in August 2025 and 30 September this year, according to a joint statement from the two companies, while Arikayce's sales grew 19% to $434 million (€396m) in 2025.
"Together, these medicines represent a significant growth opportunity with combined peak sales potential expected to exceed $10bn [€9.1bn] and to last until the very end of the next decade," Garijo told reporters on a conference call.
The US company is also developing TPIP, an inhaled drug being tested against pulmonary hypertension, a type of high blood pressure in the lungs, and fibrotic lung disease.
Insmed CEO Will Lewis said the deal would push forward its products already on the market and those in late-stage trials, which together have "multibillion-dollar peak sales potential".
Investors welcome the deal
Sanofi plans to fund the purchase with cash on hand and borrowing, while keeping room to buy smaller, early-stage businesses.
Garijo said the deal should also bring annual cost savings above $500m (€456m).
Sanofi shares were 9% higher in Paris on Tuesday afternoon as investors welcomed the deal and bought up the stock throughout the day.
The acquisition is possible "without jeopardising the dividend or the debt rating", analysts at the brokerage Jefferies said in a research note.
The deal should also "provide greater stability through the Dupixent patent cliff" and give Sanofi time to rebuild its pipeline, according to the note.
Dupixent is an anti-inflammatory treatment that generated more than €15bn in sales in 2025 for Sanofi.
Oddo BHF, an asset management firm, said the deal showed that Sanofi's new management could take "important strategic decisions" to protect its range of treatments for years to come.
The takeover is expected to be completed in the first half of 2027, subject to approval by Insmed shareholders and regulatory clearances in the US and abroad.

noticias.titulo: ‘Pervert glasses’ named Word of the Year by Macquarie dictionary
noticias.resumen: The Australian dictionary’s committee of word experts said the winning term is "a succinct reflection of the state of the world in 2026". 'Pervert glasses' follows ‘enshittification’ in 2024 and ‘AI slop’ in 2025.
noticias.texto:
The Australian dictionary’s committee of word experts said the winning term is "a succinct reflection of the state of the world in 2026". 'Pervert glasses' follows ‘enshittification’ in 2024 and ‘AI slop’ in 2025.
The accessory dubbed "pervert glasses" has faced quite the backlash this year.
Governments and companies are considering restrictions on smart glasses such as Meta's Ray-Bans, which feature built-in cameras and AI assistants, amid worries that the technology could be used to photograph, film or audio-record people without their knowledge or consent.
Smart glasses have attracted scrutiny from European privacy regulators and some lawmakers, and courts in England and Wales have prohibited their use. Even cinema operators are considering a ban on Meta AI glasses in UK cinemas.
Now, the Australian Macquarie Dictionary has named “pervert glasses” as its Word of the Year for 2026.
The committee said the phrase captured a year in which AI-powered gadgets became more capable and calls to rein in their use grew louder. It called the term “a succinct reflection of the state of the world in 2026”.
“On the one hand, we’ve seen a massive acceleration in the capabilities of AI and products that integrate it. At the same time, the undeniably critical nickname mirrors the widespread calls to hit the brakes on this seemingly unchecked development."
The committee added: “The name represents the year we’ve all endured, with AI, the manosphere, increasing surveillance in supermarkets, and more. Sure these new gadgets might be marketed as smart glasses or camera glasses, but it seems to us that pervert glasses paints a more apt reflection of the year.”
In another troubling sign of the times, other words on the shortlist included “nudify”, referring to AI-generated pornography, and “AI;DR” - short for “AI; didn’t read”.
The committee gave honourable mentions to "agentic", which describes AI that can act or make decisions independently, and "PMOS", short for polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, formerly known as PCOS.
Public voters gave an honourable mention to "digital dementia", a colloquial term for concerns about relying on devices for tasks such as remembering plans.
Earlier this month, Cambridge Dictionary crowned "human" their Word of the Year, also reflecting growing fears regarding AI. Elsewhere, “mogging” was named Collins' Word of the Year, while Dictionary.com went for "maxxing" - both rather depressing terms which are being reclaimed by Gen Z in modern slang and conversation.
