Azerbaijan, Georgia and Kazakhstan are stepping up their cooperation to develop the Middle Corridor, as the network will pass through these countries and onwards to Turkey and Europe, through a joint plan aimed at improving transport infrastructure, streamlining logistics, and making cross-border trade faster and more efficient.
The joint plan comes as European companies explore new investment opportunities along the route.
The participating countries are discussing how to connect the energy routes and markets from a so-called strategic-geography perspective, with significant political and economic benefits and growing influence.
The US-backed project is moving forward in a complex geopolitical area marked by tensions, with Iran and Russia following closely.
Both the TRIPP project and the wider Middle Corridor face geopolitical challenges, depending on the ongoing peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia, notably Armenia’s adoption of its peace treaty through a new constitution, as well as the possible challenges posed by Iran and Russia to the US-backed TRIPP project and the wider interactions of the participating countries within the current geopolitical reshaping processes.

noticias.titulo: Israeli strikes kill Hamas security chief and six others in Gaza
noticias.resumen: Two policemen died when a police station in southern Gaza was hit, while coalition talks in Israel leave caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu in charge of military operations.
noticias.texto:
Two policemen died when a police station in southern Gaza was hit, while coalition talks in Israel leave caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu in charge of military operations.
Israeli airstrikes in the Gaza Strip killed seven people on Tuesday, including Hamas's director of internal security, according to Palestinian officials, despite a ceasefire that has been in place since October 2025.
Gaza's interior ministry, which operates under Hamas authority, said an airstrike in Gaza City killed Brigadier General Naeem Abu Nahal, director-general of the Internal Security Service.
Israel's military said it had "struck a senior terrorist" from Hamas.
Mahmoud Bassal, spokesman for Gaza's civil defence agency, said several other people were in critical condition after the same strike in Gaza City's Rimal neighbourhood.
Police station hit
Bassal said three people, including a 17-year-old, had been killed earlier on Tuesday in a separate Israeli airstrike near Gaza City.
Three more were killed in a third strike, on a police station in the Al-Mawasi area of southern Gaza, he added.
Gaza's police force, which also operates under Hamas, said two policemen aged 23 and 33 were among the dead. It condemned the strike as "part of an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus".
Israel's military said it had "struck terrorists in the area" of the police station, but did not confirm the strike that is believed to have killed the 17-year-old.
Fragile truce
Israel and Hamas regularly accuse each other of violating the ceasefire, which came into effect after two years of war triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.
More than 1,650 Palestinians have been killed since the truce began, according to a tally based on data from Gaza's health ministry, which also operates under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
Over the same period, the Israeli military says seven of its soldiers and one civilian contractor have been killed.
Most of Gaza's 2.1 million people are displaced and living in tents or makeshift shelters. Israel's military says it controls more than 60% of the territory.
Coalition talks in Israel
The strikes come as talks continue in Israel to form a new government after legislative elections in October produced no clear winner.
The centrist Gadi Eisenkot is seeking to build a coalition that would end the long tenure of Benjamin Netanyahu, who is now caretaker prime minister.
But Netanyahu, who has staked his reputation on ensuring Israel's security since the 7 October attack, remains in charge of military operations while negotiations go on.

noticias.titulo: Pet passports to return from 2028 for Brits travelling to the EU with cats, dogs and ferrets
noticias.resumen: The rule change will mean pet owners no longer need to fork out for an animal health certificate each time they travel.
noticias.texto:
The rule change will mean pet owners no longer need to fork out for an animal health certificate each time they travel.
Travelling to the EU with cats, dogs and ferrets as a Brit is about to get easier – and cheaper – thanks to the reintroduction of pet passports.
From 1 March 2028, pet owners will be able to get a multiuse passport which is valid for EU travel rather than securing a new animal health certificate for each trip.
The details around how to get a multiuse pet passport will be shared in 2027. You can sign up for updates on the UK government website (or keep your eyes peeled on Euronews Travel).
The British Veterinary Association said in a statement: “This new agreement is broadly positive news and one that we've been pressing the UK government for. But it is important that the transition to the new trade rules is smooth and doesn’t negatively impact vets working across all parts of the profession.”
The news comes after the UK and EU agreed to align on sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) rules, with a number of other changes introduced.
Cats, dogs and ferrets microchipped from 1 March 2028 will need to have a code that shows the country where the animal was initially identified. This will not apply retroactively.
The UK is also set to work to ensure its microchip database system works with EU systems.
What are the current rules for travelling with pets to the EU?
Following the closure of a loophole in April that allowed Brits with holiday homes in EU countries to continue to use EU pet passports from before Brexit, all cats, dogs and ferrets have needed an animal health certificate to travel to the EU.
To get the health certificate, your pet must have either an up-to-date rabies vaccination or only need booster doses to keep the vaccination up to date. You’ll also need to take proof of your pet’s microchipping date, and vaccination history.
The certificate will be valid for 10 days, with day one being the date it is issued. It will also be valid for six months for onward travel within the EU after entering, as well as for re-entry into Great Britain.
Pets who need a rabies vaccination will need to wait for it to work, which could take as long as 30 days, before the certificate can be issued.
Only official veterinarians can sign the certificates, and prices can vary between £90 (€108) and £250 (€299), depending on factors like turnaround times and vet location.

noticias.titulo: France to create strategic reserves of rare earths and critical metals
noticias.resumen: This project was announced on Monday by Emmanuel Macron during a closed-door meeting with industrialists at the Élysée. These mineral stocks will be accompanied by a mechanism of "joint purchases".
noticias.texto:
This project was announced on Monday by Emmanuel Macron during a closed-door meeting with industrialists at the Élysée. These mineral stocks will be accompanied by a mechanism of "joint purchases".
Emmanuel Macron wants to equip France with "strategic stockpiles" of rare earths and "priority metals", modelled on oil reserves. The aim is to limit the dependence of French industry on other countries, in particular China, which concentrates 44 tonnes of rare earths out of a global total of around 110 million.
This project, which the president formalised during a behind-closed-doors meeting with industrialists at the Élysée, will be managed by the Caisse des dépôts.
The latter will now start negotiations with representatives of the sectors whose activity depends on access to these critical raw materials. Emmanuel Macron hopes the project will be up and running as early as next year.
Pooling of purchases and price guarantees
The head of state said these stockpiles would be accompanied by a mechanism of "joint purchasing", without however specifying who would be covered by these purchases or what amount is being targeted.
For reference, the United States announced at the start of the year an investment of 12 billion dollars to build up a stock of rare earths equivalent to two months of national consumption.
The precise timetable for the project has not been set out either, and its implementation could well depend on the result of the next presidential election. The idea of creating a national reserve of minerals nevertheless features in the programme of at least one candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon (La France Insoumise).
The project also provides for "price guarantee mechanisms [...] to give producers visibility and mobilise our investment tools more effectively", the Élysée added, calling on the European Commission to "go in the same direction".
The French president also announced a strengthening of the "conditioning" of public aid for the defence, aerospace and automotive sectors.
These sectors will now be required to diversify their sources of supply in strategic minerals if they are to continue receiving public support. To do so they will have to present a "desensitisation plan" to demonstrate the reduction of their dependence, in particular on China.

noticias.titulo: International Space Forum in Rome gathers 45 countries to shape future space rules
noticias.resumen: The new orbital economy is worth billions and increasingly involves private operators. Europe is seeking a strategy to avoid losing ground.
noticias.texto:
The new orbital economy is worth billions and increasingly involves private operators. Europe is seeking a strategy to avoid losing ground.
Representatives of 45 countries have gathered in Rome to discuss the future rules for space. It is a race in which the United States and China are sprinting ahead, private players are gaining ground and Europe still has to close the gap in its capacity for autonomous access to orbit. This is the backdrop to the eighth edition of the International Space Forum, returning to Italy ten years after its debut in Trento.
The numbers show how crowded the race has become. In 2026 there are about 18,000 operational satellites around the Earth, almost twice as many as in 2020. And 88 percent of the satellites launched in the past year were linked to private operators, compared with 23 percent in 2010. Space is no longer just a matter for states and government agencies, it is a rapidly expanding market in which major private companies have taken on an increasingly important role.
However, the picture of launches also shows just how far Europe still lags behind in terms of autonomy. In 2025 there were 181 American orbital launch attempts and 92 Chinese ones, compared with only eight European launches. Yet the continent has an industrial value chain that is anything but marginal: according to Eurospace, it comprises more than 750 companies and institutions and in 2025 recorded almost 11 billion euro in sales.
Traffic, debris and access to technologies
It is precisely this gap between industrial capacity and strategic autonomy that makes the European question central. The Rome Forum, entitled "The Gate to Sky: Space for Peace", addresses the other side of the competition: who sets the rules, how to ensure the peaceful and sustainable use of space and how to prevent countries with fewer resources from being excluded from the new orbital economy.
Organised by the Italian Space Agency (ASI) and the International Astronautical Federation (IAF), the forum forms part of Italy's presidency of the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS), which it took over in June for the 2026-2027 biennium. The role gives Rome a prominent position in international space diplomacy.
COPUOS, created in 1959 and made up of 110 member states, is the main multilateral United Nations body for cooperation and the peaceful use of space. Issues on the table include managing satellite traffic, dealing with debris in orbit, access to space technologies and the need to update international rules. These topics no longer concern only space agencies: satellites now underpin essential services for communications, navigation, environmental monitoring and security.
Europe, first-class expertise but autonomy lacking
This is also where Europe's position is measured. The continent has significant scientific and industrial assets, but still needs to turn them into a more autonomous strategic capability. In the new race to the Moon, Washington and Beijing have clearly defined national goals and programmes. Europe takes part in major international initiatives, but does not always manage to present itself as a single actor.
The collaboration with the United States in the Artemis programme is one example: the European Space Agency (ESA) is contributing to the mission with the service module for the Orion capsule, which is crucial for power, propulsion and life support. But the European contribution is not limited to acting as a technological partner.
The Argonaut programme, developed by ESA, aims to secure autonomous access to the lunar surface from the 2030s, with a first lander planned by 2030. The industrial consortium for the descent module will be led by Thales Alenia Space Italia, together with companies from other European countries.
The issue, therefore, is not just reaching the Moon, but having the technologies, launchers and infrastructure needed in order not to be entirely dependent on others. It is also a security challenge: in January 2026 the European External Action Service updated the EU's strategy for security and defence in space, highlighting as priorities the protection of orbital assets, reducing technological dependencies and strengthening Europe's ability to access space autonomously.
The European Union, in short, is not absent from the race. But its role remains divided between ESA's industrial and scientific dimension, EU policies and the initiatives of individual states. Coordination between these levels is precisely what makes the difference, in a field where national investment and decision making risk creating fragmentation rather than a shared strategy.
Italy is banking on space diplomacy
For Italy, the Rome forum is an opportunity to showcase its role in this landscape. The presidency of COPUOS, entrusted to it for 2026-2027, allows the country to contribute directly to the debate on international rules, from the sustainability of activities in orbit to lunar exploration. ASI president Teodoro Valente has been elected to chair the committee.
During the forum, discussions focused on three broad strands: using space technologies to tackle climate change and prevent natural disasters; ensuring fairer access to satellite technologies for emerging countries; and building an international governance framework able to keep pace with the growth of the private sector.
Since the first edition in Trento in 2016, the initiative has involved around 130 countries, with stops in Nairobi, Buenos Aires, Reggio Calabria, Panama, Manama and Manila. In Rome the delegations worked on the "Rome Page", a final declaration intended to gather recommendations and priorities for international cooperation.

noticias.titulo: West's weak response to Litvinenko's murder emboldened Putin, widow tells Euronews
noticias.resumen: Twenty years after her husband's murder in London, one of the most notorious Russian intelligence operations on foreign soil, Marina Litvinenko warns Europe against negotiating with Putin from a position of weakness and says justice requires a trial of his regime in Russia.
noticias.texto:
Twenty years after her husband's murder in London, one of the most notorious Russian intelligence operations on foreign soil, Marina Litvinenko warns Europe against negotiating with Putin from a position of weakness and says justice requires a trial of his regime in Russia.
The West's failure to respond decisively to the assassination of former Russian intelligence officer Alexander Litvinenko in London in 2006 emboldened Vladimir Putin, paving the way for Russia's war against Ukraine and its threats to wider European security, his widow Marina Litvinenko told Euronews.
Speaking on the 20th anniversary of her husband's death, following the publication of her memoir, A Life in Fragments, Litvinenko described his killing as "the first act of nuclear terrorism in London".
"And what was the reaction? It was not a very serious reaction at all. And what we have now? We have a war in Ukraine," she said.
She warned that Putin continued to test the West's resolve and that further hesitation risked an even wider conflict.
The images that shocked the world
An outspoken Kremlin critic who had served in Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB), Alexander Litvinenko fled Russia with his family in 2000 and was granted political asylum in Britain the following year.
From exile, he continued to investigate alleged corruption within Russia's intelligence services and their links to organised crime. He became a British citizen in October 2006, just weeks before his death.
On 23 November, 2006, Litvinenko died at the age of 44 after being poisoned with radioactive polonium-210.
Photographs of Litvinenko lying in a London hospital bed, his head bald and his body ravaged by radiation poisoning, appeared on newspaper front pages around the world. They became an enduring symbol of the dangers faced by Putin's opponents, even in exile.
As his condition deteriorated, his wife refused to give up hope that he would survive.
"I still believe to last moment, Sasha will survive and he will continue to fight against this monster who is the president of Russia still now," Litvinenko recalled.
"And I believed he will survive and we will have a future life, but it did not happen. And I always remember how Sasha was strong to last minute of his life."
The assassination exposed the reach of Russia's intelligence services and foreshadowed further attacks on European soil attributed to Moscow, including the 2018 poisoning of former Russian intelligence officer Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia in Salisbury and the 2019 murder of former Chechen separatist commander Zelimkhan Khangoshvili in Berlin.
A British public inquiry concluded in 2016 that Litvinenko's murder was carried out by Andrei Lugovoi and Dmitry Kovtun and that the operation was probably approved by both then-FSB chief Nikolai Patrushev and Putin himself.
In 2021, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Russia was responsible for Litvinenko's death and had failed to conduct an effective investigation. Moscow has denied responsibility.
Europe's pursuit of 'business as usual' with Putin
"It was not a strong reaction in 2006 because United Kingdom was alone," Marina Litvinenko told Euronews.
Despite the EU's economic strength, she said European governments remained reluctant to jeopardise their relations with Moscow, believing they could continue doing business with Putin.
Now, amid US-led diplomatic efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine, Western governments are once again debating the terms of engagement with Moscow.
Asked whether the West should negotiate with Putin, Litvinenko said: "Of course you have to negotiate, but not in a way what you allowed Putin to have what he wants. You need to be much stronger and believe in yourself."
She pointed to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as an example for European leaders.
"You can see the Ukrainian president who is very strong in his small country and fighting against this huge country and what everybody believes like a second army in the world," Litvinenko said.
"European Union, it's much bigger and stronger. And you just trust yourself."
Justice must ultimately come from Russia
Neither of the two men identified by the British public inquiry as responsible for Litvinenko's death faced trial in the UK.
While his widow regards the legal proceedings in London and Strasbourg as significant achievements, she believes ultimate accountability must come from within Russia itself.
"But justice only happened after Russia will have their own trial against this regime," she said.
Litvinenko sees the end of the war in Ukraine as a potential turning point, expressing confidence that her husband's case would form a central part of any future prosecution of Putin's government for crimes she attributes to it over the past two decades.
'He would be on the side of Ukraine'
Reflecting on how her husband might view Russia and Europe today, Litvinenko recalled his opposition to Putin's second war in Chechnya and his support for the Chechen independence movement.
She described his support for exiled Chechen leader Akhmed Zakayev, a close friend of the family, as part of his efforts to bring about change in Russia.
It "was a part of his Russian duty to make Russia possible to change", she said.
Twenty years after his murder, Litvinenko has no doubt where her husband would stand today.
"And now I'm 100% sure he would be on the side of Ukraine."

noticias.titulo: How Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia made the world trillions richer
noticias.resumen: Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO made him about $34 billion (€31bn) richer and added roughly $950 billion (€871bn) to the chipmaker's value in a single day. US President Donald Trump, Nvidia's staff and stock markets from New York to Seoul gained too, while Europe got a smaller lift.
noticias.texto:
Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO made him about $34 billion (€31bn) richer and added roughly $950 billion (€871bn) to the chipmaker's value in a single day. US President Donald Trump, Nvidia's staff and stock markets from New York to Seoul gained too, while Europe got a smaller lift.
Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday added about $34 billion (€31bn) to his fortune, according to Forbes' real-time billionaires list.
Nvidia's shares closed 31.5% higher, lifting the company's market value by about $950 billion (€871bn), the largest one-day gain for any company on record.
The rally also lifted US President Donald Trump's investments, the wealth of Nvidia's staff and share prices across the US and Asia, while Europe felt a smaller boost.
Trump, who had pushed for Huang's return, told CNBC on Monday that he had "convinced" Nvidia's board. "I made the deal," he boasted.
Nvidia's board received "input from senior levels of the United States government", according to a company statement.
Trump's accounts could have held between 32,000 and 370,000 Nvidia shares as of 30 September, according to a Financial Times analysis of his mandatory financial disclosures. The US president has added to his Nvidia position several times since returning to the White House.
Assuming no recent change in those holdings, the shares would have gained between $1.3 million (€1.2m) and $15 million (€14m) in value on Monday. The filings give only value ranges and do not yet cover October and November.
Trump's portfolio is run independently by third-party financial institutions, according to the White House.
A workforce of millionaires
Employees greeted Huang with cheers, applause and chants of his name when he returned to Nvidia's headquarters in Santa Clara, California, on Monday.
"Thank you all for the second chance," he told them, in footage shared online.
Many have grown rich from the company's rise. In a 2024 poll on Blind, an anonymous forum for verified tech workers, 76% of Nvidia employees who took part said they were millionaires. More than four in ten put their net worth at $10 million (€9.2m) or more.
Share-based pay cost Nvidia $6.4 billion (€5.9bn) in the financial year to January, according to its annual report. Workers can also buy a limited amount of its stock at a discount of at least 15%.
Staff turnover among its roughly 42,000 employees was 3.7% that year, according to the same filing.
Individual holdings are not public, but many staff are likely to still hold much of their wealth in Nvidia shares, which Monday's jump made significantly more valuable.
That gives them reason to see Huang as the man who made them rich and should keep running the company. More than 10,000 people who claimed to work at Nvidia reportedly signed a petition calling for his return.
Stock markets ride the wave
On Wall Street, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite closed 6.5% higher on Monday and the S&P 500 gained 4.7%, their strongest sessions since April 2025.
The S&P 500 won back about $3 trillion (€2.7trn) in market value as the rally also spread to Asia on Tuesday.
Taiwan's Taiex closed 9% higher and South Korea's Kospi rose 6.3%, back above 5,000 points.
Japan's Nikkei 225, which was shut on Monday for a public holiday, gained 3.9%.
On the other hand, Europe's gains were considerably smaller. On Monday, the pan-European Stoxx 600 rose 1.8%, while Germany's DAX added 2.2% and the UK's FTSE 100 about 1.3%.
Chip stocks such as ASML jumped on Monday, but the main European indices were actually slightly down on Tuesday morning.
A key reason for the muted reaction is that Europe's markets hold far fewer tech companies. Technology accounts for 9.5% of the Stoxx 600, according to index provider Stoxx, while banks are its biggest sector at 16.2%.
Huang now faces three House committees behind closed doors on 1 December, then a public Senate Banking Committee hearing on 3 December, a date its chair, Senator Tim Scott, confirmed on Monday.

noticias.titulo: Carbon capture was a sticking point at COP31: Is it a delay tactic or genuine solution?
noticias.resumen: The technology has been found to be “technically uncertain and very high cost” - yet the European Commission is funding it.
noticias.texto:
The technology has been found to be “technically uncertain and very high cost” - yet the European Commission is funding it.
The COP31 climate talks ended without a deal after the EU and others rejected a final deal which failed to mention fossil fuels. But another sticking point was carbon capture and storage - technologies designed to prevent CO2 from entering the atmosphere in the first place and/or to remove it after it has been emitted.
The proposed text backed carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS), including a target of at least 500 million tonnes of annual capacity by 2035 and a longer-term ambition of 1.3 billion to 2.5 billion tonnes.
Critics argue that carbon capture without a clear fossil fuel transition risks extending the lifeline of oil and gas. Questions around costs, energy requirements, environmental safeguards and long-term storage liability remain unresolved.
As one of the most divisive topics in climate action, we look into the facts about carbon capture and how the EU came to be funding this experimental technology.
How the European Commission is funding carbon capture and storage
In September this year, the European Commission celebrated their investment in what the owners are calling the “largest commercial carbon capture and storage (CCS) project in Europe”.
CO2 emitted by a fertiliser factory in the Netherlands will be stored underneath the seabed in Norway.
At an opening ceremony this week, the ammonia and fertiliser plant announced that it will capture 800,000 tonnes of CO2 a year then liquefy it to be sent by ship to Norway.
Having funded the project, the European Commission was keen to promote its investment – with the Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth attending the inauguration alongside the Prime Ministers of both countries.
While the Commission says the Sluiskil plant, run by Norwegian chemical company Yara, is a “strategic investment”, opponents say it is “risking billions in taxpayers’ money to fund a dangerous distraction that delays climate action”.
What is carbon capture and storage?
Carbon capture and storage (CCS) refers to technologies designed to prevent CO2 from entering the atmosphere in the first place and/or to remove it after it has been emitted.
As is done at the Sluiskil plant, most projects use a liquid to chemically remove the CO2 emitted from the production process, where it is then compressed into a liquid-like state and transported typically through a pipeline to a storage site. At that point, it’s either stored deep underground or is transformed into things like building materials or synthetic fuel. In the case of the latter, this technology is referred to as CCUS, where the ‘U’ stands for utilisation.
As of February 2026, there were 75 operational CCS projects around the world, according to climate change publication Carbon Brief. Almost all of them are at fossil-fuel extraction and processing sites, according to the IEA’s database. Together, these projects capture 62.5 million tonnes of CO2 (MtCO2) each year. This is equivalent to 0.2 per cent of total global emissions in 2025.
While Yara’s chief executive, Svein Tore Holsether, said in a statement, “The carbon capture facility in Sluiskil proves that large-scale industrial decarbonisation is possible today”, the cumulative emissions saved are a very, very tiny drop in the ocean.
US non-profit the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) has conducted in-depth research into CCS. Their Energy Finance Analyst, Andrew Reid, says: “Despite the political and financial support that has been pointed to CCS over the past three to four years, it remains technically uncertain, very high cost, and reliant upon huge subsidies to move from feasibility to construction and operation.”
CCS: To help the fossil fuel industry to extract and sell more oil and gas
To understand its uses, it’s important to understand where carbon technology originates from. According to Carbon Brief, it “was originally rolled out at US and Canadian oil wells in the early 1970s as a way to achieve “enhanced oil recovery”. This involves injecting captured CO2 into depleted wells – a process that stores the gas, but also helps to extract more oil.” This is by far the most significant use for carbon capture worldwide, with three-quarters of it used for this purpose.
This means that “the majority of CO2 that is both captured and used today helps the fossil-fuel industry to extract and sell more oil and gas,” according to Carbon Brief.
How did the EU end up funding carbon capture and storage?
One of the arguments against CCS, which campaigners have been making for years, is that it is a way for polluters to keep polluting, rather than emitting less of the gases which are heating up the planet at alarming rates.
“All capture and storage projects suffer from the same problem: they distract attention and resources from cutting emissions at source and give polluting industries like fertiliser production a pass to keep on polluting,” says Rachel Kennerley, Senior International Carbon Capture Campaigner at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL).
Belén Balanyá, researcher and campaigner at Corporate Europe Observatory (CEO), has been tracking the lobbying efforts of the fossil fuel industry for 25 years. She has recently focussed on lobbying by the CCS industry. The outcomes of annual COP climate talks are known to be influenced by lobbyists representing industry. Balanyá found that around 500 CCS lobbyists were at COP29 in 2024. A year earlier, at COP28, CCS proponents (largely tied to fossil fuel industries) scored a significant win with the endorsement of “abatement and removal technologies” in the agreement.
Referring to fossil fuel industries, Balanyá says, “You look at what’s on the agenda and it’s always escape hatches to stay in business,” she tells Euronews Green. “It’s where they move when they’ve been forced to – when there’s more knowledge and more acceptance about climate change and their role and that they have to decarbonise.”
CCS being endorsed in a COP agreement may have contributed to its legitimacy in political circles within the EU. The CCUS Forum (now the Industrial Carbon Management (ICM) Forum), set up by the European Commission in 2021, is an annual event with working groups that feed directly into EU policymaking. CEO found that every group has been co-chaired by the fossil fuel industry or associated organisations.
A newly released report from the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) details the risks of overshooting 1.5°C of warming and how we can limit them. It assessed what it called Carbon Dioxide Removal and found that many issues remain with the technology, such as whether it can scale sustainably (due to costs, land and energy use), whether it would actually keep CO2 out of the atmosphere permanently and who’s responsible for regulation and leaks.
CCS: Good or bad?
Wherever commentators stand on CCS, there is some agreement that for some industries, the technology can be useful. Yara’s project targets emissions from ammonia production which “provides a relatively concentrated CO2 stream, making this one of the more straightforward industrial applications of carbon capture rather than an example of the very hardest emissions to abate,” according to Domien Vangenechten, Programme Lead in Clean Economy at E3G.
“The lesson should therefore not be that Europe needs CCS everywhere, but that we should pragmatically deploy it where it can cut substantial emissions today.”
This article was published in its original form on 9th September 2026.

noticias.titulo: The Beaver Supermoon rises tonight: Where and when to see the lunar spectacle in Europe
noticias.resumen: It's worth going outside to enjoy the Moon tonight - it will look bigger and brighter than usual.
noticias.texto:
It's worth going outside to enjoy the Moon tonight - it will look bigger and brighter than usual.
We’ll be treated to a Supermoon tonight - and it’s set to be big and bright.
The night of 24th to 25th November will see the Beaver Supermoon light up the sky.
November’s full Moon is traditionally known as the 'Beaver Moon', a nickname linked to the time of year when beavers prepare for winter by building dams and gathering food.
What is a Supermoon?
The November 2026 full Moon is a Supermoon, which means it occurs when the Moon is at or near its closest point to Earth. That is possible because its orbit isn't a perfect circle. Instead, it's elliptical, or slightly egg-shaped.
That means the distance between the two bodies varies. When the Moon is at its closest point to Earth, it's at perigee. When the Moon is furthest from Earth, it's at apogee.
The technical name for a Supermoon is a perigee full Moon, and it can appear up to 14 per cent larger and 30 per cent brighter than a full Moon at apogee.
How to watch a Supermoon - and the best time to see it
A Supermoon can be seen in clear night skies without any special equipment.
Try to find a wide, open space, preferably one that's elevated, such as up a hill.
It's such an exciting spectacle because, whether a Supermoon or not, the Moon appears bigger when it's close to the horizon because of what's called the 'Moon illusion'. This is a strange visual trick that experts can't yet fully explain. "When you have a supermoon, that effect is just slightly more striking,” said astronomer William Alston with the University of Hertfordshire in the United Kingdom.
The best time to view a Supermoon
Experts say the best times to view a Supermoon are at moonrise and moonset, when the Moon is close to the horizon.
For most of western Europe, moonrise will be between 4 and 5pm today.
You can check exact moonrise times for where you live here.
If you miss moonrise, don't worry. The Supermoon will still be impressive throughout the night and into tomorrow as well (26th November).
When is the next Supermoon?
An anomalistic month (from one perigee to the next) is shorter than a synodic month (from one New Moon to the next) - but only by around two days. This means that if a full Moon falls close to perigee in one month, it is likely to do so again the following month.
The consequence of this is that, when Supermoons happen, they happen in groups - we get four or five Super Full Moons in a row (or four or five Super New Moons in a row).
Tonight’s will be the second to last Supermoon of the year. The last Supermoon of 2026 could be particularly magical, as it will rise on 24th December, celebrated as Christmas Eve in many European countries.
The next two Supermoons after that will be on 22nd January 2027 and 20th February 2027.
How do Supermoons affect tides?
The tides are caused by the gravitational forces of the Sun and the Moon on the Earth’s oceans, explains Royal Museums Greenwich. When the Moon is closer to the Earth during a Supermoon, the gravitational pull is slightly stronger, and so the tides are bigger. However this effect is almost negligible, with only a few centimetres difference between a normal full Moon and Supermoon tide.
However, full Moon and New Moon tides can be much bigger than those at other times in the lunar month, as the Sun adds its own gravitational pull into the mix, producing the so-called spring tides.
The Beaver Supermoon is set to have potentially damaging effects along the west coast of the US, for example. High tides along the Pacific Coast could break 40-year-old records and flood low-lying coastal communities, complicating travel during Thanksgiving week.
In the San Francisco Bay Area, tides could reach almost a metre above normal on Tuesday before peaking on Wednesday, says Dial Hoang, a National Weather Service forecaster.

noticias.titulo: Iran orders Hormuz closed 'further day by day' as Qatar seeks to revive peace talks
noticias.resumen: The IRGC claimed three tankers hit mines in the crucial strait while under US escort, which the Joint Maritime Information Centre said was unconfirmed, as Qatar's prime minister pressed Rubio and Vance to restart talks.
noticias.texto:
The IRGC claimed three tankers hit mines in the crucial strait while under US escort, which the Joint Maritime Information Centre said was unconfirmed, as Qatar's prime minister pressed Rubio and Vance to restart talks.
Iran's army commander-in-chief ordered his navy on Monday to close the Strait of Hormuz "further day by day" until Washington meets Tehran's conditions, warning that any new US military action would draw blows that were "more severe, more crushing and without geographical limitation."
"Until the seven conditions of the Islamic Republic of Iran are fulfilled, not only will the Strait of Hormuz not be opened, it must be closed further day by day, conditions for the enemy must become more difficult, and stronger control will be exercised over it," Major General Amir Hatami said, addressing senior commanders of Iran's armed forces.
Citing orders from Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, Hatami added that if the US "commits a new folly and starts another war, in the new phase the blows will be more severe, more crushing and without geographical limitation."
The elite paramilitary IRGC said on Monday that three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz suffered "powerful explosions and massive fires" after hitting naval mines.
One tanker was hit off the southern shores and two more in the east of the strait, "while under extensive air escort by the US army," an IRGC statement said.
The IRGC said it would publish images of the explosions and warned shipowners that "military escort by the US army is no substitute for compliance with maritime regulations."
The Joint Maritime Information Centre (JMIC), in a report covering 19 to 21 November, said it recorded 114 passages through the strait "with the assistance of the United States" and that claims of tankers hitting naval mines were unconfirmed.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Washington was seeking to impose a neither-war-nor-peace situation on Tehran, threatening there were "military ways to break the blockade that, God willing, we will pursue in the near future."
As head of the Iranian delegation in the Islamabad talks, Ghalibaf said there would be no further negotiations or action before Washington moved.
"Before the implementation of Iran's seven conditions there will be no action and no negotiation, and in response to the enemy's moves we are also ready to give a decisive answer and to change the geography of the battlefield in the event of an enemy mistake," Ghalibaf said.
Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told reporters a naval blockade was "tantamount to military aggression" and that Iran had "the right in this regard to use any available means to defend itself."
"We will certainly not tolerate this situation, and we will use all our tools to confront this US aggression," he said.
Qatar wants both sides at the table
Qatar's Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani visited Washington on Monday and met US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance to discuss efforts to restart negotiations between Tehran and Washington.
After his talks with Rubio, Al Thani said the region "cannot bear a renewed escalation of tensions between the United States and Iran" and that Doha was working to bring both sides back to the table.
Qatar and the US were also seeking to strengthen their military cooperation, he said. According to AP, citing a source familiar with the proceedings, the meeting with Vance lasted about 10 minutes.
The visit followed US President Donald Trump's statement on Sunday that military strikes on Iran could resume after the New Year. Trump had said earlier this month that he had asked Vance to shift his focus from Iran to domestic policy.
In recent days, Iran has attacked US military bases in Bahrain and Kuwait on several occasions, and Tehran's armed forces have reported almost daily that tankers it describes as violators have struck naval mines.
Qatar hosts the largest US military base in the Middle East and the regional headquarters of CENTCOM, and plays a key mediation role between Tehran and Washington.

noticias.titulo: Jensen Huang back at Nvidia: The reactions and memes breaking the internet
noticias.resumen: Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO after his resignation earlier this month. The likes of Donald Trump, Elon Musk and Sam Altman welcomed the decision as Nvidia shares surged nearly 35%. The internet has thoughts. And jokes.
noticias.texto:
Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO after his resignation earlier this month. The likes of Donald Trump, Elon Musk and Sam Altman welcomed the decision as Nvidia shares surged nearly 35%. The internet has thoughts. And jokes.
Jensen Huang wasn't unemployed for very long, as the divisive chipmaker is back as CEO of Nvidia.
This comes just days after he was ousted from the company following revelations of his extramarital affairs with employees and a suspected Chinese spy.
He resigned on 12 November and now he's back – with Nvidia's board of directors voting unanimously to reinstate Huang after input from senior US officials, concluding that his return posed no national security risk...
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman posted “Jensen!,” while Elon Musk wrote that “the mistake has been corrected.”
As for Donald Trump, he celebrated his return with a meme on his Truth Social account, showing Huang edited into the photo of Trump raising his fist after the assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania.
Huang is seen holding up a red bra with the Nvidia logo on a flag behind him.
"This is a real Trump post. He's totally lost it."
Trump even stated in a press conference yesterday that he spoke "directly and indirectly" to Nvidia's board of directors and convinced the company to reinstate Huang as its president and CEO.
Some are outraged that Huang was reinstated; many are questioning Trump's involvement; others are loving the morally bankrupt drama.
Here are some of the most viral, funniest and outraged reactions so far:
"Sir, the boogeyman has returned."
"Jensen Huang really got resurrected by the AI gods."
"Apparently having affairs with subordinates & getting tangled up with a Chinese spy isn't a career-ending event. Anyway, remember to complete your annual security awareness training."
"Even Robert Pattinson couldn't steal his job."
"Donald Trump has reinstated Sean Connery as James Bond."
"Jensen Huang's coronation at Nvidia this morning."
"So no more new affairs, right?"
A Coldplay throwback...
"This dude wishes he’d worked at Nvidia."
"Jensen Huang back as Nvidia CEO after he found out he can't cheat on Lucia in GTA VI."
Speaks for itself...
Taking precautions...
"GPU Jesus has risen!"
"Jensen Huang returning to Nvidia is proof that morality is completely performative. He cheated on his wife. Had affairs with company employees. Forced the board to step in. Yet the moment he walks back into headquarters, hundreds of employees are literally chanting his name. Why?"
Huang may be back, but the board's independent investigation into reports of a foreign intelligence effort remains open.

noticias.titulo: Grandmaster clash: World Chess enters record books as Gen Z contenders fight for title
noticias.resumen: India's Dommaraju Gukesh and Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan, two of the world's youngest chess grandmasters are meeting in Geneva to battle it out for the game's biggest title and celebrity bragging rights.
noticias.texto:
India's Dommaraju Gukesh and Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan, two of the world's youngest chess grandmasters are meeting in Geneva to battle it out for the game's biggest title and celebrity bragging rights.
Two titans of Chess go head-to-head in Geneva on Tuesday in a match that will be the most youthful world championship contest in the competition's 140-year history.
Defending the crown is India's Dommaraju Gukesh, who entered the record books in 2024, when he took the title at 18-years old.
He's up against Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan, who's also 20, and for some is favourite to win based on form, having won the World Cup and Candidates Tournament. He's currently fourth in the global rankings compared to Gukesh, who's dropped to 26th.
Sindarov also goes into the battle with a psychological advantage with two victories and one draw from their three previous encounters.
But, at the press conference on Sunday at the United Nations’ European headquarters where both players presented themselves to the world, Gukesh rejected suggestions that he faced a more difficult task this time round to protect his title.
“I don’t think I’m here to defend anything,” he said. “I’m here to win it all over again. That’s the mindset I’m in.”
The tournament is taking place at the Fondation Martin Bodmer at Cologny, one of the most important private libraries in the world, as it includes some of the oldest surviving copies of the New Testament and Shakespeare's First Folio from 1623.
The match will consist of 14 classical games. The first player to score 7.5 points or more will be crowned World Champion and claim the larger share of the total prize fund of $2.5 million. If the score is equal after 14 games, the winner will be decided by a tiebreak which will be played on 12 December.

noticias.titulo: From Ravenna to Bolzano: Emerging European rail destinations for train travel in 2027
noticias.resumen: While Paris and London remain ‘firmly established favourites’ for train travellers, Rail Europe data shows that Ravenna, Bolzano, Linz and theme-park gateways are attracting ‘growing attention’.
noticias.texto:
While Paris and London remain ‘firmly established favourites’ for train travellers, Rail Europe data shows that Ravenna, Bolzano, Linz and theme-park gateways are attracting ‘growing attention’.
The Italian city of Ravenna is among the European destinations seeing the fastest growth in searches by travel agents and tour operators, according to new data by Rail Europe.
The train booking platform’s “Track Record” report, which covers booking and search activity between 1 October 2025 and 31 October 2026, also points to growing interest in destinations from the Italian Alps to the station serving Disneyland Paris.
Paris, London and Italy’s major cities remain “firmly established favourites” for train travel, Rail Europe said. But the data suggests that the “next interesting client itinerary may begin somewhere less obvious” – from a city break in eastern Germany to a family trip to a theme park.
Ravenna tops the list for advance bookings
Known for its stunning mosaics, Ravenna is “attracting growing attention” and stood out in two parts of the report.
It was among the fastest-rising searches by travel professionals, while passengers who booked directly through Rail Europe reserved their journeys an average of 57 days before departure. That was the longest average booking lead time recorded in the report’s consumer analysis.
The two findings reflect separate groups, with one tracking where agents and tour operators searched and the other measuring how far ahead travellers booked.
Bolzano and the French Alps draw attention
Bolzano in South Tyrol also gained ground in searches by travel agents and tour operators following the 2026 Winter Olympic Games. Elsewhere in northern Italy, Bergamo drew growing interest from consumers.
Across the border in France, Chambéry and Grenoble were among the fastest-rising destinations for consumers on the platform.
Both cities are gateways to the French Alps, and travellers planning a rail trip that takes in both France and northern Italy can again use the Paris-Milan line, which reopened in 2025.
Theme parks and city breaks feature in searches
There is also a “different kind of destination emerging in the data”, Rail Europe said, with two train stations serving major European theme parks also seeing a rise in search interest among both consumers and travel professionals. Ringsheim is the railway gateway to Germany’s Europa-Park, while Marne-la-Vallée serves Disneyland Paris.
“Here, the railway station is closely tied to the experience the traveller wants to book,” Rail Europe said. “For travel professionals, knowing which stations are attracting interest can be as useful as knowing which cities are popular.”
Austria’s Linz and the German cities of Leipzig and Dresden were also among the fastest-rising searches overall. Rail Europe highlighted concert halls and Christmas markets among the attractions in these cities, offering ideas for trips built around a performance or a festive weekend.

noticias.titulo: Indonesia: Search continues for workers trapped after deadly factory fire
noticias.resumen: The death toll from a devastating fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has risen to 26. Rescue workers continue searching for victims trapped beneath the rubble.
noticias.texto:
The fire broke out on 21 November at the Fonusa Agung Mulia factory in Indonesia’s Banten province, west of Jakarta. Aerial footage filmed on Monday shows collapsed roofs and large sections of the complex reduced to ruins.
The death toll has risen to 26, with eight workers still missing. Most victims were recovered from the second floor, where rescuers said many had died trying to reach an emergency exit.
More than 600 emergency personnel have been mobilised, with unstable structures hampering searches across the 2,000-square-metre area affected by the blaze. Police are collecting DNA samples from relatives to identify the victims.
Preliminary reports suggest an electrical fault in an air-conditioning unit may have sparked the fire, although the cause remains unconfirmed.
The company, which produces the popular Milkita confectionery brand, has apologised and pledged support for victims’ families. The disaster has renewed concerns over industrial fire safety in Indonesia.

noticias.titulo: French publisher accused of sending journalists intimate images of Gisèle Pelicot
noticias.resumen: Publishing house Tinbad is accused of having used intimate images of Gisèle Pelicot to promote a book, three years after the start of her legal fight against sexual violence.
noticias.texto:
Publishing house Tinbad is accused of having used intimate images of Gisèle Pelicot to promote a book, three years after the start of her legal fight against sexual violence.
A French publishing house, Tinbad, has reportedly sent journalists intimate photographs and videos of Gisèle Pelicot that were recorded without her knowledge by her former husband, Dominique Pelicot, according to several French media outlets.
The images were allegedly used to promote Emprises, les impasses d'une success story (Coercive Control: The Dead Ends of a Success Story), an essay by the French philosopher and psychoanalyst Sabine Prokhoris. In it, Prokhoris questions the concept of "emprise", a French term for one person's psychological hold over another, and even challenges the idea that Gisèle Pelicot is a victim.
Prokhoris is known for books that take a critical stance on the #MeToo movement. She told the French daily Libération that she was not behind the decision to send the images.
Gisèle Pelicot's lawyers condemned the episode as a fresh assault on her.
"Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt," Gisèle Pelicot told the French news channel BFMTV. "I have fought to regain my dignity and my freedom. I will not let anyone take them away from me."
Publisher denies having distributed pornographic photos
Tinbad has said it will not reprint the book and that Prokhoris will no longer promote it. It described the episode as an "unfortunate communication that was not suited to the content of the book".
In a statement on its website, the publisher apologised to Gisèle Pelicot and to Prokhoris, insisting that "absolutely no image of rape, nor any video of a pornographic nature" had been sent to the press. Euronews has confirmed that the book is no longer available on the website.
According to the publisher, around 280 copies are still in circulation.
Gisèle Pelicot became an international figure in the fight against sexual violence after the Mazan rape trial, named after the town in south-eastern France where the couple lived. Between 2011 and 2020, her then-husband drugged and raped her and recruited dozens of men online to rape her while she was unconscious.
In December 2024, Dominique Pelicot and 50 other men were convicted, and he was sentenced to 20 years in prison.
The case has particular resonance in the United Kingdom, where a similar trial has just concluded. Joanne Young, 49, has been described as the "British Gisèle Pelicot".
For 13 years, the mother of three was drugged and raped by her then-husband, Philip Young, who also recruited other men online to abuse her at their home in Swindon, in southern England. He pleaded guilty to dozens of sexual offences against her earlier this year.
On 19 November, a jury at Winchester Crown Court in England found four of those men guilty of sexual offences against her. Like Pelicot, Young chose to waive her anonymity, which is guaranteed for life to victims of sexual offences in the UK.

noticias.titulo: Trump says he spoke to Nvidia board before Jensen Huang's return as CEO
noticias.resumen: US President Donald Trump says he spoke directly with Nvidia's board before CEO Jensen Huang's reinstatement, adding that he found the board "very, very reasonable".
noticias.texto:
US President Donald Trump says he spoke directly with Nvidia's board before the reinstatement of chief executive Jensen Huang, who resigned less than two weeks ago amid a scandal involving an alleged affair with a woman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence.
